Data Modelling
for Power BI

Structure, relationships and filter context, worked through one small dataset

A working manual

Data Modelling for Power BI

Most Power BI problems that look like DAX problems are model problems. This manual works through table structure, relationship mechanics and filter context using one deliberately small aircraft maintenance dataset, small enough that every number in it can be checked by hand. It opens with the operations behind the data, because you cannot model a process you cannot describe.

Running example
Meridian Aero Services, Q1 2025
Source tables
Nine, 6 to 8 rows each
Chapters
25, in seven parts

Contents

Part 0 . The domain

AHow an aircraft maintenance shop actually runs

After this chapter you will be able to read a maintenance work order, say which service line produced it, name the stage of the check that wrote each number on it, and say who owns that number. You will also know why the shape of the organisation breaks some of your joins, long before a bad extract gets the blame.

The production controller stops at your desk on a Tuesday morning. He wants one number: hours booked this month, split by service line. You have the data, so you build it in ten minutes. He reads it, points at the line maintenance row, and says that figure is wrong, because his shift supervisor had a crew on the ramp all last week. He is right. The rest of this chapter is why.

A note on one word before we start, because it is on every page from here. A work order is the shop's unit of work: one job, on one aircraft, opened, priced, worked and closed. Meridian has eight of them. Every number in this document hangs off one of those eight.

You already know how to build a model. What has been missing is the thing the columns describe. This chapter is the operations primer: no Meridian tables yet, and one measure only, because that measure makes no sense until you know the shop.

Who does the work, and who decides the work is due

MRO stands for Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul: the organisation that physically touches the aircraft, working under a maintenance organisation approval. That approval is EASA Part-145 in Europe, from the European Union Aviation Safety Agency, or 14 CFR Part 145 in the United States, from the Federal Aviation Administration. Some MROs belong to an airline. Others sell hangar capacity to several operators.

One fact shapes your data more than any other, and nobody says it out loud to a new analyst. The operator decides what maintenance is due, and the MRO performs it on the operator's instruction.

In Europe the operator carries that duty through a CAMO, a Continuing Airworthiness Management Organisation. The CAMO owns the aircraft maintenance programme. It tracks what is coming due on every aircraft registration, and it raises the demand. Under FAA rules the same duty sits with the operator's own continuing airworthiness function. Either way it is another company on another system. The shop receives an aircraft registration, a check description, a date window and a price basis. The reasoning behind those four things stays with the operator.

So an MRO source table routinely carries a foreign key to something the shop holds no master list of. The registration belongs to the customer's fleet record, that record is maintained by whoever answers the phone at the service desk, and it is late. A tail can be inducted, worked, invoiced and closed while the shop's own registry has never heard of it.

The key will not join, and Power BI will not complain. It adds a blank row on the one side and parks the unmatched facts there, where no report label points at them. Handling that is Chapter 19. What you need now is the cause, because the cause changes the fix. A data quality defect gets a ticket. This is a boundary between two companies, it recurs next quarter under a different aircraft registration, and your model has to survive it without you in the room.

Interview-level insight

Referential integrity is a property of one system under one owner. Your model spans three: the customer's continuing airworthiness function, the shop's regulated maintenance system, and planning workbooks belonging to individual managers. Clean keys would need three organisations to agree on identifiers they were never required to share. So do not chase the key. Build a dimension holding every key the facts actually use, label the recovered members as unknown, and put the count of unknown members on the report. A model that hides its own gaps is worse than one that shows them.

Six roles put their names on your columns. The planner builds the work package before arrival and owns the estimated hours. The production controller runs the check day to day and revises the forecast. Technicians book time against task cards, and a task card is one printed instruction for one piece of work. The shift supervisor decides who works which card tonight, and he keeps that on a whiteboard in the crew room. Certifying staff sign the work off, and only they can. Quality performs independent inspection. Stores issues parts and controls tooling.

Certifying authority is regulated and personal. In Europe it is a licence held under EASA Part-66. B1 covers mechanical work, B2 covers avionics, and C signs off an entire base check. In the United States the same authority sits with the A&P mechanic, meaning Airframe and Powerplant. Those letters end up in your data as a certification column, and they decide which technician rows can legally close which work.

The four service lines you support

The finance manager wants one number for the month: average hours per check. You divide the quarter's 62.0 booked hours by eight work orders and hand him 7.75. He is happy for a day. Then he asks why a three week C-check and a forty minute ramp defect are averaged together, and the honest answer is that the eight work orders come from four different kinds of work.

Four lines share one building, one technician pool and one reporting pack. In data they behave so differently that treating them as one population is the fastest route to a wrong number. So learn the four, because the finance manager's average depends on which of them he meant.

Separate the first two before anything else, because outsiders club them together every time. Line maintenance works the aircraft between flights, out where it parks. Light maintenance is a short planned input, usually in a hangar and usually overnight. Both are quick next to a heavy check, and that is where the resemblance ends. Different crews, different places, different planning behaviour, and in most shops different systems. A shop that runs both reports them separately, and your model should follow the shop.

Line maintenance

Line maintenance works the aircraft between flights. It happens where the aircraft already is: on the ramp, at the gate, or on a remote stand. Minutes to a shift, and the aircraft is expected to fly again the same day. The content is transit and pre-flight checks, defect rectification, deferred defect clearance, and servicing of oil, oxygen, hydraulics, tyres and brakes. It also covers recovering an AOG. AOG means Aircraft On Ground: an unserviceable aircraft that is stopping a departure. Certifying staff holding the licence category for that task sign it off on the stand.

Line maintenance is dispatch driven. The next departure sets the clock, and the question a line crew answers all day is whether this aircraft goes out on time. The operations desk sets that priority, a function usually called MOC, Maintenance Operations Control. Heavy maintenance planning has no say in it. Line runs its own crews on its own shift pattern, and very often on its own system. The people who need that data are standing on an apron with a phone.

What it means for the data

Very high row count, very short duration, and frequently no planned manhour figure at all. Nobody built a package a week ahead, because nobody knew the defect existed until the aircraft landed. Meridian has one line work order, WO-1007. It booked 5.0 achieved hours against a quote of 900 and against no pre-input pack whatsoever.

Then there is the problem the model cannot show you. Where line maintenance books its hours in its own system, those rows may never reach your extract at all. A service line missing from a report looks exactly like a service line that had a quiet quarter. That is what the production controller was pointing at on Tuesday morning. His crew worked the ramp, booked their time in the line system, and your extract never saw a single hour of it.

Light maintenance

Light maintenance is a short planned input, usually in a hangar and often overnight. Hours to a shift. The slot is booked in advance, and a good part of what gets done inside it is defect clearance nobody knew about when the slot was booked. The content is the daily and weekly service checks, deferred defect clearance, and small scheduled packages that need the aircraft stopped but not opened up. Light has its own bay and its own crew. Certifying staff holding the licence category for that task sign it off.

What it means for the data

High row count, short duration, unplanned. The last word is the one that matters. The work exists because a defect was reported. So frequently no package was built a week earlier, and no planned manhour figure reaches you at all.

Here is the one place in this chapter where you probably arrive holding the wrong idea, so it is worth stating flatly. A missing planned figure is not a zero, it is an absence, and coalescing the two together buries the difference. Where the pre-input row is absent there is nothing to compare the booked hours against, so the honest result is no number at all. Fill that gap with a zero and what comes back is formatted like an answer and gets read like one. Meridian has two light work orders, WO-1002 and WO-1005, and neither carries a pre-input pack. Add the line work order and three of the eight work orders in the dataset sit in exactly that state.

Heavy maintenance, usually called base maintenance

It happens in a hangar bay or dock, aircraft out of service, jacked, panels open, for days to several weeks. The content is a C-check or a heavier structural visit, plus whatever the operator bundles in while the aircraft is already down. Base maintenance certifying staff release the whole check, supported by inspection sign-offs along the way.

What it means for the data

Low row count, very long duration, planned months ahead, and dominated by one unknown: what the technicians find once the panels are off. The available, projected and achieved triad lives here, and Chapter B takes it apart. A check opened on 17 February and closed on 19 March exists in two months. So the count for a month depends on which date the slicer is wired to: opened, promised or closed. In Meridian's January the answers are three opened, two closed, two promised. Line work opens and closes inside a day, which is why nobody warns you about this.

Common mistake

Wiring the date table to the opened date, calling it done, then letting finance filter a revenue report with it. Revenue recognises at release, not at induction. The report will look sane and the totals will foot, and every check crossing a month boundary lands in the wrong month, which in heavy maintenance is most of them. The fix is one date table carrying three relationships, one active and two inactive, with a separately named measure per question.

Cabin and in-flight entertainment

Cabin work happens in a hangar, as its own input or riding inside a heavy slot because the aircraft is down anyway. Days to weeks for one aircraft, months across a fleet retrofit. The content is seats, monuments (galleys, lavatories and stowages), panels, carpets, IFE (In-Flight Entertainment) head-end and seat-back units, wiring looms, connectivity antennas, placards and livery. Most cabin reconfiguration counts as a modification. It is embodied under an STC (Supplemental Type Certificate) or an OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) service bulletin, and released through an EO (Engineering Order). Engineering owns the approval. The paper trail is a design change record, and a task card is the wrong place to look for it.

What it means for the data

Repetition helps and vocabulary hurts. The same work repeats across aircraft, so the learning curve is real and the tenth aircraft takes materially fewer hours than the first. Estimates built on the first two will be wrong by the eighth.

The vocabulary problem is worse. Cabin work uses trades that airframe work does not, and a trade is simply a skill group, such as airframe, avionics, engine or cabin. So a cabin trade arrives in a planning extract carrying real hours, and the capacity workbook has never heard of it. In Meridian, the Cabin trade carries 12.0 planned hours against zero planned capacity. That is a conformed dimension problem. It is also a planning red flag, and the shop should want it printed on the report, not normalised away by you.

One more thing about cabin work, because it changes what a total means. The aircraft sits in a bay with its panels off. From across the hangar that looks like heavy maintenance. So many shops club Cabin and IFE in with Heavy and report the pair as base maintenance. Meridian's quarter booked 38.0 achieved hours on heavy and 10.0 on cabin, so base maintenance reads 48.0. Start a retrofit programme and the same customer wants cabin broken out on its own again. Both views are legitimate, and the same person will ask for both in the same week. That is two groupings over one service line dimension, and Chapter E models it.

That is the finance manager's average answered. Hours per check across four service lines mixes minutes with weeks, so the 7.75 was arithmetic without meaning. The number he actually wanted is hours per check within one service line, and Table A.1 is the reason why.

Why a check exists at all

The planner puts two aircraft in front of you. Same type, same customer, delivered in the same month. One is due a C-check next spring and the other is due one this quarter. He wants a fleet view showing when each tail comes due, and your first instinct is to sort it by aircraft age.

Nobody in the shop invents the work. Every operator flies to an approved AMP, an Aircraft Maintenance Programme, written for each type. The AMP derives from the manufacturer's MPD, the Maintenance Planning Document. The MPD in turn derives from the MRB report, the Maintenance Review Board report. That report is agreed between the manufacturer and the authorities when the type is certified.

Tasks fall due on three counters. Flight hours (FH) count time in the air. Flight cycles (FC) count one takeoff and landing as one cycle. Calendar time counts days whether the aircraft flew or not, which is why a stored aircraft still generates maintenance.

The first two counters are why two aircraft of the same type reach the same check at very different ages. A short-haul aircraft flying several sectors a day piles up cycles against relatively few hours. A long-haul aircraft flying one long sector does the reverse. Some tasks fall due on cycles and others on hours. So two aircraft of the same type, delivered in the same month and flown on different routes, reach the same check years apart.

Which settles the planner's fleet view. Maintenance burden tracks flight hours and flight cycles. Age in years tracks neither of them, so sorting his two tails by age puts them in the wrong order and he will spot it in about four seconds. Sort by hours and cycles since the last check instead.

Two abbreviations in that last row need expanding, and the fact that they do is the lesson. A D-check is a heavy structural check in one shop, an HMV (Heavy Maintenance Visit) in the next, an IL (Intermediate Layover) in a third. One kind of work, three names, and your dimension has to carry whichever one the customer's paperwork uses.

A larger complication tends to get left out of handovers. Many operators no longer run discrete lettered checks. They run equalised or phased programmes that break C-check content into smaller packages absorbed into shorter visits, keeping the aircraft flying. Under a phased programme the C-check content arrives as a run of smaller inputs spread across what used to be a single interval. Ask the planner to point at the C-check and he will point at a series of visits.

Rule of thumb

If a dataset hands you a check type column with clean A, C and D values, somebody upstream made a simplification. Often that is the only way to report across customers running different programmes, so it can be the right call. It was still a decision, it still hid something, and the person who made it still works there. Find out who, ask what the mapping rule was, and write the answer into the model description before you build measures on it.

The lifecycle of a heavy check

The finance manager comes back with a harder question. One check, WO-1003, appears on three reports with three different hour figures. He wants to know which one belongs in the month-end pack. The first honest answer is that all three are correct.

Eight stages, in order. This is the spine every heavy maintenance table hangs off. Once you can name the stage that produced a column, most arguments about that column resolve themselves, including his.

Read the top row of four cards left to right, then the bottom row, and read the colours before the words. The terracotta cards, induction, routine work and findings, and output and release, write transaction records: something happened and a row exists because of it. The olive cards, pre-input planning and re-forecast, produce planning estimates: somebody made a judgement and wrote a number down. The grey cards produce paperwork and money. Only the terracotta stages make facts about the world, and that decides how each number may be aggregated.

1. Slot booking and contract
Months to years ahead. The check is usually priced as a fixed price for routine content plus an agreed rate for non-routine work. That pricing makes the routine against non-routine split a commercial number as well as an operational one.
2. Pre-input planning
Weeks ahead. The planner builds the package and rolls the task card estimates up by trade. A task card is one printed instruction for one piece of work, and it carries an estimate in hours. This is the heavy pre-input step, and its output is the available manhour baseline.
3. Input, also called induction
The aircraft arrives, is towed to the bay, defuelled if required, jacked and opened up. The turnaround clock starts. Planned and actual input dates routinely differ, because aircraft arrive late.
4. Routine execution and findings
Technicians work the routine cards and book time. Anything found that no routine card covers becomes a non-routine card.
5. Re-forecasting
Production control revises the expected total as findings land. This is the projected manhour figure.
6. Closure
Panels closed, systems restored, functional tests, engine runs where required, duplicate inspections, RII (Required Inspection Item) items signed, paperwork completed. Work finished with documents incomplete cannot be released.
7. Output and release
Certifying staff issue the CRS, the Certificate of Release to Service. The turnaround clock stops here.
8. Invoice and review, often called post-check
Routine content billed at the quoted price, non-routine at the agreed rate, warranty claims raised, and estimates fed back into planning.
What actually goes into a pre-input work package

The planner assembles the package from sources carrying different levels of obligation. Routine task cards due inside the window. Out-of-phase items, not due yet but worth doing while the aircraft is open. ADs, Airworthiness Directives, issued by the authority and mandatory. SBs, Service Bulletins, the manufacturer's recommendations, mandatory only when an Airworthiness Directive says so or the operator decides to embody them. Engineering Orders and modifications. Deferred defects carried under the MEL (Minimum Equipment List) or CDL (Configuration Deviation List), which permit flight with a named item inoperative, or a named secondary part missing, for a set period. Cabin defects. Customer requests.

Each card carries an estimated manhour figure from a standard time or from shop history. The planner rolls those up per trade, and that roll-up is the planned figure. Then it is frozen, because a baseline that moves cannot measure anything.

Stage 4 deserves more weight than the rest combined. A technician opens a panel and finds corrosion, a crack, a worn bushing, a chafed wiring loom. None of it is on a routine card, because nobody knew it was there. A non-routine card is raised, also called an NRC or a finding, and it becomes new work with its own hours, parts and sign-off.

This is the central economic fact of heavy maintenance. Routine hours are known before induction. Non-routine hours are not knowable before induction, by definition, because they describe the condition of one airframe nobody has looked inside since the last check. The non-routine share is commonly a large fraction of total hours, and on an older aircraft it can exceed the routine content.

Resist putting an industry percentage on that. The share varies enormously with age, type, operator, and how well the last shop did its job. Any figure you find quoted is an average over a population that does not contain your customers. Quote your own shop's history, split by type and customer, and say how few checks it covers. A mean over four C-checks is four numbers with an average on the end. Call it a benchmark and somebody will plan a year against it.

Stage 5 exists only because stage 4 does. If findings were knowable in advance there would be nothing to forecast. Each revision supersedes the one before it. A revision is an estimate of the final total, so adding it to the previous revision adds a guess to the guess it replaced.

Now the finance manager's three figures have names. Stage 2 wrote the available hours, stage 5 wrote the projected hours, and stage 4 wrote the achieved hours. For a month-end pack he wants achieved, because it is the only one of the three that records something that happened. Tell him which stage the other two came from and the argument about which number is real goes away.

Interview-level insight

The gap between projected and available hours is the findings signal, and it is readable before the check closes, which is what makes it worth reporting. Across Meridian's five planned work orders, available is 57.0 hours and projected is 63.5, so findings have added 63.5 minus 57.0, which is 6.5 hours. On the three closed heavy checks it is 44.0 against 36.0, so 8.0 hours. Here is the part a newcomer misses. A projected line that never moves usually means nobody is re-forecasting. The surprise then arrives as an overrun on the final weekend, when a revision on day nine would have warned everybody in time to move people onto it. Put the revision count on the report.

The first measure this breaks

Put the service lines and the lifecycle together. Stage 2 produces the planned hours, and line and light maintenance often never get a stage 2 at all. So the most requested measure in an MRO pack has no answer for two of the four service lines. Writing it correctly takes four lines of code. Getting the absent case wrong takes one extra argument.

DAXPerformance Factor
-- Available divided by achieved. Above 1.00 means the work
-- took fewer hours than the pre-input pack allowed.
VAR Available = SUM ( FactPreInput[PlannedHours] )
VAR Achieved  = SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( Available, Achieved )
Lines 1 to 2
State the direction of the ratio inside the measure. Shops disagree about which way up it goes, and this comment is the only place a reader can check.
Line 3
SUM rather than SUMX, because PlannedHours is already stored one row per work order per trade. SUMX would iterate to reach an identical answer, and only earns its place when the value has to be computed per row.
Line 4
Achieved hours sit in another table at another grain, one row per technician per work order per day. Each side is aggregated independently and the model joins them at the visual.
Line 5
RETURN closes the VAR block. Naming the two numbers on lines 3 and 4, then returning one expression, is what lets a reader check the direction of the ratio against the comment at the top.
Line 6
DIVIDE returns blank when Achieved is zero or blank, which is the state of every check on the morning it is inducted. It also hands blank straight back when Available is blank, because DAX carries a blank through a division instead of turning it into a zero. On a line or light work order there are no pre-input rows, Available is blank, and the measure is blank. That is the correct answer.
Why this and not that

DIVIDE rather than the slash operator, because a check inducted this morning has booked no hours yet. That is day one, not an exception, and the slash treats a zero denominator as an arithmetic error.

No third argument on DIVIDE. That argument exists to replace the result when the denominator is zero, and people supply 0 out of habit. Do it here and a check inducted yesterday reads 0.00 in the same column where WO-1003 reads 104.0 percent, and the two look like the same kind of number. Blank says nothing, and nothing is what is true so far. Zero says something false.

Do not repair the blank with COALESCE either, and do not test Available = 0. Zero planned hours and no pre-input pack at all are different facts. A pack planning zero hours for a trade is a planning statement somebody made. No pack says this service line does not plan in hours. Turn one into the other and you have hidden the absent case by hand.

Blank has its own cost, and it is worth naming before you ship this. A blank measure drops its row out of a matrix. So WO-1002, WO-1005 and WO-1007, the three Meridian work orders with no pre-input pack, leave the performance report altogether. Nothing on the page marks the hole they left. A service line that vanishes looks like a service line that behaved. Put a second measure beside the ratio that counts the work orders in the current filter with no pre-input rows, and let three of the eight show on the page where somebody has to read them.

HMCC, and why two systems disagree about a date

Two reports land on the same desk on the same morning. One says WO-1003 started on 13 January. The other says 14 January. The production controller wants to know which system is lying, and he wants it before his ten o'clock call with the customer.

HMCC stands for Heavy Maintenance Control Centre, and it needs a caveat of its own. AOG and CRS are universal terms, and you will hear them in any shop in any country. HMCC is a local name. It is what many airlines and MROs call the function that owns and controls the heavy maintenance schedule. Other shops call the identical function production control, maintenance control, or the base maintenance control centre. The line side equivalent is usually MOC, Maintenance Operations Control. Learn what the function owns rather than what it is called.

Owns
Bay and dock allocation, service line, check type, customer, planned start and finish
Does not own
Hours booked, parts issued, the release certificate
Grain
One row per work order
Usual format
A planning board export, very often a workbook maintained by hand

It also owns the daily control picture: progress against plan, what is blocking, and whether content is added to the package or taken out. The records of what physically happened all sit somewhere else. Hours live in the timesheet system, parts in stores, the certificate with certifying staff. That split is why you join three or four systems to answer one question, and it is why planned dates in the control extract and actual dates in the shop floor extract disagree. The disagreement is expected, and the gap between the two dates is the thing worth measuring.

Meridian carries a clean example of the cost. One work order has a control centre planned start of 13 January and a shop floor opened date of 14 January, because the aircraft arrived a day late. Turnaround time is the elapsed days from induction to release. Measure it from the opened date and the average across the six closed work orders is 12.0 days. Measure from the planned start and it becomes 12.17 days. One row, one day, and a headline average moves.

So both systems told the production controller the truth. The control board recorded what the shop intended, the shop floor system recorded what happened, and both entries are correct. Tell him that, then name the two dates separately on the report so the next person does not have to ask.

Demand, supply, and two columns with the same name

The resource manager sends you a workbook of capacity hours. The planner sends you a workbook of pre-input hours. Both files have a column called PlannedHours, so you put the two on one chart. The chart plots demand against demand, and it looks fine to everybody in the room.

Planned manhours are a demand on the shop: what the work needs. Capacity is supply: what the shop can provide. Different facts, different grains, different owners. Confusing them is the most common analytical error in an MRO pack, helped along by the fact that both get called planned hours. In Meridian both columns are literally named PlannedHours in two different tables.

One warning about the word demand itself, because you will meet it again. Central planning publishes its own demand figure, at service line and month grain, and that is a third number with a fourth owner. Chapter C lines all nine of these words up side by side. For this section, demand means the hours the work needs and supply means the hours the shop has.

Capacity is normally headcount multiplied by shift hours multiplied by an availability factor. That factor removes holiday, sickness, training and indirect time. It is also the number people argue about, because it is the difference between a technician being employed and a technician being able to turn a spanner. The result is split by trade and skill, because ten airframe technicians cannot do an avionics job however good the total looks.

The second constraint is physical and gets forgotten in spreadsheets: bays, docks and jigs. A shop can have work waiting and technicians idle and still be blocked, because every bay is full and the aircraft in bay one cannot move until its release is signed. Capacity reporting that counts only people will say there is room.

Capacity usually arrives at station and month grain, labour at day grain. They share a trade dimension and little else. Comparing them needs a conformed trade list, plus a decision about what happens when the grains do not line up. That is Chapter 16. Meridian plans 176 capacity hours across the quarter and books 62.0, which is 35.2 percent utilisation, and those two numbers came from two different people's workbooks.

The chart that plotted demand against demand is fixable in one step. Rename the two columns for what they hold, capacity hours and pre-input hours, before either of them reaches a visual. Do it in Power Query, where the name sticks, and the resource manager and the planner stop being able to collide.

Parts, tools and paperwork

Rotable
A repairable, serialised, high value part that cycles between aircraft and repair shop: a hydraulic pump, a landing gear assembly, an IFE server. It is not consumed, so its cost does not behave like a purchase.
Consumable and expendable
Sealant, rivets, filters, o-rings. Used up, not repaired.
Serialised versus batch
Serialised parts are tracked individually, with their own life and history. Batch parts are tracked by lot. A serial number is a key you can join on. A batch reference usually is not.
Exchange, loan and pool
Three ways of putting a rotable on an aircraft without owning one. The cost landing in your data may be an exchange fee where you expected a part price, and comparing those two produces nonsense.
Robbery, also called cannibalisation
Taking a serviceable part off one aircraft to fix another. It is controlled and recorded, and it distorts consumption analysis: the receiving aircraft consumed a part stores never issued, and the donor now needs one no defect asked for.
Tooling and GSE (Ground Support Equipment)
Special tooling is often the hidden constraint on a check. A task can be planned, staffed and stocked and still not start, because the tool is calibrated out of date or sitting in another bay.

Recognise the document set by name even though you will rarely join to it: the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual), the IPC (Illustrated Parts Catalogue), the SRM (Structural Repair Manual), the CMM (Component Maintenance Manual), the TSM or FIM (troubleshooting and fault isolation manuals), and the task card, which is what a technician books time against.

Aircraft systems are numbered under iSpec 2200, the specification published by the Air Transport Association, now Airlines for America, which is why everyone still says ATA chapter. Almost every defect, task card and finding carries an ATA chapter, which makes it the natural dimension for findings analysis.

One work order almost always touches several chapters, and one chapter appears on many work orders. That is a genuine many to many relationship, and the shop's paperwork means it. Picking a primary chapter to tidy the model loses information. If somebody upstream already picked for you, that is the same conversation as the check type column.

Performance note

Findings analysis by ATA chapter needs a bridge table, and the temptation is to make that relationship filter in both directions so slicers behave the way users expect. It works, and it is not free. A bidirectional filter makes the engine build a set on the one side instead of resolving a lookup. It pays that cost on every query touching those tables, including the queries that never needed the reverse filter. On a few thousand findings you will not notice. On three years of task card lines, you will.

What the shop reports, and where the numbers fight

The finance manager reads the utilisation figure in your pack and concludes the shop is running hot. The production controller reads the same pack, sees turnaround slipping, and concludes the shop is short of people. Both of them are quoting true numbers off your report. They will spend the whole meeting disagreeing, and the report is the reason.

The metric set is small and stable across shops. What varies is the definition underneath each name.

Two of those pull against each other structurally. Turnaround time improves when the shop has slack: a spare technician, a free bay, a trade not fully committed. With slack in the building, a bad finding on day four gets somebody moved onto it that afternoon. Utilisation improves when there is no slack at all. A shop that keeps every technician busy every hour has, by construction, nobody to redeploy, and its turnaround suffers for reasons that never appear in the turnaround report.

That is the meeting from the start of this section explained. High utilisation and slipping turnaround are one fact seen twice, and the finance manager and the production controller are both quoting it correctly. The report that prints the two side by side with no word between them is the thing at fault. Put the relationship in the pack, even in one sentence.

Common mistake

Publishing a performance factor before anybody has agreed in writing which way up it goes. Available divided by achieved gives a number above one when the work took fewer hours than planned, which most people read as good. Plenty of shops invert it and read below one as good. Both conventions are defended by people who have used them for years, and they produce mirror-image trend lines from identical data. Get the definition agreed by production control and put it in the measure description, and accept that this takes longer than writing the DAX did.

Where the data actually comes from

You ask the planner where the pre-input hours come from. He opens a folder on a shared drive, scrolls past a column of files, and opens the one with his own initials in the name. That file is a source system in your model, and nobody in the shop thinks of it that way.

Real shops run maintenance and engineering on a specialist M&E system, and only a handful of them hold most of the market. Larger operators often end up running two of them after a merger. That is a common and unglamorous reason for the same aircraft appearing under two key formats in one warehouse.

Read that table top to bottom and the pattern names itself. The further a table sits from the regulated core, the more likely it is a spreadsheet, and the more likely it is the one that breaks your model. The cause is structural. Regulated systems have referential integrity enforced by an authority that can suspend the shop's approval. Planning workbooks have it enforced by whoever last saved the file. The planner's workbook with his initials in the filename is one of those five bottom rows.

Here is the inconvenient part, better heard now than later. Most of the difficulty in this work sits in those five rows, and very little of it is DAX. Fixing them means walking to production control, asking what a column means, and writing the answer somewhere that survives you leaving. Nobody will schedule that. It will appear on no plan. The model cannot be correct without it.

The mapping you will use for the rest of this document

Everything above becomes a column somewhere. Come back to this table whenever a later chapter introduces a table without re-explaining what it represents.

What to remember
  • The operator, through its CAMO or equivalent, decides what maintenance is due, and the Part-145 shop performs it. Broken foreign keys are that boundary showing up in your data, and they recur.
  • The shop runs four service lines: Line, Light, Heavy, and Cabin and IFE. Line and Light are separate lines with separate crews, and only outsiders club them together.
  • Line and light maintenance frequently arrive with no pre-input pack and therefore no planned manhour figure, which is the case for WO-1002, WO-1005 and WO-1007 in Meridian. A planned against actual measure comes back blank for them, which is correct and also invisible, so publish the count of work orders with no pre-input pack next to the ratio.
  • Cabin and IFE is reported inside base maintenance in some months and broken out on its own in others. Both are groupings over the one service line dimension, and Chapter E builds it.
  • Heavy checks span months, so the month a work order belongs to depends on which date column the slicer filters. Name a measure per question.
  • Available is frozen at pre-input. Projected is re-forecast as findings land and each revision supersedes the last, so it is never summed. Achieved is the only transaction record of the three.
  • Non-routine work is why forecasting exists, and its share varies enormously. Quote your own shop's history, and say how few checks it covers.
  • HMCC is a local name. Other shops say production control or base maintenance control, and the line equivalent is usually MOC. Learn what the function owns.
  • Capacity is supply, planned hours are demand, and turnaround time and utilisation pull against each other by construction. Report both without saying so and the monthly review becomes an argument.
  • The further a table sits from the regulated core, the more likely it is a spreadsheet, and the more likely it is the one that breaks your model.
Part 0 . The domain

BAvailable, projected and achieved: three numbers that are three facts

After this chapter you can say precisely what each of the three manhour numbers means, when it is set, who owns it and at what grain it is recorded, and you can explain to a production controller why each of the three needs a table of its own. You will also be able to build the six measures the three numbers support without summing a forecast or dividing by a plan that was never written.

The finance manager asks for one number: forecast hours for the quarter. You drag ProjectedHours onto a card and it reads 99.5. He puts it in the month-end pack. Two weeks later the production controller sees the pack and says the shop has never forecast 99.5 hours in its life. He is right, by 36.0 hours. The card did exactly what you asked it to do, and this chapter is how a correct sum produces a number nobody in the building believes.

Three words carry the whole chapter, so here they are up front. Available is the plan. Projected is the forecast. Achieved is what was booked. A work order is one job on one aircraft, opened, priced, worked and closed, and all three numbers describe the same work order from three different moments.

One more word before the tables start, because it is used on every page from here. Grain is the answer to the question what does one row of this table mean, written as a single sentence. One row of the timesheet table is one technician's hours on one work order on one day. That is a grain. Get the grain of a table wrong and every number built on top of it is wrong in a way that is very hard to see.

This chapter sits before the curriculum, so it borrows freely from it. The DAX in here is real and it works, but several of the techniques are not properly explained until later. Read the code now for what it does, then come back for the mechanism.

  • Iterators such as SUMX, and the context transition that makes one of them work here: Chapter 9.
  • CALCULATE and the filter arguments that pick a single revision: Chapter 11.
  • Semi-additive values, the family that latest-revision belongs to: Chapter 16.
  • Building a dimension that no source system holds, which is what the trade list needs: Chapter 3.
  • Blanks, orphan keys and unknown members: Chapter 19.
  • One date table serving several date columns: Chapter 13.

The three words, one at a time

The shift supervisor keeps a whiteboard in the crew room with one number against each check in the hangar. The planner keeps a spreadsheet with a different number for the same checks. The production controller updates a third. Ask any of the three and he will tell you the other two are out of date.

Your department uses three numbers to describe the same check, and they disagree constantly. Each one is a true statement about a different moment in the life of the check. Each was made by a different person and written into a different system. So the disagreement is evidence. It is the only quantitative evidence anybody has about how well the shop plans and how well it forecasts, and a model that reconciles it away throws that evidence in the bin.

Available

Available is what the pre-input work package says the work should take. Before the aircraft arrives, the planner assembles every task card falling due in the window. A task card is one printed instruction for one piece of work, and it is what a technician books time against. He adds the out-of-phase items, the modifications and the deferred defects. He adds the ADs, Airworthiness Directives, which the authority issues and which are mandatory. He adds the SBs, Service Bulletins, which are the manufacturer's recommendation and become mandatory only when an AD or the operator says so.

Each card carries an estimated manhour figure, taken from a standard time or from shop history. The planner rolls those estimates up by trade, and a trade is a skill group such as airframe, avionics, engine or NDT, meaning non-destructive testing. That roll-up is the available figure.

It is set once, at the end of pre-input planning, then frozen at induction. Induction is the moment the aircraft arrives and the check formally opens. Frozen is the important word. A baseline that moves cannot measure anything, because every time the work turns out harder than expected you can quietly raise the plan and report that you hit it. Planning owns the number. Its grain is one figure per work order per trade, and in a stricter shop one figure per task card. In Meridian that is HeavyPreInput, eight rows covering five work orders.

The synonyms are where this starts to hurt. Planned, budgeted, estimated and sold all appear in the wild meaning roughly this, and they are not always the same number. Sold hours is the figure the customer was quoted, and it can deliberately differ from the internal estimate, which carries contingency the customer never sees. Two available numbers, both correct, and nobody will tell you which one the report you inherited uses.

Projected

Projected is the current best estimate of the final total. It is also called the forecast, or the estimate at completion, EAC. That last phrase is worth knowing, because it makes the meaning plain. It is an estimate of where the number ends up. Adding it on top of anything else is a category error. Production control owns it, and it moves during the check because findings arrive during the check.

That word findings deserves a sentence of its own, because it is the whole economics of heavy maintenance. A technician opens a panel that a routine card told them to open, and behind it is corrosion, or a crack, or a chafed wiring loom that no card mentions. They raise a non-routine card, sometimes called an NRC or a finding. Routine hours are known before induction. Non-routine hours are not knowable before induction, by definition, so production control revises the expected total as the check runs and each revision replaces the last.

Its grain is one figure per work order per revision. In Meridian that is ManhourForecast: eight rows across five work orders, two of which were never revised at all. The gap between projected and available is, in practice, what the findings cost. It is a proxy, and a weak one here. The limits section at the end of the chapter says why.

Achieved

Achieved is what technicians actually recorded against the work. Actual, booked, expended and clocked all mean this. It is the only one of the three that is a transaction record: a person did some work, and a row was written. The other two are opinions with a date attached. Keep that sentence. It settles more arguments than any modelling technique in this document.

The timesheet or labour booking system owns it, a third system separate from both of the others. Its grain in Meridian is one row per technician per work order per day, which is LaborEntries. A stricter shop books time against the task card. That is a finer grain, and it is the grain that would produce the metrics this dataset cannot.

The four derived numbers you will be asked for

Earned hours
The planned hours for the work that is actually finished so far. It is the honest progress measure. Booked hours tell you how much time went in, and they say nothing about how much of the work package is done. Earned hours requires task card completion status, which Meridian does not have.
Performance factor
Available divided by achieved, in most shops. Above one means the work took fewer hours than planned. Some shops invert it. Confirm the direction before you publish it.
Remaining to go
Projected minus achieved, also called estimate to complete. Meaningful only while the check is open, which turns out to matter.
Forecast accuracy
Achieved divided by projected, measured at close. It grades production control, not the shop floor.

The whiteboard, the planner's spreadsheet and production control's third number are the three rows of Table B.1. All of them are current, each about a different moment in the life of the check, and the model has to carry every one.

The warning that will save you the most time

This vocabulary is local to each shop. The authorities define a Certificate of Release to Service and then leave available hours to whoever is writing the report. One shop's planned is another shop's budgeted and a third shop's sold. Worse, and this is the failure mode that bites. The same word can mean the frozen baseline in one report and the live forecast in the next. Same building, two people, and no reason yet for either of them to compare notes.

Take WO-1003, a C-check on an E175 at Tucson. Planning set the baseline at 13.0 hours. Production control revised to 16.5 after findings. The check finished on 12.5 hours booked. Now put the planner and the production controller in a review where the agenda item reads hours against plan. On the planner's definition the check came in 0.5 hours under: 13.0 minus 12.5. On the production controller's definition it came in 4.0 hours under: 16.5 minus 12.5. Both figures are arithmetically correct. They tell different stories about whether this shop estimates well, and the meeting will reach whichever conclusion belongs to whoever spoke first.

So your first job on any new maintenance, repair and overhaul dataset is to write down the local definition of each term. One sentence each, with the source table named. Modelling comes after that. Take the page to somebody in production control and get it agreed in writing. Email is fine. What matters is that a named person agreed a named definition on a named date.

Rule of thumb

Put the agreed definitions into the model description and into the description property of every measure that uses them, not just into a document nobody opens. Power BI shows measure descriptions on hover in the field list, so the definition travels with the model to whoever inherits it. Two people using one word for two numbers is the most expensive failure mode in reporting for this industry, and it survives every technical review: clean data, correct relationships, right DAX, wrong answer.

The three source tables, printed in full

The shift supervisor tells you his bay is occupied and your bay report shows it free. He is standing next to the aircraft, so he wins the argument on the spot. The work order he means is WO-1005, and the reason it vanished from your report is printed in the first table below.

These three arrive on top of the six raw tables you met in Chapter 0. They add no columns to anything you already have and they change none of the totals you already know. Here they are complete, every row and every column, with the problems marked.

In a real shop this is the planning board of the Heavy Maintenance Control Centre. Be careful with that acronym. AOG (aircraft on ground) and CRS (Certificate of Release to Service) are universal. HMCC is a local name, used by many airlines and independent shops for the function that owns the heavy maintenance schedule. Elsewhere the same function is production control, maintenance control, or the base maintenance control centre. On the line side the equivalent is usually MOC, Maintenance Operations Control. Change employer and the function will still be there while the letters change. Physically this extract is very often a hand-maintained Excel workbook. Whoever is running the shift edits it at eight in the morning. That is why it is the table most likely to break your model.

Three things are wrong with it. WO-1005 has no bay, which matches its blank station code in WorkOrders. That blank is why the shift supervisor's occupied bay is missing from your report: the work order is real, the aircraft is real, and the bay label the visual groups by is empty. WO-1006 has no customer, which matches its aircraft registration N338WA being absent from the aircraft registry. WO-1003 has a planned start of 2025-01-13 while WorkOrders records an opened date of 2025-01-14, because the aircraft arrived a day late and only one system was told.

A fourth thing matters more than those three defects. ServiceLine and CheckType live only in this table, and WorkOrders holds neither of them. So every split by service line in this chapter reaches the work order through a hand-maintained spreadsheet. While you are looking at that column, notice the two values that are one letter apart. Light and Line both cover short defect work done outside a hangar bay. Many shops treat the two as one family, and Meridian's board keeps them separate. WO-1007 is the only line work order in the quarter. Label it light by mistake and 5.0 hours move from one service line to the other while the total stays at 62.0, so no reconciliation check will ever catch it.

This comes from the planning module of the maintenance and engineering system, or from the planner's own workbook, which is more common than anybody admits. Its problems are structural. Every value in it is clean and correctly typed, and the trouble is which rows are missing. Only heavy and cabin work orders appear. WO-1002 and WO-1005 sit on the light service line, and WO-1007 sits on line. All three are absent entirely. That work is defect driven, and there is nothing to plan until the defect is reported. So any measure that divides by planned hours has three work orders with no denominator. How you handle that is a design decision, and it belongs to you.

The trade value Cabin does not exist in ShopCapacity, whose four trade columns are Airframe, Avionics, Engine and NDT. Cabin and IFE work often uses different trades from airframe work, so the mismatch is normal shop life. It still has to be resolved before either number can be trusted. Quietly nastier: the column is called PlannedHours here, and the capacity table has a column called PlannedHours too. The two mean opposite things, demand here and supply there. I have watched that collision produce a chart where demand was plotted against demand.

This is production control's table, and in most shops it is a spreadsheet with one tab per check and a column added every time somebody re-forecasts. Its defining property is that it must never be summed: each revision supersedes the one before, so adding Rev 0 to Rev 1 adds an estimate to the estimate that replaced it. Only three work orders were ever revised. Either the other two had no findings large enough to move the number or nobody updated the tab, and the data cannot tell you which. One smaller detail: the Rev 0 date on WO-1003 is 2025-01-14, the actual induction date, not the 2025-01-13 the control board still shows. Production control forecast from reality. The control board never caught up.

Read the figure down the left column first. Three source boxes, three grains, three owners, and note the colours: HeavyPreInput and ManhourForecast are drawn olive because they hold planning estimates, while LaborEntries is terracotta because it is a transaction record. That colour split is the argument of this chapter in one visual convention. The three grey value cards on their right give the totals: 57.0 available hours, 63.5 projected hours, 62.0 achieved hours. The 62.0 is every labor row in the dataset, which is why it ties to the total you already know.

The upper right card traces one check across all three. WO-1003: the planner said 13.0, findings pushed the forecast to 16.5, and the check finished on 12.5, under both. Performance is 13.0 divided by 12.5, which is 104.0 percent, and forecast accuracy is 12.5 divided by 16.5, which is 75.8 percent. Hold that pair. Below it, in red, is the number nobody should ship, the eight forecast rows added together to give 99.5. The green card across the bottom is the reconciliation to keep in your head: 48.0 of the 62.0 achieved hours sit on heavy and cabin work, and the remaining 14.0 hours belong to three work orders that were never planned in hours at all. Split those 14.0 hours across the four service lines and they are 9.0 on light and 5.0 on line.

Why the three numbers need three tables

The production controller has a suggestion, and it is a reasonable one. Put the three numbers in a single table, one row per work order, three columns. It would fit on one screen and everybody could read it without being taught anything. He is asking in good faith, and you need four answers ready.

The single most valuable idea in this chapter is this one, so here are the grains stated as sentences, exactly as you should be able to recite them in a design review.

  • One row of HeavyPreInput is the planned hours for one trade on one work order, decided once before the aircraft arrived.
  • One row of ManhourForecast is one estimate of the final total for one work order, made on one date and superseded by the next one.
  • One row of LaborEntries is one technician's booked hours on one work order on one day.

Now imagine the flat alternative that somebody proposes in every project: a single table with WorkOrderID, Available, Projected and Achieved, one row per work order. It looks tidy. WO-1003 would read 13.0, 16.5, 12.5, and the report would be trivial to build. It fails for four reasons, and they are independent, which is why no clever transformation rescues it.

They are set at different times. The available column would be written weeks before induction, the projected column three separate times during the check, the achieved column every day. A row that has to be rewritten by three different processes on three different schedules is a race condition with a primary key. Whichever process writes last wins, and nothing in the table records that the other two ever ran.

They are owned by different people. Planning writes one column, production control writes another, the timesheet system writes the third. When the number is wrong you need to know who to ask, and a shared row destroys that information. It also destroys the audit trail: overwrite 13.0 with 16.5 and the evidence that the plan ever said 13.0 is gone.

They are recorded at different levels of detail. Available is per trade, so flattening it loses the fact that WO-1003's 13.0 is 8.0 airframe plus 5.0 engine. Projected is per revision, so flattening it loses when the forecast moved, which is the only evidence you will have about whether the estimate or the execution was the problem. Achieved is per technician per day, so flattening it loses every time-based analysis and every question about who did the work.

And two of the three keep changing after the first is frozen. That is the point that ends the argument. A frozen baseline sitting in the same row as two live values will eventually be edited by somebody who is updating the whole row when he meant to touch one column, and you will never find out.

Four answers, then, for the production controller: three writing schedules, three owners, three levels of detail, and one frozen value living next to two moving ones. He can have his one-screen view. Build it as a report page over three tables, and the model keeps the evidence he will want the first time a customer queries a bill.

Interview-level insight

There is a cleaner way to say this, and it generalises well beyond aviation. The three numbers have three different additive behaviours. Available is fully additive: sum it across trades, work orders, stations and months and every total means something. Achieved is fully additive too. Projected is semi-additive: it sums across work orders but never across revisions, because the revision axis holds versions of one value rather than parts of it. Three columns on one table would force a single filter context to serve three aggregation rules, and no measure can do that honestly. Filter context is the set of rows a visual has left visible at the moment a measure runs, and every measure in that visual gets the same one.

Two wrong answers, worked

Wrong answer one: summing the forecast

The wrong way

Drop ProjectedHours onto a card. Power BI defaults to a sum, because the column is numeric and it has no way of knowing what the rows mean.

DAXProjected Hours, the default
Projected Hours =
    SUM ( FactForecast[ProjectedHours] )
Result
13.0 plus 14.0 plus 13.0 plus 16.5 plus 12.0 plus 10.0 plus 13.5 plus 7.5, which is 99.5 hours. This is the number that reached the finance manager's month-end pack.
Why it is wrong
WO-1001 contributes 27.0 hours, which is its first guess plus its second guess. The check was never expected to take 27.0 hours by anybody at any point.
What you see in the report

Nothing. That is the problem. A card reading 99.5 next to an achieved card reading 62.0 looks like a shop running well under forecast, which is a pleasant story somebody will repeat in a customer meeting. No error, no blank, no warning triangle. The number is 36.0 hours too high and it is perfectly formatted.

The fix

Take the latest revision for each work order, then sum those five values. WO-1001 14.0, WO-1003 16.5, WO-1004 12.0, WO-1006 13.5, WO-1008 7.5, totalling 63.5 hours. The concept has a name, semi-additive, and it is the same shape as a stock balance: you sum across products but never across time, you take the last one. Chapter 16 covers the family properly, including the cases where last by date is not the right selector.

Common mistake

Hiding the problem by setting the forecast column to Do not summarize, or renaming it to something scary. Neither survives contact with a report builder who drags the field into a matrix. Apply the rule instead: if a table holds versions of a value rather than parts of a value, never expose its measure as a plain SUM, hide the underlying column so nobody can drag it into a visual, and write the words latest revision per work order into the measure description, where a report author sees them on hover.

Wrong answer two: dividing available by achieved on light and line maintenance

The wrong way

Build a performance factor as available divided by achieved, put it in a matrix by service line, and then tidy the empty cells away, because a matrix with holes in it looks unfinished. The usual tidy-up is a third argument on DIVIDE, written as DIVIDE ( [Available Hours], [Achieved Hours], 0 ). Now light maintenance shows 0.0 percent, and so does line maintenance. Somebody senior reads that as two teams achieving nothing against their plan, and that is a conversation you cannot take back.

The three work orders outside base maintenance appear nowhere in HeavyPreInput: WO-1002 and WO-1005 on light, WO-1007 on line. Their available hours do not exist. Nobody wrote a plan for that work, so there is no figure there to be zero. Divide a number that was never written by 14.0 hours that were genuinely worked, 9.0 of them on light and 5.0 on line, and the answer is undefined. Zero percent claims something. Undefined claims nothing, and the two are as different as an empty bank account and no bank account.

The fix

DIVIDE with no third argument. When there are no pre-input rows in the current filter context the numerator is blank, so the result comes back blank. The row still appears in the matrix, the ratio cell is empty, and an empty cell is the honest statement: we did not plan this work in hours, so we cannot grade it against a plan.

Never supply a third argument of zero to tidy the cell up, because that converts an undefined ratio into a confident false statement for exactly the rows where you know least. Say on the visual why the cell is empty instead, since a blank with no explanation gets filled in by the reader's imagination. Chapter 11 covers filter modifiers and Chapter 19 covers what blanks mean in a report.

The triad, work order by work order

Available
57.0 hours
Projected, latest revision
63.5 hours
Achieved, heavy and cabin
48.0 hours
Achieved, all work
62.0 hours

The achieved column in that table totals 48.0 and not 62.0, because it covers only the five work orders with a pre-input pack. The rest of this document works with 62.0, so here is the reconciliation. Keep it: the first question anybody asks about a heavy maintenance report is why the hours do not match the hours in the other report.

One detail is worth stating precisely. WO-1003's achieved 12.5 hours comes from two labor rows, and one of them, L-505, carries a technician key of TECH-04 with a trailing space. That defect moves 4.5 hours between technicians. It does not move them between work orders, because the work order key on that row is clean. The triad is safe from that bug and any measure sliced by technician is not. Knowing which of your numbers a given defect can reach is most of what data quality work is.

The metrics, on the three closed heavy checks only

The finance manager wants a performance figure for the quarter to show the customer on Thursday. There are eight work orders in the quarter. Three of them can honestly produce one, and the walk from eight to three is the whole of this section.

Only WO-1001, WO-1003 and WO-1006 are closed heavy checks. WO-1004 is still open, so its achieved figure is a partial count and grading it would be meaningless. WO-1008 was inducted on 2025-03-10 and has no hours booked. Filtering to completed work before you compute a completion ratio is the difference between a metric and a number. Treat that filter as a refinement and you will publish the second while calling it the first.

The arithmetic, spelled out. Performance factor is available divided by achieved: 36.0 divided by 38.0 gives 94.7 percent overall, and per check 13.0 over 13.5 is 96.3 percent, 13.0 over 12.5 is 104.0 percent, 10.0 over 12.0 is 83.3 percent. Forecast accuracy is achieved divided by projected: 38.0 divided by 44.0 gives 86.4 percent, and per check 13.5 over 14.0 is 96.4 percent, 12.5 over 16.5 is 75.8 percent, 12.0 over 13.5 is 88.9 percent.

Notice that the total row is not the average of the rows above it. The three performance figures average to 94.5 percent: 96.3 plus 104.0 plus 83.3, divided by 3, giving 94.53. The measure at the total does something different. It divides 36.0 by 38.0 and gives 94.7 percent, because bigger checks carry more weight there. Both quantities are legitimate. Only one is what your measure computes. Export the matrix to Excel, average the column, and you will get a different answer from the total.

Now WO-1003, which is the check worth understanding. The planner estimated 13.0. Production control revised to 16.5 after findings, a 3.5 hour increase. The check came in at 12.5, under the plan and a long way under the forecast. Its performance factor is 104.0 percent, the best of the three, and its forecast accuracy is 75.8 percent, the worst of the three by some distance. Those two numbers answer two different questions, so both are true at once. The planner was close. The forecast panicked. Execution beat both.

Interview-level insight

Keeping the two ratios separate is what makes the pair useful. A single hours-against-plan number cannot distinguish a shop that executes badly from one that forecasts badly, and those problems have different owners and different fixes. WO-1003 is a forecasting problem, not an execution problem. Report only performance factor and you conclude the check went well, while production control carries on adding contingency nobody measures. Report only forecast accuracy and you go and talk to the wrong team.

Here is the inconvenient part, and it is what the finance manager has to hear before Thursday. Three closed checks is a sample of three. The 94.7 percent has no statistical meaning, and putting it on a dashboard with a trend arrow invents information the data does not contain. Build this for real and you should put the count of checks beside the ratio in the same visual, and refuse to show the ratio below an agreed minimum. You will be told this makes the dashboard look empty. It does. It also stops the shop deciding on a sample of one. Give him 94.7 percent with the figure 3 printed next to it, and let the customer see both.

Rule of thumb

State the direction of the performance ratio in the measure name, not in a footnote: Performance Factor (available over achieved, above 100 percent is good). Shops genuinely invert this, and half of them read above 100 percent as favourable while the other half read it as an overspend. Nobody misreads a ratio whose direction is printed on it. The same applies to forecast accuracy, where 75.8 percent means the forecast was too high, and that is not obvious from the label either.

The trade only one system has heard of

The resource manager cannot understand why his quarterly utilisation looks comfortable while his cabin fitters are turning work away. The answer is one row. Twelve hours of cabin demand sit in the pre-input pack, and his capacity workbook has four trades, none of them cabin.

HeavyPreInput books 12.0 hours to a trade called Cabin. ShopCapacity has never heard of it: its four trade columns are Airframe, Avionics, Engine and NDT. Both tables are right about the world each one was built for. Planning knows the cabin retrofit needs cabin fitters, and the capacity workbook was built around airframe trades and never updated. The only correct response is to build the trade dimension from both sources and take the distinct union, which gives five members. That technique is Chapter 3, and it is the same move that produces the station and aircraft dimensions.

Read the Cabin row as an operational statement. Clean it up as a data defect and you destroy the signal. Twelve planned hours of cabin work exist and nobody planned the people to do it. There are at least three explanations, and the data cannot choose between them. Airframe or avionics staff may be absorbing the work and booking it under their own trade. The work may be subcontracted to a company that never appears in the capacity workbook. Or the workbook was never updated for the retrofit programme. One weak clue: the only person who booked time to WO-1004 is TECH-07, who does not exist in the human resources extract. That is consistent with an outside body and equally consistent with a data entry error. Ask.

The wider lesson is worth carrying to your next shop. Planned hours in a pre-input pack are demand. Planned hours in a capacity workbook are supply. Comparing the two needs the shared trade dimension, plus careful handling of grain. Capacity sits at station and month. Demand sits at work order and trade.

Two systems, two dates, one turnaround time

The finance manager needs an average turnaround figure for the customer review, and turnaround time is the elapsed days from induction to release. You build it and get 12.00 days. A colleague builds the same thing and gets 12.17. One row of data is the difference between you.

The control board says WO-1003 started on 2025-01-13. The shop floor system says it opened on 2025-01-14. The aircraft arrived a day late. Somebody updated one system and left the other alone. Now turnaround time, the headline metric in a heavy maintenance shop, has two defensible values.

One row of disagreement out of eight moves a quarterly headline. Both numbers are correct arithmetic on different columns. The planned start answers when were we going to start. The opened date answers when did work actually begin. Turnaround time as customers understand it usually means the second, measured from induction to the issue of the Certificate of Release to Service.

So the finance manager gets 12.00 days, taken from the opened date, with the source column named on the visual. Pick one source as the system of record for each fact, write that choice down beside the definitions you already agreed, and never let a report mix them silently. If both dates matter, and for on-time delivery analysis both do, surface both as separate named measures. The thing to keep out of production is one measure that takes its start date from whichever table happened to be joined first.

Common mistake

Relating HMCCSchedule to FactWorkOrder one to one and leaving both sets of dates live in the model. Two tables at identical grain with overlapping columns is an invitation for two report authors to pick different columns and produce two turnaround figures that both survive review. Merge the control board into the work order table in Power Query, keep the columns you decided to trust, and rename the ones you keep for reference so nobody picks them up by accident. Chapter 6 covers one to one relationships and why they are almost always a merge waiting to happen.

The measures

Six measures. The first two are trivial, the third is the only difficult one, and the last three depend on all of the above.

DAXAvailable Hours, Achieved Hours
// planning demand, frozen at induction
Available Hours =
    SUM ( FactPreInput[PlannedHours] )

// booked time, the only transaction record of the three
Achieved Hours =
    SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )
Available Hours
A plain sum is correct because available is fully additive. Every row is a distinct trade on a distinct work order, so no row overlaps another. Returns 57.0 with no filter, and blank for any light or line work order, which is the behaviour you want.
Achieved Hours
Also fully additive: every row is a separate day of a separate technician. Returns 62.0 over the whole dataset and 48.0 when the filter context is restricted to the heavy and cabin service lines, using the service line column merged onto FactWorkOrder.
DAXProjected Hours (latest revision)
Projected Hours =
SUMX (
    VALUES ( FactForecast[WorkOrderID] ),
    VAR LatestRevision =
        CALCULATE ( MAX ( FactForecast[RevisionDate] ) )
    RETURN
        CALCULATE (
            SUM ( FactForecast[ProjectedHours] ),
            FactForecast[RevisionDate] = LatestRevision
        )
)
Line 2
SUMX iterates, which means it walks a list and evaluates an expression once per item, then adds the results. The list here is one row per work order.
Line 3
VALUES returns the distinct work order identifiers visible in the current filter context. Five of them in this dataset, since only five work orders were ever forecast.
Lines 4 and 5
Inside the iteration, CALCULATE with no filter argument performs a context transition: it converts the current work order into a filter. MAX of the revision date within that filter is therefore the latest revision date for that one work order. This is the technique explained in Chapter 9.
Lines 7 to 10
The second CALCULATE keeps the work order filter and replaces the revision date filter with the single date found above, then sums. One row survives per work order.
Result
14.0 plus 16.5 plus 12.0 plus 13.5 plus 7.5, which is 63.5 hours.
Why this and not that

The obvious alternative is to keep the iterator and take MAX ( FactForecast[ProjectedHours] ) per work order instead of hunting for the latest revision date, and on this dataset that returns exactly the right answer, 63.5, because every revision in Meridian happens to revise upwards. That coincidence is the reason to reject it. The rule is take the latest, not take the largest, and the two agree only while no forecast is ever cut. The first time a production controller reduces a forecast because a finding turned out to be cosmetic, the maximum measure quietly reports the superseded number and keeps reporting it. A measure that is right for the wrong reason cannot be tested, because the test passes.

The other alternative is LASTNONBLANKVALUE, which is shorter and reads well when the model has a proper date relationship on the revision date. It is a reasonable choice. The explicit form is written out here because it makes both ideas visible, latest by date and one row per work order, and because it keeps working when the selector is not a date, such as a revision number or an approval flag.

Trace the latest revision measure by hand, work order by work order

With no filters applied, VALUES ( FactForecast[WorkOrderID] ) returns five values, and SUMX evaluates the expression once for each.

  • WO-1001. Context transition leaves two rows, dated 2025-01-06 and 2025-01-10. MAX gives 2025-01-10. The inner CALCULATE keeps Rev 1 and sums 14.0.
  • WO-1003. Two rows, 2025-01-14 and 2025-01-25. MAX gives 2025-01-25, which is Rev 1, and sums 16.5.
  • WO-1004. One row only, 2025-02-03. MAX gives that date, and Rev 0 contributes 12.0. Work orders that were never revised need no special handling, which is why this pattern is preferable to anything that filters on the text Rev 1.
  • WO-1006. Two rows, 2025-02-17 and 2025-03-01. Rev 1 wins and contributes 13.5.
  • WO-1008. One row, 2025-03-10, contributing 7.5.

14.0 plus 16.5 plus 12.0 plus 13.5 plus 7.5 equals 63.5. Now suppose RevisionDate is joined to the date table and somebody slices to February. Only WO-1004 and WO-1006 have a forecast row in February, so the card reads 12.0 plus 10.0, which is 22.0. That 10.0 is WO-1006 Rev 0, superseded on 2025-03-01 by 13.5, and the slicer has hidden the row that replaced it. Arguably correct, in that it answers what production control believed during February. Arguably wrong, in that a card labelled Projected Hours is showing a number somebody has already withdrawn. Which behaviour you want is a business decision, and every semi-additive measure forces it on you.

Performance note

This measure iterates the distinct work orders and performs a context transition on every one, which is materially more expensive than a plain SUM. At five work orders you will never notice. At forty thousand work orders in a real maintenance and engineering system, in a matrix that also slices by trade and month, you will. The usual remedy is to resolve the latest revision once, in Power Query or a calculated table, flagging each forecast row as current or superseded, then filtering on that flag at query time. That moves the work from per query to per refresh, the trade discussed in Chapter 4. The cost is that the flag is only as fresh as the last refresh, so avoid it where somebody re-forecasts mid-morning and expects the report to move.

DAXPerformance Factor, Forecast Accuracy
// above 100 percent means the work took fewer hours
// than the frozen plan. Confirm the direction locally.
Performance Factor =
    DIVIDE ( [Available Hours], [Achieved Hours] )

// measured at close only. Below 100 percent means the
// forecast was too high.
Forecast Accuracy =
    DIVIDE ( [Achieved Hours], [Projected Hours] )
Performance Factor
Grades the planner against the shop floor. 36.0 over 38.0 across the three closed checks, which is 94.7 percent. Blank for light and for line maintenance, because the numerator does not exist there.
Forecast Accuracy
Grades production control. 38.0 over 44.0 across the same three checks, which is 86.4 percent. Apply it to closed work only: on an open check the numerator is a partial count and the ratio is guaranteed to look terrible.
Why this and not that

DIVIDE rather than the division operator, in both measures, for two separate reasons. The familiar one: a plain slash raises a division by zero condition when the denominator is zero. Power BI usually renders that as infinity instead of failing the visual, and infinity in a percentage column draws the eye and means nothing. The second reason matters more here. DIVIDE gives you one explicit place to decide what an undefined ratio shows, through its optional third argument, and leaving that argument out states that undefined is undefined. WO-1008 has 9.0 available hours and 0.0 achieved hours because it was inducted on 2025-03-10 and nobody has booked time. It has no performance factor at all, and a blank cell says exactly that. Infinity would be wrong and zero would be worse.

DAXRemaining To Go
Remaining To Go =
VAR Forecast = [Projected Hours]
VAR Booked = [Achieved Hours]
VAR IsOpen =
    ISBLANK ( CALCULATE ( MAX ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] ) ) )
RETURN
    IF (
        IsOpen && NOT ISBLANK ( Forecast ),
        Forecast - Booked
    )
Lines 2 and 3
Evaluate both measures once and hold them. Beyond readability this matters because each is referenced below and the engine should not be asked to compute the forecast selection twice.
Lines 4 and 5
