The timesheet measure. SUM reads one stored column and the storage engine aggregates it in a single scan. SUMX would iterate row by row, which you need only when the value has to be computed per row, such as hours multiplied by rate.
Lines 4 to 5
The submission measure, over a different table. DeptSubmission sits at service line and month grain, and grain means the level of detail one row represents. So it relates to DimServiceLine and to the month column of your date table. Put it on a day-level axis and every day except the first of the month comes back blank. That grain behaviour is Chapter 16.
Lines 8 to 9
Two VAR declarations. Each measure is evaluated once and reused twice, which keeps the code readable and stops the engine being asked the same question again.
Lines 10 to 14
The guard. If both sides are blank there is nothing to compare, and the measure stays blank. If either side has a value, the subtraction runs.
Result
Heavy January returns 1.0. Every other populated row returns 0.0. Heavy March returns 0.0, because the department submitted a real zero and the timesheet has no rows, and those two statements agree. Light in March returns blank, because neither side has anything to say.
Why this and not that

Use ISBLANK here. A test for zero collapses two different situations into one answer, and the data proves it. Heavy in March was submitted as 0.0, a deliberate statement that the department did no heavy work. Light in March was never submitted at all. Test for zero and both cases return the same result, so the variance matrix paints a confident 0.0 across cells holding no data. The same reasoning is why IF wraps the subtraction: blank minus blank returns 0.0, and every empty cell would report perfect agreement.

Common mistake

Averaging the two numbers, or quietly taking the larger one, to make a card agree with a meeting pack. It works for exactly one month. Then a correction runs the other way, the average lands between two figures that both exist in writing, and you now have a third number that no function in the shop owns and nobody can reproduce.

The two routes to service line

Now the sharper version of the same problem, and the one that will cost you the most time if you meet it unprepared.

The production controller asks a question that sounds simple. How many hours went to heavy maintenance in the quarter? You have two ways to answer it, and both of them are already built into your model.

Route A goes through the work order. Start at FactLabor, follow the work order key to FactWorkOrder, and read the service line that came from the HMCC board on HMCCSchedule. Every labour row inherits the service line of the job it was booked to.

Route B goes through the technician. Start at FactLabor, follow the technician key to DimTechnician, look up the crew in CrewAssignment, then translate the crew code into a service line with CrewCodeMap. Every labour row inherits the service line of the crew that booked it.

What you see in the report

Two pages of the same report, built by two people six weeks apart, both with a bar labelled Heavy. One says 38.0 hours and one says 28.5. Both totals are 62.0, which is the detail that makes the argument last for months: neither side is losing hours, so neither side can be shown to be broken.

Why the two routes disagree

The gap on heavy is 38.0 minus 28.5, which is 9.5 hours, and you can name every one of them. The heart of it is TECH-04, who sits on the cabin crew, CRW-CAB. In January he booked 6.0 hours to WO-1001 and 4.5 hours to WO-1003. Both are heavy C-checks. Route A counts those 10.5 hours as heavy because heavy is what the work was. Route B counts them as cabin and IFE because cabin is whose person did it.

Two more movements complete the picture. TECH-02 is on an airframe heavy crew and booked 9.0 hours to WO-1002, a light maintenance defect job, so route B pulls those hours into heavy. TECH-05 is on the line crew and booked 8.0 hours to the heavy check WO-1003, so route B moves those into line. Route B heavy is 7.5 plus 12.0 plus 9.0, which is 28.5.

Trace this by hand, all eight labour rows

Eight rows is small enough to check with a pencil, and doing it once saves you an afternoon later. Read the two service line columns against each other. Wherever they differ, a technician worked off their own crew's service line.

Five of the eight rows are tinted, and that tells you something real: Meridian moves people across service lines constantly. The tinted hours add to 6.0 plus 9.0 plus 8.0 plus 4.5 plus 10.0, which is 37.5 of the 62.0 hours. Sixty percent of the quarter changes service line depending on the route you take.

One note on L-505. Its technician identifier arrives as TECH-04 with a trailing space, which looks identical in any table visual and matches nothing on join. Power Query trims it. Without the trim, those 4.5 hours leave TECH-04 and land in a blank technician row, so route B would report cabin and IFE at 6.0 instead of 10.5. Route A would not flinch, because it reads the work order key and never touches the technician key. Both routes would still total 62.0, so no total would reveal it. Orphan keys and blank rows are Chapter 19.

The resolution: two questions, two measure names

Both routes are correct. They answer two different questions that happen to share a word.

  • Route A answers what work was done. Use it for capacity against demand, for customer reporting, for turnaround time, and for anything that compares hours against the planned hours on a check, because the plan was written per work order.
  • Route B answers whose crew did it. Use it for roster efficiency, for the productivity factor, for headcount conversations, and for anything the resource scheduler owns, because the roster is written per crew.

Build both, name them for the question, and put the route in the description where a report author sees it on hover. Hours by Work Type and Hours by Owning Crew are good names because neither can be shortened to Heavy hours by somebody in a hurry. Calling either one Heavy hours without qualification is how two reports end up disagreeing forever, one number on the operations page and another on the manpower page, with no note saying they were never meant to match.

So the production controller gets a straight answer at last. If he is asking what work the shop did, it is 38.0 hours. If he is asking what his heavy crews spent their time on, it is 28.5. Ask him which one he wants before you open the report, and the number stops moving between meetings.

DAXTwo routes, two measures, each refusing the other's axis
Hours by Work Type =
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ),
        REMOVEFILTERS ( DimTechnician[OwningServiceLine] )
    )

Hours by Owning Crew =
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ),
        REMOVEFILTERS ( DimServiceLine[ServiceLine] )
    )
The model behind it
DimServiceLine relates to FactWorkOrder[ServiceLine], which arrived when HMCCSchedule was merged onto the work order in Power Query. DimTechnician[OwningServiceLine] is a plain text column on the technician dimension, filled in by merging CrewAssignment and then CrewCodeMap. Two separate columns, two separate axes.
Lines 1 to 5
CALCULATE is here because nothing else in DAX can change the filter context, and changing it is the whole job. Hours by work type, with the crew column's filter removed. Drop this measure into a matrix that has owning crew on rows and every row shows 38.0 for heavy, which looks odd and is meant to. The repeated value is the measure telling you that this axis does not belong to it.
Lines 7 to 11
The mirror image. Hours by owning crew ignores any selection on the work order's service line, so it cannot be silently narrowed by a slicer somebody left on another page.
What you must not build
A relationship from DimServiceLine to the technician's crew column. That would give the model two paths from one dimension to FactLabor, one through the work order and one through the technician, and Power BI will refuse to activate the second. Two paths, two possible answers, and the engine will not guess. That is Chapter 8.
Why this and not that

REMOVEFILTERS rather than ALL, even though both clear the filter on that column. ALL has two jobs in DAX: it acts as a CALCULATE modifier here, and elsewhere it returns a table you can iterate. A reader of your code has to work out which job it is doing on this line. REMOVEFILTERS has only the one job, so the intent is on the page. Also note that both take a column and not the table. REMOVEFILTERS ( DimTechnician ) would clear EmployeeType and HomeStation as well, and a user filtering to contract staff would get a number that silently included the staff technicians.

Now the inconvenient part. Those two measures refuse each other's axis, and once in a while the cross tabulation is exactly what somebody needs. The cell where work type is heavy and owning crew is cabin and IFE holds TECH-04's 10.5 hours, which is the best evidence you will ever have that the cabin crew is propping up the hangar. When you need that view, build a third measure with no modifiers, call it Hours by Work Type and Crew, and give it its own page with a title that explains the cells. Three measures is more work. It is also the only version that survives a year of other people using your report.

Performance note

Flattening CrewAssignment and CrewCodeMap into one column on DimTechnician at refresh removes two joins from every query that slices by owning crew. Be honest about the size of that win: at seven technicians it is unmeasurable, and even at four thousand the two lookups are cheap, because they run on the one side of the relationship. Do it for clarity and to avoid a second filter path, and expect no visible speed change. The cost that matters sits on the relationship from DimTechnician to FactLabor, and this changes nothing there.

The crew code map, and why it is the most fragile object you own

The manpower page has carried a bar with no label for two months. The bar is worth 10.0 hours. Nobody has asked about it, because a blank bar looks like a rendering fault and readers scroll past it. Those 10.0 hours belong to one technician, and the reason they have no home is a six row table that you typed yourself.

Route B depends on two small tables. Here they are in full, because you should see how little stands behind a number that appears on a manpower page every month.

Built CrewCodeMap is a table you typed. The roster system issues crew codes and knows nothing about service lines. The HMCC board knows service lines and nothing about crews. Somebody has to join the two vocabularies, and at Meridian that somebody is the analyst. Building a dimension your source does not contain is a normal move, covered in Chapter 3. What makes this one dangerous is that it has no owner and no test, while everything downstream looks as solid as any other column in the model.

Two problems are already sitting in these seven and six rows.

  • CRW-XX9 is missing from the map. TECH-07 belongs to it and booked 10.0 hours to WO-1004, so those hours land in a blank service line on every route B visual. That is the unlabelled bar from the top of this section. Route B still totals 62.0, and a sixth of the quarter sits in a bucket with no name.
  • CRW-LT2 is in the map and nobody is on it. Light Maintenance B has no technician assigned, so it is a mapping row with no facts. Harmless, until somebody sees it on a slicer, selects it, gets an empty page, and asks whether the report is broken.

The first problem is the one to fear. It is silent, it grows, and because you own the map, nobody else in the building will fix it. Write the check yourself and let it tell you before the business does.

MCrew codes assigned but not mapped
let
    Source = CrewAssignment,
    Anti = Table.NestedJoin (
        Source, {"CrewCode"},
        CrewCodeMap, {"CrewCode"},
        "MapRows", JoinKind.LeftAnti
    ),
    Kept = Table.SelectColumns ( Anti, {"TechnicianID", "CrewCode"} )
in
    Kept
Line 2
Start from the roster side, because the roster is the list that grows. A new crew code appears there first and reaches your map only when somebody tells you.
Lines 3 to 7
Table.NestedJoin with JoinKind.LeftAnti keeps the rows on the left that found no match on the right. This is the step the Merge dialog writes when you pick Left Anti, and it is worth reading in the formula bar so you recognise it later. The alternative, Table.SelectRows with List.Contains, gives the same answer and scans the map list once per row, which is fine at six rows and painful at six thousand.
Line 8
Keep the technician as well as the code. A code on its own tells you something is missing. A code with a name attached tells you who to ask.
Result today
One row. TECH-07 on CRW-XX9. Load it as its own small table and put it on a data quality page as a table visual with a card showing the row count.

Run the same join with the sides swapped and you get the opposite problem, crew codes you have mapped that nobody is on, which today returns CRW-LT2. That one is a tidiness issue, so a quarterly review is enough.

The Power Query check runs at refresh. You also want a number on the page saying how much of the business is parked in the blank, because a count of codes does not tell anybody whether it matters. One unmapped code covering a technician who books nothing is a note. One covering ten hours a month is a hole in the manpower report.

DAXUnmapped crew codes, and the hours sitting behind them
Unmapped Crew Codes =
    VAR Assigned = ALL ( CrewAssignment[CrewCode] )
    VAR Mapped = ALL ( CrewCodeMap[CrewCode] )
    VAR Missing = EXCEPT ( Assigned, Mapped )
    RETURN
        CONCATENATEX ( Missing, CrewAssignment[CrewCode], ", " )

Hours on Unmapped Crews =
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ),
        FILTER (
            ALL ( DimTechnician[OwningServiceLine] ),
            ISBLANK ( DimTechnician[OwningServiceLine] )
        )
    )
Lines 2 to 3
Both lists are taken with ALL so that no slicer on the page can hide a problem. A data quality check that respects the page filters will happily report all clear because somebody selected January.
Line 4
EXCEPT returns the rows of the first table that are absent from the second, and it keeps the lineage of the first table. That lineage is what lets the next line refer to CrewAssignment[CrewCode] by name. The same test written as FILTER with NOT CONTAINS finds the same rows and reads as a loop, so the intent hides behind two functions.
Line 6
CONCATENATEX turns the resulting table into a readable string for a card, so the page says CRW-XX9 instead of 1. COUNTROWS over the same variable is what gives you that 1. A count tells you something is wrong. A name tells you what to do about it.
Lines 8 to 15
The hours behind the gap. The filter keeps only the technicians whose owning service line came back blank from the map, which today is TECH-07 alone, and returns 10.0 hours. That is the unlabelled bar, now with a number and a name attached to it.
Why this and not that

ALL here, after arguing for REMOVEFILTERS two pages ago, and the difference is the point. REMOVEFILTERS is a CALCULATE modifier and cannot be used as a table expression, so it cannot feed EXCEPT or FILTER. When you need a table of every distinct value, ALL returns one. When you need to clear a filter inside CALCULATE, REMOVEFILTERS says so more clearly. Same clearing behaviour, two jobs. On the second measure, use FILTER with an explicit ALL over the one column, because ISBLANK inside a boolean filter argument is legal and reads ambiguously, and because ALL over the whole table would throw away a genuine filter on employee type or home station.

Where to keep a mapping, and how to give it an owner

  1. Keep it outside the report file. Pasting the six rows in with Enter Data feels quick and makes you the only person who can change them, with no record of what changed or when. A versioned CSV in a controlled folder, or a small list on the team's document site, costs an hour to set up.
  2. Give the file two extra columns that nobody uses in the model: who last changed the row, and the date they changed it. When a number moves eight months from now, those two columns are the only account of why.
  3. Name a real owner in a real role, which for crew codes is the resource scheduler who issues them. Ask for one thing only: tell me when you open a new crew code. That request is small enough to be agreed and specific enough to be kept. Send them the mapping once a quarter and ask them to confirm it in writing.
  4. Put the unmapped check on a data quality page, count and hours side by side. It should read zero and 0.0 nearly every day, and boring is the objective. Set a recurring note so somebody looks even in the weeks nobody opens the page, because a check that only fires when you happen to look is not a check.
Rule of thumb

If you are the only person who can change a table, then you are the system that produces it, and every rule in this chapter applies to you. Write down what your table means, when you cut it off, and who signs it. Do it now, while it has six rows, because the version with sixty rows will be inherited by somebody who has never met you.

What changes when the source system changes

The shop signs a new maintenance system and the cutover is eight weeks away. In the project meeting somebody asks whether your reports will be affected. The honest answer is that one small table you typed yourself will decide it, and the room will want to know why.

Shops replace their maintenance systems. It happens after a merger, when a contract ends, or when somebody finally wins the argument about the ageing platform. Three things then tend to happen to your data, and all three attack a hand maintained mapping.

Identifiers get reissued, so the tidy prefixed codes you built a map around become historic. Code lists get renumbered, so what was crew CRW-LT1 becomes crew 4102 and the two lists have no character in common. Vocabularies get consolidated, so two service line names collapse into one, and nobody thinks to mention it because to the operational teams it was a naming exercise.

Your map, keyed on the old codes, does not error. It stops matching. Every row falls into the blank, the totals still add to 62.0, and route B reports zero hours for every named service line while route A carries on looking normal. That is the failure mode to plan for.

The defence has two parts, and both of them have to be in place before the cutover.

  • Key the mapping on something the migration preserves, where you have the choice. A code the new system will reissue is a poor key. A stable identifier both systems carry, such as an employee number or a cost centre finance also uses, is a better one. You will not always get the choice, and when you do not, say so in the design review so the risk belongs to the project as well as to you.
  • Build the unmapped check before the cutover. On the first refresh against the new system, the count of unmapped codes tells you within seconds whether your mapping survived. Built afterwards, the same check tells you the same thing three weeks later, after the first monthly pack has already gone out with a service line breakdown that was quietly empty.

So your answer in the project meeting is one sentence long. CrewCodeMap is keyed on crew codes the new system will reissue, the check that proves whether it survived takes an afternoon to build, and it has to exist before cutover weekend.

Interview-level insight

A good answer to "how would you handle a system migration" starts with a list of the objects in your solution that have no owner and no test, because those are the ones that fail silently. In this model that list has one entry, CrewCodeMap, and being able to name it in ten seconds says more about how you work than any amount of DAX.

Back to the whiteboard

You now have something to say to the supervisor, and it does not start with the word wrong. His 27.0 is what his department submitted on the last day of January, and it is the figure central planning consolidated. Your 26.0 is what the timesheet holds today, after a booking was corrected in February. One hour, one correction, two moments.

The fix takes an afternoon. Label the dashboard card Achieved Hours (Timesheet), add a second card called Achieved Hours (Submitted), and put Submission Variance beside them so the 1.0 hour is on the page instead of in a corridor. Agree with him which one the monthly pack uses, write that decision into the measure description, and put his name on the agreement. When the same thing happens in April, nobody has to work it out again.

What to remember
  • Five functions hand the work down a chain: the CAMO decides what is due, production planning sets the available hours, resource scheduling converts hours into rostered people, production control revises the forecast, and production books the achieved hours. At month end each department submits its own figure to central planning.
  • Every number has exactly one owning function. Use the table owned by the function that owns the question, and work backwards from the question. Working forwards from the tables is how you end up with a plausible wrong number.
  • Heavy maintenance booked 26.0 hours in January according to the timesheet and 27.0 according to the departmental submission. A booking was corrected after the cutoff. Both figures are correct, and the difference of 1.0 hour belongs on the page as a measure.
  • Hours by service line have two routes. Through the work order gives Heavy 38.0, Light 9.0, Line 5.0, Cabin and IFE 10.0. Through the technician's crew gives Heavy 28.5, Cabin and IFE 10.5, Line 13.0, Light 0.0 and 10.0 unmapped. Both total 62.0. TECH-04 sits on the cabin crew and booked 10.5 hours to heavy work orders.
  • Name the two routes for the question they answer, Hours by Work Type and Hours by Owning Crew, and never let either be shortened to Heavy hours.
  • CrewCodeMap has no system behind it and no owner but you, which makes it the most fragile object in the model. Ship the unmapped check with it, keep it in a versioned file outside the report, and get the resource scheduler to confirm it in writing.
  • When the source system changes, codes get reissued and a hand maintained map stops matching without erroring. Key it on something the migration preserves, and have the unmapped check running before the cutover.
Part 1 . Reading the data

00The shop, the six tables, and how to read this document

By the end of this chapter you will know the six extracts that every later chapter works from, what is broken inside each of them, and how the rest of the manual is arranged. Nothing is repaired here: this is the raw material, printed in full so you can check every claim made later against the actual rows.

The finance manager wants one number. What did Meridian quote in the first quarter? You build a card and it reads 38,100 dollars. She likes that number, so she asks to see it split by station, and the three station bars come back adding to 36,100. Now you have to explain where 2,000 dollars went.

That gap is what this manual is about. It is a working guide to turning raw extracts into a model whose measures still return the right number when somebody clicks three slicers at once. A slicer is the filter control a user clicks on the report page, and clicking one is where most models start telling lies. A measure that is correct on an empty canvas and wrong under a station slicer is not a formula problem, it is a model problem, and rewriting the formula will not fix it. The 2,000 dollars never left the model. It just has nowhere to sit.

You already know the Power BI interface. You know where Model view is, and you have shipped reports that people use. The gap this document fills sits one layer underneath. What does a relationship actually do to a query? Why does a filter reach one table and stop before the next one? Why does a total that used to reconcile stop reconciling the week somebody adds a slicer to page two? Power BI will let you build a model that returns a plausible wrong number with no error and no warning. Nobody in the meeting catches it either, because the number looks about right. That is the failure mode this manual is written against.

The emphasis is on mechanism throughout. When a chapter tells you to do something, it also says what the engine does with it and what the obvious alternative would have done instead.

How to use this document

Part 0 sits in front of this chapter and is not about Power BI at all. Chapters A and B describe how a maintenance shop runs and what its three manhour numbers mean, because a modelling decision you cannot state in the shop's own words is a decision you cannot defend when somebody from production control disagrees with it.

Parts 1 to 4 are the spine and are written to be read in order. Part 1 teaches you to read an extract and say what its grain is and what its keys are. The grain of a table is what one row of it means, written out as a sentence: one technician booking time to one work order on one day, for example. Part 2 is Power Query, the load and transform step that runs before any data reaches the model. It covers deciding where a transformation belongs and shaping a source without hiding what you did to it. Part 3 is relationships and how a filter travels along them. Part 4 is evaluation context and the DAX that depends on it. Each part assumes the one before it, so skipping ahead to the bridge table chapter without the grain chapter will cost you more time than it saves.

Part 5 collects the hard modelling cases: role playing dates, many to many, virtual relationships, grain mismatch, cross-filtering slicers. Those chapters are full treatments, and you will want them in order too. Part 6 is diagnosis and reference. You go there when a report is already wrong and you have to find out why. It ends with a cheat sheet you will open more often than anything else in this document. Appendix C is a vocabulary list, and that one really is for looking things up.

Every number printed in this document can be reproduced by hand. The six source tables hold 8, 8, 7, 6, 6 and 7 rows, which is 42 rows in total, and none of them is larger than eight rows. That is deliberate. If a chapter claims that a measure returns 52.0 rather than 62.0 under a particular model, you can count the rows yourself in about a minute and see whether it is true. Do that at least a few times. Checking a total against the source by hand is most of what separates an analyst who trusts a model from one who hopes.

Meridian Aero Services

Meridian Aero Services is an independent MRO shop: maintenance, repair and overhaul sold to airlines and charter operators who do not carry the capability in house. It runs three working stations: MSP in Minneapolis, TUS in Tucson and LAS in Las Vegas. A fourth station code, PHX for Phoenix, exists only in the planning workbook and carries no work at all in this quarter. The period is Q1 2025, the first of January to the thirty first of March, and the currency is US dollars. Work arrives in three shapes. Scheduled inputs are planned and booked in advance. AOG call-outs are unplanned. AOG stands for aircraft on ground: the aircraft cannot fly, and what the job involves is known only once the defect has been reported. Mods are modifications or upgrades.

The six tables as they arrive

What follows is every row of every extract, unmodified. Read them once now. You will come back to them constantly, and it is worth knowing roughly what is in each one before the modelling starts.

This comes from the shop floor system. One row is one work order, which is the piece of paper a job is opened against. QuotedAmount is what the customer was told before any work started. What the job actually cost lands in two other extracts, as labor hours and as parts issues. Three date columns describe the same work order from three angles: opened, promised back to the customer, closed. Two rows have no ClosedDate because those jobs were still open on the thirty first of March. Quoted amounts sum to 38,100.

This is the timesheet export. One row is one technician booking time to one work order on one day. A single work order collects several rows, and one technician turns up on several jobs. Hours multiplied by HourlyRate gives the labor cost of that line. Total hours booked in the quarter come to 62.0. Note what is not here: no station, no aircraft, no job type. If you want labor hours by station, the station has to travel in from the work order. That is a modelling decision you make yourself, and no column in this extract makes it for you.

Rule of thumb

A key is the column two tables are joined on, such as ACREG, the aircraft registration. Before you draw a single relationship, count the distinct values on both sides of the intended key. Compare both counts against the count of their union. If the union is larger than the dimension side, you have keys in the fact that the dimension has never heard of. Decide where those rows go before somebody in a meeting asks why the total moved. Do it now on aircraft registration: WorkOrders holds 5 distinct tails, AircraftRegistry holds 6, and the union of the two is 7. Seven is larger than six, so the aircraft dimension is already known to be short of a member, and you have not built anything yet. It takes two minutes on any extract.

Stores logs one row every time a part leaves the cage against a job. Quantity multiplied by unit cost gives the value of the line. The seven lines sum to 28,245 dollars. Two structural facts matter more than any single row here. There is no aircraft registration column, so parts cost by aircraft is only reachable through the work order. Nor is there a part master. Part attributes have to be recovered from the part number itself, where the prefixes BRK, HYD, ENG and AVI carry category information that nobody bothered to store properly.

Six people from the human resources system. HomeStation is where the technician is based. The work they booked can easily have been done at another station, and that gap becomes a modelling trap later. EmployeeType separates staff from contract labor. Certifications is the column to watch. It holds a variable number of values in one cell, separated by a semicolon and a space, and D. Sandoval holds three. A person can hold several certifications, and a certification is held by several people. That shape has a name, many to many, and it has a cost. It is why one of the later chapters exists.

A spreadsheet, maintained by hand at the customer service desk, and everyone at Meridian knows it lags reality. It is still the only place the aircraft attributes live, so it cannot be discarded. Six tails are listed. The work orders reference five tails, four of which appear here, so the two lists overlap without either one containing the other. N120CE and N553KD did no work at Meridian in Q1, which is normal and is not an error.

Common mistake

Treating a file as the master list because somebody called it the registry. This file describes aircraft. It has one row per tail, and it will be the aircraft dimension in the finished model, so the assumption that it holds every tail Meridian touches costs nothing to make and everything to get wrong. It is a spreadsheet the customer service desk types into, and the work orders reference a tail it has never heard of. The pattern generalises. An MRO does not decide what maintenance is due, the operator does. The keys arriving on a work order were minted in somebody else's system, so no list held at the shop is guaranteed to be complete. Check the key coverage before you promote a file to a dimension, not after a report has shipped.

Planning publishes this workbook monthly. It states how many hours of each trade the shop expects to have available at each station in each month. The four trade columns total 80, 44, 39 and 13 reading left to right. Add those four: 80 plus 44 plus 39 plus 13 is 176 planned hours for the quarter. Do not read 14 as fourteen people or fourteen shifts. The figures here are kept small so that every utilisation percentage in this document divides cleanly. In a real shop that cell would hold headcount multiplied by shift hours multiplied by an availability factor, and the availability factor is what strips out holiday, sickness, training and indirect time. Three things about the shape of this table will matter. Airframe, Avionics, Engine and NDT are stored as column headers, when each of the four is a value that belongs in a trade column. A row is a station and a month, with no work order and no day. And the station list here disagrees with the station list in the work orders: PHX appears, LAS has no January or February row, TUS has no March row.

The colour language used in every diagram

The planner sends you a screenshot of somebody else's model and asks whether it looks right. There are eleven boxes on it and no legend. Before you can answer that, you have to sort eleven boxes into the small number of roles a table can play inside a model. This section hands you the four buckets and the colours this document uses for them.

From the next chapter onwards, every table in every diagram carries one of four tags. The colours stay the same all the way through the document. Once you have the four, you can read any diagram here without a legend, and you can sort that screenshot in seconds. The tags describe the role a table plays inside a model, not where it came from.

Fact
Terracotta. Rows recording things that happened, at one stated grain, holding the numbers you add up.
Dimension
Teal. One row per real world thing, holding the labels you slice, group and filter by.
Bridge
Olive. One row per valid pair, used where the link between two tables is many to many. Olive carries a second job in the diagrams: it also marks a table of planning estimates. A planned or forecast hour is somebody's opinion about the future, and nothing has happened yet for it to record.
Built
Teal with a dashed edge. A table that exists in no source system and is assembled in Power Query.

Take the dashed edge on a built table seriously. A dashed table is one that you own. If it is wrong, nobody upstream will fix it for you, and nobody upstream will tell you when the assumption behind it stops holding.

What is deliberately wrong in this data

Nine problems were planted in the six extracts. Every one of them has happened in a real extract on a real Tuesday. None of them is exotic. Each is repaired in a named chapter later in this document, and none of them is repaired here, because the point of Part 1 is to be able to see a problem before you know its fix.

The finance manager's missing 2,000 dollars is the first of the nine, and Table 0.1 has been showing it to you all along. WO-1005 is an AOG job quoted at 2,000 dollars with a blank StationCode. Split the quoted total by station and that row belongs to no bar, so the bars add to 36,100 while the card still says 38,100. Nothing is broken. The station is simply missing, and until you decide where that row goes, every station split in this model runs 2,000 dollars short.

  1. WorkOrders row WO-1005 has a blank StationCode, so an AOG job worth 2,000 dollars belongs to no station until you decide where to put it, and this is repaired in the chapter on the unknown member.
  2. WorkOrders rows WO-1004 and WO-1008 have a blank ClosedDate because both jobs were still open at the end of the quarter, which is correct data that breaks any measure written as if every job has closed, and it is handled in the chapter on counting open and closed work.
  3. WorkOrders row WO-1006 carries tail N338WA, which appears nowhere in AircraftRegistry. That makes it an orphan foreign key. A foreign key is a column holding the identifier of a row in another table, and an orphan is one whose row is not there. This one quietly parks 12.0 labor hours outside every aircraft grouping, and it is repaired in the chapter on building a dimension from incomplete key lists.
  4. WorkOrders carries three date columns, OpenedDate, PromisedDate and ClosedDate, and only one of them can drive a relationship at a time, which is the subject of the chapter on role playing dimensions.
  5. LaborEntries row L-505 stores the technician key as TECH-04 followed by a trailing space, which looks identical to TECH-04 in every visual and matches nothing on a join, and it is repaired in the chapter on key hygiene in Power Query.
  6. LaborEntries row L-506 books 10.0 hours to TECH-07, who is genuinely absent from the Technicians extract, and it is handled in the chapter on orphan keys and the blank row.
  7. PartsIssued row P-9007 charges 4,900 dollars of hydraulics to WO-1009, a work order that does not exist in WorkOrders, and it is handled in the same chapter on orphan keys because the header side of a header to line join fails exactly like a dimension side does.
  8. Technicians row TECH-04 holds three certifications in one cell separated by semicolons, with TECH-01 and TECH-03 holding two each, and this becomes the many to many relationship covered in the chapter on bridge tables.
  9. ShopCapacity stores its four trades as column headers, and it sits at station and month grain with no day and no work order. Its row PHX 2025-03 is the only appearance of PHX anywhere in the six extracts. All of that is dealt with in the chapter on unpivoting and grain mismatch.

Two further things are missing from the extract: an aircraft registration column on PartsIssued, and a part master anywhere at all. Both are shape problems. You fix a shape problem by building a new table, and cleaning the existing ones will not help, because there is nothing dirty in them to clean.

Interview-level insight

Nothing in these six extracts announces what it is. Fact and dimension are roles a table plays inside one particular model, not properties the table carries out of the source system. WorkOrders will end up serving as the measured event table for turn time and quoting. At the same time it is the header that labor and parts lines hang from. Same eight rows, two jobs. Candidates who answer "a fact table is the big one and a dimension is the small one" have memorised a symptom. The next chapter does the classification properly, and it does it by asking what each table records and at what grain, not by counting rows.

How to follow along

Build the six tables in Power BI Desktop before you read Part 2. There are two routes. The first is Enter Data: you paste each table from this page into the grid and load it. That is quicker, and it works for five of the six. LaborEntries is the exception. The exercise there depends on row L-505 keeping its trailing space, and clipboard paths have a habit of trimming whitespace on the way through. I have seen that space survive a paste and I have seen it vanish, and I will not claim to know which happens in your build of Desktop. What is certain is that the second query below writes that space as an explicit character, so it cannot be lost. If you do use Enter Data, check L-505 afterwards with a column that returns the text length of the key: 8 for that row, 7 for every other technician key.

MWorkOrders as a blank query
let
    Cols = type table [
        WorkOrderID   = text,
        ACREG    = text,
        StationCode   = nullable text,
        WOType        = text,
        OpenedDate    = date,
        PromisedDate  = date,
        ClosedDate    = nullable date,
        QuotedAmount  = number
    ],
    Rows = {
        {"WO-1001","N771QR","MSP","Scheduled",
         #date(2025,1,6), #date(2025,1,17), #date(2025,1,16), 3000},
        {"WO-1002","N448LM","MSP","AOG",
         #date(2025,1,8), #date(2025,1,10), #date(2025,1,13), 3200},
        {"WO-1003","N902TT","TUS","Scheduled",
         #date(2025,1,14), #date(2025,2,7), #date(2025,2,5), 12500},
        {"WO-1004","N771QR","TUS","Mod",
         #date(2025,2,3), #date(2025,2,21), null, 4000},
        {"WO-1005","N615RB",null,"AOG",
         #date(2025,2,10), #date(2025,2,12), #date(2025,2,12), 2000},
        {"WO-1006","N338WA","MSP","Scheduled",
         #date(2025,2,17), #date(2025,3,14), #date(2025,3,19), 7500},
        {"WO-1007","N902TT","LAS","AOG",
         #date(2025,3,3), #date(2025,3,5), #date(2025,3,6), 900},
        {"WO-1008","N771QR","MSP","Scheduled",
         #date(2025,3,10), #date(2025,3,28), null, 5000}
    },
    Source = #table(Cols, Rows)
in
    Source
Lines 2 to 11
The column types are declared once, in one visible place, before any data appears. StationCode and ClosedDate are declared nullable because two rows genuinely have no value. Declaring them as plain text and date would be a statement you know to be false, and a later step that assumes non-null would fail somewhere less obvious than here.
Lines 13 to 28
The eight rows in source order, two lines each, values only. Nothing is corrected on the way in. WO-1006 keeps N338WA and the blanks stay blank, because the whole document depends on loading the extract as it actually arrived.
Lines 20, 21 and 28
These are the three places a null appears: the missing ClosedDate on WO-1004, the missing StationCode on WO-1005, and the missing ClosedDate on WO-1008. A null is the absence of a value, and it behaves like an absence everywhere downstream. An empty string is a different animal. It is a value, it will take its own row in a slicer, and it will slip past a check written to look for missing data. Write WO-1005 with an empty string and the station stops looking missing at all.
Line 30
The type and the row lists are combined into a typed table in a single step, so the query has no untyped intermediate state that a later step could mistype.
Why this and not that

#table and not Table.FromRecords. Table.FromRecords wants a record per row, so you write all eight field names eight times over before you have read a single value. The row you care about ends up buried in field names you already know. Both functions accept a table type, so typing comes out the same either way. Readability is what separates them. #table takes the type once and the values as plain lists, so the shape of the table is stated in one place you can read. Enter Data is the third option. It loads the same rows, and it stores them as a compressed binary string inside the query, so the rows stop being readable the moment you open the Advanced Editor. #date and not the text "2025-01-06". A text date is parsed against a locale, so the same file loaded on a machine set to a different regional format can produce a different date or an error. #date takes three integers and has no locale to get wrong.

The other five tables take the same shape and I will not print all of them. One of the five earns the space: LaborEntries, because it is the table where a copy and paste can silently repair the defect you are supposed to study.

MLaborEntries as a blank query
let
    Cols = type table [
        LaborID      = text,
        WorkOrderID  = text,
        TechnicianID = text,
        WorkDate     = date,
        Hours        = number,
        HourlyRate   = number
    ],
    // the planted defect, written so it cannot be lost
    Space = Character.FromNumber(32),
    Rows = {
        {"L-501","WO-1001","TECH-02",
         #date(2025,1,7), 7.5, 95},
        {"L-502","WO-1001","TECH-04",
         #date(2025,1,9), 6.0, 110},
        {"L-503","WO-1002","TECH-02",
         #date(2025,1,9), 9.0, 95},
        {"L-504","WO-1003","TECH-05",
         #date(2025,1,20), 8.0, 88},
        {"L-505","WO-1003","TECH-04" & Space,
         #date(2025,1,22), 4.5, 110},
        {"L-506","WO-1004","TECH-07",
         #date(2025,2,5), 10.0, 102},
        {"L-507","WO-1006","TECH-01",
         #date(2025,2,19), 12.0, 120},
        {"L-508","WO-1007","TECH-05",
         #date(2025,3,4), 5.0, 88}
    },
    Source = #table(Cols, Rows)
in
    Source
Lines 10 and 11
The trailing space is defined once, by character code, and given a name. Character.FromNumber(32) and not the literal "TECH-04 ". A space sitting between the 4 and the closing quote is invisible on this page, invisible in the Advanced Editor, and the first editor or chat window that trims trailing whitespace will delete it without telling you. A character code cannot be trimmed by accident, and it also documents the defect for whoever reads the query next.
Lines 13 to 28
All eight timesheet rows, in source order, two lines each. Nothing is trimmed and nothing is joined. The trim belongs in a later chapter, and if you apply it now the key hygiene exercise has nothing left to find.
Line 21
L-505 is the only row whose technician key is assembled from two pieces. Every other row carries a plain literal, which is exactly the asymmetry the source extract has.
Line 30
The same single-step assembly as the WorkOrders query. Hours and HourlyRate are typed as numbers here, not text. Typed as text, 7.5 plus 6.0 would concatenate, and the first total you write on that column would fail. Typed as numbers it gives 13.5.

Eight rows is enough to reproduce every behaviour in this document, because the engine does not change what it does as data grows, only how long it takes. A relationship propagates a filter the same way over eight rows and over eighty million. The exceptions are limits on volume, not changes in logic. Some visuals cap the number of rows they will return. DirectQuery, the mode where Power BI leaves the data in the source system and sends a query out for every visual, changes what is possible at all.

That cuts the other way, and it is worth being blunt. Nothing you verify on 42 rows tells you whether your real model will be fast. Cardinality, compression, the cost of a bidirectional filter over a wide dimension: those are volume problems, and none of them can be demonstrated here. The performance notes in this document are advice, not measurements. When speed is the question, measure it on your own data at your own row counts.

Nine tables in the extract, six of them in this chapter

Meridian does not send six files. It sends nine. You have already met the other three in Chapter B: HMCCSchedule, HeavyPreInput and ManhourForecast, which between them carry the heavy maintenance planning numbers. HMCC stands for Heavy Maintenance Control Centre, the function that owns the heavy check schedule and decides which aircraft sits in which bay and when. Treat those four letters with more caution than you would treat AOG, aircraft on ground, which means the same thing in every hangar in the world. HMCC does not. Other shops call the identical function production control, maintenance control, or the base maintenance control centre, and the line maintenance equivalent is usually MOC, Maintenance Operations Control. The function exists wherever you work. The acronym travels badly.

The six printed above are the ones the modelling curriculum is built on, and the reason is that they already hold every structural problem you need to learn on. A blank key. An orphan foreign key on the dimension side, and a second one on the header side of a header to line join. One table wearing three date columns. A key with a trailing space that no visual will ever show you, a cell holding a variable number of values, and a table storing its trades as column headers at a grain nothing else in the model shares. The planning three do raise questions of their own, including a one to one relationship and a forecast table that must never be summed. Each of those is a question about what to do with a table you have already classified. Put all nine in front of you before you can look at an extract and say what its grain is, and the extra three are noise. Learn to classify first. Then the planning tables have somewhere to land.

What those three add is the vocabulary you use every day and the numbers underneath it. HeavyPreInput is the heavy pre-input pack. One row is one work order and one trade, and it holds the available hours: what the planner said the job should take. Those hours are fixed at induction, so performance has something stable to be measured against. ManhourForecast holds the projected hours, the current best estimate of the final total, revised as findings land, one row per revision, each revision replacing the one before it rather than adding to it. Achieved hours are the timesheet, which you have already read as Table 0.2. Across the quarter the three totals are 57.0 available, 63.5 projected and 62.0 achieved, although only 48.0 of those achieved hours sit on work orders that had a plan at all. Add the forecast rows together instead and you get 99.5, which is not a manhour figure at all, and Chapter B is where that number gets taken apart.

One consequence of the split is inconvenient enough to say out loud. The counts in this chapter, six extracts and 42 rows, describe what this chapter prints and not what the shop sends. Load Chapter B as well and your file holds nine queries, and 42 stops being the size of the whole model. The reading order is also the reverse of the working order. Pre-input planning happens weeks before the aircraft is towed into the bay, and the bay date is the one WorkOrders records as OpenedDate. So the planned hours in HeavyPreInput were written before the row you would naturally call the start of the job. Teaching order and business order are different things, and this document chose the first. On your own extract nobody hands you a curated six. You get the folder on day one. Several of the files inside it are maintained by hand in a spreadsheet, and those are reliably the ones that break the model.

What to remember
  • Six extracts, 42 rows, nothing larger than eight rows. Every number in this document can be checked by hand against Tables 0.1 to 0.6.
  • Meridian runs three real stations, MSP, TUS and LAS, and one planning-only station, PHX, that appears in ShopCapacity and nowhere else.
  • Nine problems are planted on purpose. Learn the row numbers: WO-1005, WO-1004 and WO-1008, WO-1006, the three date columns, L-505, L-506, P-9007, TECH-04, and the wide PHX row in ShopCapacity.
  • Two more issues are shape problems, not dirt: PartsIssued has no aircraft registration, and no part master exists anywhere.
  • Terracotta is a fact, teal is a dimension, olive is a bridge or a table of planning estimates, and a dashed edge means a table you built yourself and therefore own.
  • Small data proves correctness and proves nothing about speed. Keep those two questions separate for the rest of this document.
Part 1 . Reading the data

01Facts, dimensions and the grain test

After this chapter you can look at any table in the Meridian export, say in one sentence what a single row of it means, classify it as a fact or a dimension, and name which of the three fact patterns it follows. You will also be able to test that claim against the rows instead of trusting your reading of the column names.

The production controller wants to know how many work orders Meridian closed in February. You drop a count of work orders onto a card, filter the page to February, and it reads 3. He shakes his head and says 2, and he is looking at his own whiteboard while he says it. You are both right. The reason is sitting in three columns of one table, and it takes this whole chapter to say properly.

Almost every decision you make later in this model (relationship direction, measure design, refresh strategy) inherits from two judgements you make in the first ten minutes. What is each table? What does one row of it mean? Get either wrong and the model still loads. It still refreshes. It just answers questions incorrectly, quietly, in a way that survives review because the totals look plausible.

Meridian Aero Services hands you six tables covering Q1 2025. WorkOrders has 8 rows, LaborEntries 8, PartsIssued 7, Technicians 6, AircraftRegistry 6, ShopCapacity 7. That is 8 plus 8 plus 7 plus 6 plus 6 plus 7, which is 42 rows in total. Small enough to check by hand, which is the only reason this chapter can prove its claims. On a real extract you will not have that luxury, and that is why the tests below matter.

What a fact table actually is

The shift supervisor asks what the shop is charging out per hour. LaborEntries[HourlyRate] is sitting right there in the extract, so you drop it on a card. The card reads 808. He asks whether that is dollars, and you have to tell him you do not know what it is. Hold on to 808. It comes back at the end of this section.

A fact table records measurements of events. Something happened at a point in time, somebody wrote down how much of it happened, and that record is one row. A fact table earns the name from that one property: the row is a measurement. The name on the table and the system it came out of tell you nothing.

Four consequences follow, and all four are diagnostic. Fact tables grow as time passes, because time keeps producing events. They are narrow and deep: mostly foreign keys pointing outward, plus a small set of numeric columns. A foreign key is a column holding the identifier of a row in another table, and LaborEntries[WorkOrderID] is one, because it names a row over in WorkOrders. Their text is thin, since the description lives in the dimensions those keys point to. And their numeric columns fall into three additivity classes that you must be able to tell apart.

Additive columns can be summed across every dimension in the model. LaborEntries[Hours] is additive. 62.0 hours in Q1 is a real number whether you slice it by station, by technician, by month or not at all. PartsIssued[Qty] is additive too. So are the four trade columns of ShopCapacity, once they are unpivoted into a single FactCapacity[PlannedHours]. Semi-additive columns can be summed across some dimensions but not across time, and the classic case is a balance. Meridian has no genuinely semi-additive column, and saying so is more useful than inventing one. It means nobody on this model needs the closing balance pattern yet. That pattern wraps LASTDATE around the measure instead of leaving it as a plain SUM, because the right answer for a quarter is the value standing on the last day, not the three month end balances added together. Non-additive columns cannot be summed at all.

LaborEntries[HourlyRate] is the non-additive one, and the card that read 808 is worth taking apart. The eight rates are 95, 110, 95, 88, 110, 102, 120 and 88. Add them: 95 plus 110 is 205, plus 95 is 300, plus 88 is 388, plus 110 is 498, plus 102 is 600, plus 120 is 720, plus 88 is 808. The number 808 will render happily in a card visual. It means nothing at all. The blended rate the shift supervisor was asking for is total labor cost divided by total hours. That is 6,326.50 divided by 62.0, which is 102.04 dollars per hour. Hand him 102.04 and take the 808 card off the page. A ratio of two sums, never a sum of ratios.

What a dimension actually is

A dimension is the vocabulary you slice by. One row per real world thing: one aircraft, one technician, one station, one part number, one calendar date. Where a fact answers "how much", a dimension answers "which one".

Dimensions have the opposite shape to facts. They are wide and shallow, heavy on descriptive text, and their row count is bounded by the real world. Time passing adds nothing to them. AircraftRegistry has 6 rows, and it grows only when Meridian's customers acquire airframes. A quarter passing on its own would never take it to 600. Technicians has 6 rows and changes when somebody is hired, leaves, moves station or earns a certification. That is what "slowly changing" means, and it is why the phrase slowly changing dimension exists while nobody has ever said slowly changing fact.

One heuristic catches most misclassification. Every label that appears on the axis of a chart, in a slicer, or in the rows of a matrix should come from a dimension. If you find yourself putting a text column from a fact table on an axis, either that column is a degenerate dimension (covered later in this chapter, and legitimate) or you have a dimension trapped inside a fact and it needs to come out. Technicians shows the trapped case in miniature. At row level it is a clean dimension, one row per person. But Technicians[Certifications] holds "A&P; NDT" in a single cell. The row is one technician. That one column is at a finer grain than its own row, which is why it eventually becomes a bridge table with 10 rows.

A three question test you can apply to anything

Column names lie. Table names lie more. Ask the rows three questions instead.

  1. Does a row record something that happened at a point in time, or something that simply is? Events are facts. States of being are dimensions.
  2. Would you ever put a sum over a numeric column in it, or only a distinct count? Sums point to facts. Counting how many distinct members exist points to a dimension.
  3. If you double the time period covered, does the row count grow? Six months of Meridian data means roughly twice the labor rows. It means the same six technicians.

Three yes answers for facts, three no answers for dimensions, and the interesting tables are the ones that split. Question two is the one people skip, so make it concrete in DAX before you trust your instinct. A measure is a DAX formula a visual evaluates, and it returns one value for whatever that visual is currently filtered to.

DAXAdditivity probe
// question 2, written out: what does each table let you do?
Planned Hours = SUM ( FactCapacity[PlannedHours] )

Stations Planned = DISTINCTCOUNT ( FactCapacity[StationCode] )
Line 2
SUM and not SUMX. The value is already stored in a column, so there is nothing to evaluate row by row. SUMX would build an iterator over the table to read a column it could have read directly. Across all stations and months this returns 176 planned hours.
Line 4
DISTINCTCOUNT and not COUNTA. COUNTA counts non-blank values, so it would return 28, the row count of FactCapacity once ShopCapacity has been unpivoted (7 source rows times 4 trade columns), not the 4 stations that actually appear (MSP, TUS, LAS, PHX). The fact that the second measure is the only sensible one for StationCode, while the first is sensible for PlannedHours, tells you the table holds both a key and a measurement. That is a fact table.
Common mistake

ShopCapacity looks exactly like a lookup table and gets modelled as one. It is wide (four trade columns), it has only 7 rows, the leftmost column is a station code, and it came out of a planning workbook, not a transaction system. Every surface signal says dimension. Apply the test and it collapses. ShopCapacity[Airframe] and its three siblings are hours. Sum them across stations and months and you get 176, a number the shop actually uses. Feed the table another month of planning and it gains rows. It is a fact table whose columns were laid out for a human to read. Model it as a dimension and you cannot compare planned hours against the 62.0 actual labor hours. The denominator of your utilisation measure ends up on the wrong side of the model.

Grain is a sentence, and you write it first

The shift supervisor is reading a labor listing over your shoulder and stops you. TECH-02 appears twice, he says, so the timesheet has double counted the man. He is wrong, and you need one sentence to show him why. That sentence is the grain of the table, and writing it comes before everything else in this chapter.

The grain of a table is the business meaning of one row, stated as a sentence in plain language. It is a sentence, with a subject and enough qualifiers that a shop supervisor would recognise it as true. A list of key columns is a different thing, and it will not settle an argument on the shop floor.

One row of LaborEntries is one technician booking time to one work order on one day. Hand that sentence to the supervisor and the argument is over. TECH-02 sits on L-501 and on L-503, which are two different work orders on two different days, so both rows are real and neither is a duplicate. That sentence is the whole contract. It tells you that hours can be summed, that the same technician can appear many times, that a work order can accumulate hours across days, and that if you ever see two rows with the same technician, work order and date, something upstream has broken or your sentence was wrong. It also tells you what the table cannot answer: it holds no start and end clock times, so you cannot ask when in the day the work happened.

Grain
The business meaning of one row, stated as a sentence, before any keys are named.
Candidate key
The smallest set of columns whose combination is unique across every row, used to check a grain claim against the data.
Grain mismatch
Two tables in the same model whose rows describe periods or events of different sizes, so a relationship between them can only be built at the coarser of the two.

Read the ShopCapacity sentence again, because it is the only one that needed a clause about layout. Its row grain is station plus month, but its value grain is station plus month plus trade, since each of the four numbers on a row means something different. Those two grains disagree, and unpivoting is the operation that reconciles them: 7 source rows times 4 trade columns gives 28 rows in Built FactCapacity, each holding exactly one measurement. A table whose row grain and value grain disagree is always a table that needs reshaping.

Rule of thumb

Write the grain sentence for every table before you draw a single relationship or write a single measure. If you cannot finish the sentence without using the word "and" to join two different things, the table has more than one grain in it and needs to be split. If you can finish it but nobody in operations recognises it, you have described the export format, and the business process is still unwritten.

Verifying a grain instead of assuming it

A grain sentence is a claim. Claims get tested. The test is the candidate key check. Identify the columns your sentence says make a row unique. Count the distinct combinations of those columns. Compare that count to the row count. Equal counts mean the data does not contradict your sentence. Unequal counts mean one of two things: your sentence is wrong, or your source is duplicating rows. You need to know which before anything else happens.

You can run this in Power Query with Group By on the candidate columns and a row count aggregation, then filter for counts above one. That is the right home for it during load, because a failure should stop the refresh. During modelling it is faster to keep a diagnostic measure on hand.

DAXLabor Grain Violations
// returns 0 when the claimed grain holds in the loaded data
Labor Grain Violations =
VAR RowsInTable = COUNTROWS ( FactLabor )
VAR DistinctKeys =
    COUNTROWS (
        SUMMARIZE (
            FactLabor,
            FactLabor[WorkOrderID],
            FactLabor[TechnicianID],
            FactLabor[WorkDate]
        )
    )
RETURN
    RowsInTable - DistinctKeys
Line 3
COUNTROWS and not COUNT. COUNT takes a column and skips blanks, so a table with blank values in the counted column would report fewer rows than it has and the check would silently pass. COUNTROWS counts rows regardless of their contents, which is the only correct denominator for a duplicate test.
Lines 4 to 12
Group the table down to its distinct key combinations and count what survives. SUMMARIZE is used here purely as a grouping function with no added columns, which is the one job it does without controversy.
Lines 13 to 14
The difference is the number of rows the grain sentence cannot account for. Put it on a card. For FactLabor it reads 0, because there are 8 rows and 8 distinct combinations of work order, technician and date.
Why this and not that

DISTINCT is the obvious first reach, and it is the wrong one here: given a column reference it returns the distinct values of a single column, and a composite key needs three columns grouped together, not three separate distinct lists. SUMMARIZECOLUMNS is the modern grouping function and is genuinely better in a query window. Inside a measure it raises an error under certain modified filter contexts. That makes it unreliable for a diagnostic you want to drop into any visual on any page. GROUPBY would also work and exists for the case where you need to iterate the groups with a nested expression, which this check does not. SUMMARIZE earns its place by being the plainest grouping available in a measure. Note the boundary of the claim: this measure tests the data currently loaded, under the current filter context. It says nothing about the source system.

Trace this by hand, row by row, and see why the composite is necessary

Take each candidate key in turn and count distinct combinations across the 8 rows of LaborEntries. Single columns fail immediately. WorkOrderID gives 6 distinct values across 8 rows, because L-501 and L-502 both book to WO-1001 (on 2025-01-07 and 2025-01-09) and L-504 and L-505 both book to WO-1003 (on 2025-01-20 and 2025-01-22). The remaining four rows sit on four separate orders: WO-1002, WO-1004, WO-1006 and WO-1007. WorkDate gives 7 distinct values, because L-502 and L-503 both fall on 2025-01-09 while working different orders. TechnicianID gives 5 distinct values after trimming, because TECH-02 appears on L-501 and L-503, TECH-04 on L-502 and L-505, and TECH-05 on L-504 and L-508.

Those overlaps are what kill every single column key. L-501 and L-502 share WO-1001 on two different dates, so the work order alone cannot identify a row. L-502 and L-503 share the date 2025-01-09 across two different orders, so the date alone cannot either. L-501 and L-503 share TECH-02 on two different days, so the technician alone cannot. One column is never enough here, which leaves the combinations.

Look at what the middle three rows are telling you. All three pairs are unique across this quarter, so the data alone would let you adopt any of them and feel verified. Adopt WorkOrderID plus TechnicianID and you have written a rule saying a technician may book to a work order once and once only. That rule is false. WO-1003 ran for 22 days, and nothing stops TECH-05 from booking to it on Monday and again on Wednesday. The sample happens not to contain that case. The business process does.

One detail worth carrying forward. L-505 stores its technician as "TECH-04 " with a trailing space, so before trimming the untrimmed column has 6 distinct values instead of 5. The trim changes the distinct count of that column but does not change the composite, because L-505 is the only labor row on WO-1003 dated 2025-01-22. A cleaning step that alters a key can break a grain. Re-run the check after cleaning, not before.

Table
LaborEntries
Rows
8
Grain
Technician, work order, day
Additive
Hours only

Now the part nobody enjoys, and it is worth stating without softening. The candidate key test can disprove a grain. It can never prove one. Uniqueness in the rows you happen to hold is evidence, not proof, and on a three month extract of 8 rows it is weak evidence. The grain sentence comes from the business process, from asking a supervisor whether a technician can book twice to the same order on the same day and what it would mean if they did. The test only confirms that today's data does not contradict what you were told. A grain you have not tested is a guess. A grain you have tested on a sample is a better guess.

Running the same test on the other five tables

Table 1.2 holds six grain sentences, which is six claims, and every one of them has to be checked. LaborEntries got the long treatment above because its grain is the only composite one in the extract, and the other five still need the same test run against their own rows. Doing that by opening six queries and clicking Group By six times is how the check stops happening by the third sprint, so write it once as a function and call it.

MfnGrainCheck
// fnGrainCheck( LaborEntries,
//   {"WorkOrderID","TechnicianID","WorkDate"} )
// returns [ Rows = 8, DistinctKeys = 8, Violations = 0 ]
let
    fnGrainCheck =
        ( Source as table, KeyColumns as list ) as record =>
        let
            RowsIn = Table.RowCount( Source ),
            KeysIn = Table.RowCount(
                Table.Distinct(
                    Table.SelectColumns( Source, KeyColumns ) ) ),
            Report = [
                Rows         = RowsIn,
                DistinctKeys = KeysIn,
                Violations   = RowsIn - KeysIn ]
        in
            Report
in
    fnGrainCheck
Lines 5 to 6
A function taking the table and the key column names, so you write the check once. The check has to be re-run after every cleaning step that touches a key, and six copies of a query are six things that drift apart the first time somebody improves one of them.
Lines 10 to 12
Table.SelectColumns first and then Table.Distinct, and not the two argument form Table.Distinct( Source, KeyColumns ). Both return the same count. Readability separates them. Projecting first makes the step you read on screen the claim you made: these columns, and nothing else, are what the grain sentence names.
Line 16
A difference, not a true or false. Zero is the pass. A non-zero number tells you how much duplication you are looking at, which is the difference between one row that arrived twice and a join upstream that fanned every row out.
Report
A record and not a table, because three numbers render in the query preview without another click. To test every table at once, call it six times inside Table.FromRecords and load the result as a small check table.
What it does not do
It reports, it does not stop anything. Replace Report with if RowsIn <> KeysIn then error "grain violated" else Report and the refresh fails instead. Do that for a dimension key, where a duplicate makes every measure over that path wrong. Think harder before doing it on a fact, because a failed refresh at 6am means the report shows yesterday, and yesterday is sometimes worse than a flagged duplicate.

Six passes. Now read that result correctly, because a column of zeroes is the easiest thing in this document to over-trust. Three of those six tables carry a key the source system generated for its own purposes, WorkOrderID, IssueID and LaborID, and a generated identifier passes a uniqueness test by construction. The pass tells you one thing only: the export delivered each row once. The question the grain sentence answers, what one row of the table actually means, sits outside the reach of that test altogether.

The four tables where the test does real work are the ones whose keys describe the business itself, not the shape of the export. PartsIssued at work order plus part number plus date says a part can be issued to the same job on more than one day. P-9003 and P-9004 prove it: ENG-8802 on 2025-01-21 and BRK-2210 on 2025-01-24, both against WO-1003. ShopCapacity at station plus month says planning publishes one figure per station per month, and the 7 rows are 7 distinct station months, MSP three times, TUS twice, LAS once, PHX once.

Then there is the other direction, which is the part that catches people. Several columns in this extract pass the uniqueness test and are not keys at all.

Five columns, five clean passes, five wrong answers. PartsIssued[IssueDate] is the one to sit with: 7 distinct dates across 7 rows, a perfect score, and adopting it would encode a rule saying stores may issue parts on at most one line per day. Nobody in stores has ever agreed to that. The test cannot see the difference between a key and a coincidence, because both look like a matching pair of counts.

Common mistake

Running the check on the identifier column and calling the grain verified. LaborID is distinct across all 8 rows, so fnGrainCheck( LaborEntries, {"LaborID"} ) returns zero violations and you have learned nothing. LaborID is a surrogate key, an identifier the source system invented for its own bookkeeping, and a surrogate key is unique because it was minted to be unique. The check earns its keep only when you feed it the columns your sentence names. If your sentence says one technician, one work order, one day, then those three columns go into the call, and the surrogate stays out of it.

One more property of ShopCapacity is worth pinning down before Part 2, because it is the case where a passing test and a correct sentence still leave you with work to do. The row grain is station plus month and it passes at 7 out of 7. The value grain is station plus month plus trade, because the four numbers on a row mean four different things. After the unpivot, Built FactCapacity holds 7 times 4, which is 28 rows, and its candidate key is StationCode plus MonthKey plus Trade: 28 distinct combinations across 28 rows. Re-run the check after any reshape, because reshaping a table is the act of changing its grain, and the number that was verified belonged to the old shape.

The same three numbers apply to the dimensions you are about to build, and there the test stops being diagnostic and becomes structural. A duplicate key on the one side of a relationship is not a warning, it is a refusal: the engine will not create the relationship at all. Chapter 3 runs this check over every table built for the Meridian model, and adds the second half of it, whether the dimension covers every key the facts actually use.

The three kinds of fact table

This is the classification that pays for itself. Facts come in three patterns, and the pattern determines how the table refreshes, which dates it needs, and what kinds of measure make sense on it. Meridian has all three, which is unusual for a dataset this size.

Transaction facts: LaborEntries and PartsIssued

One row per event, written once and then left alone. A timesheet booking happened on 2025-01-07 and that fact will never change. A part left stores on 2025-01-24 and that is settled. Transaction facts carry exactly one date and they are insert-only. That makes them cheap to refresh a slice at a time, because yesterday's rows never change. Their measures are the straightforward additive ones, 62.0 total hours and 28,245 in total parts cost.

The tell is the single date column. LaborEntries[WorkDate] and PartsIssued[IssueDate] each answer one question: when did this happen. There is no ambiguity about which date the row belongs to, which is why these two tables get a plain active relationship to the date table and nothing more complicated.

Periodic snapshot: ShopCapacity

A row exists because the calendar turned, not because anything happened. MSP has a row for January, February and March whether or not a single hour was worked. The measurement is taken at a regular interval, and it describes a period of time. No single event lies behind it.

Snapshots have a property transaction facts do not: rows can exist with nothing behind them. PHX appears in ShopCapacity for March with 8 plus 4 plus 3 plus 1, that is 16 planned hours, and PHX appears nowhere else in the entire dataset. No work orders, no technicians, no labor. Its utilisation is 0 percent of 16 hours, which is a legitimate answer. The snapshot is what makes that answer possible, because a transaction fact would simply have no row and PHX would vanish from the report.

Meridian's snapshot is also incomplete, and the distinction matters. LAS has no January or February rows and TUS has no March row. A missing row means planning published no figure at all, which is a different thing from planning zero hours. For TUS in March there is no denominator, so utilisation is undefined rather than 100 percent or zero. Any measure that divides labor hours by planned hours needs to return blank there, and not an infinity or a misleading figure. An incomplete periodic snapshot is a data quality problem that masquerades as a modelling problem. Fix it upstream if you can, and if you cannot, handle the blank denominator explicitly and tell the report consumer what a blank means.

Accumulating snapshot: WorkOrders

One row per thing that moves through a pipeline, with a column for each milestone, and the row is updated in place as the thing progresses. WorkOrders has OpenedDate, PromisedDate and ClosedDate side by side on the same row. WO-1004 opened on 2025-02-03 with a promise of 2025-02-21 and a blank close. WO-1008 opened on 2025-03-10 with a promise of 2025-03-28 and a blank close. Both rows will be rewritten, not added to, when those work orders eventually close. Six of the eight are closed, two are open.

Two consequences, and they are the reason this classification matters more than the other two.

The first is refresh. An accumulating snapshot cannot be incrementally appended, because the rows you already loaded are the rows that change. Power BI's incremental refresh partitions a table on a date range and, by default, leaves older partitions untouched. Partition WorkOrders on OpenedDate and WO-1004 lands permanently in the February partition. Close it in April and the February partition is never revisited, so your model will carry an open work order that closed months ago and your on time percentage will be wrong in a direction nobody notices. There are two escape hatches. One is a full reload of the table every cycle. The other is incremental refresh with the detect data changes option, pointed at a last-modified timestamp that the source system must actually maintain. At 8 rows you reload the table and think no more about it. At 4 million rows this is a real design conversation, and the cost is real: you either pay for the full reload every cycle or you depend on a source column you do not control.

The second consequence is that three date columns on one row force a role-playing date dimension. You cannot answer "how many work orders in February" until somebody says which February: opened, promised or closed. Those are three different questions with three different answers.

Look at how many date tables there are in that picture. One. The three lines running from it into the same fact table are the three milestone columns, and the picture prints their names beside the fact box: OpenedDate, PromisedDate, ClosedDate. Only the top line is solid, and it is the one labelled active, so that is the line the engine follows by default. The two beneath it are dashed and labelled inactive. They exist, and nothing travels down them until a measure asks for one by name. That is what the USERELATIONSHIP in the measure card underneath is doing. The other card counts the same January twice on the strength of that switch, 3 work orders by opened date against 2 by closed date. That is the shape an accumulating snapshot always produces, and it is the reason a beginner's instinct, three copies of the calendar, is the wrong answer.

Read the February column and the argument from the first page of this chapter settles itself. Three work orders opened in February. Two closed. Your card was counting openings, the production controller was counting closures at his whiteboard, and the model has to be able to answer both questions from the same eight rows.

The closed row totals 2 plus 2 plus 2, which is 6 and not 8. That is the correct answer: WO-1004 and WO-1008 have no close date to be counted under. Somebody will eventually put two of these visuals on the same page and ask why the totals disagree. The answer is that they are measuring different milestones of the same eight objects, and the model is what makes it possible to ask both questions from one date table. How that is wired, one active relationship plus two inactive ones, comes later in the course.

Performance note
