Accumulating snapshots are usually the smallest fact table in a model and the most expensive to refresh per row, because the whole table is rewritten each cycle. That trade is fine while the table is small. Watch the ratio, not the row count. If your accumulating snapshot approaches the size of your transaction facts, the pipeline it describes probably has more milestones than it needs, or you are carrying closed work orders that could be archived out of the hot table.

Degenerate dimensions: keys that stay on the fact

A degenerate dimension is a dimension key that lives on the fact table and has no attributes of its own to hang anywhere else. LaborEntries[LaborID] is the purest example in Meridian. It identifies the row, there is no descriptive information attached to it anywhere in the business, and building a DimLaborID table would produce a dimension with exactly as many rows as the fact and exactly one useful column. PartsIssued[IssueID] is the same shape.

WorkOrderID would be a degenerate dimension too, in a version of Meridian where WorkOrders did not exist. Imagine only the timesheet extract had landed. You could still group hours by work order, still see 13.5 hours on WO-1001 and 12.5 on WO-1003, still filter to one order. The identifier carries meaning on its own and belongs on the fact. What you could not do is ask which aircraft, which station or which work order type, because none of that is in the timesheet.

That is exactly the promotion rule. A degenerate dimension should be promoted when it acquires attributes. The moment somebody hands you WorkOrders, WorkOrderID has an aircraft registration, a station, a type, a quoted amount and three dates attached to it. Those attributes have to live in a table of their own. Store them on every labor row and every parts row and you are maintaining the same fact in several places at once. Keep the degenerate keys that never acquire attributes. Promote the ones that do. And keep LaborID on the fact for audit traceability, even though it will never appear in a visual. You accept a cost when you do that. A unique text column is the worst case for compression in the storage engine, because there is no repetition for the engine to exploit. At 8 rows that costs nothing measurable. At 40 million it can be the largest column in your model.

Header and line: one table doing two jobs

The finance manager asks what Meridian spent on parts for the E175 fleet in Q1. It is a fair question and you cannot answer it. Open PartsIssued and every row carries a part number, a quantity, a unit cost and a work order, with no aircraft registration anywhere on it. The answer is 12,680 dollars, and this section is about how the filter gets there.

WorkOrders is simultaneously a Fact at its own grain and the header Dimension for two other facts. Both statements are true at the same time and the model depends on both.

As a fact it has 8 rows and an additive QuotedAmount summing to 38,100. It also carries measures that only make sense at work order grain: average turn time of 12.0 days across the 6 closed orders, and on time performance of 50.0 percent. As a header, it supplies context that LaborEntries and PartsIssued do not carry. PartsIssued has no aircraft registration column at all. So the filter has to travel from DimAircraft into WorkOrders and only then down into PartsIssued, and that path is what turns the finance manager's blank visual into 12,680 for the E175 fleet.

The relationship from WorkOrders[WorkOrderID] to LaborEntries[WorkOrderID] is one to many, single direction, filtering from the header side to the line side. Mechanically it is an ordinary relationship. It is called a header to line relationship, or a fact to fact relationship, and it is legitimate for one specific reason: the header side has a genuinely unique key. Eight work orders, eight distinct WorkOrderID values. If that were not true the relationship could not be created at all, and the fix would be to go back and find the real header grain.

Follow one work order across the two grains in that picture, which shows the first three work orders and the five labor rows that hang off them. WO-1001 is a single row on the header side carrying one quoted amount of 3,000. The curved lines fan it out into two rows on the line side, 7.5 hours and 6.0 hours, and WO-1003 fans out the same way into 8.0 and 4.5. Every header attribute repeats down the fan. That is exactly why the red card, which pulls QuotedAmount down to line grain, lands on 3,000 plus 3,000 plus 3,200 plus 12,500 plus 12,500. WO-1001 and WO-1003 are each counted twice. The same card names the second error, and it runs the other way. A work order with no labor line has nothing to fan out into, so WO-1005 and WO-1008 drop out of the flattened sum entirely. The green card keeps each measure on the table that owns it, 38,100 of quoted amount from the header and 6,326.50 of labor cost from the lines. Count the rows on the header side, not the rows arriving at the line side. Parts behave the same way, though this picture does not draw them: PartsIssued fans off the same header, and P-9003 and P-9004 both hang off WO-1003.

This is the single thing analysts most often get wrong when they have read one book on star schemas. A star schema is the layout where one fact table sits in the middle and the dimensions surround it, each joined straight to the fact. The rule they remember is that facts connect only to dimensions, so they do one of two things. The first is to flatten. They copy aircraft registration, station and work order type down onto every labor row and every parts row in Power Query, and now WO-1005's blank station has to be fixed in three places instead of one. The second is to build a separate DimWorkOrder holding the same 8 rows as the fact. Then they have to decide which of the two identical tables owns QuotedAmount, and that question has no good answer. A single table serving as both fact and header is the correct model here. The goal is a correct number, and textbook purity buys you nothing on its own.

Interview-level insight

The header to line relationship filters in one direction only. Put technicians on the rows of a matrix with a measure summing WorkOrders[QuotedAmount], and every row shows 38,100. TECH-03 and TECH-06 booked no hours at all and they show 38,100 too. DimTechnician filters LaborEntries, but LaborEntries does not filter WorkOrders, so the quoted amount is never restricted. Most people meet this and reach for bidirectional cross filtering. Do not. The visual is telling you something true: a quoted amount belongs to a work order, and there is no defensible way to split 3,000 dollars of quote between the two technicians who worked WO-1001. If you need cost per technician, sum labor cost, which is measured at that grain. Knowing which measures are meaningful at which grain is most of this job.

Factless fact tables

A factless fact table records that an event or a relationship happened, with no numeric measure on the row at all. The classic case is a scheduled event. Meridian's six source tables stop short of one, so be clear about the status of what follows. This is a shape you would add to the Meridian model yourself, and the example below is built to show you the pattern.

Suppose maintenance planning gives you a list of inspections due: one row per airframe per inspection code per due date, covering the 7 aircraft registrations that end up in DimAircraft. The row itself is the fact, and counting rows is the whole measure. You count it, using COUNTROWS and not COUNT of a column, for the reason given earlier: there is no numeric column to count, and a text column would be counted only where it is non-blank.

Factless facts earn their place in two ways. They let you count scheduled events, for example how many inspections fall due in March across the Northwind Regional fleet. More usefully, they let you ask negative questions, which no other table shape supports well: which aircraft have an inspection due this month and no work order opened against them. That question needs a table of what should happen, so it can be compared against the table of what did happen. Without the factless table there is nothing for the absence to show up against.

The classification, all six tables

Four facts and two dimensions. That is the opposite of the ratio most people expect from a star schema diagram, and it is why the finished Meridian model will need built dimensions. Two source dimensions cannot supply the vocabulary for four facts. Stations, work order types, parts and dates all have to be constructed from the facts themselves, which is the subject of the next part of this course.

What to remember
  • A fact records a measurement of an event, grows as time passes, and holds mostly keys and numbers. A dimension holds one row per real world thing and grows only when the world does.
  • Three questions settle almost every case: did it happen or does it simply exist, would you ever sum a number in it, and does the row count grow when the period doubles.
  • The grain is a sentence about one row, written before any relationship or measure. One row of LaborEntries is one technician booking time to one work order on one day.
  • Test the grain with a candidate key check, comparing distinct key combinations to the row count. The test can disprove a grain but never prove one, so the sentence still has to come from the business.
  • Run that check on all six tables, not the interesting one. All six pass at the key their sentence implies, and five other columns pass by coincidence, including PartsIssued[IssueDate] at 7 distinct across 7 rows. Feeding the check a surrogate key such as LaborID proves nothing at all.
  • LaborEntries and PartsIssued are transaction facts, ShopCapacity is a periodic snapshot, WorkOrders is an accumulating snapshot. The last one must be fully reloaded, never appended to, and its three dates are what force a role-playing date dimension.
  • Degenerate dimensions like LaborID stay on the fact. Promote a key only when it acquires attributes, as WorkOrderID has.
  • WorkOrders is a fact at its own grain and the header dimension for two other facts at the same time. That dual role is normal and correct because the header key is unique. Forcing it into a textbook star costs you either duplicated data or two tables that both claim to own QuotedAmount.
Part 1 . Reading the data

02Why the star schema is the right shape

After this chapter you will be able to say, in storage terms, what a wide flat table costs Meridian. You will also be able to decide, for any dimension, whether to flatten it or split it out.

The finance manager wants one number before the quarter closes. What did Meridian quote? Your report says 46,600. Her ledger says 38,100. Nothing on the page is broken and no measure has an error in it, and the answer is still 8,500 dollars wrong. The cause is the shape of the tables underneath. This chapter shows you how to price that shape in storage terms, so you can judge the trade yourself and stop quoting a convention at people.

Most people meet the star schema as a convention. Facts in the middle, dimensions around the edge, someone senior said so. A star schema is one table of measurements, called the fact table, surrounded by the tables that describe those measurements, called dimension tables. As a convention it stops helping the moment it looks like it is costing you something, because a convention gives you no way to price the trade. Storage gives you one, so build the argument up from there.

How the engine actually stores a column

Power BI holds imported data in memory using an engine called VertiPaq. VertiPaq is a column store, which means it keeps each column as its own separate object. So the eight rows of Fact FactLabor you met in Chapter 1 live in memory as six columns. Each one is compressed on its own, in its own region of memory. The engine reassembles rows at query time, and only for the columns the query actually touched. A measure is a calculation the model performs on demand, and a measure that reads FactLabor[Hours] never pays for FactLabor[HourlyRate] sitting next to it.

Each column gets one of two encodings. Value encoding applies to integers. The engine looks for a linear transform, usually subtracting a base, that holds every value in fewer bits. FactLabor[HourlyRate] contains 88, 95, 102, 110 and 120. Subtract 88 and the range becomes 0 to 32, which fits in six bits per row. A plain integer column wants thirty-two. No dictionary is needed here, because the original value is recoverable by arithmetic.

Dictionary encoding handles everything else: text, dates, decimals, and integers where the value trick does not pay. The engine lists the distinct values, gives each an integer id, and stores the column as a list of ids. Table 2.1 does that by hand for FactWorkOrder[StationCode], after the blank on WO-1005 has been mapped to UNASSIGNED.

Four distinct values need two bits to identify. Eight rows times two bits is sixteen bits, two bytes for the whole column, plus one dictionary of four short strings. "MSP" is stored once, not four times. I assigned the ids in order of first appearance for readability; the real assignment is the engine's business, but the count of entries is exactly what you control.

On top of that sits run length encoding. The engine works in segments, and a segment is a block of roughly a million rows in an import model. Inside each segment it reorders the rows so identical values line up, then stores each run as one value and one count. A station column reading MSP two hundred thousand times becomes a single pair. There is a tension in that, and it is worth knowing about. One row order has to serve every column in the segment. An order that gives long runs for StationCode may give short runs for ACREG, and the engine picks its compromise by heuristic. You cannot direct it.

Now the consequence, which is the whole chapter in one line. The cost of a column is set by its distinct count, not by its row count. The number of distinct values in a column is called its cardinality, and that word will come back in every section below. Four distinct values across a hundred million rows is nearly free: four dictionary entries, two bits per row, enormous runs. A hundred million distinct values across a hundred million rows is close to worst case: a dictionary as large as the table, twenty-seven bits per id, no runs anywhere. Every modelling decision below is a decision about cardinality.

The flat table, and the two bills it sends you

Go back to the finance manager and her 46,600. That number came out of the obvious approach, and the obvious approach is genuinely tempting, so build it here and watch it break. Meridian has six source tables. You want hours by aircraft type, by technician and by station, so you join everything in Power Query down to one table and load that. Down to what, though? Grain is the sentence that says what one row of a table means, and the grain you pick here is one row per labor line. Eight rows in, eight rows out, no relationships to explain to anyone. Table 2.2 is that table.

The figure takes the first five of those rows and tints every cell that is a repeat. That tinting separates the harmless repetition from the fatal kind. ACREG and AircraftType repeat because WO-1001 and WO-1003 each carry two labor lines, and neither repeat costs you an answer. The same is true across the wider Table 2.2, where Cascade Air appears four times and D. Sandoval twice. QuotedAmount repeats for exactly the same reason, and there it is fatal. A number that belongs to a work order has been copied onto every labor line that work order happens to have. Sum that column down the five rows drawn and you get 34,200, with 3,000 and 12,500 each counted twice. Sum it down all eight rows of Table 2.2 and you get 46,600, against a true total of 38,100.

The first bill is storage, and here I am going to argue against the version of this you have probably read. Repeating a low-cardinality text value is cheap. That is the exact case dictionary encoding and run length encoding were built for. AircraftType has four distinct values here, and it would still have four across a hundred million rows. The real storage penalty is narrower than the folklore. It comes from high-cardinality header attributes dragged down to line grain, and from the segment sort compromise, because twenty columns force one row order that cannot suit all of them. At eight rows, flattening costs zero bytes. Say so out loud. A reader who has been told the flat table is slow, and then measures it, will stop believing you about anything else.

The second bill is correctness, and that one you have to pay in full. QuotedAmount is an attribute of the work order header, which means it has one value per work order. In Table 2.2 it has one value per labor line instead. WO-1001's 3,000 appears twice and WO-1003's 12,500 appears twice. Meanwhile WO-1005 and WO-1008 have vanished from the table entirely, because neither has a labor row to hang on.

The wrong way

Sum the header amount from the flattened table, because it is right there as a column.

DAXQuoted Total, flat
// FlatLabor is one row per labor line
Quoted Total =
    SUM ( FlatLabor[QuotedAmount] )
Line 3
SUM reads one physical column and adds every value it finds. It cannot know that two of those values are copies, because nothing in the model says so. Returns 46,600.

The usual repair is to deduplicate inside the measure.

DAXQuoted Total, patched
Quoted Total =
    SUMX (
        SUMMARIZE (
            FlatLabor,
            FlatLabor[WorkOrderID],
            FlatLabor[QuotedAmount]
        ),
        FlatLabor[QuotedAmount]
    )
Line 2
SUMX and not SUM, because SUM can only read a column that physically exists. You are adding the rows of a table built at query time, which needs an iterator.
Line 3
SUMMARIZE and not VALUES, because you need the work order key paired with its amount. VALUES returns one column, which would collapse two work orders that share an amount.
Cost
It removes the duplicates and still cannot invent WO-1005 and WO-1008. It also runs this grouping on every visual, every slicer click, forever.
The fix

Keep the header amount at header grain, in its own table, and sum it there.

DAXQuoted Total, star
Quoted Total =
    SUM ( FactWorkOrder[QuotedAmount] )
Line 2
SUM is right here precisely because the grain is right: eight rows, eight amounts, one per work order. No deduplication needed, so no iterator needed.
Result
38,100, which matches what finance quotes. WO-1005 and WO-1008 are included, because they exist whether or not anyone booked time to them.

The measure got shorter. That is the tell. When the shape matches the grain, measures stop containing corrections.

What you see in the report

A card labelled Total Quoted reads 46,600. Nobody questions it. It is roughly the right size, and it sits beside a labor hours card reading 62.0, which is correct. Three weeks later the finance manager says the quarter was 38,100 and asks why you are 8,500 high. You will not find that by staring at the visual, because the visual is doing exactly what you asked it to do.

Trace the 8,500 by hand

Flat sum, straight down the last column of Table 2.2: 3,000 plus 3,000 plus 3,200 plus 12,500 plus 12,500 plus 4,000 plus 7,500 plus 900 equals 46,600.

Reconcile that against the true total of 38,100. Remove WO-1005 at 2,000 and WO-1008 at 5,000, because neither has a labor row to carry it into the flat table. That leaves 31,100. Now add the copies back. WO-1001 sits on two labor lines, so its 3,000 counts twice, and WO-1003 sits on two lines, so its 12,500 counts twice. 31,100 plus 3,000 plus 12,500 equals 46,600. The overstatement is 8,500, which is the figure the finance manager put to you.

A left outer join from work orders to labor does not save you. WO-1005 and WO-1008 come back with blank hours, giving ten rows, and the quoted sum becomes 46,600 plus 2,000 plus 5,000, which is 53,600. You added the missing work orders back and the number got worse. That is the signature of a grain problem rather than a data problem.

Common mistake

Treating the deduplicating measure as the fix. It is a tax, and you pay it on every measure that touches a header column: quoted amount, promised date, turn time, on time percentage. Each has to be written defensively by someone who remembers why. The next person to open the file will write SUM, get 46,600, and ship it.

The star

So the finance manager gets her 38,100 as soon as the quoted amount goes back to the grain it belongs at, one row per work order. That table is the one in the middle of the picture that follows.

One Fact table sits in the centre in terracotta, FactWorkOrder at eight rows, one per work order. The four Dimension tables that describe it sit around it in teal: DimDate above, DimAircraft to the left, DimStation to the right, DimWOType below. Follow any line and count the hops. Each line carries a 1 at the dimension end and a star at the fact end, and every one of them is a single hop. That is the whole idea. A slicer is the filter control a report user clicks, and everything a slicer touches sits one relationship away from the numbers it filters. A dashed border means somebody built the table. Not one of these four arrives from a source system as a table you can simply load.

The full model runs wider than that one star. The facts are FactWorkOrder at eight rows, FactLabor at eight, FactParts at seven and FactCapacity at twenty-eight after the unpivot. Only FactWorkOrder is drawn above. Five dimensions have to be Built, because no source system hands them to you. DimAircraft is the registry appended with the tails found in the work orders, which gives N338WA a home instead of a blank row. DimStation is the union of three sources plus an UNASSIGNED member. DimTechnician gains a row for the orphan TECH-07. DimPart is derived from the fact itself, since no part master exists. DimDate is generated from a start date and an end date.

Fact tables
4
Dimension tables
7
Bridge tables
1
Deepest active path
Two hops

Here is what happens when the production controller clicks A320-200 in that slicer. The engine restricts DimAircraft to the two matching rows, N771QR and N615RB. It reads their ACREG values as a set of dictionary ids and pushes that set onto FactWorkOrder[ACREG]. Then it scans that one column once and keeps the row positions that match: WO-1001, WO-1004 and WO-1008 on N771QR, plus WO-1005 on N615RB. The surviving set propagates on to FactLabor the same way. Hours comes back as 23.5, which is WO-1001 at 13.5 plus WO-1004 at 10.0. WO-1005 and WO-1008 contribute nothing, because neither has a labor row. Nothing was widened and nothing was duplicated. The work is proportional to the number of distinct keys, not to the size of the fact.

Now the inconvenient part, and you should say it out loud in a design review. Meridian's model is a star with one extra layer in it. FactWorkOrder plays two roles at once. It is a fact, because QuotedAmount lives on it and gets summed. It is also the header dimension for FactLabor and FactParts, neither of which is drawn in the star above. That puts DimAircraft two hops from FactLabor instead of one. The chain is what makes hours by aircraft type reachable at all, since neither line table carries an aircraft registration. Two hops is the price of keeping the header amount at header grain, and it is worth paying.

What a relationship costs at query time

The planner has been told that every relationship you add makes the report slower, and he wants to know how many the model can carry. It is a fair question and it has a specific answer, so work out what one relationship actually costs the engine.

A relationship in a tabular model is not a SQL join, and the engine does not evaluate it like one. At load time, for each many-to-one relationship, the engine builds a structure that maps every value on the many side to the position of the matching row on the one side. Following the relationship afterwards is a lookup. There is no matching phase, no hashing of one side against the other, no loop over rows. Many-to-one is the direction almost every relationship in this model runs: many fact rows point at one dimension row.

Be precise about what is certain here. The internal representation is an implementation detail. Microsoft has changed it across versions and does not publish it as a contract. What is stable, and what you design against, is the cost profile. A many-to-one hop costs roughly in proportion to the distinct values involved, and it stays cheap into the millions of rows. So the planner's answer is that relationships of this shape are close to free, and you should add the ones the questions need.

Many-to-many is a different animal. There is no single row on the one side to point at, so that prepared structure cannot exist. The engine expands the filter through a distinct list of the shared key at query time and holds an intermediate result. That work happens per query and per filter combination, and it cannot be prepared at load. It also gives up the property that made the star worth building, because filters that travel both ways can take more than one route.

Rule of thumb

Every relationship should be many-to-one, single direction, from the one side outward. When you want a many-to-many, first check whether you are missing a dimension. Meridian's certification case is genuinely many-to-many, so BridgeTechCert exists for it: ten rows joining the six certified technicians to four certifications, producing hours by certification that add to 85.0 against a true total of 62.0. That gap is real, and it gets its own chapter.

Snowflaking, and when it is worth it

A colleague reviews your model and says the aircraft dimension repeats the operator name seven times, so it should be split out. The instinct behind that is a good one, and here it is wrong. Work through what the split buys and what it costs, because you will have this argument again.

Read this one from the left. DimOperator and DimEngineType both feed DimAircraft, and only DimAircraft touches FactWorkOrder. That is four boxes and three lines, each line labelled 1 at the outer end and a star at the inner end. Count the hops from a filter on Operator to the fact and you get two, where the star figure had one. The selection resolves to operator keys, then to aircraft registrations in DimAircraft, then to fact rows. The picture is tidier. The query has more to do.

Snowflaking means normalising a dimension, which is to say lifting the repeated attributes out into their own table. Here DimAircraft splits three ways. DimAircraft keeps the aircraft registration, the aircraft type and two outer keys, OperatorID and EngineID. DimOperator holds the three real operators plus an unknown member. DimEngineType holds the three engine families plus its own unknown member. The benefit is real. If the customer service desk renames Northwind Regional, there is one row to change and it cannot be changed inconsistently.

Read the last column twice, because it is the argument your colleague needs to hear. Snowflaking is sold as a way to remove duplication. Dictionary encoding has already removed it. "Northwind Regional" is stored once either way. The flat dimension holds seven small ids inside one table. The snowflake holds those same seven ids, plus a four-row operator table, plus a four-row engine type table, plus two more relationships in the model. Rows held goes up: 7 becomes 7 plus 4 plus 4, which is 15. The saving you were promised has already been taken by the compression.

So take a position. Flatten by default. Snowflake in two situations only. First, when the outer table is large enough that duplicating its attributes genuinely costs something, such as a five million row product dimension carrying a two hundred character description, where the dictionary itself becomes the expensive object. Second, when the outer table is truly shared, meaning two or more dimensions need the same attributes and the same maintenance.

Neither situation holds at Meridian, so tell your colleague the split stays out. DimAircraft has seven rows and DimOperator would have four. You would add a table, a relationship and a hop to every operator filter, all to avoid repeating an integer id seven times. There is a second cost you cannot measure in bytes. Report authors open the field list, find aircraft attributes sitting in three places, and start guessing which one to use.

Several facts, one set of dimensions

The production controller wants one line on a page: how busy was MSP in January. Busy against what, though. He means the hours the shop actually worked, set against the hours it planned to have available. Those two numbers live in two different fact tables, and nothing so far in this chapter lets you put them in the same row.

A model with more than one fact sharing the same dimensions is called a galaxy, or a fact constellation. The name matters less than the mechanism. DimStation has a single-direction relationship to FactWorkOrder[StationCode], and a second one to FactCapacity[StationCode]. A dimension used this way is conformed, which means one member list and one meaning serving both facts.

Put DimStation[StationCode] on the rows of a matrix and the engine takes each station in turn, pushing that filter down both relationships independently. Labor hours resolves through the work orders. Planned hours resolves through the capacity rows. Both answers land in the same matrix row, and that is the whole mechanism behind utilisation.

DAXUtilisation
Labor Hours =
    SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )

Planned Hours =
    SUM ( FactCapacity[PlannedHours] )

Utilisation =
    DIVIDE ( [Labor Hours], [Planned Hours] )
Lines 1 to 2
One physical column of one fact. Under a station filter this gives MSP 34.5, TUS 22.5 and LAS 5.0, adding to 62.0.
Lines 4 to 5
A different fact through the same dimension. MSP 90, TUS 50, LAS 20, PHX 16, adding to 176. PHX has planned hours and no work booked against them. That is a fact about the business, and the report should show it.
Lines 7 to 8
Divides the two. By station and month: MSP January 22.5 over 30 is 75.0%, TUS January 12.5 over 25 is 50.0%, LAS March 5.0 over 20 is 25.0%, PHX March 0 over 16 is 0%, and 62.0 over 176 is 35.2% for everything.
Why this and not that

DIVIDE rather than the / operator, because the denominator goes blank in a way you will actually hit. The relationship into FactCapacity is at month grain, so a report filtered to 7 January returns 7.5 labor hours and a blank planned hours. In DAX a non-blank number divided by blank returns infinity, and your card shows a symbol nobody wants to explain. DIVIDE returns blank, which is the honest answer to a day-level question asked of month-level capacity.

SUM and not SUMX in the two base measures, because both columns physically exist and need no per-row arithmetic. SUMX would build an iteration where a single column scan does the job. It earns its place only when the value has to be computed row by row, such as hours times rate.

So the production controller gets his line. MSP in January is 22.5 hours worked against 30 planned, which is 75.0%. Take DimStation away and that measure has nowhere to stand. The two totals would sit in unrelated tables with no shared filter, and the only way to line them up would be a Power Query merge at a grain that fits neither. The conformed dimension is what makes the comparison expressible at all.

Cardinality as a design input

The shift supervisor asks for something reasonable. Every labor line has a note where the technician types what they did, and he wants it in the report so he can read the story behind a long job. Loading one more column sounds like a two minute job. Before you agree, count what that column would contain.

Cardinality is the distinct count of a column, and once distinct count drives cost, cardinality becomes something you check before you load anything. Table 2.4 is the census for the columns already in the model. The bit width is the smallest number of bits that can address that many distinct values. Treat it as a lower bound on the id width, not a promise about final size.

So make the judgement column by column. FactWorkOrder[ACREG] has five distinct values across eight rows. It would still have five across five million rows, because Meridian works the same small fleet. Three bits per row, a dictionary of five short strings, and it is the key that reaches DimAircraft at all. Keep it without thinking twice. Low-cardinality keys on a fact are the cheapest thing in the model.

Now price the supervisor's column. Call it WorkDescription, one free-text note per labor line. Every value in it would be distinct, because no two people write the same sentence. The dictionary would hold one entry per row, so it would be as large as the table it describes. The ids would need as many bits as there are rows. Run length encoding would find nothing at all to compress. On eight rows that costs nothing. On eight million rows, that one column would outweigh the rest of the model put together.

Cardinality is only half the argument, though. Ask what the column is for. Nobody groups a chart by free text, and nobody filters on it, because it cannot be selected usefully in a slicer. It exists to be read one row at a time, at the level of a single labor line. So the answer to the shift supervisor is that the note stays where it is. He reads it in the shop floor system, one job at a time, which is how he reads it today, and the model carries the hours he wants to group and compare. If he ever needs the note inside Power BI, that is a decision to take again against a real row count and a measured refresh, and to write down. The same logic condemns FactLabor[LaborID]. It is distinct per row, and no visual will ever group by it, so once the relationships are built it is dead weight.

Performance note

Two numbers decide what a column costs you. The first is its distinct count, which sets the width of every id and the length of every run. That is why a five value rate column is free and a per row identifier is expensive. The second is whether anything in the report actually needs the column, which decides whether you should be paying at all. Hiding a column leaves it exactly where it was. A hidden column is still loaded, still encoded, still refreshed, and it still gives the segment sort heuristic one more column to compromise over. Hiding takes it out of the field list and stops there, which makes it a usability choice. If a column has no measure, no relationship and no visual behind it, remove it in Power Query, or stop selecting it in the source query so it never crosses the wire. Two things to check first in any inherited model: the surrogate row id on every fact, and any free-text note field.

The reason that actually matters

The shift supervisor at MSP comes back with a printed page. Your report says his station did 34.5 hours in the quarter. His whiteboard says 28.5, and he has been running that whiteboard for nine years. One of you is wrong, and this section is about the possibility that neither of you is.

First deal with cost, because at Meridian's size every cost in this chapter is zero. Eight work orders, eight labor rows, seven parts rows and twenty-eight capacity rows will not stress anything. If performance were the only argument for the star, the honest answer for this model would be to flatten it and move on.

The real argument is ambiguity, and the supervisor's whiteboard is where it shows up. Look at what the relationship list deliberately leaves out. There is no relationship from DimStation[StationCode] to DimTechnician[HomeStation], even though the columns match and Power BI would happily create it. Draw that line and there are two routes from DimStation to FactLabor. One goes through FactWorkOrder and answers hours performed at this station. The other goes through DimTechnician and answers hours worked by technicians based at this station. Both are legitimate questions. They are different questions.

Work it out from the rows. Through the work order, MSP is 34.5, TUS is 22.5, LAS is 5.0. Through home station it comes out differently. TECH-01 at 12.0 and TECH-02 at 16.5 are both MSP, giving 28.5. TECH-04 at 10.5 is TUS. TECH-05 at 13.0 is LAS. TECH-07 at 10.0 has no home station at all. So the second route reads MSP 28.5, TUS 10.5, LAS 13.0 and unassigned 10.0. Both columns total 62.0. Every single row differs. LAS more than doubles, TUS halves, and nothing on the visual tells you which path the engine took.

So the supervisor is right and so are you. He counts the people who report to him. Your report counts the aircraft that came into his hangar, including the 10.0 hours TECH-07 booked there. Because the model holds one path and only one, you can tell him which of the two his 34.5 is, and build the other number as its own measure if he wants both. In a model carrying both paths at once you could not have answered him, because you would not know which one the visual used.

Interview-level insight

The star schema earns its place on one property above every other. It gives each measure exactly one path from every dimension to every fact, so a number means the same thing in every visual on every page. Performance is the secondary benefit. Ambiguity is what makes a measure behave differently in two visuals that look identical, and it is close to undebuggable from the report surface, because the report shows you a number and never shows you the route it took. Keep one path and the argument about which answer is right never starts.

What to remember
  • VertiPaq compresses each column separately, so a column costs what its distinct count costs, not what its row count costs.
  • Flattening to line grain repeats header attributes. The storage penalty is smaller than folklore claims; the correctness penalty is fatal. Summing QuotedAmount over the flat labor table gives 46,600 instead of 38,100.
  • Meridian's star is four facts, seven dimensions and one bridge, with one extra layer in the middle: FactWorkOrder is also the header for FactLabor and FactParts, which is what makes hours by aircraft type reachable.
  • A many-to-one hop is a prepared lookup, so it is cheap. Many-to-many expands a distinct list per query and gives up the single-path guarantee.
  • Flatten dimensions by default. Snowflake only when the outer table is large enough for its attributes to cost something, or when two dimensions genuinely share it. Seven aircraft rows against four operator rows means the Meridian snowflake buys nothing and costs a hop.
  • Conformed dimensions make cross-fact measures possible. DimStation feeding both FactWorkOrder and FactCapacity is the only reason 62.0 over 176 equals 35.2% can be written.
  • Remove unused columns. Hiding one changes nothing in memory: it is still loaded, still encoded and still refreshed.
  • The payoff is one unambiguous filter path per measure. Hours at MSP is 34.5 through the work order and 28.5 through home station, and a model containing both paths would let the engine pick.
Part 1 . Reading the data

03Building the dimensions your source does not contain

By the end of this chapter you will be able to build a complete, unique and stable dimension table out of source systems that never shipped one. You will also be able to prove that the dimension covers every key value any fact actually uses.

The planner asks for planned hours by station for the quarter. You build the chart in five minutes. Three bars come back, MSP 90, TUS 50 and LAS 20, and a fourth bar with no label on it holding 16. The total reads 176, which is right, and one station's worth of capacity is sitting in a bar nobody can name. This chapter is about where that unlabelled bar comes from and how to make it impossible.

Meridian's six source tables give you four facts and almost no dimensions. A dimension is the table that describes something a fact refers to: a station, a part, an aircraft, a date. There is no station master, no part master, no calendar and no work order type list. The one dimension that does exist, AircraftRegistry, is missing an aircraft registration that a work order already references. This is normal. Operational systems are built to record transactions, not to describe the world those transactions happen in.

So you build the descriptions yourself. That is the job, and this chapter is how it is done. A dimension is the list of values your model agrees are allowed to exist. The moment a fact holds a value that list does not contain, the model starts telling a quieter kind of lie: the totals stay right and the breakdowns go wrong. The planner's total of 176 is correct, and the breakdown underneath it is the half that fails him.

The four properties every dimension table must have

Before any M code, agree on what you are aiming at. A table qualifies as a dimension when all four of these hold. Miss one and you get a predictable failure, and it is worth knowing which failure belongs to which property.

  1. The key is unique. One row per key value, no exceptions. The engine enforces this on the one side of a relationship and will simply refuse to create the relationship if you break it. The deeper reason is arithmetic: a duplicated key fans the fact rows out across both matching dimension rows, and every measure over that path doubles without warning.
  2. The key has no blank. A blank in a dimension key is ambiguous, because Power BI already uses a blank member for something else. When a fact holds a key the dimension lacks, the engine adds an invisible blank row on the dimension side and parks the unmatched facts there. If your dimension also contains a real blank key, a blank category on a visual could mean either thing and you can no longer tell which.
  3. The key covers every value that appears in every fact referencing it. Complete coverage, across all facts, not just the convenient one. This is the property everyone misses, and it is the direct cause of the blank rows people see in visuals and cannot explain.
  4. The key is stable. The same code means the same thing next refresh. If the shop floor system starts sending MSP1 where it used to send MSP, every report level filter, every bookmark, every saved slicer selection and every measure that tests for "MSP" keeps working syntactically and returns nothing. Filters store the value, not the row. That failure is invisible at build time and expensive at read time.
Common mistake

Taking the distinct values from the largest fact and calling that a dimension. It feels safe because the biggest table surely has everything. At Meridian, WorkOrders is the biggest table that uses a station code, and it does not contain PHX at all. Build DimStation from WorkOrders alone and every capacity row for PHX, 16 planned hours, loses its home and lands behind a blank member. The station list has to be the union of everything that uses the key, not a sample of it.

DimStation, assembled from three partial lists

So where did the planner's fourth bar go. The station code lives in three places at Meridian and no two of them hold the full list. Look at what each source actually contains.

There is the planner's missing bar. Only the planning workbook knows PHX exists. Phoenix has capacity rows and no work orders, which is exactly the situation his chart should be showing him. Leave PHX out of DimStation and the relationship from DimStation[StationCode] to FactCapacity[StationCode] orphans those four capacity rows. An orphan is a fact row whose key has no match in the dimension, and the engine has to park it somewhere. It parks it in an unlabelled row, which splits the planned hours total into a labelled 160 and an unlabelled 16.

The blank on WO-1005 needs a different answer. A blank means nobody recorded a station. Keep it out of the key list you union together, because a key list holds codes and a blank is the absence of one. The work order itself is real, though, and its hours have to land somewhere a person can see, so you add a member with a real code, UNASSIGNED, and map the blank to it on the fact side. Two separate acts, in this order: drop the blank from the key list, then create a member that means "we know this one is missing".

  1. Create three reference queries from WorkOrders, Technicians and ShopCapacity, and reduce each one to the single station column.
  2. Rename HomeStation to StationCode so all three columns carry the same name, because an append matches columns by name and not by position.
  3. Append the three into one stack.
  4. Trim the text, then remove nulls and empty strings.
  5. Remove duplicates. What remains is the key list.
  6. Attach the descriptive attributes, either by merging a maintained mapping table or by joining a small inline table written in M.
  7. Append the single UNASSIGNED row.
MDimStation
let
    // one column from each source, all named StationCode
    FromWorkOrders =
        Table.SelectColumns( WorkOrders, {"StationCode"} ),

    FromTechnicians =
        Table.RenameColumns(
            Table.SelectColumns( Technicians, {"HomeStation"} ),
            {{"HomeStation", "StationCode"}} ),

    FromCapacity =
        Table.SelectColumns( ShopCapacity, {"StationCode"} ),

    Stacked =
        Table.Combine(
            {FromWorkOrders, FromTechnicians, FromCapacity} ),

    Trimmed =
        Table.TransformColumns(
            Stacked, {{"StationCode", Text.Trim, type text}} ),

    NoBlanks =
        Table.SelectRows( Trimmed,
            each [StationCode] <> null
                 and [StationCode] <> "" ),

    Keys = Table.Distinct( NoBlanks ),

    Attributes = #table(
        type table [ StationCode = text, StationName = text,
                     StationRole = text ],
        {
            {"MSP", "Minneapolis", "Line and Base"},
            {"TUS", "Tucson",      "Base"},
            {"LAS", "Las Vegas",   "Line"},
            {"PHX", "Phoenix",     "Planned, no activity"}
        } ),

    Joined =
        Table.NestedJoin( Keys, {"StationCode"},
            Attributes, {"StationCode"}, "attr",
            JoinKind.LeftOuter ),

    Widened =
        Table.ExpandTableColumn( Joined, "attr",
            {"StationName", "StationRole"} ),

    Unassigned = #table(
        type table [ StationCode = text, StationName = text,
                     StationRole = text ],
        {{"UNASSIGNED", "Unassigned", "n/a"}} ),

    DimStation = Table.Combine( {Widened, Unassigned} )
in
    DimStation
FromTechnicians
The rename is the load bearing step. Table.Combine aligns on column name, so an unrenamed HomeStation would produce a second column full of nulls instead of stacking underneath, and you would find out only when the distinct count came back wrong.
Trimmed
Trim before deduplicating, never after. "TUS" and "TUS " are two distinct values to Table.Distinct and one value to your eyes. Meridian already has this exact defect in LaborEntries on TECH-04, so treat the trim as a certainty. It has happened here once already.
NoBlanks
Nulls and empty strings are different values in M and both have to go. This removes the WO-1005 blank from the key list. It does not lose the work order, which still carries its hours and gets mapped to UNASSIGNED on the fact side.
Attributes
An inline #table is honest about what it is: a hand maintained mapping with four rows that a human owns. When it grows past roughly twenty rows or a second person needs to edit it, move it to a real file and merge instead, because nobody outside your team can find a table that only exists inside a query.
Joined
A left outer join keeps every key, even the ones the mapping has no entry for. That is the point of choosing it. If a new station code called RNO appears next quarter, it arrives in DimStation carrying a null name. An inner join would have dropped it on the floor. A null name in a report is a question somebody asks.

The same union can be expressed in DAX as a calculated table, and you should know how. On some datasets you genuinely cannot touch the queries. A live connection, a shared semantic model owned by another team, a certified dataflow you have no rights to edit: any of those leaves you working inside the model instead of upstream of it. Take the block below for what it is. It returns the key list and stops there, so the descriptive columns and the UNASSIGNED member are a second step, described under the code.

DAXDimStation key list, calculated table fallback
DimStation =
VAR Keys =
    DISTINCT (
        UNION (
            DISTINCT ( WorkOrders[StationCode] ),
            DISTINCT ( Technicians[HomeStation] ),
            DISTINCT ( ShopCapacity[StationCode] )
        )
    )
RETURN
    FILTER ( Keys, [StationCode] <> "" )
DISTINCT
DISTINCT is the function to reach for, and VALUES is the trap sitting next to it. The two are identical except for one thing that matters here: VALUES returns the blank virtual row that the engine adds when a relationship has unmatched fact keys, and DISTINCT leaves that row out. Building a dimension out of VALUES would import the very blank member you are trying to eliminate.
UNION
UNION concatenates and keeps duplicates, so MSP would appear three times without the outer DISTINCT. It also matches its arguments by position rather than by name, which is why Technicians[HomeStation] can sit in the middle with a different column name and still land in the same column.
FILTER
FILTER is the operator that applies here, because it iterates whatever table expression you hand it. The habit to break is reaching for CALCULATETABLE. That function works by modifying filter context over model tables, and Keys is an anonymous table held in a variable, which has no filter context to modify.
<> ""
One comparison against "" does the whole job. In DAX a true blank compares equal to an empty string, so that single test removes an empty text value and a real blank together. The obvious looking alternative, NOT ISBLANK, returns FALSE for an empty string and would let it through.
What is not here
One column comes back, StationCode, so this is not yet the five row table in Table 3.2. Wrap the result in ADDCOLUMNS with a SWITCH over the code to attach StationName and StationRole, then UNION that with a one row table constructor holding UNASSIGNED. SWITCH rather than a merge because a calculated table has no join step, and the mapping is small enough that hard coding it in the expression is readable. That is three more layers of DAX to reproduce two Power Query clicks, which is itself an argument for the next box.
Why this and not that

Power Query is the correct home for a built dimension and DAX is the fallback. Three reasons, in order of what they cost you. A calculated table is evaluated during refresh and stored in the model, so no query can reference it, column quality cannot profile it, and a second report cannot reuse it. The DAX version also has no access to the source, so it can only union what is already loaded, which forces you to import ShopCapacity as a model table even if you wanted it only for its station list. Last, and this is the one that bites in a design review, the dimension build becomes invisible: someone auditing the extract and transform layer sees six queries and no station logic anywhere, because it is hiding in a table definition. Use the DAX version when the queries are genuinely out of reach, and write a comment saying why.

Trace the station union by hand, row by row

The append stacks 8 rows from WorkOrders, 6 from Technicians and 7 from ShopCapacity, which is 8 plus 6 plus 7 = 21 rows before anything is removed. One of those 21 is the blank on WO-1005, leaving 20. Deduplicating 20 values leaves 4: MSP appears 4 plus 3 plus 3 = 10 times, TUS 2 plus 2 plus 2 = 6 times, LAS 1 plus 1 plus 1 = 3 times, PHX once, and 10 plus 6 plus 3 plus 1 = 20. Adding the UNASSIGNED member gives the 5 row DimStation. If your row count after deduplication is not 4, the trim step did not run or did not run first.

Load that table and the planner's chart changes. The fourth bar is now labelled Phoenix and carries the same 16 hours it always carried. Nothing about the arithmetic moved. The total was 176 before and it is 176 now, which is the point that makes this defect so easy to ship: the number you would have checked was already right. What the fifth row bought him is a bar he can point at and ask about.

Interview-level insight

A dimension is a contract about what values are allowed to exist. Building it from the union of every source that uses the key is what makes that contract true. Anyone can write a lookup table from the values they happened to see. The discipline is deriving it from every producer of the key, including the producers that generate no transactions at all. PHX is the one that generates none.

DimTrade, where planning and capacity keep different lists

The production controller asks the question the whole shop runs on: do we have the people for the work booked this quarter. You give him a chart with demand and capacity side by side, split by trade. Four bars, all of them comfortably inside their limit, meeting over in ninety seconds. The chart is missing a fifth bar, and the fifth bar is the only one worth talking about.

Meridian has a second key with exactly the same defect as the station code. It is worth working through, because the two sources that produce it sit on opposite sides of the shop and have never had to agree on anything. Start with what a trade is, since the word carries no meaning outside this industry. A trade is the skill group a technician works in: airframe, avionics, engine, NDT (Non-Destructive Testing, the inspection specialism that finds cracks and corrosion without dismantling the structure), and at some shops cabin. Everything about resourcing a hangar is split by trade, for one reason. Ten airframe technicians cannot do an avionics job. A headcount on its own tells you almost nothing about whether the work in front of you can be done.

Two extracts carry a trade code, and neither of them is a list of trades.

ShopCapacity
Supply, at station and month grain. Grain is the sentence that says what one row of a table means, and one row here means one station in one month. It comes out of the monthly planning workbook the resource manager owns. A capacity figure is normally headcount multiplied by shift hours multiplied by an availability factor that strips out holiday, sickness, training and time booked to no job, then split by trade. In this workbook the four trades arrive as column headers: Airframe, Avionics, Engine and NDT. Unpivoting turns a set of columns into rows, one row per column per original row, and until that unpivot runs "Airframe" is the name of a column instead of a value in one. You cannot build a relationship on a column name.
HeavyPreInput
Demand, at work order and trade grain. This is the heavy pre-input tab: the planner's work package for a base maintenance visit, assembled in the weeks before the aircraft physically arrives. Input, also called induction, is that arrival, so pre-input is everything the planner does while the aircraft is still flying. He pulls together four kinds of work: the routine task cards falling due in the window, the ADs (Airworthiness Directives, which are mandatory), the service bulletins and modifications the customer has bought, and the defects carried over from earlier visits. He puts an estimated manhour figure against each card. Then he rolls the total up per trade. One row is one work order and one trade. The figure is then frozen at induction, because a baseline that moves cannot measure anything. Here the trades are values in a column, and there are five of them: the four above, plus Cabin.

That fifth member is the one that matters, and it appears nowhere else in the model. WO-1004 is a cabin retrofit on N771QR at Tucson, carrying 12.0 planned hours. Three systems describe that one job in three vocabularies. The shop floor system types it Mod. The HMCC board records the service line as Cabin and IFE. The planner's pack calls the trade Cabin. HMCC stands for Heavy Maintenance Control Centre. That is what many airlines and MROs (maintenance, repair and overhaul organisations) call the function that owns the heavy schedule. Plenty of shops call the identical function production control, or base maintenance control, so do not expect the acronym to travel with you. IFE is In-Flight Entertainment, the seat-back screens and the head-end equipment behind them. None of those three words appears anywhere in the capacity workbook.

One caution about the figures before you model them. What Meridian calls available hours, other shops call planned, budgeted, estimated or sold. The same word can mean the frozen baseline in one report and the live forecast in the next. Every shop settles this locally and no industry standard settles it for them. So write down the definition your production control team actually uses, get it agreed in writing, and put it in the model description. Note also that the hours column is called PlannedHours in both extracts and means opposite things: demand in one, supply in the other. Name the measures apart even if you leave the columns alone. A report author browsing the field list then sees Available Hours and Capacity Hours, and cannot add them together by accident.

The union arithmetic is smaller than the station one. The capacity workbook names four trades, the pre-input pack names five, the union is five, and the single member that separates the two lists is Cabin.

  1. Reference FactCapacity, the query that has already unpivoted ShopCapacity, and reduce it to the trade column.
  2. Reference HeavyPreInput and reduce it to the trade column.
  3. Append the two into one stack. No rename is needed here, provided the unpivot named its output column Trade and did not leave the default name in place.
  4. Trim the text, then remove nulls and empty strings.
  5. Remove duplicates. Five rows remain, and that is the entire dimension.
  6. Stop. There is no attribute table to join and no unknown member to add.
MDimTrade
let
    // FactCapacity is ShopCapacity after the unpivot, so Trade
    // is a value here and a column header in the source
    FromCapacity =
        Table.SelectColumns( FactCapacity, {"Trade"} ),

    FromPreInput =
        Table.SelectColumns( HeavyPreInput, {"Trade"} ),

    Stacked =
        Table.Combine( {FromCapacity, FromPreInput} ),

    Trimmed =
        Table.TransformColumns(
            Stacked, {{"Trade", Text.Trim, type text}} ),

    NoBlanks =
        Table.SelectRows( Trimmed,
            each [Trade] <> null
                 and [Trade] <> "" ),

    DimTrade = Table.Distinct( NoBlanks )
in
    DimTrade
FromCapacity
Point at FactCapacity and not at Table.ColumnNames( ShopCapacity ). Reading the headers looks like the shorter route and it returns StationCode and Month along with the four trades, so you would have to strip two names by hand. That exclusion list is one more thing a human maintains, and the day planning adds a Notes column to the workbook it starts admitting a trade called Notes. Reading the unpivoted column instead means the values come from a column whose only content is trades.
Both named Trade
This works because the unpivot renamed its output. Table.UnpivotOtherColumns produces columns called Attribute and Value, and Attribute has to become Trade at that step, not at this one. Leave it as Attribute and Table.Combine aligns nothing: you get two columns, each mostly null, and Table.Distinct returns 4 plus 5 = 9 rows that all look plausible in the preview.
NoBlanks
Neither source has a blank trade today. The guard stays because the pre-input pack is a planner's workbook, and workbooks behave the way workbooks behave. A row with hours in it and the trade cell left empty is an ordinary Friday. DimStation got an UNASSIGNED member and this dimension gets none, because there is no blank here to catch. Add the member on the day the data needs it.
Table.Distinct
The key is the whole row, as it will be for DimCertification later in this chapter. Meridian has no trade master, no skill grouping and no rate band, so there is nothing honest to attach. Resist in particular the temptation to add a flag saying whether the trade appears in the capacity workbook. That is a fact about this quarter's rows, it will be wrong the moment planning rosters a cabin technician, and freezing it into a dimension puts a measurable thing where a descriptive thing belongs.
Trace the trade union by hand, row by row

The unpivot turns 7 capacity rows times 4 trade columns into 28 rows, so the capacity side contributes 28 trade values, 7 each of Airframe, Avionics, Engine and NDT. The pre-input pack contributes its 8 rows: Airframe 4 times, on WO-1001, WO-1003, WO-1006 and WO-1008, then one each of Avionics, Engine, Cabin and NDT. The append is therefore 28 plus 8 = 36 values, made up of Airframe 11, Avionics 8, Engine 8, NDT 8 and Cabin 1, and 11 plus 8 plus 8 plus 8 plus 1 = 36 confirms nothing was dropped on the way in. Deduplicating 36 values leaves 5. A result of 4 rows means you appended the capacity side only. A result of 9 means the two columns never shared a name.

Common mistake

Building the trade list from the pre-input pack alone and letting the coverage check bless it. Today that check passes. HeavyPreInput happens to name all four capacity trades as well as Cabin, so the check comes back empty against both facts and the model ships. The list is complete by accident rather than by construction. Delete one row, the 2.0 NDT hours on WO-1008, and the dimension drops to four members while the 13 planned NDT hours in the capacity workbook lose their home. A check that passes on today's rows tells you about today's rows. A rule that keeps passing next quarter is a different thing, and construction is what buys it.

The wrong way

Take the four column headers out of the capacity workbook and call that the trade list, on the reasonable sounding grounds that the resource manager is the person who owns trades.

Available hours by trade then reads Airframe 34.0, Avionics 4.0, Engine 5.0 and NDT 2.0. Those four add to 34.0 plus 4.0 plus 5.0 plus 2.0 = 45.0. The card above the chart says 57.0, because the unmatched 12.0 is still in the total, parked behind the blank member the engine added the moment it met a fact key the dimension did not contain.

No error, no warning, and the one work order in the quarter whose entire package is cabin work has no bar at all.

The fix

Union both producers. Five members, with Cabin among them whether or not anybody has rostered for it.

The same chart now reads Cabin 12.0 against a planned capacity of 0, alongside Airframe 34.0 against 80, Avionics 4.0 against 44, Engine 5.0 against 39 and NDT 2.0 against 13. The labelled rows add to the total, and the one line with a zero on the supply side is the line a planner reads first.

That 12.0 is 21.1 percent of the 57.0 available hours, computed as 12.0 divided by 57.0, and it sits on a single work order out of eight.

What you see in the report

With four members, a demand against capacity chart is four comfortable bars adding to 45.0 against 176 planned hours of capacity. Everything inside its limit, nothing to discuss, meeting over. Two things are wrong with that picture and only one of them is the dimension. The missing bar is the dimension. The other is that the 57.0 covers heavy and cabin work only, because light maintenance never gets a pre-input pack, so the demand side is understated by whatever the line work consumes and the chart flatters the shop twice over.

The comparison also holds only at trade and quarter grain, which is worth knowing before somebody asks for it by month. Capacity sits at station and month. A pre-input row has a work order, a trade and an hours figure, and no date of any kind. So a monthly demand against capacity chart has to borrow a date from the work order, and then decide which of the three dates on it counts. That is an easy problem to solve and a decision somebody has to make out loud. A chart that splits by month before anybody has made it is answering a question nobody asked.

Now the payoff, and it is an operations finding. Cabin carries 12.0 planned hours against zero planned capacity. Read that the way the production controller reads it. The work package says the cabin job needs twelve hours of somebody's time, and the roster for the quarter puts nobody in that trade at any of the four stations, in any month. That is his answer, and it is the opposite of the comfortable one his four bar chart gave him. The five member dimension made a fact that had been sitting in the data all along reachable by a visual. The gap itself was already there, and it stays there until somebody rosters for it. With a four member trade list, nothing in the report could have got near it.

Then stop short of the conclusion, because two different situations produce this identical row and nothing in the extracts separates them. Either nobody was rostered for cabin work, which is a resourcing gap somebody has to answer for before the aircraft is in the bay. Or the capacity workbook runs a coarser trade list than the planning module does, and the people who will do the job are already counted inside Airframe. Cabin work frequently uses trades other than airframe, which is the usual reason a cabin code turns up in a planning extract and is missing from a capacity workbook. Shops genuinely differ on whether cabin is a trade of its own or a specialism sitting inside another one. Your model has produced a question. Production control owns the answer, and it is worth having in writing before the number reaches a page.

One more detail sharpens the question, and stops short of settling it. The only labor ever booked against WO-1004 is 10.0 hours from TECH-07, an identifier that appears nowhere in the HR (human resources) extract. One row takes you exactly this far. The single job with no planned capacity is also the single job whose hours were booked by a technician the roster does not know about. Whether that means a contractor nobody set up in the system, or somebody mistyping a digit, one row of data cannot settle. That combination is worth raising with a human being.

Finish the build the way this chapter finishes every other one. The grain sentence is one row per trade that either producer names. The key is Trade, with 5 distinct values across 5 rows. The coverage check is two anti joins, one for each fact that uses the key. An anti join returns the rows on one side that have no match on the other, so it is the question "which keys does the fact use that the dimension has never heard of" written down. FactCapacity[Trade] holds 4 distinct values with none missing. FactPreInput[Trade], which is HeavyPreInput typed and keyed, holds 5 with none missing. Build the dimension from the capacity workbook alone and the second check returns exactly one row, Cabin, which is this whole section compressed into one output. The model figure later in this chapter leaves out DimTrade and FactPreInput, because that figure is the twelve table core model and the pre-input pack arrives with the heavy maintenance extension. FactCapacity is drawn there, with its Trade column listed and no trade dimension yet attached to it.

DimAircraft, where the dimension you were given is the incomplete one

The finance manager wants labor hours split by aircraft type, because she is preparing a customer conversation about the A320 fleet. Your chart gives her three types adding to 50.0 hours. She has already seen the quarter total on another page and it says 62.0. Twelve hours have gone somewhere between the two pages, and she asks the obvious question.

Here the source did ship a dimension, which makes this the most dangerous case in the chapter. AircraftRegistry has 6 tails, maintained on a spreadsheet by the customer service desk, and it is stale in the way fleet spreadsheets always are. WorkOrders references 5 distinct tails. The two lists overlap, and neither one contains the other.

Notice the asymmetry. N120CE and N553KD sit in the registry with no work orders against them, and that costs you nothing. A dimension member with no facts is legitimate. It returns blank measures and drops out of visuals, unless you switch on "show items with no data". N338WA is the expensive case, and it is where the finance manager's twelve hours went. The fact references a key the dimension does not contain, and the engine has to put those rows somewhere.

MDimAircraft
let
    Registry =
        Table.SelectColumns( AircraftRegistry,
            {"ACREG", "AircraftType", "Operator",
             "EngineType", "YearBuilt"} ),

    FactTails =
        Table.Distinct(
            Table.SelectColumns( WorkOrders, {"ACREG"} ) ),

    // registry first: its rows win the deduplication
    Stacked = Table.Combine( {Registry, FactTails} ),

    Deduped = Table.Distinct( Stacked, {"ACREG"} ),

    Filled =
        Table.TransformColumns( Deduped,
            {
                {"AircraftType",
                 each if _ = null then "Unknown type"
                      else _, type text},
                {"Operator",
                 each if _ = null then "Unknown operator"
                      else _, type text},
                {"EngineType",
                 each if _ = null then "Unknown engine"
                      else _, type text}
            } )
in
    Filled
Stacked
Table.Combine with mismatched column sets fills the absent columns with null, so the N338WA row arrives carrying an aircraft registration and four nulls. That is the shape you want going into the deduplication.
Deduped
Append order decides the outcome here. Table.Distinct with a key column keeps the first row it meets for each key, so putting Registry first means the described rows win. The bare fact key then survives only where the registry had nothing to say. Reverse the append order and you wipe out the attributes for all five tails that appear in both lists.
Filled
Literal text, not a blank. "Unknown type" is a value a report reader can see, filter on, count and complain about. A null is a value they scroll past.
YearBuilt
Deliberately left null. Every other unknown gets a label, but a year is a number that measures will average, and inventing 0 or 1900 would poison the average silently. When the unknown value feeds arithmetic, leave it blank; when it feeds a label, fill it.

Now the payoff. Put the two versions of the chart side by side, because the principle is easier to believe with the arithmetic attached. The measure is total labor hours, sliced by DimAircraft[AircraftType], with the filter travelling from DimAircraft to FactWorkOrder to FactLabor.

The wrong way

Load AircraftRegistry as the dimension, unchanged, six rows.

The three real types sum to 23.5 plus 9.0 plus 17.5 = 50.0. The remaining 12.0 belongs to WO-1006 on N338WA and sits in a row with no name, no operator and no way to drill into it.

The fix

Load the built DimAircraft, seven rows, with the recovered key labelled.

Same 62.0 total, same 12.0. The 12.0 now carries a label the finance manager can act on, and clicking it filters to N338WA and WO-1006. Her missing twelve hours were on an airframe the registry has never listed.

What you see in the report

Both versions total 62.0, which is why this defect survives review. Nobody reconciles a breakdown against its own total. The reader sees three aircraft types adding to 50.0. The fourth row never registers, because a blank category label reads as visual noise, and she leaves believing the fleet consumed 50 labor hours. That understates it by 19.4 percent, computed as 12.0 divided by 62.0. The engine did nothing wrong here. It added the blank member because you asked it to relate a fact key to a dimension that did not contain that key.

Rule of thumb

Never let a fact contain a key value that the dimension does not contain. Not a blank, not an orphan, not a code that arrived last Tuesday. If you cannot describe the value, add it anyway with an explicit unknown label, because a labelled unknown gets investigated and an unlabelled blank gets ignored.

That rule is only useful if you test it, and the test is three lines of DAX you can run in a table visual after every refresh.

DAXCoverage assertion, should return zero rows
Missing Aircraft Keys =
EXCEPT (
    DISTINCT ( FactWorkOrder[ACREG] ),
    DISTINCT ( DimAircraft[ACREG] )
)
Why this and not that

EXCEPT and not a FILTER wrapped around NOT CONTAINS. Both return the same rows. EXCEPT is a set operator, so the engine resolves it as one set difference rather than iterating the fact key list and probing the dimension once per value. It also reads as the question you are actually asking: which fact keys are missing from the dimension. The CONTAINS form states that question backwards. It invites the classic error of putting the arguments in the wrong order, which returns dimension members with no facts, a completely different and usually harmless condition. Note that EXCEPT matches columns by position, so both arguments must be single column tables in the same order.

DimPart, built out of the fact that uses it

The finance manager comes back a week later wanting parts cost grouped by category, so she can see how much of the quarter went on brakes. Meridian has no part master anywhere. Nobody holds a list that says BRK-2210 is a brake. You have seven rows in a stores issue log and a customer waiting.

PartsIssued has 7 rows carrying 4 distinct part numbers, and that is the entire universe of parts as far as this model is concerned. When the only producer of a key is a single fact, the fact is where the dimension comes from.

MDimPart
let
    Keys =
        Table.Distinct(
            Table.SelectColumns( PartsIssued,
                {"PartNumber"} ) ),

    Prefix =
        Table.AddColumn( Keys, "Prefix",
            each Text.BeforeDelimiter( [PartNumber], "-" ),
            type text ),

    Category =
        Table.AddColumn( Prefix, "PartCategory",
            each if [Prefix] = "BRK" then "Brakes"
            else if [Prefix] = "HYD" then "Hydraulics"
            else if [Prefix] = "ENG" then "Engine"
            else if [Prefix] = "AVI" then "Avionics"
            else "Unmapped prefix", type text ),

    Class =
        Table.AddColumn( Category, "PartClass",
            each if [Prefix] = "BRK" then "Consumable"
                 else "Rotable", type text ),

    DimPart =
        Table.SelectColumns( Class,
            {"PartNumber", "PartCategory", "PartClass"} )
in
    DimPart
Text.BeforeDelimiter
Split on the delimiter, because that encodes the rule that actually exists, which is "everything before the hyphen". Text.Start( [PartNumber], 3 ) returns BRK today as well, so the two look interchangeable. Text.Start hard codes the assumption that every prefix is exactly three characters, and the first four character prefix the stores system invents will produce a silently truncated category.
else "Unmapped prefix"
The catch all branch earns its place. It decides whether a new prefix shows up as a visible label in a report or as a blank that nobody investigates. Put an unmapped count on your refresh check page.
Prefix dropped
The helper column comes out at the end. Leave it visible and report authors get a second way to group parts, one you never documented and never intended. Two groupings that agree today will not agree forever.

So the finance manager gets her brakes figure. Now say the caveat out loud, because you should be able to state both halves of it in a design review. Extracting a category out of a key is acceptable here and a smell in general. Acceptable, because no alternative source exists and the mapping is small enough to audit by eye. A smell, because the source system is encoding meaning inside an identifier, and encodings drift. The day stores renumbers a brake assembly from BRK-2210 to ASM-2210, for a purchasing reason that has nothing to do with you, that part changes category. Every historical parts cost by category figure moves with it. DimPart has no memory of what BRK used to mean. The permanent fix is a part master that stores owns, and the prefix parse is what you run until somebody funds one.

DimWOType, three rows and the argument for bothering

The shift supervisor filters the page to LAS to look at one station, and the work order type slicer beside it loses two of its three options. He calls you and says the report is broken. The slicer is behaving exactly as it was built to, he is right to call, and the fix is a three row table.

WorkOrders[WOType] holds three values across eight rows. Scheduled sits on WO-1001, WO-1003, WO-1006 and WO-1008. AOG (aircraft on ground, unplanned work that the shop learns about when the defect is reported) sits on WO-1002, WO-1005 and WO-1007. Mod sits on WO-1004 alone. Meridian has no work order type master anywhere, and the column has no blank and no orphan in it. This is the smallest built dimension in the model and the one most likely to be skipped, so be explicit about what building it buys and what it costs.

The case for skipping it is real. WOType is already on the fact, it has three values, and dragging FactWorkOrder[WOType] onto a slicer works today. That is the degenerate dimension argument from Chapter 1, and for a key with no attributes it is the right call. The question is whether this key has attributes, and it does: a definition that operations cares about, a display order that is not alphabetical, and the fact that AOG means unplanned while the other two do not.

MDimWOType
let
    Keys =
        Table.Distinct(
            Table.SelectColumns( WorkOrders, {"WOType"} ) ),

    Attributes = #table(
        type table [ WOType = text, WOTypeDesc = text,
                     WOTypeSort = Int64.Type,
                     IsUnplanned = logical ],
        {
            {"Scheduled", "Planned input, booked in advance",
             1, false},
            {"AOG", "Aircraft on ground, unplanned",
             2, true},
            {"Mod", "Modification or upgrade",
             3, false}
        } ),

    Joined =
        Table.NestedJoin( Keys, {"WOType"},
            Attributes, {"WOType"}, "attr",
            JoinKind.LeftOuter ),

    DimWOType =
        Table.ExpandTableColumn( Joined, "attr",
            {"WOTypeDesc", "WOTypeSort", "IsUnplanned"} )
in
    DimWOType
Keys
The key list comes from the fact, not from the three strings you are about to type underneath. Type them and a fourth type arriving next quarter, Warranty say, has no row in the dimension and its work orders fall behind the blank member. Derive the list and the new code arrives in the dimension by itself, with a null description that somebody notices on the first report that groups by it.
WOTypeSort
An integer, because Scheduled, AOG, Mod is the order the shop thinks in and alphabetical order is AOG, Mod, Scheduled. Setting the Sort by Column property on WOTypeDesc to this column is a manual step in the model that no query can do for you, and it is forgotten roughly as often as the same step on month names.
IsUnplanned
A logical column holding the definition of unplanned work in one row of one table. The alternative is every measure that cares testing WOType = "AOG" for itself, which works and which scatters the rule across the model. When Meridian adds an AOG-Ferry code, one row changes here and nothing else does.
JoinKind.LeftOuter
