Left outer and not inner, for the same reason as DimStation. An inner join silently drops any key the attribute table has no entry for, which is the one case you need to see.
No unknown member
DimStation got an UNASSIGNED row and DimAircraft got a recovered one. This dimension gets neither, because WorkOrders[WOType] has no blank and no orphan. Adding an unknown member anyway would put a row in every slicer that can never be selected usefully. Add the member when the data needs it, not as a habit.

Check that arithmetic against Chapter 0 before you use it. Scheduled hours are WO-1001 at 13.5 plus WO-1003 at 12.5 plus WO-1006 at 12.0 plus WO-1008 at nothing, which is 38.0. AOG is WO-1002 at 9.0 plus WO-1005 at nothing plus WO-1007 at 5.0, which is 14.0. Mod is WO-1004 at 10.0. Those add to 62.0. Quoted runs 3,000 plus 12,500 plus 7,500 plus 5,000 = 28,000 for Scheduled, 3,200 plus 2,000 plus 900 = 6,100 for AOG, 4,000 for Mod, and 28,000 plus 6,100 plus 4,000 = 38,100.

Here is the behaviour behind the supervisor's phone call, and you can reproduce it in two minutes. Put a station slicer and a work order type slicer on a page. Set the station slicer to LAS, which has exactly one work order, WO-1007, an AOG job. If the type slicer reads FactWorkOrder[WOType], Scheduled and Mod vanish from it. The station selection filtered the fact, and the slicer is reading the surviving rows of that fact. If it reads DimWOType[WOType], all three options stay put, because filter flows from the dimension into the fact and never back up the other relationship. So point his slicer at the dimension and the list stops moving. He was right to call: with the fact column feeding the slicer, he could not tell whether Mod was absent because LAS does no mods, or because somebody had removed the option.

The cost is honest and small. You have added a table, a relationship and a maintenance job, all to hold three strings that were already in the model. If Meridian had shipped a work order type master, this whole section would be one merge. Whatever you gain here, you do not gain it in bytes. Three distinct values cost two bits per row on the fact either way, and building the dimension leaves that column exactly where it was.

DimCertification and BridgeTechCert, from a delimited column

The production controller wants to know how many hours went to work needing an NDT ticket, because he is deciding whether to send a second technician for the qualification. The certifications are in the model. They are sitting three to a cell in one text column, which means no visual can group by them. Getting from that column to his number takes one new table and one uncomfortable piece of arithmetic.

Technicians[Certifications] holds multiple values per row, delimited by a semicolon. TECH-04 carries "A&P; Avionics; Engine Run". A&P is Airframe and Powerplant, the Federal Aviation Administration mechanic certification. Meridian uses A&P and the European licence categories appear nowhere, which tells you which authority the shop answers to. A column shaped like this cannot be filtered or grouped reliably. "Avionics" as a substring appears inside three different technicians' text, and a text filter for it stops matching anything useful the moment somebody reorders their list. Split it to rows.

MBridgeTechCert
let
    Kept =
        Table.SelectColumns( Technicians,
            {"TechnicianID", "Certifications"} ),

    // split on the semicolon only, then trim
    ToList =
        Table.TransformColumns( Kept,
            {{"Certifications",
              each Text.Split( Text.From( _ ), ";" ),
              type list}} ),

    ToRows =
        Table.ExpandListColumn( ToList, "Certifications" ),

    Clean =
        Table.TransformColumns( ToRows,
            {{"Certifications", Text.Trim, type text}} ),

    Renamed =
        Table.RenameColumns( Clean,
            {{"Certifications", "CertCode"}} ),

    BridgeTechCert = Table.Distinct( Renamed )
in
    BridgeTechCert
Text.Split on ";"
Split on the delimiter you can rely on, then trim what is left. Splitting on "; " works on every current row, because every current row has the space. Then a single row typed as "A&P;NDT" produces one certification called "A&P;NDT" and quietly creates a fifth member of DimCertification.
ExpandListColumn
This is the step that changes the grain. Six technician rows become ten technician and certification rows, which is why this output cannot live on DimTechnician: loading it there would duplicate TECH-04 three times and break the uniqueness property from the start of this chapter.
Table.Distinct
Guards against the same certification being listed twice on one technician, which is a data entry outcome you will eventually meet. A duplicate pair in a bridge multiplies that technician's contribution to a certification, and unlike a duplicate dimension key the engine will not warn you.

DimCertification is then the distinct CertCode from this output: A&P, Avionics, NDT and Engine Run, four rows. Build it from the bridge rather than typing it, so that a new certification appearing in HR cannot reach the bridge without also reaching the dimension. Two queries, one dependency, and the coverage property from the start of this chapter now holds by construction. Vigilance stops being part of the design.

MDimCertification
let
    Codes =
        Table.SelectColumns( BridgeTechCert,
            {"CertCode"} ),

    DimCertification = Table.Distinct( Codes )
in
    DimCertification
BridgeTechCert
Reference the bridge, not Technicians. The bridge has already been split, trimmed and deduplicated, so the dimension inherits every one of those cleaning steps for free and cannot drift away from the values the bridge actually holds. Point this query at the raw delimited column instead and you have written the split twice.
No attributes
The code is the whole row. Meridian has no certification master, no issuing authority, no expiry, so there is nothing honest to add and a fabricated grouping column would be worse than none. Add columns when a source for them exists.
The cost
Deriving the dimension from the bridge means a certification that nobody currently holds cannot appear in the model at all. If Meridian needs to report on a qualification the shop is trying to hire for, this build cannot show it, and you will need a maintained list upstream of the bridge instead. That is a real limitation of the pattern, not a detail to wave past.

Row counts per technician are 2, 1, 2, 3, 1 and 1, and 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 1 plus 1 = 10. A Bridge is its own kind of table, sitting outside Fact and Dimension both. It holds a relationship written down as rows, one row for each pairing that exists, and that is the only way a relational model can carry a many to many association. It has no measures on it, and it has no descriptive attributes and no single column key either, which is why it fits neither of the other two categories. A bridge exists to be traversed by a filter, and nobody should be reading it. Hide it from the field list. An author who drops BridgeTechCert[CertCode] onto a visual instead of DimCertification[CertCode] gets a result that looks plausible and behaves differently under cross filtering.

Now the production controller gets his NDT number, and it comes with a warning about the arithmetic. Grouping the 62.0 total labor hours by certification produces rows of 39.0, 10.5, 12.0 and 23.5, which add to 85.0. Those four rows are the correct answer to the question "hours performed by somebody holding this certification". TECH-04 holds three certifications, so every hour he books lands under all three of them. The number the production controller came for is the NDT row, 12.0 hours, and it overlaps the other rows on purpose. Those 12.0 hours are all TECH-01's, because TECH-01 and TECH-03 are the only two NDT holders and TECH-03 booked nothing this quarter. Chapter 14 deals with how to put that on a page without anybody reading 85.0 as a total.

DimDate, the dimension that has no source at all

The finance manager selects Feb in a month slicer and asks for the year to date labor hours. The card returns February's number and labels it year to date. Nothing errors, nothing goes blank, and the page answers a different question from the one printed on it. That failure has one cause and one setting behind it, and both are in this section.

Every date column in the model needs one shared calendar, and there are six date columns across four facts. Meridian's period runs 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31, which is 31 plus 28 plus 31 = 90 days.

Grain
One row per calendar day
Rows
90
Range
2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31
Key
DimDate[Date]
DAXDimDate as a calculated table
DimDate =
VAR FirstDay = DATE ( 2025, 1, 1 )
VAR LastDay = DATE ( 2025, 3, 31 )
RETURN
ADDCOLUMNS (
    CALENDAR ( FirstDay, LastDay ),
    "Year", YEAR ( [Date] ),
    "MonthNo", MONTH ( [Date] ),
    "MonthName", FORMAT ( [Date], "mmm" ),
    "MonthKey", YEAR ( [Date] ) * 100 + MONTH ( [Date] ),
    "MonthStart",
        DATE ( YEAR ( [Date] ), MONTH ( [Date] ), 1 ),
    "Quarter", "Q" & QUARTER ( [Date] ),
    "DayOfWeek", WEEKDAY ( [Date], 2 ),
    "IsWeekend", WEEKDAY ( [Date], 2 ) > 5
)
ADDCOLUMNS
One expression, holding all eight columns at once. That gives you one object to review, one place to change the fiscal logic, and no risk of a colleague deleting the column that a sort order depends on. Adding the eight as separate calculated columns through the interface scatters all three of those. The trade off is that you cannot edit a single attribute without reopening the whole table definition.
WEEKDAY( , 2 )
Return type 2 makes Monday 1 and Sunday 7, so the weekend test is one comparison against 5. The default return type 1 starts the week on Sunday, which would need = 1 || = 7 and would also make any day of week sort order start on the wrong day.
MonthKey
2025 times 100 plus 1 = 202501. An integer month key sorts correctly by nature, joins to FactCapacity[MonthKey] without date coercion, and costs one byte column instead of a text column with 3 distinct values that sorts alphabetically.
MonthName
FORMAT returns text, so MonthName sorts as Feb, Jan, Mar until you set its Sort by Column property to MonthNo. Setting that property is required, and it is the single most common omission in a hand built calendar.
QUARTER
QUARTER returns the integer 1 to 4 with no format string to get wrong, and the concatenation makes it Q1. The habit people carry over from Excel and from report builders is FORMAT( [Date], "q" ). The list of custom date codes that DAX documents does not include q at all, so whatever a q returns here is undocumented behaviour, and you would be trusting it to survive the next version and the next locale. That is a thin thing to hang a column on.
Why this and not that

CALENDAR and not CALENDARAUTO. CALENDARAUTO scans every date column in the model and returns whole years spanning the minimum and maximum it finds. Here that gives 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31: 365 rows for 90 days of data, and nine months of empty rows that report readers will slice into and find blank. Worse, the range becomes a function of the model's contents. The day somebody adds a source with a date typed as 1900-01-01, your calendar grows by 125 years and the model doubles in size, with nobody having changed a line of code. CALENDAR with explicit bounds fails loudly instead. Data outside the range simply does not match, and an orphan check catches it.

The Power Query version does the same work upstream, and for the same reasons given for DimStation it is the one to prefer in a new model.

MDimDate
let
    FirstDay = #date( 2025, 1, 1 ),
    LastDay  = #date( 2025, 3, 31 ),
    DayCount = Duration.Days( LastDay - FirstDay ) + 1,

    Dates =
        List.Dates( FirstDay, DayCount,
            #duration( 1, 0, 0, 0 ) ),

    Base =
        Table.TransformColumnTypes(
            Table.FromList( Dates,
                Splitter.SplitByNothing(), {"Date"} ),
            {{"Date", type date}} ),

    A = Table.AddColumn( Base, "Year",
            each Date.Year( [Date] ), Int64.Type ),
    B = Table.AddColumn( A, "MonthNo",
            each Date.Month( [Date] ), Int64.Type ),
    C = Table.AddColumn( B, "MonthName",
            each Date.ToText( [Date], "MMM" ), type text ),
    D = Table.AddColumn( C, "MonthKey",
            each [Year] * 100 + [MonthNo], Int64.Type ),
    E = Table.AddColumn( D, "MonthStart",
            each Date.StartOfMonth( [Date] ), type date ),
    F = Table.AddColumn( E, "Quarter",
            each "Q" &
                 Text.From( Date.QuarterOfYear( [Date] ) ),
            type text ),
    G = Table.AddColumn( F, "DayOfWeek",
            each Date.DayOfWeek( [Date], Day.Monday ) + 1,
            Int64.Type ),
    DimDate = Table.AddColumn( G, "IsWeekend",
            each [DayOfWeek] > 5, type logical )
in
    DimDate
DayCount
Duration.Days of the difference gives 89, and the plus 1 makes 90 because both endpoints are included. Off by one here produces a calendar that stops on 2025-03-30, and the only symptom is that one day of March data goes missing from every date sliced visual.
List.Dates
Generates the sequence directly with a one day step, which guarantees contiguity by construction. The alternative of pulling distinct dates out of the facts produces a calendar with holes wherever the shop was quiet, and holes are the one thing a date table must not have.
Date.DayOfWeek
This function is zero based, so the plus 1 aligns it with the DAX WEEKDAY( , 2 ) convention. Keep the two versions of the calendar numerically identical or you will spend an afternoon on a discrepancy that is entirely of your own making.

Mark as Date Table, and what it actually does

Marking a table as the date table changes how the engine behaves, which is why the finance manager's card came back wrong. You nominate the date column, and the engine records that this column is a contiguous, unique, day grain date key for the whole table. The consequence that matters lives inside the time intelligence functions. DATESYTD, TOTALYTD, DATEADD and SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR all work the same way. Each one returns a set of dates and applies that set as a filter. To do it safely, each one must first clear whatever date filters are already in play. When the table is marked, that implicit clearing is a REMOVEFILTERS over the entire date table, every column of it. When the table is unmarked, the clearing reaches only the date column passed into the function.

That difference is the whole reason the setting exists. Put DimDate[MonthName] in a slicer, select Feb, and ask for a year to date total. With the table marked, the function clears the February filter along with everything else on DimDate, and the year to date figure comes back correct. Leave it unmarked and the February filter survives. It intersects with the year to date date set, and you get February's number wearing a year to date label. That is exactly what happened on her page, and marking the table is the whole fix.

Contiguity is the price of that guarantee. Time intelligence treats the date column as a continuous axis and shifts along it by position, so a missing day breaks every shift that crosses it. Power BI therefore refuses to mark a table with gaps, duplicates or blanks in the nominated column. Filtering weekends out of the calendar is how people usually break this. Exclude weekends with a column such as IsWeekend, never by deleting rows.

Here is the inconvenient consequence for Meridian specifically. The calendar covers 90 days, so any measure that shifts a year backwards returns blank. There are no 2024 rows to shift to. Year over year is out of reach in this model, and no amount of DAX will bring it into reach. If the business asks for it, the answer is to extend the calendar and load prior year facts. A cleverer measure will not do it.

Look at the figure in two passes. First pass, ignore the lines and count the shapes. Twelve tables, and the note printed with them breaks that twelve down as four facts, seven dimensions and one bridge. The note also records that nine of the twelve are absent from the source and get built in Power Query. Count them off against the boxes. DimStation, DimWOType, DimPart, DimCertification and BridgeTechCert have no source table of their own. Each one was reconstructed out of columns buried inside tables built for another purpose. DimDate is the extreme case. It has no source anywhere in the six extracts and is generated from two dates and a step. DimAircraft and DimTechnician arrived as source extracts, and both had to be repaired and extended before they could be used. FactCapacity only takes the shape drawn here after the unpivot. That leaves three tables, FactWorkOrder, FactLabor and FactParts, which loaded more or less as they arrived. Three tables out of twelve. That ratio is the honest picture of what modelling work looks like on operational data.

Second pass, follow the lines out of DimStation. Every solid line in the figure carries a 1 at one end and a * at the other. That pair of labels is the whole statement of direction. The 1 marks the one side, the * marks the many side, and filter flows from the 1 towards the *. DimStation reaches FactWorkOrder and FactCapacity directly, which is why one station slicer can drive both actual hours and planned hours. Look for a line from DimStation to DimTechnician and you will find none, even though DimTechnician[HomeStation] holds station codes. That omission is deliberate. Adding the line would create a second route from DimStation to FactLabor, one through FactWorkOrder and one through DimTechnician, and the engine cannot choose between two paths. HomeStation stays a descriptive attribute. Note also the single line into BridgeTechCert from each side, and that the bridge sits between two dimensions rather than between a dimension and a fact. That placement is the visual signature of a many to many association.

One line is drawn differently from the rest. The curve from DimDate to FactCapacity is dashed and labelled month grain only, because that join is made on MonthStart rather than on a day, unlike every other link out of DimDate. The label is a warning left in the picture on purpose: the relationship is genuine, it simply answers nothing below month level. Chapter 16 is where that costs something.

Testing the tables you built

You are in a design review and somebody asks the fair question: how do you know these eight tables are right. You have about a minute, and the answer that works is a table of checks that ran during the last refresh. Saying that you built them carefully buys you nothing in that room.

Everything above is a claim. Eight tables now exist that no source system shipped, and each one asserts a grain, a unique key and a complete list of allowed values. Grain is the sentence that says what one row of the table means. Chapter 1 tested the grain of the six source tables with a candidate key check, which is a count of distinct key values set against a count of rows. Run that same check here. Then run the second half of it, the half the source tables did not need: does the key list cover every value the facts actually hold.

Start with the sentences, because a built table needs a grain sentence exactly as much as an extract does. It is easier to write a wrong one when you built the table yourself. You already know what you meant, so nobody checks.

Seven of the eight have a single column key and pass. The bridge is the one that cannot, and that is by design. TechnicianID alone has 6 distinct values across its 10 rows and CertCode alone has 4, so neither column identifies a row and only the pair does. Six technicians times four certifications gives 24 possible pairs, of which 10 exist. A table whose only key is the whole row is the shape of a bridge, and it is why a bridge can never sit on the one side of a relationship.

Note what the DimCertification sentence gives away. It says "held by at least one technician on the roster", not "recognised by Meridian", because the query derives the list from the bridge. The sentence is the honest description of what the query built, and writing it forced the limitation into the open. That is most of what grain sentences are for on tables you assembled yourself.

Now the coverage half. The check is one anti join per relationship, so write it as a function too and point it at every pair.

MfnMissingKeys
// fnMissingKeys( FactLabor, "TechnicianID",
//     Technicians, "TechnicianID" ) returns one row: TECH-07
let
    fnMissingKeys =
        ( Fact as table, FactKey as text,
          Dim as table, DimKey as text ) as table =>
        let
            FactKeys = Table.Distinct(
                Table.SelectColumns( Fact, {FactKey} ) ),
            DimKeys = Table.Distinct(
                Table.SelectColumns( Dim, {DimKey} ) ),
            Missing = Table.NestedJoin(
                FactKeys, {FactKey},
                DimKeys,  {DimKey},
                "match", JoinKind.LeftAnti )
        in
            Table.SelectColumns( Missing, {FactKey} )
in
    fnMissingKeys
JoinKind.LeftAnti
The anti join is the question written down in one step, and it never carries the matched dimension rows through only to throw them away. The alternative people write is JoinKind.LeftOuter followed by an expand and a filter for nulls. That outer form is three steps, and three steps can be reordered by the next person to open the query.
FactKey and DimKey
Two separate parameters because Table.NestedJoin takes a key list for each side and the two columns do not have to share a name. That is not hypothetical here: Technicians[HomeStation] and DimStation[StationCode] hold the same key under two names, and a function that demanded matching names could not check that pair at all.
Table.Distinct on both sides
On the dimension side it is redundant if the dimension is really a dimension. Leave it in anyway: this function gets pointed at half finished tables, and a duplicated dimension key would otherwise multiply the fact key rows in the join and give you an answer whose row count means nothing.
Making it fail
Wrap the call as if Table.IsEmpty( fnMissingKeys( ... ) ) then Source else error "coverage" and the refresh stops. Do that where a gap is genuinely unacceptable. Meridian is the case where you must not: TECH-07 and WO-1009 are known, tolerated orphans, so a hard error would block every refresh over data the business considers normal. Put the output on a page somebody reads instead, and reserve the error for a dimension you control end to end.
Against the DAX form
The EXCEPT expression earlier in this chapter asks the same question, at query time, over data that is already loaded. Use it when the queries are out of your hands. This version answers during refresh, before anybody has looked at a number, which is where you want the answer if you can get it there.

Fourteen clean rows and two failures, and the two failures are the ones this dataset keeps on purpose. FactLabor books 10.0 hours to TECH-07, who is absent from the HR extract. FactParts charges 4,900 dollars to WO-1009, a work order Meridian has never raised. Both are fixed the same way DimAircraft was, by appending the distinct fact key and labelling it, and Chapter 19 covers what that does to the numbers on a report page. So that is your answer in the design review. The table above found both of them during a refresh, before anybody sat down in a meeting.

Read the ClosedDate row carefully as well, because a zero there is easy to misread. Six distinct close dates, no missing keys, and two work orders, WO-1004 and WO-1008, that carry no close date at all. A foreign key is the column on the fact that points at a dimension, and ClosedDate is one. A blank foreign key is not an orphan. It matches nothing, it contributes to nothing, and this check will never report it. Counting closed work orders therefore needs a test of its own, and a coverage check will not supply it.

Why DimStation needs both fact columns checked, not one

Take the two station rows of Table 3.12 apart. FactWorkOrder[StationCode] holds MSP, TUS, LAS and, after the blank on WO-1005 is mapped, UNASSIGNED. Four distinct values, all present in DimStation. FactCapacity[StationCode] holds MSP, TUS, LAS and PHX. Also four distinct values, also all present. Neither fact uses all five members, and no single fact would have told you the dimension was complete.

Now build DimStation from the work orders alone, which is the shortcut in the Common mistake box at the top of this chapter, and re-run both rows. Against FactWorkOrder it still reports zero missing, so the check passes and you ship. Against FactCapacity it reports one: PHX, carrying 8 plus 4 plus 3 plus 1 = 16 planned hours. Planned hours by station now reads MSP 90, TUS 50, LAS 20 and a blank row of 16, and the quarter total of 176 is still correct, which is exactly why nobody catches it.

The UNASSIGNED member goes the other way. It appears in FactWorkOrder and never in FactCapacity, because planning does not publish hours for a station that does not exist. A dimension member with no rows in one of its facts is normal, and a coverage check only ever reads in one direction: from the keys a fact uses, to the list the dimension allows.

Those two station rows are what the word conformed means in practice. DimStation is conformed because one member list, one set of codes and one set of names serves both FactWorkOrder and FactCapacity. MSP therefore means the same thing on both sides of a utilisation figure, and a single slicer drives both. The same holds for DimDate, which serves six date columns across four facts, and for DimTechnician, which serves FactLabor and the bridge. Every dimension here is conformed by construction, because each key list was built from the union of every producer of the key. Whichever table you happened to open first has no say in it.

The counter case is worth naming, so the word does not turn into decoration. Build a station list from WorkOrders for the work order report, and a second one from ShopCapacity for the planning report. Both reports are individually correct. Put them side by side and MSP reads 34.5 hours against 90 planned in one, and 34.5 against 90 in the other, right up until the day somebody adds PHX to the second list and leaves the first alone. Two lists that agree today are still two lists, and two lists drift.

Interview-level insight

Conformance is a property of the member list, not of the relationship. Two facts joined to two separate station tables holding identical values will produce identical numbers and still be unconformed, because nothing keeps them identical: the next refresh, the next station code, the next person to edit one query. Test for conformance with one question. Is there exactly one query that decides what a station is? Whether the numbers currently agree is a weaker question, and it is the one people ask instead. At Meridian the answer to the real question is DimStation, whose inputs are all three producers of the code, which is why PHX cannot be lost and a blank cannot get in.

CrewCodeMap, the table that exists because you typed it

The resource manager wants hours by crew before his Monday call. You have the tables, so you build it in four minutes. Four rows come back. Three carry a crew name, the fourth carries no label at all, and 10.0 hours are sitting in it. He points at the unlabelled row and asks whose crew that is. Nobody at the table can answer him, and the reason is a spreadsheet on your laptop.

Two tables produce that visual. CrewAssignment comes out of the roster system and has 7 rows, one per technician, each carrying a crew code. A crew code is the shop's identifier for a working team, and it looks like CRW-AF1. CrewCodeMap has 6 rows and turns a crew code into two readable things: a crew name and a service line. A service line is the kind of work Meridian sells, and there are four of them, Line, Light, Heavy, and Cabin and IFE. Almost every planning number the shop reports is grouped by service line, so the map decides where the hours land.

Built Every key list in this chapter so far came out of a column that some system produces. The station codes come from three extracts, the part numbers come from the stores issue log, the certifications come from an HR column. CrewCodeMap breaks that pattern. The roster system issues the crew codes and nothing anywhere issues their meaning. No source system holds this table, no extract refreshes it, and the dataset records its source as the analyst. That is you. Six typed rows decide the service line of every hour that reaches a report through a crew.

Two lists of six that overlap on five. The roster uses 6 distinct crew codes across its 7 technician rows, the map holds 6 crew codes, and only 5 of them appear on both sides. That is the same shape as DimAircraft earlier in this chapter, where the registry held 6 tails and the work orders referenced 5 and the union came to 7. The difference is that the registry has a keeper at the customer service desk. The crew map has you.

Read the two red rows, because they are the two ways a mapping table goes wrong and they point in opposite directions. CRW-XX9 is on the roster and missing from the map, so the 10.0 hours TECH-07 booked to WO-1004 have no crew name and no service line. That is 16.1 percent of the quarter, computed as 10.0 divided by 62.0, against a visual whose total still reads a correct 62.0. Look back at Table 3.12 and you will find the same technician in the red row there: FactLabor books hours to TECH-07 and the HR extract has never heard of him. The roster system is the one list that does know him, and it puts him on CRW-XX9. So two lists have a hole, the HR extract and the crew map, and both holes sit on the same 10.0 hours.

CRW-LT2 is the other direction. Light Maintenance B is in the map and no technician is assigned to it, so it contributes nothing to any measure. A dimension member with no facts is ordinary and this chapter has already kept two of them on purpose, PHX with its 16 planned hours and no work orders, and N120CE with no activity at all. What separates those from CRW-LT2 is ownership. PHX sits in a workbook the resource manager maintains, so you can ask him whether Phoenix is a real station and get an answer. Nobody maintains the crew map, so nobody can tell you whether Light Maintenance B is a crew that exists and is currently unstaffed, or a crew that was disbanded last spring and never deleted. The row is evidence that the map and the roster have drifted, and the evidence has been sitting there quietly.

Common mistake

Tidying the map. A row with no hours against it looks like clutter, so during a cleanup somebody deletes CRW-LT2 and the file gets shorter. What went with it was the only visible sign that the typed map no longer matches the roster. The next report reads clean, and the question of whether Light Maintenance B still exists is now unaskable, because there is nothing left to ask about. Keep the row. Let the check flag it every refresh until a human answers.

So hold the map as a proper table with a proper build, the same as every other dimension in this chapter. Seven steps, and the last one happens outside Power Query altogether.

  1. Move the map into a workbook in a shared location, on one worksheet, formatted as a named Excel table called CrewCodeMap with the three columns it has today.
  2. Create a query parameter called CrewMapPath holding the full path to that file, so the path lives in one place a person can see.
  3. Load the named table, set the three columns to text, trim the crew code and the service line, and drop any row with a blank crew code.
  4. Assert that the crew code is unique and fail the refresh when it is not.
  5. Reference that query and append a labelled row for every crew code the roster uses that the map has no entry for. This is the DimAircraft append from earlier in this chapter, done again on a different key.
  6. Build the exception query, load it, and put it on a page the resource scheduler actually opens.
  7. Write down who owns the map and how a change to it gets agreed.
MCrewCodeMapSource
let
    // one workbook, one named table, one owner
    Source =
        Excel.Workbook(
            File.Contents( CrewMapPath ), true ),

    Map =
        Source{[ Item = "CrewCodeMap",
                 Kind = "Table" ]}[Data],

    Typed =
        Table.TransformColumnTypes( Map,
            {{"CrewCode", type text},
             {"CrewName", type text},
             {"ServiceLine", type text}} ),

    Trimmed =
        Table.TransformColumns( Typed,
            {{"CrewCode", Text.Trim, type text},
             {"ServiceLine", Text.Trim, type text}} ),

    NoBlanks =
        Table.SelectRows( Trimmed,
            each [CrewCode] <> null
                 and [CrewCode] <> "" ),

    CrewCodeMapSource =
        if Table.IsDistinct(
               Table.SelectColumns( NoBlanks, {"CrewCode"} ) )
        then NoBlanks
        else error "CrewCodeMap: duplicate crew code"
in
    CrewCodeMapSource
CrewMapPath
A query parameter and not a path typed into the step. The file will move, because files that people edit always move, and a parameter turns that into one edit in a dialog instead of a hunt through M under time pressure. Note where the file has to live: somewhere the resource scheduler can open it. A mapping only one person can reach has already failed, whatever the query does.
Kind = "Table"
Point at a named Excel table inside the workbook, not at the worksheet. Kind = "Sheet" reads the used range, so the day somebody types a note two rows under the data, that note arrives as a crew code with a null service line. A named table has an edge the person editing the file can see on screen, which is the only kind of boundary a hand maintained file ever respects.
Trimmed
Both text columns, for the reason this chapter keeps repeating. "CRW-LT1 " and "CRW-LT1" are one crew code to your eye and two to a join. A person typing into a spreadsheet produces trailing spaces the way a system never does, and ServiceLine gets the same treatment because it is the value every planning visual groups by.
Table.IsDistinct and error
The Making it fail note above said to reserve a hard refresh failure for a dimension you control end to end. This is that dimension. TECH-07 and WO-1009 are orphans the business tolerates, so blocking a refresh over them would be wrong. A crew code typed twice is your own defect in your own file. It fans every technician on that crew across two rows. Stop the refresh and fix the file.
Why not an inline table
DimStation keeps its four station names in an inline #table written into the query, and that was defensible: four rows, no other editor, no expected change. The crew map fails both halves of that test. The resource scheduler has to be able to read it, and the row that is missing today can only be filled in by him. A mapping that changes on somebody else's schedule belongs in data, where they can reach it.

The second query is short enough to describe. Reference CrewCodeMapSource, run the coverage check to find the crew codes the roster uses that the map has no row for, add CrewName as "Unknown crew" and ServiceLine as "Unmapped", and append. That is the move that recovered N338WA into DimAircraft, applied to a different key. The loaded CrewCodeMap then has 7 rows, and the 10.0 hours reach a report under a label somebody can click instead of a blank somebody scrolls past.

Now the check, and it is the piece most people never write. Point fnMissingKeys at the crew code in both directions.

MCrewMapExceptions
let
    NotMapped =
        fnMissingKeys( CrewAssignment, "CrewCode",
            CrewCodeMapSource, "CrewCode" ),

    NotStaffed =
        fnMissingKeys( CrewCodeMapSource, "CrewCode",
            CrewAssignment, "CrewCode" ),

    Flagged =
        Table.AddColumn( NotMapped, "Issue",
            each "On the roster, missing from the map",
            type text ),

    Idle =
        Table.AddColumn( NotStaffed, "Issue",
            each "In the map, nobody assigned to it",
            type text ),

    CrewMapExceptions =
        Table.Combine( {Flagged, Idle} )
in
    CrewMapExceptions
Called twice
The first call is the ordinary coverage check from the previous section, keys used against keys allowed. The second call swaps the arguments, which the EXCEPT box earlier in this chapter described as the classic error, returning dimension members with no facts, a usually harmless condition. On a table you type by hand it is the interesting one. It is how you learn that the map has stopped matching the roster while every number on every page still adds up.
CrewCodeMapSource
Point the check at the typed file, before the recovered row is appended. Run it against the loaded CrewCodeMap instead and it returns nothing at all, because that table already contains a row for CRW-XX9 that the query invented. A dimension that heals itself hides the gap it healed. Check the source, load the healed version, and never let the two swap places.
Issue
Two plain English sentences instead of a code or a flag. The person who can fix either row reads a page, not your query, and "On the roster, missing from the map" tells him what to do without a legend. A column called ExceptionType holding 1 and 2 would need you in the room.
Table.Combine
Both tables carry CrewCode and Issue under the same names, so the append stacks them into one list. Same rule as the station union at the top of this chapter. Table.Combine aligns on column name, so a rename in one branch and not the other gives you two half empty columns and a result that looks fine in the preview.

Here is the part the query cannot do. The check tells you CRW-XX9 exists and is unmapped. It cannot tell you whether that crew does light work or heavy work, and no amount of M will decide it, because the fact is not in any file you can read. Somebody in the roster office knows. Until you ask, the honest label for those 10.0 hours is Unmapped, and a report that shows an Unmapped row is doing its job. The technical fix makes the gap visible. The gap itself closes in a conversation.

That is the governance point, and it is worth stating flatly because it is the one thing in this chapter you cannot solve with a query. This map has no owner, no change control and no test. Without an owner, the day a new crew code is issued nobody is responsible for adding it, and your first warning is a blank row in a meeting. Without change control, nobody records who changed a service line or when, so a number that moved between two months has no explanation anybody can retrieve. Without a test, both kinds of drift stay invisible: codes arriving upstream that never reach the map, and rows in the map that stopped meaning anything. A mapping table with those three holes in it rots quietly, one row at a time, while every total on every page keeps reconciling. Nothing breaks, so nothing gets escalated.

So fix it in the shop as well as in the model. Name a person in resource scheduling who owns the crew list, and get his agreement in writing that a new crew code comes with a service line on the day it is issued. Put CrewMapExceptions in front of him on the same cadence as the month end submission, since he is already looking at hours then. Add two columns to the file that the model will never load, one for who last changed the row and one for when. None of that is Power Query, and all of it is the reason the map still works in a year. The most fragile object in a Meridian dashboard is six rows long, it lives in a spreadsheet, and the tool that keeps it alive is a named human being.

Which answers the resource manager, most of the way. The unlabelled 10.0 belongs to TECH-07, whose crew code is CRW-XX9, and after the append the row on his visual reads Unknown crew instead of nothing. Which service line those hours belong to is a question for the roster office, and you can now put it to them in one sentence with the number attached.

Reference, duplicate, and keeping staging out of the model

Everything above depends on one habit. Use Reference, not Duplicate, when a query starts from another query's output. Duplicate copies the M script, so you get two scripts that agree today and drift the first time somebody fixes a type conversion in one of them. Reference points at the upstream result instead, so a change made once flows downstream to everything built on it.

A reference re-evaluates, and that is the cost you pay. Each downstream query triggers its own run of the upstream chain, so three references over WorkOrders can mean three reads of the source. On eight rows that is free. On eight million rows it is expensive, and the fix is a staging layer that lands the data once. Chapter 5 covers that layer along with query folding. Turn off Enable load on every staging query. A query with load disabled still runs during refresh and still feeds its consumers. What it stops doing is occupying model memory and offering report authors a half finished table to build visuals on.

Performance note

Built dimensions are small: DimStation 5 rows, DimPart 4, DimAircraft 7, DimDate 90. Storage is the smaller bill here. The one you pay is refresh time. Every union re-reads its sources, so the station list alone touches WorkOrders, Technicians and ShopCapacity again, on top of the reads that load the facts. Set that against a breakdown which quietly excludes 12.0 of 62.0 hours and it is an easy trade. Set it against a source that takes four minutes to query and you will want the staging layer first.

What to remember
  • A dimension needs four properties: a unique key, no blank in the key, complete coverage of every key value in every fact that references it, and stability of meaning across refreshes. Coverage is the one people miss.
  • Build the key list from the union of every source that produces the key. At Meridian only ShopCapacity knows PHX exists, and only WorkOrders knows N338WA exists.
  • An unmatched fact key keeps its measure and loses its label. Labor hours by aircraft type totals 62.0 either way, and with the incomplete registry the visible types sum to 50.0 while 12.0 sits in a blank row.
  • Fill unknown text attributes with a readable label, leave unknown numeric attributes blank so nothing averages them.
  • A bridge is a relationship stored as a table. It has no measures and no unique key, it belongs hidden, and it makes category subtotals exceed the grand total by design.
  • Build the small dimensions too. DimWOType holds three rows that were already on the fact, and what it buys is a stable slicer list, a non-alphabetical sort order and one place to say what AOG means.
  • Every built table gets the same treatment as a source table: a grain sentence, a candidate key check, and then a coverage check per relationship. Fourteen of the sixteen key relationships in the core model come back clean, and the two that do not are TECH-07 and WO-1009.
  • Conformed means one query decides what a station is, not that two station lists currently agree. Checking DimStation against FactWorkOrder alone passes and still loses PHX and its 16 planned hours.
  • The one table in this model that no system produces is CrewCodeMap, six rows you type yourself, and it decides the service line of every hour that reaches a report through a crew. CRW-XX9 is missing from it, so 10.0 of the 62.0 hours land unmapped, and CRW-LT2 sits in it with nobody assigned. Give it an owner first, then a labelled unknown member, then a check that runs in both directions.
  • Mark as Date Table gives time intelligence functions an implicit REMOVEFILTERS across the whole date table. Skip it and year to date measures silently inherit filters from your own month and year columns.
  • Power Query is the right home for a built dimension. The DAX calculated table is the fallback for when the queries are out of your control, and it hides the logic from anyone auditing the model.
Part 2 . Shaping the data

04Power Query or DAX: deciding where work belongs

After this chapter you will be able to take any transformation request, place it in one of four layers, and say out loud what that choice costs at refresh time and at query time. You will also be able to check whether your Power Query steps are still being pushed back to the source, and fix the ones that are not.

The production controller stops at your desk at nine in the morning. He wants the work order board grouped by how long each job took: under a week, one to two weeks, over two weeks. You already have turn days working. You wrote it last week as a measure, which is a DAX formula Power BI works out fresh every time a visual asks for it. Now you try to put those turn time buckets on the axis of a chart, and Power BI will not let you. Nothing is broken. The calculation is sitting in the wrong layer.

You asked when to use DAX and when to use Power Query in the cases where both would work. That is most cases. Either tool will strip the trailing space from TECH-04 in row L-505, derive the category Brakes out of the BRK-2210 prefix, and work out that WO-1003 took 22 days to turn. Both tools give you the same number. What separates them is when the work runs, how many times it runs, and how much of the world the work can see while it runs.

Four places the work can happen

Every transformation in a Power BI solution lands in one of four layers. They run in a fixed order. Each layer can see things the layer before it could not. Knowing the order is most of the skill. Once you can say where a piece of logic runs, you can say what it costs.

1. The source system, before Power BI is involved

A view in the shop floor database, a computed column in the timesheet system, a corrected data type agreed with the vendor. Work here is done once, by an engine designed for set based work. The result is then available to every report that reads that table, including reports nobody has built yet. If someone else builds a report on the same timesheet table next quarter, they inherit your fix for free. This is the cheapest layer to run and the most expensive layer to get access to. At Meridian it is mostly closed: the WorkOrders extract arrives as a file, the fleet list is a spreadsheet kept by the customer service desk, and ShopCapacity is a planning workbook that a scheduler edits by hand. You cannot push a computed column into a workbook. That is a real limit and it is worth naming early. Half the advice in this chapter only becomes usable the day someone gives you a connection to the system behind the export.

2. Power Query, at refresh

M runs when the semantic model refreshes. A refresh is the scheduled or manual reload that pulls current data out of the source and rebuilds the model from it. Whatever M produces is handed to the storage engine, encoded, sorted and compressed. From that moment it is indistinguishable from a column that came straight out of the source. Power Query is where reshaping belongs: unpivoting, splitting, appending, trimming, deriving row level attributes, building small dimensions. The cost is paid once per refresh and never again.

3. DAX calculated columns and calculated tables, at model load

These are evaluated after the imported data has landed, in the pass usually called process recalc. They can see the whole model, including relationships, which M cannot: RELATED works in a calculated column and has no equivalent in Power Query without a merge. The result is materialised and stored in the model, so it costs memory and it costs refresh time, every refresh.

4. DAX measures, at query time

Nothing is stored. The expression is evaluated when a visual asks for a value, inside whatever filter context the report has produced at that instant. Filter context is the set of filters in force at that moment: the slicers the user clicked, the row and column headings of the visual, and anything else narrowing the data. A slicer is the button, list or date range on a report page that a user clicks to filter it. This is the only layer that can see what the user selected. It is also the only layer that runs again every time anyone touches anything.

Read that diagram as a timeline running left to right. Each band has already finished by the time the band to its right begins. That is why a measure can use a Power Query column and a Power Query step can never use a measure. The three Power BI bands each name the moment they run: at refresh, at load and at query time. The axis underneath turns those moments into a price. At the left hand end the work is computed once, per refresh. At the right hand end it is computed per visual, per user, per click.

The picture leaves one thing for you to carry in your head. Each layer can see a different amount of the world. The source knows nothing about your model. Power Query knows about one query and whatever it merges in. A calculated column knows the whole model and knows nothing about the report page. Only the measure layer can see the slicers. Sight and cost run in the same direction, and that is the reason the order is worth memorising. The line above the green card, push work as far left as you can and then move it right for one reason only, is the rule stated below in upstream and downstream terms. The green card itself is that one reason.

The principle, and why it holds

Rule of thumb

Push each piece of work as far upstream as it will go, because upstream work is computed once and downstream work is computed again for every visual, every user and every interaction.

The arithmetic behind that sentence is dull and decisive. Deriving PartCategory from the prefix of PartNumber in Power Query runs 7 times per refresh, once for each row in PartsIssued, and the answer sits in DimPart as 4 rows afterwards. Deriving the same category inside a measure runs whenever a visual needs it: on the parts page, on every drill through, for the scheduler and the shop manager and the customer service desk, at nine in the morning when all three of them open the report at once. The logic stayed exactly as simple. What changed is the number of times it ran.

There is a second reason, quieter but more important on large models. A column produced in Power Query is compressed by VertiPaq along with everything else in the table. VertiPaq is the storage engine inside Power BI that keeps imported data column by column, and its compression is what makes the model fast. A value computed at query time is never compressed, because it never exists until the query asks for it. Upstream work becomes part of the compressed structure. Downstream work has to be rebuilt on top of it.

Meridian will not make you feel any of this. The finished model is 8 work order rows plus 8 labor rows plus 7 parts rows plus 28 capacity rows plus 10 bridge rows plus 90 date rows plus the dimensions at 7, 5, 7, 4, 3 and 4 rows. That totals 181 rows in the entire model. Every choice in this chapter runs instantly at that size. You are learning the discipline here so that it is already a habit the day the timesheet extract arrives with millions of rows and a four minute refresh turns into forty.

The exception, which is the real dividing line

The planner set the baseline three weeks ago and is now being asked why average turn days moved. She filters the report to MSP and reads 15.0 days. She clears the filter and reads 12.0 days. Both numbers came out of the same model on the same afternoon. Both are correct. Here is why one stored column could never have produced both.

The upstream principle on its own is wrong. Follow it blindly and you produce reports that lie. Work has to move downstream whenever the result depends on what the user selected. Anything a slicer can change cannot be precomputed, because at refresh time nobody has clicked anything yet.

Interview-level insight

Forget the lists of tasks. The question that decides the layer is: can a slicer change this number? If the answer is yes, the number does not exist until query time, and no amount of upstream cleverness can precompute it. Everything else in this chapter is a refinement of that one test.

Turn time on a work order shows both sides of the line in the same calculation. WO-1003 opened on 2025-01-14 and closed on 2025-02-05, which is 22 days. That 22 is a property of the row. It holds whether the user filters to MSP, to March, or to AOG work. It belongs upstream, as a column. Average turn days across closed work orders is a different animal. Across all six closed work orders it is 12.0 days, from a sum of 72 over 6 orders. Filter the report to MSP and the closed work orders are WO-1001 at 10 days, WO-1002 at 5 days and WO-1006 at 30 days. The average becomes 45 divided by 3, which is 15.0 days. Two numbers from one dataset, both correct, and only a measure can produce the second one.

That is the planner's pair of numbers. Her 12.0 and her 15.0 are the same measure read under two filter contexts, which is why nobody moved the baseline. It also answers the production controller from the opening of this chapter. Turn days on one work order is a property of the row, so it belongs in Power Query as a stored column. Once it is stored, you can bucket it, put the buckets on an axis, and count work orders in each bucket. A measure could only ever have printed the number in a card.

The procedure, in the order to run it

  1. Ask whether the answer changes when the user changes a slicer. If it does, it is a measure. Stop here, the remaining questions do not apply.
  2. Check whether it is a row level attribute that you will group by, filter on, sort by, or join on. If it is, it belongs in Power Query as a column. Axes, slicers and relationships all need a stored column to point at.
  3. Ask whether the calculation needs values sitting in the current filter context of another table, for example planned hours from FactCapacity beside actual hours from FactLabor. That combination only exists at query time, so it is a measure.
  4. Decide whether the thing has to exist before relationships are built: a key, a dimension member, an Unknown row. Put it in Power Query. A relationship can be built on a calculated column and it will work, but you have then stored the key twice. The dirty version stays in the model for someone else to pick up by mistake.
  5. Ask whether it is a table that depends on other model tables and could never have been produced upstream, such as a what-if scenario table. That is a DAX calculated table, and you accept that it is rebuilt on every refresh.

Run the questions in that order and take the first match. The order matters because question one dominates everything else. A late flag looks like a row level attribute, and it is one. Then somebody asks for a tolerance slicer that changes the definition of late. The flag stops being an attribute and becomes a measure. Upstream discipline will not save you there.

Fifteen decisions, with the failure mode attached

Three of those rows deserve their function named. Naming a function without a reason is how bad habits spread.

Ranking technicians uses RANKX and not TOPN. TOPN returns a table of the best n rows and never produces a rank number you can put on a visual. RANKX returns a position for the current row in the current filter context, which is what a rank on a visual means.

Year to date hours uses CALCULATE with DATESYTD. TOTALYTD is shorter and it hides the CALCULATE inside itself. It does accept an extra filter argument, but that argument is positional and sits next to an optional year end date. The next person reading the formula cannot see what is filtering what. The explicit form puts the context modification on the page where it can be read. CALCULATE and not a plain filter expression, because only CALCULATE can replace the filter context that the visual has already applied.

If you ever do build turn days as a measure rather than as a column, use DATEDIFF with the DAY interval. Subtracting one date from the other carries the time component with it and hands you a decimal that then needs rounding. DATEDIFF states its unit in the code where the next reader can see it. Average turn days over a stored column uses AVERAGE and not AVERAGEX, because there is nothing left to iterate once the value sits on the row.

Query folding, and how to tell whether you still have it

The planner messages you at seven in the morning. The overnight refresh has gone from four minutes to forty, her report was still building when she needed it, and nobody changed the data. You changed something. You added one step to the labor query on Friday afternoon. That step is the reason, and the reason has a name.

Query folding
The mechanism by which Power Query translates your applied steps into a single native query and sends that to the source, instead of downloading the table and doing the work locally.
Materialised
Stored as real values in memory. Imported columns and calculated columns are materialised, so they occupy space. A measure is computed on demand and stores nothing.
Process recalc
The pass after data load in which the engine evaluates calculated columns, calculated tables and hierarchies, in dependency order.

Filter LaborEntries to Q1 2025 against a real database and Power Query writes a SQL statement with a WHERE clause. The database runs it. Only the Q1 rows ever cross the network. That is folding, and it matters for three reasons that all point the same way: the source is better at set based work than the mashup engine is, far less data travels, and the source can use its own indexes on your behalf. A folded query on a large table is often an order of magnitude faster than the same steps evaluated locally. It is the single biggest refresh lever you have.

To check, right click the last applied step and look at View Native Query. If it is available, everything up to that step folded and you can read the SQL. If it is greyed out, folding has already stopped. Click back up the step list until the option becomes available again; the first step where it goes grey is the one that broke it. This is the whole diagnostic, and it takes twenty seconds.

Folding is a prefix property. Once a step breaks it, everything after that step runs locally, no matter how foldable those later steps look on their own. That gives you the practical rule: filter rows and remove columns first, while folding is still alive. Put the index column, the buffer and your clever custom function at the end, where they can only slow down a table that is already small.

MFactLabor, ordered to keep folding
// Filter and drop columns first, while folding is still alive.
let
    Source  = Sql.Database("shopfloor01", "MRO"),
    Labor   = Source{[Schema="dbo", Item="LaborEntries"]}[Data],
    Kept    = Table.SelectColumns(Labor,
        {"LaborID", "WorkOrderID", "TechnicianID",
         "WorkDate", "Hours", "HourlyRate"}),
    Q1      = Table.SelectRows(Kept, each
        [WorkDate] >= #date(2025, 1, 1) and
        [WorkDate] <= #date(2025, 3, 31)),
    Trimmed = Table.TransformColumns(Q1,
        {{"TechnicianID", Text.Trim, type text}})
in
    Trimmed
Lines 2 to 4
The let block opens, then the connection on line 3 and the table on line 4. Nothing has been fetched yet; M is lazy and only executes when the result is demanded.
Lines 5 to 7
Column removal goes first. It becomes the SELECT list, so the six columns you keep are the only ones that ever cross the network.
Lines 8 to 10
The date filter becomes a WHERE clause. It is written as an explicit range, because a plain comparison is the form the connector translates most reliably. A date helper function is where folding often stops.
Lines 11 to 12
The trim that fixes L-505. Text.Trim and not a text replace of every space, because replacing spaces would also destroy any key that legitimately contains one. Against SQL Server this folds to a trim in the native query. Against another connector, check View Native Query before you assume anything.

The order in that query is the whole lesson. Move the trim to the top and it still gives the right answer. On a large table you may have pulled every column and every year across the wire to get it.

That is the planner's forty minute refresh. The step you added on Friday was an index column, and an index column cannot fold. Because folding is a prefix property, every step after it stopped folding too, including the date filter that used to keep the whole quarter at the source. Move the index column to the end of the query, behind the filter and the column removal, and the database goes back to doing the heavy work.

What a calculated column actually costs

A DAX calculated column appears the instant you type it in a model of a few hundred rows, so most people treat it as free. It costs memory and it costs refresh time, every single refresh. The reason is worth stating plainly.

Performance note

A calculated column is materialised into the model exactly like an imported one, so it consumes memory. It is also usually compressed less effectively, because the engine loads and compresses the imported columns first and picks a segment sort order based on what it can see at that moment. Your calculated column is evaluated after that sort has been chosen, so the sort was never optimised for it. How much worse the compression turns out to be depends entirely on the data, so measure your own model before you quote a ratio. On DimDate at 90 rows this is noise. On a labor table of tens of millions of rows it can be the difference between a model that fits in memory and one that does not.

There are two more costs that surprise people. First, a calculated column is recomputed on refresh and on any model change. That is why adding an innocent measure to a large model sometimes triggers a wait you did not ask for. Second, a calculated column that reads another table creates a dependency. The engine must finish that table before it can evaluate your column. Chain a few of these together and process recalc has to walk the chain in order. Picture a column on FactLabor that reads DimTechnician, and a column on DimTechnician that reads DimStation. Nothing here is catastrophic on its own. Together they turn a refresh you understood into one you have to investigate.

What a measure costs, which is the mirror image

A measure stores nothing, so it adds not one byte to the model. It pays for that at the other end. It is evaluated when a visual asks, and it is asked often. Put technicians on the rows of a matrix and months on the columns. DimTechnician has 7 rows and Q1 has 3 months, so that is 7 times 3, or 21 body cells. Add 7 row subtotals, 3 column subtotals and the grand total, and one measure has produced 32 values in one visual. Add a second visual and a slicer. Then multiply by however many people have the report open.

Be careful with how you picture that. The engine is smarter than the cell count suggests: for a simple aggregation it will often satisfy the whole matrix with one or two storage engine scans and slice the results up afterwards. The cell count becomes real when the measure manipulates filter context in ways the engine cannot batch, and that is where badly written CALCULATE logic hurts. A measure that forces per cell evaluation over a large fact table is the most common cause of a report that feels slow without any single thing looking wrong.

The middle case nobody argues about honestly

The finance manager wants one number for the month: what labor cost. He does not care which table it comes from, and he should not have to. On the face of it this is the easiest request in the chapter, and it is the case that sits exactly on the fence. FactLabor has Hours and HourlyRate on every row. Line cost is one multiplication. You can store it as a Power Query column, or you can never store it and let a measure do the multiplication at query time.

DAXLabor Cost
Labor Cost =
SUMX (
    FactLabor,
    FactLabor[Hours] * FactLabor[HourlyRate]
)
Why this and not that

SUMX and not SUM, because SUM takes a single column and there is no single column here to sum. The product has to be formed row by row before anything can be added up, and SUMX is the iterator that creates that row context. If you had stored a LineCost column in Power Query then SUM would be correct and SUMX would be pointless extra machinery, which is exactly the trade being argued below.

The case for storing the column: the multiplication happens once per refresh instead of on every query, and a plain SUM over a stored column is a pure scan with no expression to evaluate. On a very large fact table that difference is measurable.

The case against: the stored column costs memory, and it costs more than people expect. Cardinality means the number of distinct values in a column. The cardinality of a product is roughly the cardinality of hours multiplied by the cardinality of rates, and high cardinality columns are the expensive ones in a columnar model. Meridian has 8 distinct line costs, so this is invisible here. In a real timesheet table LineCost is often one of the worst compressing columns in the model. The stored column also cannot respond to a what-if rate slicer, ever, because it was computed before anyone selected anything.

DAXLabor Cost at Scenario Rate
Labor Cost at Scenario Rate =
VAR ScenarioRate =
    SELECTEDVALUE ( 'Rate Scenario'[Rate] )
RETURN
    IF (
        ISBLANK ( ScenarioRate ),
        [Labor Cost],
        SUMX ( FactLabor, FactLabor[Hours] * ScenarioRate )
    )
Lines 2 to 3
Read the single rate the user selected. SELECTEDVALUE and not VALUES. VALUES returns a table, and it throws an error the moment more than one value is in context. SELECTEDVALUE returns blank in that same situation and lets you decide what to do about it. Not MIN either, because MIN would silently pick a value when the user has selected several and hide the ambiguity.
Lines 5 to 7
ISBLANK and not a comparison to zero, because in DAX a blank compares equal to zero and a scenario rate of zero is a selection a user could legitimately make. Line 7 falls back to the real Labor Cost measure, so the visual shows actuals until somebody moves the slicer.
Line 8
The scenario branch multiplies hours by the selected rate and ignores HourlyRate entirely. This is the line a stored LineCost column can never produce.
Trace both versions by hand, row by row

Eight rows, one multiplication each. The stored column would hold the right hand values below and SUM would add them. The measure forms them at query time and adds them in the same pass.

Now set the scenario rate to a flat 100 per hour. The measure returns 62.0 times 100, which is 6,200.00, so the scenario sits 126.50 below the actual 6,326.50 (6,326.50 minus 6,200.00). A stored LineCost column returns 6,326.50 no matter where the slicer is, because the numbers in the fourth column above were fixed at refresh time.

So what should you actually do. Store the column when the inputs are immutable and the row level arithmetic is simple. A closed period fits that description: HourlyRate is the rate that was billed and nobody is going to reprice history. Use SUMX the moment the rate could ever be parameterised. Retrofitting a what-if onto a stored column means rewriting every measure that already depends on it.

For the finance manager's monthly number, both versions print 6,326.50 and he will never know which one you built. Choose for the request that comes after his. The day somebody asks what the month would have cost at a flat 100 per hour, only the measure can answer, and the answer is 6,200.00.

The storage argument is also weaker than it used to be. SUMX over a multiplication of two columns in the same table is one of the patterns the storage engine handles well. It can do the arithmetic inside the scan without materialising an intermediate table, so you are paying for a scan you were going to pay for anyway. The stored column usually wins only on very large fact tables. Even then, the compression penalty on a high cardinality product eats into the gain. This decision is genuinely close. A colleague who argues the other side with a measured refresh time and a measured query time in front of them is probably right for their model.

The lookup that should have been a relationship

The shift supervisor tells you the report is wrong. His whiteboard says TECH-04 booked 10.5 hours this week. Your technician page says 6.0. He is right, you are wrong, and the cause is one calculated column that somebody wrote to avoid building a relationship.

Common mistake

Adding a calculated column to a fact table that pulls an attribute across with LOOKUPVALUE, instead of building the relationship. It is the single most common symptom of a model whose author has not committed to the star schema. It is usually written by someone who could not get the relationship to work and quietly went around it.

DAXThe column you should not write
// Calculated column on FactLabor. Do not do this.
TechName =
LOOKUPVALUE (
    DimTechnician[TechnicianName],
    DimTechnician[TechnicianID], FactLabor[TechnicianID]
)
Line 2
A new stored column on the fact table, duplicating text that already exists once per technician in the dimension. On 8 labor rows that is 8 copies of a name. On a large fact table it is millions of copies of a string that VertiPaq already stored efficiently in one small dimension.
Lines 3 to 6
A filtered scan of DimTechnician for every row of FactLabor at process recalc, with no relationship to make it cheap. It also fails hard: L-505 with its untrimmed key returns blank, and if two dimension rows ever matched the same key the expression raises an error rather than picking one.
Everything
The deeper damage is that no relationship exists, so filter context never propagates. Slicing by HomeStation, by EmployeeType or through BridgeTechCert is impossible, and the 10.0 orphan hours from TECH-07 disappear into a blank with nothing to catch them.

The fix is not a better formula. Trim the key in Power Query. Add the Unknown row for TECH-07. Build the relationship from DimTechnician[TechnicianID] to FactLabor[TechnicianID]. Then drag TechnicianName onto the visual straight from the dimension. No column is required at all, and TECH-04 comes back to 10.5 hours, which is the number on the supervisor's whiteboard. If you genuinely need the value materialised on the fact row, for example to sort a fact level visual by an attribute, then this is what it should look like.

DAXOnly if the value must sit on the row
HomeStation = RELATED ( DimTechnician[HomeStation] )
Why this and not that

RELATED and not LOOKUPVALUE, because RELATED follows a relationship that already exists in the model. The engine resolves it through the many to one path it has already built, so it is cheaper, and it cannot silently disagree with what the rest of the model does. LOOKUPVALUE performs an independent filtered lookup with no relationship behind it. That means it works in places RELATED cannot, for example matching on a column pair that is not the relationship key. That case is the only one where reaching for it is defensible. If RELATED will not compile, the honest reading is that your relationship is missing or inactive, and that is the thing to fix.

One last honest note

None of these choices will change a single millisecond on 181 rows. You could put every calculation in this chapter in the wrong layer and Meridian would still render instantly. That is what makes it a good place to build the habit and a bad place to test it. The moment your model stops being a teaching set, the cheapest diagnostic you own is the question at the top of the procedure, asked before you write anything: can a slicer change this number.

What to remember
  • Work happens in four layers that run in order: the source, Power Query at refresh, calculated columns and tables at model load, measures at query time. Each layer sees more than the one before and costs more to run.
  • Push work as far upstream as it will go, because upstream work runs once and downstream work runs for every visual, every user and every interaction.
  • The exception overrides the principle: anything a slicer can change cannot be precomputed, so it is a measure. Ask that question first and take the first match.
  • Row level attributes used to group, filter, sort or relate belong in Power Query, along with keys, unknown members and anything that must exist before relationships are built.
  • Folding means your steps are executed by the source. Check with View Native Query, remember it is a prefix property, and do filtering and column removal before anything that breaks it.
  • Calculated columns are materialised, compress less well because they are computed after the segment sort is chosen, and are rebuilt on every refresh and model change.
  • Measures store nothing and pay for it at query time, which is fine until filter context manipulation forces evaluation cell by cell.
  • LineCost is a genuinely close call. Store it when the rate is fixed history, compute it with SUMX when the rate could ever become a parameter.
  • A LOOKUPVALUE column on a fact table is almost always a relationship someone gave up on.
Part 2 . Shaping the data

05Power Query mechanics that matter for modelling

By the end of this chapter you will be able to predict the exact row count that comes out of every unpivot, append, merge and group in the Meridian load, and you will know which of those steps quietly changes the meaning of a number that is already on a report page.

The finance manager wants one number: what has the shop quoted this quarter. You put a card on the page and it reads 53,600. He has the quotes in front of him and says the figure is 38,100. Nothing in the report shows an error, and every work order looks correct when you drill into it. The card is still wrong by 15,500. A merge you built in the query editor last week is counting two work orders twice.

Most Power Query training is a tour of the ribbon. Your problem is narrower than that. A handful of these transformations change the grain of a table. Grain means what one row of a table stands for. One row of WorkOrders stands for one work order. One row of LaborEntries stands for the hours one technician booked on one day. Grain is the thing your model is built on, so get the grain wrong in the query editor and no amount of DAX will rescue the report.

This chapter works through the transformations that actually move the model: unpivot, append, merge and its six join kinds, expand versus aggregate, group by, and the query dependency choices that decide how often your source gets hit. Each one is also argued against its DAX equivalent. Most of them have one, and it usually returns the same number, which is exactly what makes the choice look optional. Every example runs on Meridian rows. Every row count is one you can check by hand against the source tables.

Unpivot: turning column headers back into data

The planner keeps ShopCapacity in a workbook and edits it by hand every month. She asks for a chart of planned hours by trade, which sounds like five minutes of work. In her workbook the trades are column headings, and a column heading cannot go on the axis of a chart. One step in the query editor turns those headings into data she can slice.

ShopCapacity arrives from the monthly planning workbook as a matrix. Someone in planning built it to be read by a human, so the trades run across the top.

Airframe, Avionics, Engine and NDT are four values of one attribute called Trade. The numbers under them are all the same measurement, planned hours. A model can only slice by a column, and here Trade is spread across four column names. No relationship can point at a column header either. Unpivot fixes both problems in one step.

MFactCapacity, the version that survives change
let
    Source = ShopCapacity,
    Unpivoted = Table.UnpivotOtherColumns(
        Source, {"StationCode", "Month"},
        "Attribute", "Value"),
    Renamed = Table.RenameColumns(Unpivoted, {
        {"Attribute", "Trade"},
        {"Value", "PlannedHours"}}),
    Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Renamed, {
        {"Trade", type text},
        {"PlannedHours", Int64.Type}})
in
    Typed
Line 3
Table.UnpivotOtherColumns takes the list of columns to keep. Everything you leave out of that list gets folded down into two new columns. Read that twice. You name the survivors, and the ribbon label suggests the opposite.
Line 5
The two literals name the output columns. The generated names are always Attribute and Value when you use the ribbon, which is why the next step exists.
Line 6
Rename immediately. Attribute becomes Trade because a column called Attribute tells a report reader nothing, and because a field list full of Attribute columns from four different queries is unusable.
Line 9
Type immediately. Unpivot returns Value as type any. An untyped numeric column will still sum, but it stores as a variant, compresses badly, and any implicit measure you build on it can silently become a text count.

Now the ribbon. The Transform tab offers three commands and their names do not map to the generated functions the way you would expect. Read the formula bar after every unpivot, because the formula bar is the only honest description of what you did.

Unpivot Only Selected Columns generates Table.Unpivot with the four trade names written into the step as a literal list. Unpivot Columns and Unpivot Other Columns both generate Table.UnpivotOtherColumns. They differ only in which columns you had highlighted when you clicked. So the practical test is the function name in the formula bar. Read that, and ignore the menu label you clicked to get there.

MThe hard coded variant, from Unpivot Only Selected Columns
let
    Source = ShopCapacity,
    Unpivoted = Table.Unpivot(
        Source,
        {"Airframe", "Avionics", "Engine", "NDT"},
        "Attribute", "Value")
in
    Unpivoted
Line 5
The trade list is frozen into the query. Today it produces the same 28 rows as the other version. Next month, when planning adds a Structures column to the workbook, this step unpivots the same four trades and carries Structures through as a fifth, still wide, column that nothing in the model reads.
Failure mode
No error, no warning. Planned capacity is understated and the utilisation measure quietly goes up, because the denominator lost hours.

The anchored version behaves the other way. Table.UnpivotOtherColumns names StationCode and Month. Those two are the grain keys, and they are the columns least likely to change. A new Structures column is absent from that list, so it gets unpivoted along with everything else and arrives as a new Trade value on the next refresh. That is why anchoring on keys is the default. You name the stable columns and let everything else flow through. The rule is short. Select the two key columns, use Unpivot Other Columns, and confirm the formula bar reads Table.UnpivotOtherColumns before you move on.

Common mistake

Assuming the auto-generated Changed Type step above the unpivot will catch a source change. It will stay silent and it will keep working. Table.TransformColumnTypes only touches the columns it names. When planning adds Structures, that step ignores it and passes it through as type any. Pair that with Unpivot Only Selected Columns and the refresh succeeds, the query still reports 176 planned hours, and an entire trade is missing from the model. A Changed Type step does fail loudly when a column it names is renamed or removed at source. A column being added is the quiet case.
