The only thing they lack is permission to carry a filter unless a measure asks for them by name. The card headed Why it matters puts the consequence in numbers: the same January selection returns 3 work orders by opened date and 2 by closed date.

Try to make a second one active and Power BI stops you. Depending on where you do it, you either get a refusal naming the existing active relationship, or, in the Manage relationships dialog, the tool deactivates the one that was active so that only one survives. Neither behaviour is arbitrary. Suppose two active paths ran from DimDate to FactWorkOrder. A filter of January against a count of work orders would then have two defensible answers, 3 by opened date and 2 by closed date, and the engine has no basis for preferring either. So it holds one path open and no more. The finance manager's three and the shift supervisor's two both live in that one table. Getting both onto one page means writing the second as a measure that names the dormant relationship. That refusal is a feature. It is also the same check that will bite you later, when a well meant extra relationship creates a second route between two tables you thought were connected one way.

To use a dormant relationship, name it inside a measure.

DAXWork Orders Closed
Work Orders Closed =
CALCULATE(
    COUNTROWS( FactWorkOrder ),
    USERELATIONSHIP( DimDate[Date], FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] ),
    NOT ISBLANK( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
)
Line 1
This has to be a measure. The relationship swap happens while a filter context exists, and a calculated column has no filter context at query time.
Line 2
CALCULATE rather than CALCULATETABLE because the result is a single number for a card or a matrix cell. Both accept the same modifiers; the only difference is scalar against table, and USERELATIONSHIP is valid in either.
Line 3
COUNTROWS, and not COUNT( FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID] ). COUNT counts non blank values in a column, so it silently changes meaning the day that column contains a blank. The question is how many work orders, which is a question about rows.
Line 4
The relationship swap. For the duration of this CALCULATE only, the closed date relationship becomes the active path from DimDate to FactWorkOrder and the opened date relationship steps aside. Nothing about the stored model changes.
Line 5
Excludes the two work orders with no closed date. Without it the measure returns 6 across the quarter and 2 in each of the three months. With no date filter at all it returns 8. The two unmatched rows attach to the blank row on DimDate, and that blank row is included whenever nothing filters the date table.
Why this and not that

USERELATIONSHIP rather than a second date table. Loading DimDate a second time and calling it DimClosedDate also works, and it has one real advantage: the two dates can then be sliced independently on the same page. The cost is that every date attribute exists twice, every slicer has to be duplicated, and a user who filters the quarter slicer is puzzled when half the page does not move. One date table with named relationships keeps a single slicer driving every date measure. Use the second table only when the report genuinely needs two independent date filters at once.

USERELATIONSHIP, and not CROSSFILTER. They look similar and do unrelated jobs. CROSSFILTER changes the direction of a relationship that is already active. It cannot wake a dormant one. Reach for it here and you get either no effect or an error, depending on what else is set.

NOT ISBLANK, and not a comparison against BLANK(). Comparing a column to blank drags in the engine's blank coercion rules, where blank equals zero for numeric types. Copy the same pattern onto an amount column later and it behaves in a way nobody expects. ISBLANK tests emptiness and nothing else.

Interview-level insight

A relationship is a design assertion about the data, and the engine will hold you to it. Most people add one so that a visual will work, which is how the assertion gets made by accident. Many to one asserts that a key is unique on the one side and stays unique through every future refresh. Single direction asserts that this dimension describes the fact, and that the fact says nothing back about the dimension. Active asserts that this, out of every possible route between these two tables, is the one route a report author gets without asking. Every one of those assertions is enforced. So when a relationship fails, look past the relationship. What changed is almost always the world the assertion described.

Four constraints people trip over

One column on each side, and no exceptions

The planner is back, and she wants planned hours beside booked hours, by station and by month. It takes two columns to identify a capacity row, station and month, and Power BI will only let you draw a relationship on one. So you build a key out of both parts. It works. By the end of this section you will have deleted it.

A relationship uses exactly one column on each side. There is no composite key relationship in Power BI. If your two tables share a two part key, you build a single column that holds both parts and relate on that.

Build it in Power Query, and put a separator between the parts. The separator does real work. Join part A straight onto part B and you get a string that another pair of parts could also produce. A station code of AB with a month of C gives the same result as a station code of A with a month of BC. In Meridian that collision cannot happen today. Every station code is three characters and every month key is six digits, so the split point is always in the same place. That safety is a property of the seven rows currently in the planning workbook. Your model does nothing to hold it there. The day somebody adds a two character code, every affected row joins to the wrong parent and nothing errors.

MFactCapacity, station and month composite key
let
    Source = ShopCapacityUnpivoted,
    AddKey = Table.AddColumn(
        Source,
        "StationMonthKey",
        each [StationCode] & "|" & Text.From([MonthKey]),
        type text
    )
in
    AddKey
Line 2
Starts from the unpivoted capacity table, so the key lands on all 28 rows and not on the 7 wide ones.
Line 3
Table.AddColumn rather than Table.TransformColumns because you want a new column beside the two originals. Keep the parts. You will need them for grouping, and a key you cannot decompose is a key you cannot debug.
Line 6
The pipe is the separator. It is chosen because it cannot occur in a station code or a month key, which is the only property a separator needs.
Line 6
Text.From, and not Number.ToText. The planning workbook has already changed the type of that column once. Text.From converts whatever arrives, where Number.ToText errors on anything that is not a number. Also not Text.Combine, which ignores null items and hands back a shorter string, so a row with a missing station code would produce a key that looks perfectly valid.
Line 7
The type is declared, not inferred. A column typed as any will not participate in a relationship, and the failure message does not mention typing.

Now the inconvenient part. You should not do this in Meridian. The composite key gives you MSP|202501, and four trade rows share that value, so it repeats inside FactCapacity. The capacity table would have to be the many side, and you would need a new seven row station month table on the one side. That table is a junk dimension nobody wants to slice by, sitting next to two dimensions that already cover the same ground. Station and month are independent of each other. DimStation and DimDate[MonthStart] filter FactCapacity correctly on their own, and between them they give the planner her report. Build a concatenated key when the parts genuinely cannot be separated into dimensions of their own. Not before.

Rule of thumb

Before you concatenate, try to decompose. A two part key usually means two dimensions, and two dimensions give the report author two independent slicers plus everything each dimension knows. A concatenated key gives one slicer full of strings like MSP|202501 that nobody can read and nobody can filter usefully.

Data types must match

A whole number key will not relate to a text key. The two columns can render identically in a table visual and still refuse to connect. The comparison happens on stored type, and the displayed text has no say in it. DimDate[MonthKey] holds 202501 as a whole number. Derive a month key on FactCapacity by taking the text "2025-01" and removing the dash, and what you have is the text "202501". The relationship dialog refuses to create the link. This is why the shipped model relates DimDate[MonthStart] to FactCapacity[MonthStart], both typed as date. No derived key comes into it.

Fix types in Power Query. A type change there is one operation applied during load, and the relationship is built directly on the loaded column. A calculated column adds a second stored column, materialised after load, and that column cannot fold back to the source.

The one side cannot contain blanks

The engine reserves the blank slot on the one side for its own use, so a genuine blank in your key column collides with something already sitting there. What the engine puts in that slot is the unknown member. When the many side holds a key value with no match on the one side, Power BI adds a blank row to the one side table and attaches the unmatched fact rows to it. That is deliberate design, and the reason for it is arithmetic. A total should never come out quietly smaller than the sum of its parts.

Meridian shows it in one place. FactParts contains issue P-9007 against WO-1009, and WO-1009 does not exist in FactWorkOrder. So FactWorkOrder carries a blank row and P-9007 hangs off it. Total parts cost is 28,245 whatever you do. Slice by anything that comes from the work order table, though, and the labelled rows add up to 23,345, with 4,900 sitting in an unlabelled blank row at the bottom of the visual. Report consumers scroll past that row. They have been trained to read blanks as noise.

The other blank in the dataset behaves differently and is worth separating. WO-1005 has no station code at all, which puts a blank on the many side of the station relationship. Many side blanks are allowed. They fall to the blank row on DimStation. The build handles this one by mapping the blank to an UNASSIGNED member, so the report shows a named row where an anonymous one would have sat. Labor hours by station then read MSP 34.5, TUS 22.5, LAS 5.0, UNASSIGNED 0 and PHX 0, totalling 62.0. Every one of those rows means something to a reader.

Circular paths are rejected

Power BI will not accept a set of active relationships that lets a filter leave a table and arrive back at it. It applies the same refusal to a set that gives one table two routes to another. Meridian has a live example, deliberately left out of the model. DimTechnician[HomeStation] holds station codes, and relating it to DimStation[StationCode] is tempting. Do that and DimStation can reach FactLabor two ways, once through FactWorkOrder and once through DimTechnician. Filtering to MSP would then mean either "labor on work orders raised at MSP" or "labor by technicians based at MSP". Two different questions, two different answers. Power BI will not choose between them, so it deactivates one of the paths. HomeStation stays as a plain descriptive column. If the shop later wants hours by the technician's home station, that is a measure, and Chapter 7 writes it.

Follow the two routes leaving DimStation on the left. Both arrive at FactLabor on the right, one across the top through FactWorkOrder and one across the bottom by way of DimTechnician. The top route is labelled path A and drawn solid. The lower one is labelled path B and drawn dashed, which is what the model looks like after the engine has refused to leave a second route active. The red card underneath is the reason. Select MSP and path A gives 34.5 hours, the work performed at that station, while path B gives 28.5, the hours booked by technicians based there. Both are defensible, and neither is what a bare MSP label on an axis promises. That is the shape the engine will not leave fully active. Train your eye to catch it in a diagram before the tool catches it for you. By the time the tool tells you, you are usually looking at a relationship that has been silently dormant for a fortnight.

Assume Referential Integrity

There is a checkbox on the relationship editor called Assume Referential Integrity. It appears only for DirectQuery relationships, where the model queries the source live at report time. Import mode never offers it. So if your model is fully imported you can skip this section, though you should still know what the checkbox does before somebody hands you a DirectQuery model to fix.

What it does is narrow and specific. It tells the engine that it may write an inner join in the native query it sends to the source. Without the checkbox the engine writes an outer join, which is what preserves unmatched fact rows. Inner joins let the source apply predicates earlier and ship fewer rows back. On a large DirectQuery fact that is a real difference.

It is safe when two things are true and provable: every key value on the many side exists on the one side, and the many side key is never blank. Not "usually true". Provable, by a constraint in the source or a check you run.

The consequence when it is not true is the reason this setting has a bad reputation. Rows that do not match are dropped by the inner join. No error is raised. No blank row appears, because there is nothing left to put in it. The number simply gets smaller. In Meridian, tick this box on the relationship from FactWorkOrder to FactParts in a DirectQuery model and P-9007 drops out entirely. Total parts cost goes from 28,245 to 23,345, with nothing anywhere to tell you that 4,900 has left the building. Now tick it on the station relationship, in a version of the model that has not yet mapped WO-1005's blank station code to UNASSIGNED. That work order disappears from every station sliced result, for the same reason. A blank many side key matches nothing, and an inner join has nowhere to put a row that matches nothing. Once the build maps the blank to a real member, the setting is safe on that relationship. That is a decent illustration of how narrow the safe case is. It depends on a Power Query step, and the checkbox knows nothing about Power Query steps.

Performance note

Assume Referential Integrity trades correctness for speed. Most settings only trade one cost for another, so treat this one with more care than the rest. If a DirectQuery model is slow, exhaust the ordinary work first: reduce the number of visuals on the page, push aggregations into the source, and check whether an import mode aggregation table over the DirectQuery detail would solve it outright. Come back to this checkbox last, and only for relationships where the source enforces the foreign key itself.

Deciding, in one table

One last note on the alternative to a physical relationship. TREATAS applies a set of values to a column as though a relationship existed, entirely inside a measure. That makes it the escape hatch for the case where a physical link would create ambiguity you cannot live with. It leaves no permanent path, so the ambiguity check never sees it. The cost is that the behaviour lives in one measure rather than in the model. A report author dragging raw columns onto a visual gets nothing. Prefer a physical relationship whenever the model can carry one honestly.

What to remember
  • A relationship is a stored mapping from one side values to many side row positions, built at refresh. Direction exists because that mapping is asymmetric.
  • Cardinality is inferred from the data present when you click OK. That makes it a snapshot of one refresh. Know what upstream rule keeps the one side unique, and write it down.
  • Many to one and one to many are the same relationship. One to one usually means a merge you have not done. Many to many usually means a dimension you have not built.
  • Meridian's one genuine one to one is HMCCSchedule to FactWorkOrder: eight rows each, one row per work order, both keys unique. Merge it in Power Query rather than relate it, and accept what the merge forces. The control board says WO-1003 started on 2025-01-13 and the shop floor says 2025-01-14. Somebody has to write down which date the turnaround measure uses, before an average of 12.0 days or 12.17 days means anything.
  • One to one is locked at Both, so the companion table filters the dimension whether you meant it to or not. A six row HR companion beside the seven row DimTechnician takes labor hours from 62.0 to 52.0 and A320-200 from 23.5 to 13.5, with nothing on the page to show where the hours went. Accept it only when you cannot merge and the two key lists are guaranteed identical forever.
  • Before accepting many to many, ask whether you can list the distinct values, whether unmatched keys need to stay visible, and whether a filter has to continue past that hop. A yes to any of the three means build the dimension.
  • Many to many produces a weak relationship: no blank row for unmatched values, and propagation that does not extend through the chain the way a regular relationship does.
  • One active relationship per path. Extra ones are stored and dormant, and a measure wakes one with USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE. In Meridian, OpenedDate is active and PromisedDate and ClosedDate are not.
  • One column each side, matching data types, no blanks on the one side, no second route between two tables. Concatenate a composite key only when the parts cannot become dimensions of their own, and always with a separator.
  • Unmatched many side keys land on a blank row added to the one side. That is how 4,900 of the 28,245 parts cost ends up in a row report consumers ignore.
  • Assume Referential Integrity is DirectQuery only and drops unmatched fact rows without telling you. Turn it on only where the source enforces the key.
Part 3 . Relationships and filter flow

07How a filter actually travels through the model

After this chapter you will be able to point at any number in any visual and say which rows of which tables survived, in what order the engine eliminated the rest, and why a slicer that looks connected sometimes does nothing at all.

The production controller wants labor hours by aircraft type before the morning meeting. You build the matrix in about thirty seconds. E175 comes back 17.5 hours, and he asks the one question that matters: which jobs is that? Nothing in the measure mentions aircraft. Nothing in the labor table mentions aircraft either. This chapter answers him, row by row.

A filter is a set of surviving rows.

You almost certainly learned filtering in Excel. A condition sits on a column, rows that fail it get hidden, and everything else stays visible. That picture holds up fine when you have one table. It stops working the moment you have twelve tables and a measure that reads from one of them while the slicer sits on another. Keep the Excel picture and filter propagation will feel like a rule you memorised. Replace the picture and it becomes something you can work out from first principles.

Here is the replacement. In the tabular engine, a filter context is a set of surviving rows on every table in the model at the same time. Twelve tables, twelve row sets, all decided at once. Before a single measure runs, the engine has already worked out for each table exactly which rows are in play. DimAircraft Dimension might be down to two rows out of seven while DimStation still holds all five. A dimension table is a list of the things you describe work by, one row each, so DimAircraft holds one row per aircraft. FactLabor Fact might be down to three rows out of eight. A fact table holds events, and one FactLabor row is one booking of hours by one technician against one work order. That whole collection of row sets, one per table, is the filter context. Only then does the measure evaluate, and it evaluates against those sets.

Every cell in a visual gets its own filter context, built from scratch. A matrix with four visible rows evaluates the measure four times for the body and once more for the total. Five separate contexts, five separate sets. Nothing carries over between cells. The only thing they share is the model itself.

Rule of thumb

When a number surprises you, do not ask "why is this measure wrong". Ask "which rows survived". The measure is almost never the problem. The set it was handed usually is.

The order of operations inside one cell

Three things happen, always in this order, and the order is why propagation behaves the way it does.

  1. The engine collects every filter that applies to this cell and applies each one directly to the table that owns the column being filtered.
  2. The engine follows relationships outward from those tables, narrowing other tables as it goes, until nothing more can be narrowed.
  3. The measure runs, reading only the rows that survived on whichever table it aggregates.

Step two is propagation. It is a graph walk, and the rule for whether a hop is legal is short: you may cross a relationship from the one side to the many side. Crossing the other way is not allowed unless you explicitly enable it. Everything else in this chapter follows from that single restriction.

Read the top row of boxes left to right and look at where the arrowheads sit. Both arrows point the same way. Each is marked 1 at the end it leaves and * at the end it arrives, so every hop runs from the one side to the many side. Only the first arrow leaves a dimension. The second leaves FactWorkOrder and lands on FactLabor, header to line, and it is legal for the same reason: one work order row, many labor rows. Nothing points back the other way. That is the constraint the engine enforces, drawn, and it means the reachable set from any starting table is fixed and knowable before you run anything.

The three numbered cards underneath sit directly below the box each one belongs to, and they hold the whole idea. Card 1 is what survives on DimAircraft once the diagram's E175 filter lands, two aircraft registrations. Card 2 is what is left on FactWorkOrder after the first hop, two work orders. Card 3 is what is left on FactLabor after the second hop, three labor rows with their hours printed beside them. The green card on the right adds those three hours to 17.5. Each card is a set of surviving rows, never a condition, and the measure only appears at the end, on whatever the last card still contains.

Hand trace: Labor Hours for the E175 row

Build a matrix. Put DimAircraft[AircraftType] on rows and one measure in values.

DAXLabor Hours
Labor Hours =
    SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )
Line 1
The measure name. It aggregates FactLabor, and nothing in its definition mentions aircraft. That matters: the connection to DimAircraft lives entirely in the model, not in the code.
Line 2
SUM adds one stored column across whatever rows survive. Nothing here needs a row by row expression, so SUMX would only add an iterator the engine has to unwind. Use SUM when you are adding a single physical column and save SUMX for the cases where you are multiplying two columns together.

Now trace the E175 row in full. The three cards in the diagram above give you the shape and the answer; what follows is every row at every stage, so you can see what was dropped as well as what was kept. Four steps, because the measure evaluating is a step in its own right, and at each one the only question is which rows are still standing.

Step 1. The visual filters DimAircraft

The row header is a filter on DimAircraft[AircraftType] with the value E175. That column lives on DimAircraft, so the filter lands there first, before any propagation happens at all.

The surviving set is exactly two aircraft registrations, N902TT and N553KD. Note that N553KD survives even though it has never had a work order. Nothing about the dimension knows or cares about that yet.

Step 2. DimAircraft propagates to FactWorkOrder

There is one relationship out of DimAircraft, from DimAircraft[ACREG] to FactWorkOrder[ACREG], and it runs from the one side to the many side. Legal hop. The engine keeps the FactWorkOrder rows whose ACREG is in the surviving set from step 1.

N553KD contributed nothing, because no work order references it. The set from step 1 had two members and the set here has two members, but that is coincidence: one tail supplied both.

Step 3. FactWorkOrder propagates to FactLabor

The header to line relationship runs from FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID] to FactLabor[WorkOrderID], one side to many side. Legal hop again. FactLabor keeps the rows whose work order is in the surviving set from step 2.

Step 4. The measure runs

SUM over FactLabor[Hours] sees exactly three rows: 8.0 plus 4.5 plus 5.0 equals 17.5. That is the number in the E175 cell. Every step that produced it was a set operation, and the only arithmetic happened at the very end. It is also the production controller's answer. Two work orders, WO-1003 and WO-1007, three labor bookings between them.

Now look at what else the engine did on the way. People skip this part and find it confusing later. The filter context for that one cell is a state of the entire model, and the E175 selection is only the piece of it you asked for.

Two things in that table are worth stopping on. First, FactParts narrowed to two rows without anyone asking, because it hangs off FactWorkOrder exactly the way FactLabor does. Drop a Parts Cost measure into the same matrix and the E175 row returns 10,200 plus 2,480, which is 12,680. You did no extra work to get it. Second, the dimensions listed lower down the table still have every row. Nothing touched them, because reaching them would mean walking a relationship backwards.

The total row is the same measure evaluated one more time, with no filter on DimAircraft at all. Nobody adds the four rows up. The total agrees with their sum here because every labor row belongs to exactly one aircraft, and that agreement is a property of this data. Hold onto the distinction. It breaks in the bridge table chapter, and it breaks again later in this one.

The expanded table, and why it is the abstraction that matters

The planner points at a slicer on part category and asks whether it changes labor hours. You could trace it: filter the part table, walk every relationship out of it, write down what survives. That is twenty minutes with a pen. There is a way to answer her in about ten seconds, and this is it.

Doing that trace by hand every time would be exhausting. There is a shortcut, and once you hold it most propagation questions become something you can settle in your head.

Conceptually, every table in the model is expanded to include the columns of every table you can reach from it by following many to one relationships. Many to one only, in the direction a fact row points at its dimension row. So the expanded version of FactLabor carries its own six columns (LaborID, WorkOrderID, TechnicianID, WorkDate, Hours and HourlyRate). On top of those it carries the columns of FactWorkOrder, plus DimAircraft, DimStation, DimWOType, DimTechnician and DimDate. All of them, as if they had been joined into one very wide table.

Now restate propagation using it. A filter on DimAircraft[AircraftType] is a filter on a column of the expanded FactLabor, so it filters FactLabor. A filter on DimTechnician[EmployeeType] is also a column of expanded FactLabor, so it filters FactLabor too. A filter on DimPart[Category] is not a column of expanded FactLabor, because DimPart sits outside every many to one hop that leaves FactLabor. So it does nothing to labor hours, however prominently the slicer sits on the page. That answers the planner, and it took one look at the expansion list.

Interview-level insight

Expanded tables also explain why CALCULATE filter arguments work the way they do. When you write a filter on a dimension column inside a measure that aggregates a fact, you are filtering a column of the fact's expanded table directly. As far as that filter is concerned, the dimension is already part of the fact. So the filter arrives whether or not the dimension appears anywhere in the visual, and the direction of the relationship decides what is reachable. Your intuition about which table should reach which gets no vote.

Write out the expansion for your own model once, on paper, and keep it. For Meridian it takes ten minutes and it answers roughly eighty percent of the "why doesn't this slicer work" questions you will ever be asked.

Why filters only travel one way

The shift supervisor asks this one first, and then everybody else asks it. Why does the slicer work in one direction and sit there in the other? The stock reply, that this is just how Power BI works, gives you nothing to use the next time the model surprises you. Here is the mechanism.

Going from the many side to the one side is deterministic. Take FactWorkOrder row WO-1003. Its ACREG is N902TT, and DimAircraft[ACREG] is unique, so that row points at exactly one dimension row. Always one. The lookup is a single hash probe and the answer is a scalar. Every fact row in the model behaves this way, which is what makes the expanded table well defined in the first place.

Going the other way loses that guarantee. Take DimAircraft row N771QR. It is referenced by WO-1001, WO-1004 and WO-1008, three rows. A different tail would give a different count. So propagating from the one side to the many side returns a set, and the engine has to build that set before it can apply it. That is more work, and the work scales with how many distinct keys survive.

The second problem is worse than the cost. Sets can arrive by more than one route. Suppose both directions were open by default. A filter on DimStation could then reach FactLabor through FactWorkOrder. Had somebody built the relationship, it could reach the same table through DimTechnician[HomeStation] as well. Those two routes give different answers to the same question. The Meridian model leaves out DimStation[StationCode] to DimTechnician[HomeStation] for exactly this reason. With one direction, the reachable set from any table is unique, and the model has exactly one interpretation.

Many to one
One row, always
One to many
A set, size varies
Default direction
One side to many side
What it buys you
Exactly one answer

Five ways to make a filter go the other way

The production controller who staffs the LAS line wants hours by the technician's home station. He is asking what his own people booked, wherever the aircraft happened to be sitting. The model holds a work order station and a technician home station, with no relationship between them. He has asked a filter to travel in the one direction this model refuses to send it.

Sometimes you genuinely need the flow reversed. There are five options and they are not equal. They are listed here in the order you should consider them, which is not the order most people try them in.

Option 1 is the one people skip, and it is usually correct. Before reaching for anything clever, check whether the filter could come from a dimension both facts already touch. Labor hours and planned capacity share DimStation and DimDate. You do not need any reverse flow between them, and the utilisation trace at the end of this chapter shows why.

Option 3 has a concrete home in this model. Meridian deliberately refuses to relate DimStation to DimTechnician[HomeStation], because that would give a filter on DimStation two routes to FactLabor. But "how many hours did technicians based at MSP book, wherever they booked them" is a fair question. TREATAS answers it without a relationship.

DAXLabor Hours by Home Station
Labor Hours by Home Station =
VAR SelectedStations =
    VALUES ( DimStation[StationCode] )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        [Labor Hours],
        REMOVEFILTERS ( DimStation ),
        TREATAS (
            SelectedStations,
            DimTechnician[HomeStation]
        )
    )
Line 2 to 3
Capture the station codes currently visible. VALUES rather than DISTINCT: VALUES includes the blank row the engine adds for unmatched keys. When you hand a set to a virtual relationship, you want that blank travelling with it. DISTINCT leaves it behind.
Line 5
CALCULATE is the only function that can modify a filter context. A bare FILTER would build a table, but it cannot change what the surrounding measure sees, so it is not an alternative here.
Line 7
REMOVEFILTERS on DimStation stops the original station filter from also propagating through FactWorkOrder. Without it you get the intersection of two different definitions of station. ALL would do the same job, but it reads as a table function and this is a modifier, so REMOVEFILTERS states the intent.
Line 8 to 11
TREATAS takes the captured values and applies them as a filter on DimTechnician[HomeStation], a column with no relationship to DimStation at all. That filter then propagates normally down to FactLabor.
Why this and not that

TREATAS rather than a physical relationship, because a physical relationship here is the exact thing this model was built to avoid. TREATAS and not CROSSFILTER: CROSSFILTER can only change the direction of a relationship that already exists, and here there is none. TREATAS and not INTERSECT on the technician table, because INTERSECT hands you a table to compare against, where what you need is a filter the engine will propagate. The trade is that nothing in the model diagram hints this measure exists.

Run it and the answers differ from the station route, which is the point. Technician home station and work order station are two different facts about the same hours.

LAS is the interesting cell, and it is the production controller's answer. Five hours of work happened at LAS. K. Ibrahim is based there and booked thirteen hours in total, most of them on a Tucson work order. Both figures describe his line. Put the two columns on one page without labelling them clearly and somebody will build a staffing plan on the wrong one.

Performance note

Reversing filter direction has a price, and the price tracks the number of distinct keys that survive. Table size barely comes into it. Making FactWorkOrder to FactLabor bidirectional on eight rows costs nothing you could measure. Do it on a work order table with four million keys and the engine materialises a key set of up to four million values, then hands it across on every query that touches both tables. This is why a bidirectional relationship on a small bridge, where the key is a certification code with four values, is usually fine. It is also why a bidirectional relationship on a transaction identifier is usually what you find at the bottom of a slow report.

When there is no path at all

The finance manager wants parts cost split by employee type. Staff against contract, one figure each, on the Friday pack. It sounds like a five minute job, and the model already holds every column the question names.

Put a slicer on DimTechnician[EmployeeType] with Staff and Contract on it. Put a card next to it showing Parts Cost, defined as follows.

DAXParts Cost
Parts Cost =
    SUMX (
        FactParts,
        FactParts[Qty] * FactParts[UnitCost]
    )
Line 2
SUMX and not SUM, because there is no stored extended cost column on FactParts and SUM cannot multiply two columns. A calculated column would also work and would let you use SUM, but it materialises a value into the model that you only ever need at query time.
Line 3 to 4
The iterator walks whatever rows of FactParts survive the filter context, multiplying quantity by unit cost for each and adding the results.
What you see in the report

The slicer works. Buttons highlight, the selection sticks, the other visuals on the page respond. The Parts Cost card reads 28,245 with Staff selected, 28,245 with Contract selected, and 28,245 with nothing selected. It never moves.

Explain it as a graph walk and the reason is immediate. From DimTechnician the engine can hop to FactLabor, because that relationship runs one side to many side. From FactLabor the only relationship that leads anywhere new is FactWorkOrder to FactLabor, and taking it would mean walking from the many side to the one side. Not allowed by default. The other two relationships touching FactLabor come in from DimDate and DimTechnician, and they point the wrong way as well. The walk stops there. FactParts is never reached, all seven rows survive, and the measure returns the same 28,245 every time. Said the other way: DimTechnician is not in the expanded table of FactParts, so it cannot filter it.

Common mistake

Assuming a slicer that visibly reacts is a slicer that is doing something. Slicer interactivity is a property of the slicer visual. Whether the selection reaches your measure is a property of the model. They are unrelated, and a slicer that filters nothing looks exactly like a slicer that filters everything.

Three fixes get proposed whenever this comes up. One of them can be built against this data. One cannot be built here at all. The third is the correct answer, and it is the one that almost never gets built.

Fix A. Push the filter through with CROSSFILTER

DAXParts Cost Pushed Through Labor
Parts Cost Pushed Through Labor =
    CALCULATE (
        [Parts Cost],
        CROSSFILTER (
            FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID],
            FactLabor[WorkOrderID],
            BOTH
        )
    )
Line 2
CALCULATE again, because the relationship direction is part of the filter context and only CALCULATE can alter it.
Line 4 to 8
CROSSFILTER names the two columns of an existing relationship and sets its direction to BOTH for this evaluation only. USERELATIONSHIP is the function people reach for first. It wakes an inactive relationship, and this relationship is active already, so it does not apply here. Setting the relationship bidirectional in the model view would work too, and it would change every measure in the file, which is exactly what you are trying to avoid.

Now the filter reaches. DimTechnician narrows FactLabor, FactLabor narrows FactWorkOrder because the direction is temporarily open, and FactWorkOrder narrows FactParts as usual. You get numbers. Read them carefully.

Two independent errors are stacked in that table and both are structural. WO-1001 was worked by TECH-02, who is Staff, and TECH-04, who is Contract, so its 1,240 of brake parts appears in both rows. WO-1003 does the same with 12,680. That is 13,920 counted twice. Meanwhile the rows are missing 1,875 from WO-1005, which has parts but no labor at all, and 4,900 from P-9007, whose work order WO-1009 does not exist in FactWorkOrder. Those two add to 6,775, which is exactly the gap between 28,245 and the 21,470 the rows actually cover. Double count 13,920, omit 6,775, and you land 7,145 above the correct grand total.

Fix B. Denormalise the technician onto the parts fact

Add a TechnicianID column to FactParts in Power Query and relate it to DimTechnician. This is option 5 from the ranked list, and in many situations it is the best answer available. Here it is not available at all, because the source has no such column. PartsIssued arrives with IssueID, WorkOrderID, PartNumber, Qty, UnitCost and IssueDate. There is no technician anywhere in it. You could allocate parts cost to technicians in proportion to hours booked, and that is a legitimate thing to build, but be honest about what it is: an assumption you invented, not a fact you loaded.

Fix C. Change the question

This is the correct answer, and it is the inconvenient one. The stores log records that a part left the shelf against a work order. Nobody wrote down who fitted it, and no amount of relationship configuration will conjure a fact that was never captured. So a part issue in this data belongs to a work order and to nothing else. "Parts cost by employee type" is a question with no defined answer, given these six source tables. The obstacle sits in the source data, and Power BI will hand you a number for it anyway if you ask. Building a model that returns one is worse than returning nothing, because the number looks authoritative.

What you can answer, precisely, is "parts cost on work orders that contract technicians booked time to". That is 13,920, and Fix A computes it correctly. Two rules come with it. You may show it as a single filtered figure. You may never put it in a matrix with a total row, because the moment two employee types appear side by side the shared work orders get counted twice. Rename the measure to say so. A measure called Parts Cost On Work Orders Touched will get questioned by the person reading it. A measure called Parts Cost will sail through. That is the honest version of the finance manager's Friday number, and part of the job is telling him why the other version does not exist.

How the filters stack

The shift supervisor says the report is wrong. His whiteboard shows more MSP work on the A320s this month than your matrix does. He has been counting jobs and the matrix has been adding hours, and neither of you has noticed that yet. There are three filters on that page, and he can see two of them.

One cell usually has more than one filter arriving at it. The sources are report level filters, page level filters, visual level filters, every slicer on the page, the row, column, legend and small multiple fields of the visual itself, cross highlighting from a selection in another visual, row level security if it is configured, and any filter the measure applies with CALCULATE. All of them contribute.

They combine by intersection. Each filter produces a set of surviving rows, and the engine keeps the rows that survive all of them, which is logical AND. There is one exception worth knowing. A filter argument inside CALCULATE overwrites any existing filter on the same column. Everything arriving from outside the measure intersects.

Work an example on the A320-200 row. Three filters, from three different places, landing on three different tables.

WO-1008 survives all three filters and still contributes nothing, because it has no labor rows yet. That is the difference between a work order sitting in the filter context and a work order having something to add. Both are true here, and only one of them shows up in the number. That answers the shift supervisor. He counted two jobs, the matrix added the hours on one of them, and both of you were right.

One habit will save you a great deal of time. When a number looks wrong, start with the visual and leave the DAX alone for a minute. Strip the visual back to one row and one measure, then add the filter sources back one at a time and watch where the number changes. You are looking for the filter that removed a row you expected to keep. The formula is rarely where the trouble lives.

Trace this by hand, row by row: Utilisation at MSP in January

The first trace had a single chain. This one has two branches that converge, which is the more common shape and the one worth practising. The measures:

DAXPlanned Hours and Utilisation
Planned Hours =
    SUM ( FactCapacity[PlannedHours] )

// Utilisation compares booked hours to planned hours
Utilisation =
    DIVIDE ( [Labor Hours], [Planned Hours] )
Line 2
SUM over the unpivoted capacity fact. The trade columns became rows during the unpivot, so a station month now has four rows and adding them is a plain column sum.
Line 6
DIVIDE and not the division operator. LAS has no capacity row for January, so [Planned Hours] is blank there, and DIVIDE returns blank rather than raising an error. The operator would fail on the same cell, and a visual that errors on one cell shows nothing at all.

Put DimStation[StationCode] on rows, DimDate[MonthName] on columns, and read the cell at MSP and January. Two filters land, and neither one touches FactLabor or FactCapacity directly.

Branch one, the station filter

DimStation is filtered to the single row MSP. It has two relationships out, both one side to many side, so both propagate.

  • DimStation to FactWorkOrder leaves WO-1001, WO-1002, WO-1006 and WO-1008.
  • DimStation to FactCapacity leaves the twelve rows that belong to MSP, four trades in each of three months.

The work order set then propagates one more hop to FactLabor, leaving L-501, L-502, L-503 and L-507.

Branch two, the date filter

DimDate is filtered to the thirty-one January dates. It also has more than one relationship out.

  • DimDate[Date] to FactLabor[WorkDate] leaves L-501, L-502, L-503, L-504 and L-505.
  • DimDate[MonthStart] to FactCapacity[MonthStart] leaves every row whose MonthStart is 2025-01-01, which is MSP January, TUS January, and no others.
Where the branches meet

L-506 and L-508 are omitted from that table because they fail both branches. Labor Hours for the cell is 7.5 plus 6.0 plus 9.0, which is 22.5.

Twelve MSP rows from the station branch, intersected with the eight January rows from the date branch (four trades at MSP and four at TUS), leaves four. They add to 14 plus 8 plus 6 plus 2, which is 30. DIVIDE then returns 22.5 divided by 30, which is 0.75, shown as 75.0 percent.

Two things about this trace are worth carrying forward. First, the capacity relationship is on MonthStart, not on Date, so it only matches when the date filter includes the first of the month. Filter the page to January and it works, because 2025-01-01 is in the set. Filter the page to 2025-01-15 alone and FactCapacity keeps nothing. [Planned Hours] goes blank, and DIVIDE returns blank. A blank cell is easier to question than a percentage computed against nothing. That is the grain mismatch behaving as designed, and it is the reason the measure was written with DIVIDE in the first place.

Second, DimDate can reach FactLabor two ways in this model: directly through FactLabor[WorkDate], and indirectly through the active FactWorkOrder[OpenedDate] relationship followed by the header to line hop. For MSP in January both routes land on the same three rows, so 22.5 is correct either way. In a model where labor is booked in a different month from the one the work order opened in, they would not agree. Before you trust a date slicer against a header and line pair, filter to a single day and check that the number is what you expect. If it comes back blank, you have found this.

Working the ranked list

Four requests have landed on your desk this month, one from nearly everybody in this chapter. The planner wants planned hours beside booked hours. The production controller wants hours by home station. Somebody in the training office wants hours by certification, which here means A&P, Avionics, NDT and Engine Run. A&P is the Airframe and Powerplant licence a mechanic holds. The finance manager still wants parts cost by employee type. Four requests, one list, and four different answers.

A ranked list is only useful if you can watch someone climb it and reject rungs out loud. Here are those four requirements. Three of them land on a different rung each, and the fourth never reaches a rung at all.

The second row is the one worth climbing in full, because four of the five rungs are technically available and only one of them is right.

Rung 1, re-point at a shared dimension. Is there a table that both DimCertification and FactLabor already touch? No. DimCertification has exactly one relationship, out to BridgeTechCert. A bridge table is a small table of pairs that joins two tables which cannot relate to each other directly, and this one holds ten rows, one per technician and certification pair. The bridge holds no measures. There is nothing to re-point, and no dimension you could build would change that, because a certification describes a technician and never a labor row. Rung 1 does not apply here at all, and cost never enters into it.

Rung 2, CROSSFILTER inside one measure. This works. Wrap the hours measure in CALCULATE with CROSSFILTER over BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID] and DimTechnician[TechnicianID] set to BOTH, and A&P returns 39.0. The arithmetic is fine. The objection is to the premise of rung 2, which is false in this case. Rung 2 is right when one or two measures need the hop. Hours by certification, cost by certification, headcount by certification and average hours per certified technician all need it. Every one of them then carries its own copy of the modifier, which is four places for the next person to keep in step, and a fifth measure that will be written without it.

Rung 3, TREATAS. Also works, and the next chapter writes it out in full: capture VALUES ( BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID] ) in the outer filter context and restamp it onto DimTechnician[TechnicianID]. Same 39.0. It has the same repetition problem as rung 2, and one extra risk on top, because TREATAS matches by value with no stored relationship behind it. Had the build left the keys untrimmed, the "TECH-04 " on L-505 would fail to match. A&P would come back 34.5, and nothing in the visual would say that 4.5 hours had gone missing.

Rung 4, a bidirectional relationship. Set DimTechnician to BridgeTechCert to Both and every measure gets the hop without asking for it. The joining key has four distinct values, so the reverse materialisation the engine has to perform is four rows wide. This is the answer. It is the documented exception to the general preference for measure scope over model scope. When every query needs the hop, pay for it once in the model. The alternative is paying for it in four measures and forgetting the fifth.

Rung 5, denormalise the certification onto FactLabor. This looks like the cheapest option on the list and it is the only one that damages the data. A labor row has to be repeated once per certification the technician holds. TECH-04 holds three, so L-502 becomes three rows and L-505 becomes three. TECH-01 holds two, so L-507 becomes two. TECH-07 holds none, so L-506 and its ten hours disappear from the fact table altogether. Eight labor rows become twelve. Total labor hours become 7.5 plus 18.0 plus 9.0 plus 8.0 plus 13.5 plus 24.0 plus 5.0, which is 85.0. That figure is then stored, permanently, for every measure and every user in the file. Rung 4 leaves FactLabor at 62.0 and confines the double count to the certification slice, where you can label it. Rung 5 makes 85.0 the truth.

One last thing about the order. It is a sequence of consideration, and the ranking says nothing about quality. Rung 4 beats rung 2 for the bridge, and rung 2 beats rung 4 for a one off requirement on a wide fact. The list is ordered the way it is because the early rungs are the cheapest to undo. A re-pointed model is a conversation. A modifier inside one measure is one delete. A bidirectional relationship is a property that half a dozen reports have quietly come to depend on by the time anybody thinks to question it.

What to remember
  • A filter context is a set of surviving rows on every table in the model at once. The measure runs last, against whatever survived.
  • Propagation is a graph walk in which every hop must go from the one side to the many side. If no such walk exists between two tables, the slicer does nothing and looks perfectly functional while doing it.
  • Every table is conceptually expanded to include the columns of everything reachable by many to one hops. FactLabor expanded carries FactWorkOrder, DimAircraft, DimStation, DimWOType, DimTechnician and DimDate. Learn this and most surprises stop.
  • One direction is the default because many to one always returns exactly one row, while one to many returns a set that can arrive by more than one route. Single direction is what makes the model unambiguous.
  • To reverse the flow, try re-pointing the model first, then CROSSFILTER, then TREATAS, then a bidirectional relationship, then denormalisation. Most people try them in the opposite order.
  • The ranking is an order of consideration. Different Meridian requirements land on different rungs: utilisation on rung 1, hours by certification on rung 4, hours by home station on rung 3. What the order buys you is that the early rungs are the cheapest to undo.
  • Rung 5 is the one to watch. Denormalising certification onto FactLabor turns eight labor rows into twelve, drops TECH-07 entirely, and makes 85.0 the stored total for everybody, where rung 4 leaves the fact at 62.0.
  • Filters from slicers, page filters, visual filters and the visual's own fields intersect with logical AND. A filter argument inside CALCULATE is the exception: it overwrites any filter already on that column.
  • Some questions have no answer in the data you loaded. Parts cost by employee type is one of them, and forcing a number out of it produces 35,390 against a true total of 28,245.
Part 3 . Relationships and filter flow

08Single versus bidirectional cross-filtering

After this chapter you will be able to say exactly which rows a Both relationship adds to a query. You will be able to name the three costs you pay for it. You will also be able to choose between a model change, a CROSSFILTER modifier and TREATAS for any requirement in the Meridian model.

The production controller wants Q1 hours by certification. He runs four certifications on his board and he wants to know how many hours went to each one. You put DimCertification on the rows of a table visual and drop the Labor Hours measure into the values. All four rows come back 62.0. That is the whole quarter's hours, printed four times under four different labels, and nothing on the page warns you.

A measure is a calculation the engine runs once for every cell of a visual. It runs over whatever rows are still visible at that moment, and that set of visible rows is called the filter context. So the four identical numbers are telling you something specific. The certification the reader picked never reached the labor rows at all. The reason is one property on one relationship, and most people have never opened it.

Cross-filter direction looks like a preference sitting in a properties pane. What it states is which way the engine may walk a relationship when it builds the filter context. Change it and you change the answer to questions you were not thinking about at the time.

Every relationship in the Meridian model has two properties that matter here. Cardinality says which side is the one and which is the many. Cross-filter direction says which of those two sides can filter the other. Section C of the model spec sets every relationship to single, which means the filter runs from the one side to the many side and stops. Dimension filters Fact. Never the reverse.

Set a relationship to Both and you add a second, opposite hop. The filter can now run from the many side back to the one side. That sounds symmetric. Underneath, the two hops are different operations, and the reverse one is the expensive half.

Default direction
Single, one to many
Legitimate use of Both
Bridge in a many to many
Costs you pay
Ambiguity, performance, RLS
Measure-level equivalent
CROSSFILTER inside CALCULATE

Look at the arrows first. Both panels draw the same two tables, DimTechnician above FactLabor, joined on TechnicianID with the 1 on the dimension and the * on the fact. In the left panel, the one titled Single, the default, a single arrow runs downward from the dimension into the fact. The note beside it says a selection on FactLabor does not reach DimTechnician. In the right panel, titled Both, bidirectional, that same pair of boxes is joined by a double headed arrow. The note beside that one says a selection on FactLabor now narrows DimTechnician as well. The boxes, the columns and the keys are identical on both sides. The arrow is the only thing that changes. Under the left panel sits a green card headed one path, one answer. Under the right one sits a red card headed convenient, and the usual source of ambiguity. That single changed property is the whole subject of this chapter, and it stays invisible in a report visual until it produces a number you cannot defend.

What actually changes when you set Both

Going from the one side to the many side is a lookup. The engine has a filtered set of keys on the dimension and it needs the fact rows whose key is in that set. Column storage is built for exactly this. Going from the many side to the one side is a different job. The engine has to work out which distinct key values survive in the filtered fact. It builds that set in memory, which is what the word materialisation means, and only then applies it as a filter on the dimension. A lookup reads what is already indexed. A materialisation builds something new on every query that needs it.

The practical consequence is that selecting fact rows now restricts the dimension. Say a report page filters FactLabor to March, and the relationship from DimTechnician to FactLabor is set to Both. DimTechnician is then reduced to the technicians who booked labor in March. In Meridian that is TECH-05 alone, because L-508 is the only March labor row. A slicer built on DimTechnician would show one name. A slicer is the on-page control a user clicks to choose values. Nothing about your report definition changed. Only the relationship property did.

Row three is the production controller's problem, written out as a filter path. Rows one and two only change what a slicer displays. Row three changes a number from wrong to right, and it is the one case here where the reverse hop answers a business question. The next section takes it apart. Then it shows you the same answer written as DAX, so you can see that the model property is a convenience. The capability was there all along.

The legitimate use: a bridge in a many to many

Meridian technicians hold multiple certifications, and each certification is held by multiple technicians. That shape is called many to many. The model spec resolves it by splitting Technicians[Certifications] to rows, which produces Bridge BridgeTechCert with 10 rows. A bridge table is a table whose only job is to hold one row for each valid pairing. This one sits on the many side of two relationships, one from DimTechnician and one from DimCertification.

With both of those relationships left at single, a selection on DimCertification filters the bridge and stops there. The bridge carries no measures. FactLabor never hears about the selection, so an hours measure returns its unfiltered 62.0 on every one of the four certification rows. Note what that is not. It is not a blank, which people expect and would at least notice. It is the grand total, wearing four different labels.

Set the DimTechnician to BridgeTechCert relationship to Both and the chain completes. Here is the walk for A&P.

Hop 3 is the one that only exists under Both, and 39.0 is the number the production controller asked for. Note that L-505 appears in the result at 4.5 hours. That is only true because FactLabor was built with the technician key trimmed. Untrimmed, "TECH-04 " would fail the join and A&P would come out at 34.5. Cross-filter direction and key hygiene fail in ways that look identical in a card visual, so check the keys before you touch the relationship properties.

You do not have to change the model to get this number. The same behaviour is available as a measure.

DAXHours by Certification
Hours by Certification =
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ),
        CROSSFILTER (
            BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID],
            DimTechnician[TechnicianID],
            BOTH
        )
    )
Line 2
CALCULATE because the visual cell wants one number. CALCULATETABLE returns a table, and a table will not fit in a cell.
Line 3
SUM because Hours is a stored column with no expression around it. SUMX would open a row context and make the engine iterate it for no arithmetic benefit.
Lines 4 to 8
CROSSFILTER flips the direction of one named relationship for the duration of this CALCULATE only. Outside this measure the relationship is still single.
Why this and not that

CROSSFILTER rather than USERELATIONSHIP, because the two solve different problems that are easy to confuse. USERELATIONSHIP chooses which of several relationships between two tables is the active one for the duration of a CALCULATE. That is what Chapter 12 does for the three date columns on FactWorkOrder. CROSSFILTER changes the direction of an already active relationship, or switches it off entirely. Those are different axes. There is only one relationship between DimTechnician and BridgeTechCert and it is already active. Pointing USERELATIONSHIP at it is legal and completely inert, because it has no argument that says which way the filter runs. Only CROSSFILTER has that argument.

There is nothing special inside the engine about Both. Write the reverse hop yourself and you get the same 39.0.

DAXHours by Certification, manual reverse hop
Hours by Certification Manual =
VAR TechsWithCert =
    VALUES ( BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID] )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ),
        TREATAS (
            TechsWithCert,
            DimTechnician[TechnicianID]
        )
    )
Lines 2 to 3
The variable is evaluated in the outer filter context, where A&P is already filtering the bridge. It returns TECH-01, TECH-02, TECH-04. VALUES rather than DISTINCT because VALUES keeps the blank member the engine adds when a fact holds a key the dimension does not. Meridian still has one of those: FactParts carries WO-1009, which has no header row in FactWorkOrder. On this bridge column the two functions return the same three rows, so the choice looks arbitrary here. It stops being arbitrary the moment you point the same pattern at a column that sits on the one side of an imperfect join.
Lines 5 to 11
The captured list is applied as a filter on DimTechnician. From there it propagates forward to FactLabor down the existing single relationship. Result: 39.0, identical to the Both version.

That is all a bidirectional relationship does. It reads the distinct keys surviving on the many side and applies them as a filter on the one side. The model setting does it for every query that touches the relationship, whether or not the query needed it.

Interview-level insight

Setting a bridge relationship to Both makes the per-certification numbers computable. It does not make them additive. A&P 39.0 plus Avionics 10.5 plus NDT 12.0 plus Engine Run 23.5 comes to 85.0 against a true total of 62.0. TECH-04 holds three certifications, so his 10.5 hours are counted once under each. The 23-hour gap is what correct arithmetic on a many to many looks like. The fix is a total row computed on its own labor rows, so that it stops being the sum of what the reader can see. Bidirectional filtering solves half of a many to many. Additivity is the half it leaves you.

The illegitimate use, and the symptom it produces

The shift supervisor at MSP comes over with a printout. Your report says MSP did 34.5 hours in the quarter. His whiteboard says 28.5, and he has been keeping that whiteboard for eleven years. You check your figure twice and it holds. So does his. Two people, one word, and the word is MSP.

Follow the two routes leaving DimStation on the left. Path A, the solid line across the top, goes to FactWorkOrder and continues into FactLabor on the right through the header to line relationship, the one that joins each work order to its own labor rows. Path B, the dashed line across the bottom, goes to DimTechnician and its HomeStation column, then continues into FactLabor through the technician key. Both routes start at the same table and end at the same table. That is the shape the engine refuses. The card underneath puts the consequence as a question: select MSP, and which of the two answers is correct, the 34.5 hours path A produces or the 28.5 path B produces? Both are defensible, and neither is what the axis label says.

The model spec marks DimStation[StationCode] to DimTechnician[HomeStation] as deliberately not created, and this is why. The relationship looks obviously correct. Technicians do have a home station, and it is the same list of station codes. The relationship is factually right. The trouble is that it hands DimStation two ways to reach FactLabor, and the two ways disagree.

The disagreement runs wider than MSP. Ask for labor hours down each path, station by station.

Trace both MSP numbers by hand, row by row

Path A, through FactWorkOrder. MSP work orders are WO-1001, WO-1002, WO-1006 and WO-1008. Their labor hours are 13.5, 9.0, 12.0 and 0. That is 13.5 plus 9.0 plus 12.0 equals 34.5. This is work performed at the MSP shop, whoever did it. TECH-04 is a TUS technician and his 6.0 hours on WO-1001 are inside this number.

Path B, through DimTechnician[HomeStation]. The technicians whose home station is MSP are TECH-01, TECH-02 and TECH-06. Their hours are 12.0, 16.5 and 0. That is 12.0 plus 16.5 plus 0 equals 28.5. This is work booked by MSP staff, wherever it was performed. That is the supervisor's whiteboard, and he is counting his own crew.

The other rows in Table 8.3 come out the same way. TUS home station is TECH-03 at 0 plus TECH-04 at 10.5, which is 10.5. LAS is TECH-05 alone at 13.0. TECH-07 has no row in the HR extract, so the built DimTechnician gives him an unknown row with an Unassigned home station. His 10.0 hours land there, which is why Path B shows 10.0 where Path A shows 0. Both columns reach 62.0 because every labor row is counted exactly once in each. They just get counted under different labels.

What you see in the report

Power BI refuses to activate the relationship. A message says it would introduce ambiguity between tables, and the new relationship drops to inactive. No wrong number has appeared yet. The message reads as an obstacle, so somebody makes it go away. They deactivate the older relationship so the new one can go active, or they flip a direction to Both somewhere else and keep clicking until the model saves. Now the report returns a number, and that number comes from whichever path was left standing. Nobody wrote down which one it was, and it will not be the same after somebody adds a table next quarter.

The engine will not choose, because there is nothing to choose between. Both answers are defensible. 34.5 is what the MSP shop manager means by MSP hours. 28.5 is what the MSP shift supervisor means. One label, two questions, and no rule the engine could apply that would be right for both readers.

Common mistake

Turning every relationship in the model to Both to make a stuck measure move. Put DimCertification on rows with a parts cost measure and all four rows read 28,245, the unfiltered total. That happens because FactParts is only reachable from FactWorkOrder, and there is no path at all from a certification to a work order. Set every relationship to Both and a path appears: certification to bridge to technician to FactLabor to FactWorkOrder to FactParts. Now the rows do move. WO-1003 contributes its full 12,680 of parts to A&P, to Avionics and to Engine Run, because TECH-04 and TECH-05 booked labor to it and between them hold those three certifications. The report went from obviously stuck to plausibly wrong, which is the worse of the two states. A measure that will not respond to the rows you put it against is the model telling you there is no path from those rows to that number. Treat that as information about the model and go looking for the missing path.

The fix: two measures with two names

The two numbers answer two questions, so give them two names and leave the model alone. The supervisor gets his 28.5 back and the shop manager keeps his 34.5.

DAXTwo questions, two measures
Labor Hours =
    SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )

Labor Hours by Home Station =
VAR Stations =
    VALUES ( DimStation[StationCode] )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ),
        REMOVEFILTERS ( DimStation ),
        TREATAS (
            Stations,
            DimTechnician[HomeStation]
        )
    )
Lines 1 to 2
The plain measure. Station comes from the work order, because that is the only station relationship in the model. On MSP it returns 34.5.
Lines 5 to 6
Capture the selected station codes before anything is removed. The variable is evaluated in the outer filter context, which is the whole reason this pattern works.
Line 10
REMOVEFILTERS on DimStation, and not on FactWorkOrder. Clearing the intermediate table achieves nothing, because DimStation still holds the selection and re-propagates it down the work order path. You have to remove the filter at its source.
Lines 11 to 14
TREATAS applies the captured codes to DimTechnician[HomeStation] as though a relationship existed. From there the normal single relationship carries the filter into FactLabor. On MSP it returns 28.5, which is the supervisor's number.
Why this and not that

REMOVEFILTERS rather than ALL: they do the same thing when used as a CALCULATE modifier, but ALL is also a table function. A reader six months from now has to work out which of the two jobs it is doing on that line. REMOVEFILTERS only ever means one thing.

TREATAS, and not INTERSECT or a FILTER over DimTechnician. Lineage is the engine's record of which model column a set of values came from, and it is what lets those values travel down a relationship. INTERSECT returns a table you then have to feed back into CALCULATE, and it keeps the lineage of its first argument instead of restamping it. A set of station codes stays a set of station codes, so it never lands on DimTechnician[HomeStation] and never reaches FactLabor. TREATAS restamps the lineage of the captured values onto the target column, which is exactly what a relationship does. FILTER over the dimension would work, but it forces a scan of DimTechnician on every evaluation and it reads as a loop where the model wanted a join.

The alternative is to denormalise the home station onto the fact, which means copying the value from the dimension onto every labor row.

DAXFactLabor calculated column
FactLabor[TechHomeStation] =
    RELATED ( DimTechnician[HomeStation] )
Line 2
RELATED rather than LOOKUPVALUE, because a many to one relationship already exists from FactLabor to DimTechnician. RELATED follows it. LOOKUPVALUE performs its own match and would still return the right value, but it ignores the relationship you already maintain. A later key change then stops being reflected in one place and keeps being reflected in the other.

Here is the inconvenient part. You cannot then relate DimStation to that new column, because you would recreate the two paths you were trying to avoid. The denormalised column needs its own station table, a second copy of DimStation called something like DimHomeStation. The report then carries two visibly different station slicers. That duplication is the honest price of asking two station questions on one fact, and it is a steep price for something the measure pair above already gives you. If you go that way, name the slicers so nobody has to guess: "Work performed at" and "Technician based at".

The three costs of Both

Six months later the planner asks for one more breakdown, and you open model view to add the relationship it needs. Power BI refuses to activate it and says the model would become ambiguous. You did not draw the path it is complaining about. Somebody drew it to close a ticket, and nobody wrote down why. That is the first of the three costs. The other two are quieter and you pay them the whole time.

1. Ambiguity

Covered above. Power BI blocks you, and the blocking is the visible part. What matters is what people do next. Both is the tool they reach for to get past being blocked, so a model with several bidirectional relationships saves cleanly and then quietly narrows what anyone can add to it later. Every Both setting creates extra paths, and the next relationship has to avoid crossing all of them. The person who hits that wall is rarely the person who set the direction. What they have to unpick is a decision nobody recorded, which is exactly the position the planner has just put you in.

2. Performance

The reverse hop is a scan plus a materialisation. It runs whenever a filter lands on the many side of that relationship, and the author of the query never gets asked. Set DimTechnician to FactLabor to Both, then drop a date slicer on the page. The slicer filters FactLabor. The reverse hop then reads the technician keys that survived and applies them to DimTechnician. Every visual on that page which touches DimTechnician now pays for the materialisation, including a plain table of technicians with a count of the certifications each one holds. That table asked for none of it. The cost is attached to the relationship, not to the measure, so no measure on the page shows any sign of it.

Performance note

On the Meridian data you will not be able to measure this. Eight labor rows and ten bridge rows fit in a cache line, and the reverse hop costs nothing you can detect in Performance Analyzer. That is the trap. The cost scales with the cardinality of the relationship column on the many side. A FactLabor with two hundred million rows and forty thousand distinct technician keys can materialise a set of up to forty thousand rows on every affected query, while your test model tells you the change is free. Here you have to reason about the mechanism, because a benchmark on development data will never show you the bill.

3. Row level security

Row level security, RLS, is a rule that limits which rows a named group of users is allowed to see. Security predicates are filters. They enter the filter context before your measures run and they propagate along relationships like anything else. So a bidirectional relationship extends the reach of a security rule to tables the rule author never considered. Give a TUS manager an RLS rule on DimStation. With single direction throughout, that rule reaches FactWorkOrder, then FactLabor and FactParts. It never reaches DimTechnician. The manager still sees all seven technicians in a slicer while their measures show only TUS work. Now set DimTechnician to FactLabor to Both and switch on that relationship's security filter property. The station rule reaches DimTechnician as well, and the manager's technician slicer shrinks to the people who booked hours at TUS. Nobody edited the rule. Somebody changed a relationship.

Two things are certain here and worth stating separately from the rest. First, cross-filter direction and security filter direction are different settings. Each relationship has an "Apply security filter in both directions" property, and it is off by default even when the cross-filter direction is Both. Power BI treats security propagation as a decision you make on purpose. Second, Power BI Desktop validates the model against your roles and will refuse to save some combinations of bidirectional filtering and RLS, returning an error instead of a warning. The exact set of blocked combinations has moved across product versions. Read that error as the model telling you the security path is ambiguous, and change the design.

Choosing between the three tools

Rule of thumb

Change the model when the requirement is structural and permanent. Change the measure when the requirement belongs to a question. A many to many is structural: the link between a technician and a certification is a fact about the business, and it does not vary by report page. "Hours booked by technicians based at this station" is a question, and questions get measures. If you cannot say which of the two you are looking at, you are looking at a question.

The same trap in the vocabulary you use every day

The production controller asks for Q1 hours split by service line. A service line is the kind of work a job belongs to, and Meridian runs four of them: Heavy, Light, Line, and Cabin and IFE. You build the visual and send it out. Two people come back the same afternoon. The cabin crew chief says his crew booked more than the 10.0 hours you gave him. The light maintenance chief says the shop did nine hours of light work and his crew is showing zero. Neither of them is wrong.

Service line arrives from the Heavy Maintenance Control Centre planning board, the HMCC, and it is merged onto FactWorkOrder in Power Query. The shop floor system never carries it. So route A runs DimServiceLine to FactWorkOrder to FactLabor, using the header to line relationship you already have. It answers one question: what kind of work was done.

There is a second route to the same word. Every technician belongs to a crew. CrewAssignment gives each technician a crew code, and CrewCodeMap turns that crew code into a service line. So TECH-04 on CRW-CAB belongs to Cabin and IFE. Merge those two in Power Query and DimTechnician gains a CrewServiceLine column. Route B then runs DimServiceLine to DimTechnician to FactLabor. It answers a different question: whose crew did the work.

Two routes, one dimension, one fact. That is the station shape again with different table names, and this time all four service line rows disagree.

Start with TECH-04, because he moves the most. He sits on CRW-CAB, the cabin crew. In Q1 he booked 10.5 hours: 6.0 on WO-1001 and 4.5 on WO-1003. Both of those are Heavy C-checks, the scheduled inspection that takes an aircraft out of service for weeks at a time. Route A files that 10.5 under Heavy, because Heavy is the work that was done. Route B files it under Cabin and IFE, because the cabin crew is who did it. One technician, 10.5 hours, and the service line he lands on depends on which route you took.

Interview-level insight

Cabin and IFE reads 10.0 down route A and 10.5 down route B, so the pair looks like a rounding argument. The two numbers share no labor rows at all. Route A's 10.0 is one row, L-506, booked by TECH-07 to WO-1004, the cabin retrofit. Route B's 10.5 is two different rows, L-502 and L-505, both booked by TECH-04 to heavy checks. Half an hour of visible difference, and a complete change of the rows underneath it. Numbers that nearly agree are harder to defend than numbers that obviously do not, because nobody opens an investigation over half an hour.

TECH-07 carries the rest of the gap. His crew code is CRW-XX9, and CrewCodeMap has no row for it. Route B cannot give his 10.0 hours a service line at all, so they land in a blank row. Remember who owns that map. No system produces it, you maintain it by hand, and no refresh will ever tell you that a new crew code turned up.

The resolution is the one this chapter has already argued. Leave DimServiceLine and DimTechnician[CrewServiceLine] unrelated. Relating them hands DimServiceLine two ways to reach FactLabor, and you are back in front of the same ambiguity message. Write two measures instead. Name them so the difference sits in the field list where the production controller can read it.

DAXLabor Hours by Crew Line
Labor Hours by Crew Line =
VAR SelectedLines =
    VALUES ( DimServiceLine[ServiceLine] )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ),
        REMOVEFILTERS ( DimServiceLine ),
        TREATAS (
            SelectedLines,
            DimTechnician[CrewServiceLine]
        )
    )
Lines 2 to 3
Capture the service lines the visual is asking for, before anything is cleared. The variable is evaluated in the outer filter context, which is what makes the pattern work. VALUES again here, and not DISTINCT, for the reason given earlier: VALUES keeps the blank member the engine adds when a fact holds a key the dimension does not. On today's four service lines the two functions return the same rows. That stops being true the first time the HMCC board emits a fifth one.
Lines 5 to 6
