CALCULATE because the visual wants one number here. CALCULATETABLE returns a table to iterate, which is a different job. SUM because Hours is a stored column with no expression wrapped round it, so SUMX would iterate for nothing.
Line 7
REMOVEFILTERS on DimServiceLine, and not on FactWorkOrder. Clearing the middle table gains you nothing, because DimServiceLine still holds the selection and pushes it straight back down the work order route. Take the filter off at its source. REMOVEFILTERS again in place of ALL, for the reason given earlier: ALL also works as a table function, so a reader has to stop and decide which job it is doing.
Lines 8 to 11
TREATAS stamps the captured service line values onto DimTechnician[CrewServiceLine], and the existing single relationship carries the filter on into FactLabor. TREATAS rather than a real relationship, because a real relationship is exactly what creates the second path.

Now the cost, and it is a real one. TECH-07 has a blank CrewServiceLine, so TREATAS matches nothing for him and his 10.0 hours drop out of the crew measure. The crew measure totals 62.0 minus 10.0, which is 52.0, while Labor Hours totals 62.0 on the same page. Ten hours go missing and nothing on screen says so. Put both measures in one table visual and add a third measure holding the difference between them. Then the unmapped crew code has a number attached to it, and somebody will fix the map.

The model stays as it is. The field list carries two names and each name answers one question. The production controller gets Heavy at 38.0, which is the work the shop did. The cabin crew chief gets 10.5, which is what his crew booked. Neither of them has to learn what a filter path is.

The slicer case, which is almost always the wrong tool

The shift supervisor picks LAS on the station slicer, clicks a technician name in the technician slicer, and the page goes blank. He tries two more names and gets the same empty page. Then he raises a ticket saying the report is broken. This is the most common reason a bidirectional relationship ends up in a production model, so it gets its own treatment.

The wrong way

Select LAS on the station slicer. The technician slicer still lists all seven members of DimTechnician. That includes TECH-03 and TECH-06, who have no labor rows anywhere, and TECH-01, who has hours but not at LAS.

Set DimTechnician to FactLabor to Both. The technician slicer now shows TECH-05 alone, because L-508 is the only LAS labor row. The ticket closes.

What you actually changed is global. The model now has a new path running from FactLabor back up to DimTechnician, and forward from there into BridgeTechCert. It stops at the bridge, because the bridge to certification relationship is still single. Any filter that reaches FactLabor in any report now narrows the technician list, whether the visual wanted that or not, and the next relationship anyone adds is likelier to be rejected as ambiguous.

The fix

Put a visual level filter on the slicer itself: Labor Hours is not blank, or Labor Hours > 0 if you want to drop technicians whose hours net to zero. The slicer evaluates that measure per member in the current filter context and hides the members that fail.

The cost is paid by that one visual, on that one page. It is visible to the next person who opens the report, because it sits in the filter pane where they will look.

It also survives the requirement changing. When somebody asks for technicians with hours in the last 90 days instead, you edit a measure. You do not renegotiate the model.

What you see in the report

Both approaches produce a slicer showing TECH-05, and the supervisor's ticket closes either way. They are indistinguishable in the screenshot attached to that ticket, which is why this decision gets made badly. The difference only surfaces later, in a query plan you did not write and a relationship you cannot create.

Slicer behaviour deserves more room than a paragraph in a relationships chapter. "The slicer shows the wrong items" has at least five distinct causes, and only one of them is about cross-filter direction. Chapter 17 works through the diagnosis properly. Until then, the rule is short: if the only thing you want to change is which items appear in a slicer, leave the relationship alone.

What to remember
  • Single direction means the filter runs one way, from the one side to the many side. Both adds a reverse hop that reads the surviving keys on the many side and applies them to the one side. That reverse hop is a scan and a materialisation, and it costs more than the forward lookup.
  • The legitimate case is a bridge in a many to many. Setting DimTechnician to BridgeTechCert to Both lets an A&P selection reach FactLabor and return 39.0. It does not make the certification rows additive: they sum to 85.0 against a true total of 62.0.
  • Two filter paths from one table to another is ambiguity, and the engine refuses it because both answers are defensible. MSP is 34.5 hours through the work order and 28.5 hours through technician home station. Two questions, one label.
  • Hours by service line has the same two routes. Through the work order it is Heavy 38.0, Light 9.0, Line 5.0 and Cabin and IFE 10.0. Through the technician's crew it is Heavy 28.5, Cabin and IFE 10.5, Line 13.0, Light 0.0 and 10.0 hours on a crew code that is not in the map. Both total 62.0 and all four service lines disagree, because TECH-04 sits on the cabin crew and booked 10.5 hours to heavy checks. Answer it with two named measures and leave the model alone.
  • Force the ambiguity through and the number comes from whichever path is left standing. That choice is not written down anywhere, and it will not survive the next model change.
  • Three costs, all real: ambiguity, a per-query materialisation you cannot measure on small data, and security filters reaching tables the rule author never considered.
  • Bidirectional relationship when every measure needs the reverse hop. CROSSFILTER when one or two do. TREATAS when the tables should not be related at all.
  • A slicer showing too many items is a visual problem. Fix it with a visual level measure filter. A model property makes every query in the model pay for it.
Part 4 . Evaluation context and DAX

09Row context and filter context

After this chapter you will be able to look at any DAX expression in the Meridian model and say which context it is running in. You will be able to say what the engine did to produce that context, and why two expressions that look almost identical return 62.0 and 52.0.

The production controller wants a technician scorecard for the quarter. One row per technician, hours booked, sorted. You build it, and the total under the column reads 52.0. On the same page, a card showing total labor hours reads 62.0. Both numbers come out of the same eight labor rows, and you wrote both of them yourself.

Most DAX that returns a wrong number is not doing wrong arithmetic. It is doing correct arithmetic over the wrong set of rows. Everything in this chapter exists to let you predict, before you press enter, exactly which rows the engine will hand your aggregation. By the end of it you will know where those ten hours went, and you will be able to say whether 52.0 or 62.0 is the number the production controller actually asked for.

There are two independent mechanisms at work, and the whole of DAX rests on telling them apart. Once you can, a result that looked arbitrary becomes one you can derive on paper before the engine ever runs it.

Two different questions

Filter context
The set of rows currently visible on every table in the model. It is created by slicers, by report and page filters, by the rows and columns of a visual, and by CALCULATE. A slicer is the on-page control a user clicks to choose values. The filter context is what a measure sees, and a measure is a calculation the engine runs once for every cell of a visual. A filter context always exists, even if it is empty, and an empty filter context means every row of every table is visible.
Row context
A pointer to one specific row of one specific table. It is created by a calculated column and by any iterator function. An iterator is a function that walks a table one row at a time. A row context leaves every row of the table visible. Its only job is to say which row the words FactLabor[Hours] refer to right now.

Here is the sentence to write on the whiteboard. A row context knows which row you are on. A filter context knows which rows exist. Those are different questions. DAX keeps them separate on purpose, because collapsing them would make it impossible to write an expression that compares one row against the whole table.

A row context leaves an aggregation free to see everything. This is the part that gets missed on a first read, so say it out loud: being positioned on row L-505 still lets SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ) return 62.0. Position and visibility stay unrelated until you deliberately connect them, and connecting them is what the second half of this chapter is about.

Filter context, seen on the Meridian report

The finance manager wants one number for the month. Hours booked at MSP in January, and he does not care how you get it. You give him a matrix so he can see the other months too.

Put Dimension DimStation[StationCode] on the rows of that matrix, put DimDate[MonthName] on the columns, and drop a Labor Hours measure into the values. The MSP and January cell returns 22.5. Trace where that came from. The visual applies two filters, one from each axis. DimStation is cut to the single row MSP. DimDate is cut to the 31 rows of January. Those filters then travel along the relationships in the direction the arrows allow: DimStation to Fact FactWorkOrder, which leaves WO-1001, WO-1002, WO-1006 and WO-1008; then FactWorkOrder to FactLabor along the header to line relationship; and separately DimDate straight into FactLabor[WorkDate].

What survives both filters is three labor rows: L-501 at 7.5 hours, L-502 at 6.0 and L-503 at 9.0. That is 7.5 plus 6.0 plus 9.0, which is 22.5. The finance manager has his number. The measure asked what was left, summed it, and returned. Filter context did all of that work on its own.

Rule of thumb

Every number in a visual is one measure evaluated once per cell, in a filter context assembled fresh for that cell. If you cannot list the filters in a cell, you cannot debug the number in it. Write them down before you write DAX.

Row context, seen on the same rows

Now add a calculated column to FactLabor. A calculated column is worked out once per row when the model refreshes, and the answer is stored in the model like any other column.

DAXLineCost, calculated column on FactLabor
// Evaluated once per row at refresh time.
LineCost =
    FactLabor[Hours] * FactLabor[HourlyRate]
Line 3
Two bare column references with no aggregation around them. In a measure this would fail. Here it works, because a calculated column is given a row context automatically, once for every row of the table it sits on.
Result
On L-501 the row context points at 7.5 and 95, so the column stores 712.50. On L-507 it points at 12.0 and 120, so it stores 1,440.00. Eight rows, eight independent evaluations, and the column total is 6,326.50, the same figure the Labor Cost measure returns.
Name
LineCost and not Labor Cost. The model already carries a measure called Labor Cost, and a column may not share a name with a measure in the same table. Chapter 4 and Chapter 10 weigh up whether to store this column at all. The point here is only that the expression compiles as a column and would not compile as a measure.

Look at what the calculated column actually did. It resolved two column names against a row pointer and multiplied. There was no slicer to consult, because slicers do not exist at refresh time. The rest of the model still saw all eight rows of FactLabor throughout. That is the entire behaviour of a row context.

A measure begins with no row context at all

This is the cleanest proof that the two mechanisms are separate.

DAXOne works, one cannot
// Works. SUM walks the visible rows itself.
Labor Hours = SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )

// Fails. No row context exists, so DAX cannot decide
// which of the eight values of Hours you meant.
Broken Hours = FactLabor[Hours]
Line 2
SUM is an aggregator that opens its own internal row context over the column you hand it, walks every visible row, and folds the values together. That internal context lives and dies inside the function.
Line 6
A measure is evaluated once per cell, not once per row. With eight visible rows of FactLabor and no pointer to any of them, the engine refuses. It reports that a single value for column Hours in table FactLabor cannot be determined. That error message is the engine telling you, in its own words, that there is no row context.
Why this and not that

SUM here, because the expression to be summed is a plain column with nothing computed per row. SUMX would give the same 62.0, but it would open a row context you do not need and evaluate an expression eight times instead of scanning one column. On a real fact table that costs. Reach for SUMX only when the thing you are summing has to be worked out row by row, such as Hours multiplied by HourlyRate.

Where row context comes from

Two sources, and only two. Calculated columns get one for free. Iterators create one over whatever table you pass as their first argument, and they create it fresh for every row of that table. These are the iterators you will actually meet in this model.

SUMX
Sums an expression evaluated per row. Chosen over SUM whenever the per row expression involves more than one column, because SUM accepts a single column reference and nothing else.
AVERAGEX
Same shape, averaging instead. Chosen over AVERAGE for the same reason, and also because AVERAGE would average the eight Hours values instead of the eight computed costs.
FILTER
Returns a table, keeping the rows where a condition evaluated in row context is true. Chosen over a plain boolean predicate inside CALCULATE when the condition compares two columns of the same table, or calls a measure, neither of which a simple predicate can express.
ADDCOLUMNS
Returns the source table plus new evaluated columns. Chosen over SELECTCOLUMNS when you want to keep everything you already had and add to it, because SELECTCOLUMNS discards any column you do not list.
RANKX
Ranks each row of a table by an expression. Chosen over the newer RANK window function when you are writing a calculated column or a measure outside a query with a defined window, since RANK expects an ordering and partition supplied by the surrounding query shape.
MAXX
Largest value of an expression across rows. Chosen over MAX when the value has to be computed for each row, because MAX takes a column or two scalars and cannot take an expression over a table.
GENERATE
For each row of the first table, evaluates the second table in that row context and joins the results. Chosen over CROSSJOIN when the second table must depend on the current row, which CROSSJOIN cannot do because it evaluates both sides once.

Look at the two panels first. Both draw the same five labor rows, L-501 through L-505, so whatever differs between them is the mechanism and not the data. On the left, under the heading Row context, one row is outlined and carries a small arrow beside it. The other four are drawn exactly as they always were: still there, still visible, still countable. That is row context, a cursor. On the right, under the heading Filter context, three of the five rows are greyed out and two stay lit. The two that stay lit are the ones booked to TECH-04, which is the selection that panel's note names. Nothing is marked as current, because nothing needs to be. That is filter context, a knife. The card running the full width underneath is context transition, and its arrow runs from the words row context to the words filter context with CALCULATE sitting on it. That is the only thing in DAX that turns the first picture into the second. The last line of that card states a result this chapter reaches later, that SUMX ( DimTechnician, [Labor Hours] ) returns 52.0 and not 62.0. Hold the question until Hours C, which is where the production controller's scorecard gets settled.

Context transition, which is the hard part

When CALCULATE is invoked while a row context is open, it does something before it does anything else. It takes the current row context on the table being iterated. It converts that into a filter context which cuts the table down to that row, using every column of the table. Then, with the new filter in place, it evaluates its expression.

That conversion is called context transition. It cannot be switched off, and it happens even when CALCULATE has no filter arguments at all. CALCULATE ( [Labor Hours] ) written inside an iterator is doing real work despite looking like it does nothing.

Two consequences trip up almost everybody.

  1. A measure referenced inside an iterator gets an implicit CALCULATE wrapped around it by the engine. Writing [Labor Hours] is exactly the same as writing CALCULATE ( [Labor Hours] ). So the measure undergoes context transition automatically, every time, whether or not you wanted it. This is why SUMX ( FactLabor, [Labor Hours] ) does not do what a beginner expects.
  2. Context transition on a table with no unique key filters to every row that matches on every column. A unique key is a column whose values never repeat. Without one, two identical rows are indistinguishable to the transition and both stay visible. Your iteration then silently includes more rows than you intended, and the total comes out too high with no error and no warning.
Interview-level insight

Context transition also overwrites, rather than intersects with, any existing filter on the columns of the transitioned table. This matters when a measure containing an iterator sits inside a visual that already filters that same table. The iterator still only walks rows visible in the outer filter context, so the slicer still controls the loop. Inside each iteration, though, the row filter replaces the outer one on those columns. Saying which of those two rules applies to a given expression is the fastest way to demonstrate you actually understand CALCULATE.

Three expressions on the Meridian rows

Define the measure once and leave it alone for the rest of the chapter.

DAXLabor Hours
Labor Hours = SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )
Line 1
One aggregation over one column, with no filter modifier and no iterator. SUM because there is nothing to compute per row, so SUMX would open a row context for no gain. Plain SUM with no CALCULATE wrapper, because nothing here changes a filter. Whatever filter context the measure is called in, it sums the Hours values that survive it.
Baseline
With no slicers and no visual axes, the filter context is empty, all eight rows are visible, and the measure returns 62.0. Every result later in this chapter is a variation on that one number.

These are the eight rows it will be working over. FactLabor is LaborEntries with TechnicianID trimmed, which is what repaired L-505 back onto TECH-04.

The shaded row is L-506, whose technician TECH-07 does not exist in the HR extract. Hold on to that row. It is what makes the third expression interesting, and it is where the production controller's ten hours are hiding.

DAXThree expressions, two results
// 1. Row context only. No transition anywhere.
Hours A = SUMX ( FactLabor, FactLabor[Hours] )

// 2. Measure inside an iterator. Implicit CALCULATE,
// so context transition on every one of the 8 rows.
Hours B = SUMX ( FactLabor, [Labor Hours] )

// 3. Same measure, different table iterated.
Hours C = SUMX ( DimTechnician, [Labor Hours] )
Line 2
First argument is a table, second is an expression evaluated in the row context that table opens. SUMX rather than SUM because SUM accepts only a column reference and cannot be handed an expression to work out per row.
Line 6
The only change from line 2 is the second argument. Here it is a measure reference in [Name] form, where line 2 had a column reference in Table[Column] form. That single difference is what invites the implicit CALCULATE and therefore context transition.
Line 9
Identical expression to line 6, iterating Dimension DimTechnician instead of Fact FactLabor. Nothing else moves. The result does.

Hours A, 62.0, no transition

SUMX opens a row context over FactLabor and moves through the eight rows. On each one, FactLabor[Hours] resolves against the row pointer and yields a stored number. The engine reads 7.5, 6.0, 9.0, 8.0, 4.5, 10.0, 12.0 and 5.0 straight off those eight rows, and adds them to 62.0. Every value comes from storage exactly as it sits there. The one thing that could convert a row context into a filter is CALCULATE, and this expression contains none, explicit or implicit. This is the boring case, and boring is what you want.

Hours B, also 62.0, for a completely different reason

Same eight iterations, but the second argument is a measure, so the engine rewrites it as CALCULATE ( [Labor Hours] ). On the first iteration the row context is sitting on L-501. Context transition takes that row and builds a filter on FactLabor covering every column of it: LaborID equals L-501, WorkOrderID equals WO-1001, TechnicianID equals TECH-02, WorkDate equals 7 January 2025, Hours equals 7.5, HourlyRate equals 95. Only one row in the table satisfies all six conditions, because LaborID alone is already unique. FactLabor is now filtered to a single row. Only then does SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ) run, over a table of one row, returning 7.5.

Repeat that seven more times and you get 6.0, 9.0, 8.0, 4.5, 10.0, 12.0, 5.0, and the outer SUMX adds them to 62.0. The number is identical to Hours A and the machinery underneath is a different animal. A read of a stored value happened eight times in A. In B, eight filter contexts were constructed, eight filtered scans of the fact table were performed, and eight aggregations were run. The result agrees only because the transition happened to isolate exactly one row each time.

Performance note

Hours B is the expensive way to get 62.0. On eight rows nobody notices. On a labor table with two million rows, an iterator with a transitioning measure inside it can force the engine out of its fast column scan and into a much slower row by row evaluation, and query time can go from milliseconds to minutes. Reserve transition inside an iterator for when you genuinely need per row aggregation of related data, and never write it just because it reads nicely.

Hours C, 52.0, and this one is genuinely useful

This is the scorecard the production controller asked for, and here is where its 52.0 comes from. Change nothing but the iterated table. Take DimTechnician at the point in the build where it holds the six cleaned rows from the HR extract, TECH-01 through TECH-06. SUMX now walks six rows, not eight. On each one the implicit CALCULATE transitions that technician row into a filter on DimTechnician. Because TechnicianID is unique in that table, the transition isolates one technician. That single row filter then propagates down the one to many relationship into FactLabor, cutting it to that technician's labor rows, and SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ) totals whatever is left.

12.0 plus 16.5 plus 0 plus 10.5 plus 13.0 plus 0 is 52.0. The ten hours on L-506 are simply never reached, because the loop is over technicians and TECH-07 is not a technician as far as this table is concerned. The engine reports this as a clean success. No error is raised and no blank row appears. The number is quietly ten hours short of the fact table total, which is why the scorecard and the card beside it disagree.

One precision point before you use Table 09.3 as gospel. For TECH-03 and TECH-06, SUM over an empty set returns BLANK, not zero. The table above shows 0 because that is the arithmetic contribution, and SUMX treats blank as zero when it adds the six values together. In a matrix visual those two technicians would show an empty cell where this table shows 0, and by default their rows would disappear from the visual entirely.

Trace this by hand, row by row

Six iterations of SUMX ( DimTechnician, [Labor Hours] ). Read the middle column as the filter that context transition installed on DimTechnician, and the right column as what survived in FactLabor after that filter propagated across the relationship.

  1. Row context lands on TECH-01. Implicit CALCULATE fires. Transition filters DimTechnician to TechnicianID = TECH-01, Name = R. Okafor, HomeStation = MSP, EmployeeType = Staff. That is one row. Propagation cuts FactLabor to L-507 only. SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ) returns 12.0.
  2. Row context moves to TECH-02. Transition isolates M. Halvorsen. FactLabor keeps L-501 and L-503. 7.5 plus 9.0 gives 16.5.
  3. Row context moves to TECH-03. Transition isolates J. Prieto. Propagation leaves FactLabor with zero rows, because J. Prieto logged no time in the quarter. SUM over nothing returns BLANK, which contributes 0.
  4. Row context moves to TECH-04. Transition isolates D. Sandoval. FactLabor keeps L-502 and L-505. 6.0 plus 4.5 gives 10.5. Note that L-505 only arrives here because the trailing space in its TechnicianID was trimmed in Power Query. Without that trim this iteration would return 6.0 and the grand total would be 47.5.
  5. Row context moves to TECH-05. Transition isolates K. Ibrahim. FactLabor keeps L-504 and L-508. 8.0 plus 5.0 gives 13.0.
  6. Row context moves to TECH-06. Transition isolates L. Petrov. No labor rows survive, so the result is BLANK and contributes 0.

The outer SUMX adds 12.0, 16.5, 0, 10.5, 13.0 and 0, and returns 52.0. L-506 was never visited by any of the six iterations, so its 10.0 hours are absent by construction. Nothing malfunctioned. The loop simply never went near that row.

Now the inconvenient part. In the finished Meridian model, DimTechnician has seven rows, because an Unknown technician member was added for TECH-07 exactly so that orphan facts have somewhere to land. Run the same expression against that seven row version. A seventh iteration isolates TECH-07, reaches L-506, and returns 10.0. That brings the total to 62.0, matching the fact table. The 52.0 belonged to an incomplete dimension all along, and SUMX was doing its job both times. That is why the unknown member work in Part 3 earns its keep.

Common mistake

Building a technician scorecard by iterating the dimension, then reconciling it against a plant total that iterates the fact table, and concluding that DAX is unreliable when the two disagree. They disagree because they are answering different questions. Iterating a dimension answers "how much for each of these people", which by definition excludes anyone not in the list. Iterating the fact answers "how much in total". Decide which question the business is asking before you decide which table to iterate. If the answer is the first, then the completeness of your dimension has just become a reporting requirement, and you should write it into the spec as one.

When transition cannot isolate one row

The planner wants planned hours compared across trades, with the month taken out of the way. She builds a small helper table that strips the month columns off capacity, points a measure at it, and asks you why MSP airframe now shows 72 planned hours when the source workbook says 44. Nothing on her screen is flagged. Both iterated tables so far had a unique key, and hers does not.

DAXCapByTrade, calculated table
CapByTrade =
    SELECTCOLUMNS (
        FactCapacity,
        "StationCode", FactCapacity[StationCode],
        "Trade", FactCapacity[Trade],
        "PlannedHours", FactCapacity[PlannedHours]
    )
Why this and not that

SELECTCOLUMNS rather than SUMMARIZE, and the choice is the whole point. SUMMARIZE would group the rows and collapse the duplicates, which hides the problem and produces a table with a natural key again. SELECTCOLUMNS keeps every one of the 28 rows exactly as they were, minus the two month columns, which is what a rushed modeller actually ends up with.

MSP planned 14 airframe hours in January and 14 again in February. Drop the month and those two rows become MSP, Airframe, 14 and MSP, Airframe, 14, identical in all three remaining columns. March is MSP, Airframe, 16, still distinct. Now compare two ways of totalling the MSP airframe hours.

DAXThe same total, two ways
Planned Trade Hours = SUM ( CapByTrade[PlannedHours] )

// Row context only. Correct.
MSP Airframe A =
    SUMX (
        FILTER (
            CapByTrade,
            CapByTrade[StationCode] = "MSP"
                && CapByTrade[Trade] = "Airframe"
        ),
        CapByTrade[PlannedHours]
    )

// Transition on a table with no unique key. Inflated.
MSP Airframe B =
    SUMX (
        FILTER (
            CapByTrade,
            CapByTrade[StationCode] = "MSP"
                && CapByTrade[Trade] = "Airframe"
        ),
        [Planned Trade Hours]
    )
MSP Airframe A
Three rows survive the FILTER. The iterator reads 14, 14 and 16 straight off each row and returns 44. That agrees with the source workbook, where MSP planned 14 airframe hours in January, 14 in February and 16 in March.
MSP Airframe B
Same three rows, but the measure triggers transition. On the January row the filter becomes StationCode = MSP, Trade = Airframe, PlannedHours = 14. Two rows match that, so the measure returns 28. On the February row the filter is character for character the same, so it returns 28 again. The March row is unique and returns 16. 28 plus 28 plus 16 is 72, which is 28 hours of capacity that Meridian does not have.

The planner had the B version. No error, and no warning triangle. Any utilisation percentage sitting on top of that number now divides by 72 where it should divide by 44. Every airframe utilisation figure at MSP therefore reads about 61 percent of its true value, and the shop manager is told there is slack that does not exist. The defence is a unique key on any table you intend to iterate with a transitioning expression. In practice that means keeping MonthKey on FactCapacity instead of throwing it away for tidiness.

Nested row contexts, and why EARLIER exists

The shift supervisor wants to know, for each work order, which labor line was the biggest. He is chasing a pattern in who gets handed the long jobs. That is a ranking inside each work order, and writing it is where row contexts start sitting on top of one another.

Row contexts nest. If you write a calculated column on FactLabor, you already have one row context over FactLabor. If that column then calls FILTER ( FactLabor, ... ), the FILTER opens a second row context over the same table. Inside the FILTER, a bare reference to FactLabor[Hours] resolves to the inner context, the row FILTER is currently testing. The outer row is shadowed. The value you actually want, the one belonging to the row the column is being computed for, can no longer be reached by name.

EARLIER exists to reach past the shadow. It means "the value this column had in the row context one level out". The name misleads on first reading, because it sounds temporal and it is not. Here is a ranking column on FactLabor that ranks each labor entry by hours within its own work order.

DAXHours Rank in WO, the EARLIER form
Hours Rank in WO =
    COUNTROWS (
        FILTER (
            FactLabor,
            FactLabor[WorkOrderID]
                = EARLIER ( FactLabor[WorkOrderID] )
                && FactLabor[Hours]
                >= EARLIER ( FactLabor[Hours] )
        )
    )
Lines 5 and 6
The bare FactLabor[WorkOrderID] on the left of the comparison is the row FILTER is testing. The EARLIER ( FactLabor[WorkOrderID] ) on the right is the row the calculated column is being written for. Same column name, two different rows, and nothing in the syntax tells you which is which except the wrapper.
Line 8
Greater than or equal, not greater than, so that the largest entry counts itself and ranks 1. Plain greater than would rank it 0.
Line 2
COUNTROWS turns the surviving table into the rank. Written this way the whole expression is correct and almost unreadable, which is the case against EARLIER.

The same logic, with the outer values captured by name instead.

DAXHours Rank in WO, the VAR form
Hours Rank in WO =
    VAR CurrentWO = FactLabor[WorkOrderID]
    VAR CurrentHours = FactLabor[Hours]
    RETURN
        COUNTROWS (
            FILTER (
                FactLabor,
                FactLabor[WorkOrderID] = CurrentWO
                    && FactLabor[Hours] >= CurrentHours
            )
        )
VAR lines
The two variables are evaluated in the outer row context, before FILTER opens anything, and their values are then fixed. A variable in DAX is a constant once assigned, so no later context can change what CurrentWO means.
FILTER line
Inside FILTER, FactLabor[WorkOrderID] refers to the row being tested, and CurrentWO refers to the row being computed. The comparison reads left to right as English, which the EARLIER version never manages.
COUNTROWS
Counting how many rows in the same work order have hours greater than or equal to this row's hours gives that row's rank, with 1 for the largest.

Both forms return the same values. L-501 ranks 1 and L-502 ranks 2 within WO-1001, since 7.5 beats 6.0. L-504 ranks 1 and L-505 ranks 2 within WO-1003, since 8.0 beats 4.5. L-503, L-506, L-507 and L-508 each rank 1, being the only labor line on their work order. That column answers the supervisor's question: filter it to rank 1 and he has the biggest line on every work order, with the name attached. Use the second form in all new code. EARLIER still works and is still supported, but it forces the reader to count nesting levels in their head. It takes an optional second argument for skipping more than one level that almost nobody remembers. And it breaks the moment somebody wraps your expression in another iterator.

Why this and not that

COUNTROWS rather than COUNT. COUNT counts non blank values in one column, so it would silently undercount any row where the counted column happened to be blank. COUNTROWS counts rows regardless of content, which is what a rank needs. And FILTER in place of a boolean predicate inside CALCULATE, because the condition compares a column against a value captured from a different row of the same table, which a simple predicate cannot express.

The calculated column trap that follows from all this

The production controller wants the work order list to carry two extra columns: how many labor lines each order has, and how many hours they add up to. It sounds like a five minute job. The first attempt fails to compile, and the reason is the rule this chapter opened with.

Row context points at a row and leaves every other row visible. Say it once more, because this is where it produces its most confusing symptom. In a calculated column, a reference to a column of a related table on the many side resolves to all the rows that match. That is a table, and DAX will not put a table into a scalar column.

Which function you need depends entirely on which side of the relationship you are reaching towards.

The wrong way

A column on FactWorkOrder to see how much labor each order absorbed.

DAXDoes not work
Labor Lines =
    RELATED ( FactLabor[LaborID] )
Line 2
RELATED promises a single scalar. It can only deliver one when the target sits on the one side.

FactLabor is on the many side of the header to line relationship. WO-1001 has two labor rows, so there is no single LaborID to return and the expression is rejected outright.

The fix

Ask for the table, then aggregate it.

DAXLabor Lines, column on FactWorkOrder
Labor Lines =
    COALESCE (
        COUNTROWS (
            RELATEDTABLE ( FactLabor )
        ),
        0
    )
Line 4
RELATEDTABLE returns the labor rows belonging to the current work order, as a table.
Lines 3 and 2
COUNTROWS reduces that table to a number, and COALESCE turns the blank into 0 for WO-1005 and WO-1008.
Why this and not that

RELATEDTABLE rather than FILTER ( FactLabor, FactLabor[WorkOrderID] = FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID] ), because RELATEDTABLE uses the relationship the model already holds. The FILTER version rebuilds that join by hand, which is longer to read and much slower on a large fact table. Under the hood RELATEDTABLE is CALCULATETABLE of the target table, so it performs context transition and then lets the filter propagate along the relationship. That is the same mechanism as Hours C, applied to a table result instead of a scalar. And COALESCE in place of IF ( ISBLANK ( ... ), 0, ... ), because COUNTROWS of an empty table returns BLANK and not zero. COALESCE handles that in one evaluation, where the IF form makes you write the count expression twice.

That table is the production controller's two columns, finished. The Labor Hours column is the same idea with a different aggregator, written as SUMX ( RELATEDTABLE ( FactLabor ), FactLabor[Hours] ). SUMX here, and not a bare SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ), and the reason is the whole subject of this chapter. SUM reads the filter context. A calculated column on FactWorkOrder supplies a row context, and row context does not travel across a relationship. So a bare SUM would see all eight labor rows on every single work order and write 62.0 into all eight cells. SUMX over RELATEDTABLE states the row set explicitly instead of hoping one arrives. CALCULATE ( SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ) ) would also work, by forcing the transition, and it is the shorter form. It also hides the mechanism behind a function that looks like it is doing nothing. The two shaded rows are WO-1005 and WO-1008, which have no labor at all. Without COALESCE those cells would be blank, and a blank in a numeric column has a way of turning into an unexpected gap in a chart later.

Reaching the other direction is easier, and it works across more than one hop.

DAXAircraft Type, column on FactLabor
// Two hops: FactLabor to FactWorkOrder to DimAircraft.
// Both hops go many to one, so RELATED can follow them.
Aircraft Type =
    RELATED ( DimAircraft[AircraftType] )
Hop 1
FactLabor[WorkOrderID] is on the many side of the relationship to FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID]. One work order per labor row, so the value is unambiguous.
Hop 2
FactWorkOrder[ACREG] is on the many side of the relationship to Built DimAircraft[ACREG]. One aircraft per work order, again unambiguous, so RELATED keeps walking and returns the type.
Limit
RELATED follows a chain only while every step goes from many to one. The instant one step goes the other way, it fails, and you need RELATEDTABLE plus an aggregator for that step.
Why this and not that

RELATED, and not LOOKUPVALUE ( DimAircraft[AircraftType], DimAircraft[ACREG], RELATED ( FactWorkOrder[ACREG] ) ). Both return the same string. LOOKUPVALUE performs its own search and does not require a relationship, which makes it the right tool when no relationship exists. Here one does, and RELATED uses the relationship the engine has already indexed. Choosing LOOKUPVALUE when a relationship is available is paying for a search you have already paid for once.

Grouped by type that is 23.5 hours on the A320-200 fleet, 9.0 on the B737-800, 17.5 on the E175 and 12.0 against the recovered tail N338WA. L-507 returns a value at all because DimAircraft was built as an append of the registry and the distinct tails from the work orders. N338WA is therefore a real dimension row with placeholder attributes. Against the raw registry, RELATED would find nothing and those 12.0 hours would vanish from every type breakdown on the report.

One last honest caveat about calculated columns generally. Every column here is computed at refresh and stored in the model, so it costs memory in proportion to its cardinality and it cannot respond to a slicer. Aircraft Type on FactLabor is a reasonable trade, since the model already stores the same values on DimAircraft and the dictionary is tiny. Labor Lines on FactWorkOrder is fine at eight rows and would be worth questioning at eight million. At that size a measure using COUNTROWS over the filtered fact table gives you the same answer without materialising anything. Reach for a calculated column when you need the value on a slicer or an axis. Reach for a measure otherwise.

What to remember
  • A row context knows which row you are on. A filter context knows which rows exist. Neither one implies the other.
  • Calculated columns and iterators create row context. Slicers, visual axes, report filters and CALCULATE create filter context. A measure starts with filter context only, which is why SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ) works and a bare FactLabor[Hours] does not.
  • Context transition is CALCULATE converting the current row into a filter on all columns of the iterated table. Any measure reference inside an iterator triggers it, because the engine wraps measures in an implicit CALCULATE.
  • SUMX ( FactLabor, FactLabor[Hours] ) and SUMX ( FactLabor, [Labor Hours] ) both return 62.0 by completely different routes, and only the first is cheap.
  • SUMX ( DimTechnician, [Labor Hours] ) returns 52.0 over the six HR technicians, because TECH-07 on L-506 is not in the dimension and is never iterated. Add the Unknown member and it returns 62.0. What you iterate decides what you can possibly count.
  • Transition on a table without a unique key filters to every row matching on all columns, which inflates totals with no error. Keep a key on anything you intend to iterate.
  • Use VAR to capture the outer row value instead of EARLIER in all new code. Same result, and it survives being nested inside somebody else's iterator.
  • In a calculated column, RELATED reaches towards the one side across any chain of many to one hops, and RELATEDTABLE with an aggregator reaches towards the many side. Wrap the count in COALESCE unless you want blanks for work orders with no activity.
Part 4 . Evaluation context and DAX

10Calculated column or measure

After this chapter you will be able to look at any Meridian requirement and decide, before writing code, whether it belongs in a calculated column, a measure, a calculated table or Power Query. You will also be able to name the exact symptom each wrong choice produces, and prove it with the row counts in the model.

The finance manager wants one number. What did Meridian quote for the quarter? You put a card on the page and it reads 46,600. She writes it down and it goes on a slide. The true figure is 38,100.

The card is doing its arithmetic correctly. The mistake was made three weeks earlier, when somebody chose to store a value in a column instead of computing it in a measure. A calculated column and a measure share one formula bar and run on completely different machinery underneath. Most of the reporting bugs that get blamed on DAX come from that choice made wrong. Two failures account for nearly all of them: values that refuse to respond to a slicer, and totals that come out too high. This chapter works through both, and it ends with the 38,100.

One difference, and everything else follows from it

Start with the calculated column. A calculated column is a new column you add to a table with a DAX formula, and the engine evaluates that formula once per row of the table. The evaluation happens during data refresh, which is the load step that pulls source data into the model. It runs before any report is open and before any user exists. The result is written into the model as a real column. It is encoded and compressed next to the columns that came from the source, and it occupies memory whether a single visual uses it or not. Once refresh finishes, the value is frozen until the next refresh.

Now the measure. A measure is a DAX formula that returns one value, and the engine evaluates it once per cell, at query time. Nothing is stored. When a visual renders, the engine works out the filter context for each cell of that visual. Filter context is the set of filters in force at that moment, arriving from slicers, from the rows and columns of the visual, and from page filters. The engine applies that filter context and runs your expression inside it. Change a slicer and every cell is recomputed against a different filter context. The measure has no memory of yesterday and no existence outside the query that asked for it.

That is the whole difference between a calculated column and a measure. Everything else in this chapter follows from it. Hold those two paragraphs in your head and you can derive most of the guidance yourself, with nothing left to memorise.

Symptom one: a number that ignores the slicer

The shift supervisor at TUS wants a leaderboard. Who logged the most labour hours, ranked, so he can put it on the wall. You build it, he opens it, and he clicks TUS in the station slicer. The technician at the top of his list is ranked fourth, and nobody on screen is ranked first. He tells you the report is broken.

Here is how the ranking was built. Ranking feels like an attribute of a person, so it went on DimTechnician as a calculated column. The code below is careful. It handles context transition correctly, which is more than most first attempts manage. Context transition is the step where the row the engine is currently sitting on becomes a filter, and line 5 is where it happens.

DAXDimTechnician[HoursRank], calculated column, wrong tool
// Calculated column on DimTechnician
HoursRank =
RANKX (
    DimTechnician,
    CALCULATE ( SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ) ),
    ,
    DESC,
    DENSE
)
Line 3
RANKX and not RANK. RANK is the newer window function and it needs an explicit ORDERBY relation. That makes it a good fit for visual calculations and DAX queries, and a poor fit for a stored model object. RANKX takes a table expression and an expression to evaluate over it, which is exactly the shape needed here.
Line 4
The table to rank over is the whole of DimTechnician, all seven rows including the Unknown row that catches TECH-07.
Line 5
CALCULATE earns its place here. Inside a calculated column the engine has row context, which means it knows which row of DimTechnician it is sitting on. It has no filter context at all. So a bare SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ) would see the entire fact table and return 62.0 on every single row. CALCULATE performs context transition. It converts the current row of DimTechnician into a filter, and that filter propagates down the relationship to FactLabor. SUM and not SUMX because Hours is a stored column, so SUM can be answered straight from the compressed column.
Line 6
The third argument is left empty deliberately. RANKX accepts an optional value to place in the ranking, and omitting it tells the engine to evaluate the expression in the current context and rank that result. The bare comma has to stay, because the two arguments after it are positional. Delete the empty slot and DESC slides into the value position, which changes the meaning of the call rather than raising a clean error.
Lines 7 and 8
DESC so the highest hours get rank 1. DENSE so tied ranks do not leave gaps behind them. TECH-03 and TECH-06 both have zero hours and both sit at the bottom, so DENSE and the default SKIP happen to agree in this dataset. They stop agreeing the moment a tie appears mid-list. Write the argument explicitly every time and the question never comes up.

Refresh the model and the column materialises. It is correct, in the narrow sense that it answers the question it was asked.

Now put a station slicer on the page and select TUS, the way the shift supervisor did. Note carefully which field that slicer has to use. The Meridian model deliberately has no relationship between DimStation and DimTechnician. Creating one would give two filter paths from DimStation into FactLabor: one through FactWorkOrder, one through DimTechnician. The station attribute that filters technicians directly is DimTechnician[HomeStation], and that is the field on the slicer.

Select TUS. The visual now shows two technicians, TECH-03 and TECH-04. The rank column still says 6 and 4. Nobody is ranked first, which is exactly the screen the shift supervisor was looking at. The usual next move is to decide DAX is broken and start adding CALCULATE wrappers to a value that was written to disk before anyone opened the file.

It is not broken. HoursRank was computed at refresh time, when a TUS selection did not exist. The column answers one fixed question, permanently: where does this technician rank among all seven technicians in the model. The user is asking a different one: where does this technician rank among the technicians on screen right now. Only an object evaluated after the click can answer that.

DAXLabor Hours and Technician Rank, measures
Labor Hours =
SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )

Technician Rank =
RANKX (
    ALLSELECTED ( DimTechnician[TechnicianName] ),
    [Labor Hours] + 0,
    ,
    DESC,
    DENSE
)
Line 6
ALLSELECTED over the technician name column. This removes the filter that the current row of the visual puts on the technician, so each cell can see its peers. It keeps the filters that arrived from outside the visual, and the slicer is one of those.
Line 7
The expression is the measure itself. A measure reference carries no table name, so it is written [Labor Hours], while the column it sums is written FactLabor[Hours]. The ranking is computed from whatever Labor Hours returns under the current filters. The + 0 is deliberate. TECH-03 has no rows in FactLabor at all, so SUM returns a blank, and I do not want the rank order to depend on how blanks sort. Adding zero makes the value explicit and the result deterministic. It also keeps TECH-03 visible in the table, because a blank measure result would drop the row from the visual entirely.
Lines 9 and 10
Same tie handling as the column version, for the same reason. Line 8 is the same empty value slot, kept for the same positional reason.
Why this and not that

ALLSELECTED and not ALL: ALL would strip the slicer as well as the row filter, so under a TUS selection it would rank TECH-04 against all seven technicians and hand back rank 4 again. You would have written a measure that reproduces the calculated column's bug with more effort. ALLSELECTED and not VALUES: VALUES returns the technicians visible in the current filter context. Inside a row of the visual that context has already narrowed to one technician. Every cell would rank a single-row table, and every cell would return 1.

Remove the slicer and Technician Rank returns 4 for TECH-04, matching the column exactly. Same logic as the column, evaluated against a context that is allowed to change. The column is a photograph and the measure is a window. The shift supervisor gets the leaderboard he asked for: with TUS selected, TECH-04 is first on 10.5 hours and TECH-03 is second on 0.0.

Symptom two: duplicated rows and inflated totals

Back to the finance manager and her 46,600. She wants the quoted value of the quarter's work, one number, for a slide. This failure costs money because the number looks completely normal. A stuck rank announces itself on screen. An inflated total sits there looking like a number, in a card, on a slide.

Grain is the question of what one row of a table stands for, and the whole bug lives in the answer. FactWorkOrder is at header grain: one row per work order, eight rows in all. QuotedAmount lives there because a quote is a property of a work order. FactLabor is at line grain: one row per labour line, eight rows spread unevenly across only six work orders. WO-1001 has two labour lines. WO-1003 has two. WO-1005 and WO-1008 have none at all. That uneven spread is the whole mechanism of the bug.

Look at the curved lines leaving the header rows on the left. WO-1001 fans out into two labour lines, L-501 and L-502, and WO-1003 fans out into L-504 and L-505, so anything copied down those lines arrives twice. WO-1002 has a single labour line and looks perfectly healthy. The extract drawn here is three of the eight work orders and five of the eight labour lines. That is enough to show the fan, and not enough to show the opposite failure. The red card states that one in words instead: work orders with no labor line vanish entirely. In the full data those are WO-1005 and WO-1008. That same red card adds only the five lines drawn, 3,000 plus 3,000 plus 3,200 plus 12,500 plus 12,500, and the full eight labour lines take the same arithmetic to 46,600. The green card shows the shape to aim for. Quoted Amount reads 38,100 from FactWorkOrder, Labor Cost reads 6,326.50 from FactLabor, and each measure is left on its own table. The picture is the bug. Everything below is just the arithmetic of that picture.

The page the finance manager was reading is a labour page, built around hours and technicians. She wanted quoted value on it too. The obvious move is to bring the quote down onto the labour table so it sits next to the hours.

The wrong way

A calculated column on FactLabor that pulls the header value down to line grain, then a measure that sums it.

DAXFactLabor[WOQuoted]
WOQuoted =
RELATED ( FactWorkOrder[QuotedAmount] )

Quoted Amount =
SUM ( FactLabor[WOQuoted] )
Line 2
RELATED and not LOOKUPVALUE, because a relationship from FactLabor to FactWorkOrder already exists and RELATED walks it. The DAX on this line is valid. It is pointed the correct way, many side to one side, and it returns exactly what it promises.
Line 5
The damage happens at this line. The line above it is innocent. SUM now aggregates a header value that has been copied onto eight line rows, so the row count of FactLabor decides the answer and the row count of FactWorkOrder stops mattering.

It refreshes without an error, the column populates, the measure returns a plausible currency figure. Result: 46,600.

The fix

Leave QuotedAmount where it belongs, on FactWorkOrder, and aggregate it with a measure.

DAXQuoted Amount
Quoted Amount =
SUM ( FactWorkOrder[QuotedAmount] )
Line 2
SUM and not SUMX, because QuotedAmount is a stored column and there is no row-by-row expression to evaluate, so the engine answers from the compressed column. No CALCULATE either: nothing about the filter context is being modified, and wrapping an aggregation in CALCULATE for decoration only makes the code harder to read.

Eight rows in, eight values summed, one per work order. Result: 38,100, in every filter context that reaches FactWorkOrder.

Wrong total
46,600
True total
38,100
Overstatement
8,500
Independent causes
Two
What you see in the report

A quoted value card that reads 46,600, which is 22 per cent above the truth of 38,100. The damage spreads from there. A margin card built as quoted minus actual reads 16,928.50 instead of 8,428.50. The whole 8,500 of phantom quote lands in the margin and nothing offsets it, so the job book looks roughly twice as profitable as it is. Slice it by station and the individual station figures are wrong too. Each one is wrong by a plausible amount, so nothing triggers suspicion. The number only fails a check if somebody adds the eight quotes up by hand. That is exactly the check nobody performs on a dashboard that has been live for a quarter.

Trace this by hand, row by row

Every row of FactLabor gets the quote of its parent work order stamped onto it. The relationship is many to one from FactLabor to FactWorkOrder, so RELATED resolves cleanly and no error is raised anywhere.

The arithmetic, spelled out: 3,000 plus 3,000 is 6,000. Plus 3,200 is 9,200. Plus 12,500 is 21,700. Plus 12,500 is 34,200. Plus 4,000 is 38,200. Plus 7,500 is 45,700. Plus 900 is 46,600.

The true total is 3,000 plus 3,200 plus 12,500 plus 4,000 plus 2,000 plus 7,500 plus 900 plus 5,000, which is 38,100.

The gap is 8,500, and it is made of two errors pulling in opposite directions.

  1. Over-count. WO-1001 has two labour lines, so its 3,000 is counted twice. WO-1003 has two labour lines, so its 12,500 is counted twice. That adds 15,500 that does not exist.
  2. Under-count. WO-1005 and WO-1008 have no labour lines whatsoever, so they contribute nothing. That silently drops 2,000 plus 5,000, which is 7,000 of real quoted value.

15,500 minus 7,000 is 8,500, which reconciles exactly to the gap. The two errors are independent of each other. Fixing the duplication alone would still leave you 7,000 short. The two work orders that vanished are the ones a shop manager is most likely to ask about, because one of them is still open.

Common mistake

RELATED inside a calculated column on a fact table is the most reliable way to inflate a total in Power BI. The function itself is fine. It is the right choice over LOOKUPVALUE when a relationship already exists, because it follows that relationship instead of scanning the target table for a match. The mistake is what you do next. Pull a header value down to line grain and it inherits the line table's row count, so any SUM over it counts each header once per line. Two labour lines means the quote counts twice. Zero labour lines means it disappears. One question before you type RELATED in a column: is the value I am pulling repeated across the rows I am pulling it into. If yes, write a measure against the table where the value lives.

The correct approach, and then the harder case

The finance manager gets her number here, and it is 38,100. SUM ( FactWorkOrder[QuotedAmount] ) is the model working exactly as designed. Slice by DimStation and the filter reaches FactWorkOrder directly, so MSP returns the sum of its own work orders and nothing else. Slice by DimWOType and the same thing happens. Put labour hours beside it and both measures answer independently at their own grain, which is what measures are for. SUM and not SUMX because QuotedAmount is a stored column that needs no row-by-row expression, so the engine answers from the compressed column without materialising anything.

That claim is worth proving, because "it works under a slicer" is the exact thing the calculated column failed at. Put the same measure on two different fields and add the columns up.

Check the station column by hand: 18,700 plus 16,500 plus 900 plus 2,000 is 38,100. Now the type column: 28,000 plus 6,100 plus 4,000 is also 38,100. Each work order is counted exactly once in each decomposition. Each work order is one row of FactWorkOrder, and it belongs to exactly one station and exactly one type. PHX returns a blank. That is correct, and most report consumers will read it as a bug, so decide deliberately whether you hide the row or coalesce it to zero. A zero would claim PHX quoted nothing, which says something different from PHX having no work orders at all. The same measure over FactLabor[WOQuoted] would have split 46,600 across those members instead, and every one of those station figures would have looked individually defensible.

The genuinely harder case is quoted against actual, because actual comes from two facts at two different grains. Labour is at technician-day grain, parts are at issue-line grain, and neither can be added to the other by putting a column somewhere. Five measures handle it.

DAXThe quoted versus actual measure set
Labor Cost =
SUMX ( FactLabor, FactLabor[Hours] * FactLabor[HourlyRate] )

Parts Cost =
SUMX ( FactParts, FactParts[Qty] * FactParts[UnitCost] )

Actual Cost =
[Labor Cost] + [Parts Cost]

Quoted Amount =
SUM ( FactWorkOrder[QuotedAmount] )

Variance =
[Quoted Amount] - [Actual Cost]
Labor Cost
SUMX and not SUM because the value being summed is a product of two columns and does not exist as a stored column. SUM only accepts a single column reference, so it cannot express this at all.
Parts Cost
Same shape, different fact. Note there is no ACREG on FactParts, so slicing parts by aircraft routes through FactWorkOrder. Solve that routing with a relationship. Adding an aircraft registration column to FactParts would be the same header-to-line error wearing a new costume.
Actual Cost
Plain addition of two measures, and not an iterator over a combined table. Each measure resolves at its own grain in the current filter context, and adding two scalars is safe. Building a UNION of labour and parts rows to iterate over would give the same answer at more cost. It would also need reconciling every time either fact changes shape.
Variance
Positive means Meridian quoted more than it spent. Negative means the job ran over. Written as a subtraction of measures so it inherits both filter contexts automatically and needs no maintenance when either side changes.

WO-1008 deserves a look. It shows 5,000 quoted and nothing spent, which is correct: it opened on 10 March and has neither labour nor parts against it yet. Under the calculated column approach that row did not appear at all. WO-1004 shows a favourable variance of 2,980.00 that will shrink, because the order is still open and the remaining cost has not landed. Both rows are business facts, and the measure is honest enough to put them on screen. The fix is a filter on closed work orders. The calculation stays as it is.

One display detail before you check those figures against your own screen. Where a work order has no rows in a fact, the measure returns a blank. WO-1008 has neither labour nor parts, so Labor Cost, Parts Cost and Actual Cost are all blank on that row. The same is true of the parts columns on WO-1004 and WO-1007. The zeros are written out in the table only so that the arithmetic reads cleanly down each column. The row still appears in the visual because Quoted Amount has a value, and Variance still reads 5,000.00, because subtracting a blank subtracts nothing. If you want the zeros for real, wrap the measure in COALESCE. Adding zero would also work, and COALESCE states the intent in the formula instead of hiding it in an arithmetic side effect.

Now the inconvenient part of that table. The visual on your screen will carry a ninth row, blank, holding 4,900 of parts cost. That is P-9007 charged to WO-1009, and WO-1009 does not exist in FactWorkOrder. A fact row whose key has no match like that is an orphan, and the engine parks every orphan against the blank member. With that row included, Actual Cost totals 34,571.50 and Variance totals 3,528.50, both derived from the same measures. Both figures are correct. They answer a question that includes an orphan. Decide deliberately whether your page shows it, and tell your users what you chose.

Performance note

The measure-first rule has a real cost and you should know what you are buying. Labor Cost iterates FactLabor on every query. On eight rows that is free. On forty million rows it is not. A stored LineCost column computed once at refresh aggregates faster, because the engine scans one compressed column instead of multiplying two. That case is legitimate, precisely because line cost is a property of the labour line that does not change when anyone clicks. Reach for it after you have measured a problem, and compute it in Power Query rather than DAX if the source can produce it.

Deciding, in six questions

Work down this list and stop at the first question that answers itself. It resolves nearly every case without argument.

  1. Ask what the value is a property of. A property of a technician, a date or a work order points toward a column on that table. A property of a set of rows points toward a measure.
  2. Ask whether the answer should change when the user changes a slicer. If yes, it must be a measure. No calculated column responds to selection.
  3. Ask whether the value needs to be aggregated, averaged, ranked or compared across rows. If yes, measure.
  4. Ask whether the value lives at a different grain from the table you were about to put it on. If yes, do not put it there at any price. That is the 46,600 error.
  5. Ask whether you need it on an axis, in a slicer, as a sort-by key, inside a hierarchy, as a relationship key or in a security filter. Those six require a physical column, and a measure cannot do any of them.
  6. If you have reached here you need a column. Ask whether Power Query can compute it, and if it can, compute it there.
Interview-level insight

The real question behind "column or measure" is what the value is a property of. Quoted amount is a property of a work order, so it belongs on FactWorkOrder and stays there. Hours are a property of a labour line. A technician's rank is a property of a comparison, and a comparison only exists once someone has chosen who is in it. That is why rank can never be stored and quoted amount must never be moved. Answer the property question and the DAX object follows.

Ten Meridian tasks, decided

When a calculated column is the right answer

The planner asks for a slicer that splits work orders into small, medium and large jobs. You have just been burned by the 46,600 bug, so your instinct says measure. You spend an afternoon trying to drop a measure into a slicer and Power BI refuses every time.

Analysts burned by that bug swing to a rule of "never write a calculated column", and the planner's slicer is where the rule breaks. Six situations require a physical column, and the size band is one of them.

  • Relationship keys. A relationship binds two physical columns. If the key needs cleaning or concatenating, the cleaned key has to exist as a column.
  • Sort-by columns. DimDate[MonthName] is text and sorts alphabetically, putting February first. Sort by Column fixes it, and it needs MonthNo present as a column on the same table at the same grain.
  • Static row-level classification. The work order size band, an IsWeekend flag, an employee type grouping. Each is decided by the row's own values and by nothing the user does.
  • Anything that goes in a slicer. Slicers read columns. The product enforces that boundary, and the size band the planner asked for is exactly this case.
  • Columns used by a security role. Row-level security filters are written against columns, so a role that restricts a user to their home station needs that station as a column.
  • Hierarchy levels. A hierarchy is an ordered list of columns. Station to work order to labour line needs each level physically present.
Rule of thumb

A calculated column is right when the value is a property of the row and does not depend on what anyone selects. Read that twice, because both halves matter. Line cost passes both tests. Turn time passes both. Technician rank fails the second test. Quoted amount on a labour row fails the first, because it is a property of the work order and the labour line only borrows it. If a requirement fails either half, write a measure.

Calculated tables, briefly and honestly

The production controller puts his check dates on a chart and the months come out in alphabetical order, February first. He asks for calendar order. Meridian's source system has no calendar table to point at, so you have to build one inside the model.

A calculated table is the same idea one level up: a DAX expression returning a table, evaluated at refresh and stored in the model. The case where it earns its place in Meridian is DimDate, and the controller's month order is the reason.

DAXDimDate, calculated table, 90 rows
DimDate =
ADDCOLUMNS (
    CALENDAR ( DATE ( 2025, 1, 1 ), DATE ( 2025, 3, 31 ) ),
    "Year",      YEAR ( [Date] ),
    "MonthNo",   MONTH ( [Date] ),
    "MonthName", FORMAT ( [Date], "mmmm" ),
    "MonthKey",  YEAR ( [Date] ) * 100 + MONTH ( [Date] ),
    "MonthStart",
        DATE ( YEAR ( [Date] ), MONTH ( [Date] ), 1 )
)
CALENDAR
CALENDAR and not CALENDARAUTO. CALENDARAUTO inspects every date column in the model and expands to whole years. That would hand you 365 rows covering all of 2025, when Meridian only reports on Q1. Explicit bounds give exactly 90 rows, 31 plus 28 plus 31, and a date table with no stray empty months.
ADDCOLUMNS
One expression producing the whole table. The alternative is creating the calendar first and then stacking five separate calculated columns on top of it. One expression means fewer objects in the dependency graph and one place to read the definition. The remaining DimDate columns that Meridian needs, Quarter, DayOfWeek and IsWeekend, follow the same pattern and are left out here only to keep the block readable.
YEAR, MONTH
These read the numeric parts straight from the date value. FORMAT could produce them too, but it returns text, and text sorts alphabetically on an axis, which is the problem you are trying to avoid.
FORMAT
Used only where text is actually wanted, for the display month name. Because it returns text, MonthName must then be sorted by MonthNo. That is the sort-by case from the list above, and it is the reason MonthNo is in this table at all. It is also what gives the production controller January, February, March in that order, with February back where it belongs.
MonthStart
DATE and not STARTOFMONTH. STARTOFMONTH is a time intelligence function that operates on a column of dates within a filter context, and inside ADDCOLUMNS you are in row context working with one scalar date. DATE constructs the value directly. This column is what FactCapacity joins to at month grain.

The honest caveats. A calculated table is recomputed at every refresh and stored like any other table, so it costs memory and refresh time. It cannot be edited in Power Query, so the analyst who inherits your file will look for it in the query editor and not find it. DirectQuery restricts it further. Check the current limitation list before you assume Import behaviour carries over. For a date table in an Import model the trade is usually worth it, because the definition is self-contained and does not depend on a source system having a calendar table. For most other tables, if the source or Power Query can produce it, let them.

The third option people forget

Back to the planner and the size band. There is a third place to build that column, and for anything that could be a calculated column and does not need to see the rest of the model, the third place is usually the better answer. Power Query is the load step where you shape a table before it enters the model. The size band belongs there.

Read this left to right. The four bands are the four places a calculation can live: the source system, then Power Query, then DAX calculated columns and tables, then DAX measures. Each band after the first carries the moment it runs, at refresh, at load, at query time. The axis underneath them runs from computed once, per refresh on the left, to computed per visual, per user, per click on the right. That is the cost you trade every time you move one step further along. The rule is printed beneath the bands: push work as far left as you can, then move it right for one reason only. The green card names that reason. If the answer depends on what the user selects, it cannot be precomputed, and no amount of refresh time will make it so.

MFactWorkOrder size band
let
    Source = WorkOrders,
    Banded = Table.AddColumn (
        Source,
        "SizeBand",
        each
            if [QuotedAmount] < 3000 then "Small"
            else if [QuotedAmount] < 7500 then "Medium"
            else "Large",
        type text
    )
in
    Banded
Table.AddColumn
The user interface Conditional Column button writes the same function call, and it omits the final type argument, so the column arrives typed as any. Writing type text by hand gives the engine a known type to encode. On a column destined for a slicer that is worth the extra few characters.
The bands
Under 3,000 is Small, 3,000 to 7,499 is Medium, 7,500 and above is Large. Against the eight Meridian quotes that puts WO-1005 at 2,000 and WO-1007 at 900 in Small, WO-1003 at 12,500 and WO-1006 at 7,500 in Large, and the remaining four in Medium. The planner drops SizeBand straight into a slicer and it works, because it arrived in the model as a real column.

Two reasons to prefer this over the DAX equivalent. First, a Power Query column arrives with the table and is encoded in the same pass as every column that came from the source. A calculated column is added after the table has already been loaded, and it usually compresses less well. Second, and this is the reason I would defend hardest, a calculated column becomes a node in the model's dependency graph. Every measure, relationship, hierarchy and other calculated column that touches it now depends on it. Refresh has to evaluate it in the right order, and changing it later can force recalculation you did not plan for. A Power Query column stays outside that graph. It arrives as a plain column and the engine treats it exactly like the columns that came from the source.

The exception is real and you will hit it. If the expression needs to see another table through a relationship, or needs a measure, Power Query cannot help you. Relationships do not exist yet at that stage of the pipeline. That is when a calculated column is the correct tool, and nobody is compromising. Everything else belongs upstream. Chapter 4 covers where each transformation belongs and why moving work upstream keeps paying you back long after the model is built.

What to remember
  • A calculated column is evaluated once per row at refresh and stored. A measure is evaluated once per cell at query time and stores nothing. Every other difference follows from that one.
  • A calculated column cannot respond to a slicer, because it was computed before the report was opened. HoursRank says 4 for TECH-04 whatever is selected. The measure using ALLSELECTED says 1 under a TUS home station slicer.
  • Pulling a header value to line grain with RELATED inflates totals. Quoted amount on FactLabor sums to 46,600 against a true 38,100: 15,500 over-counted because WO-1001 and WO-1003 each have two labour lines, 7,000 lost because WO-1005 and WO-1008 have none.
  • Keep QuotedAmount on FactWorkOrder and aggregate it with a measure. It returns 38,100 in every filter context that reaches that table.
  • The real question is what the value is a property of, and whether that property depends on what anyone selects.
  • Columns are still required for relationship keys, sort-by columns, static row classification, slicer fields, security filters and hierarchy levels. Build them in Power Query unless they need to see the model.
Part 4 . Evaluation context and DAX

11CALCULATE and every filter modifier you need

After this chapter you will be able to predict the number a CALCULATE expression returns before you write it, name which modifier changes which part of the filter context, and explain why a measure that hard filters AOG still shows AOG hours when the slicer says Scheduled.

The production controller sets the work order type slicer to Scheduled. He wants to see the scheduled work and nothing else. The labor hours card drops to 38.0, which is right. The card beside it, the one labelled AOG Hours, still reads 14.0. He asks you why a report filtered to Scheduled is showing him AOG hours, and it is a fair question.

The answer is in one function. CALCULATE is the only function in DAX that can change the filter context an expression is evaluated in. Filter context is the set of filters in force when a value is computed, arriving from slicers, from the rows and columns of a visual, and from page filters. Every other function reads that context. CALCULATE writes it. That is why CALCULATE appears in almost every measure of any substance you will ship, and why almost every measure of any substance you will debug turns out to be a CALCULATE you did not fully understand.

The mechanism is small. There are five things CALCULATE does and they happen in a fixed order. Once you can recite that order you can reason about any expression in the language. One of those five steps is counterintuitive on first contact, and nothing in the interface tells you it happened. That step is what put 14.0 on the controller's screen, and this chapter ends by resolving it.

What CALCULATE does, in order

CALCULATE takes an expression as its first argument and zero or more filter arguments after it. When the engine hits a CALCULATE call it runs this sequence.

  1. It creates a new filter context that starts as a copy of the current one.
  2. It evaluates each filter argument. Every filter argument is evaluated in the outer filter context, the one that existed before CALCULATE started, and in any row context that is open. Filter arguments never see each other. Two filter arguments in the same CALCULATE are evaluated independently, so the second one cannot depend on what the first one did.
  3. If there is a row context, CALCULATE performs context transition. Every column of the table being iterated becomes a filter in the new context. This is the step covered in Chapter 9, and it happens whether you wanted it or not.
  4. It applies the CALCULATE modifiers. ALL, REMOVEFILTERS, ALLEXCEPT, ALLSELECTED, KEEPFILTERS, USERELATIONSHIP and CROSSFILTER belong in a category of their own. They instruct CALCULATE about how to build the context, and they run after context transition, in step four.
  5. It applies the evaluated filter arguments to that context, then evaluates the expression.

This is the same pair of panels you met in Chapter 9, and it repays a second look now that the five steps are in front of you. In the left panel one FactLabor row is outlined and the other four sit there untouched. An iterator knows which row it is on. That knowledge filters nothing until something converts it into a filter. Step three above is that conversion, and CALCULATE is the only function that performs it. Read the full width card along the bottom for the rest of it. Follow the arrow that runs from the words row context to the words filter context. That arrow is the step that makes a measure reference inside an iterator return a different number from the same reference sitting in a card visual on the page. The card gives the Meridian case underneath: SUMX ( DimTechnician, [Labor Hours] ) returns 52.0 and not 62.0.

Step five carries the fact that explains most of the confusion in this language. When CALCULATE applies a filter argument on a column, it does not add that filter to whatever filter was already sitting on the column. It replaces it. The old filter on that column is gone. Filters on every other column survive untouched.

Interview-level insight

Ask why CALCULATE replaces instead of intersecting and the answer is that a filter argument is a table. DimWOType[WOType] = "AOG" expands into a table of the values that satisfy it, built from ALL on that column. Applying a table to a column sets the context for that column to exactly those values. Nothing of what was there survives, because nothing of what was there was consulted. Whether that should have been the default is a fair question. The practical answer is that the opposite behaviour costs you one keyword, KEEPFILTERS. Starting from an intersecting default would instead mean adding a filter remover for every column you touched.

The two syntaxes, and why one is sugar for the other

Take the Meridian measure [Labor Hours], defined as SUM(FactLabor[Hours]), which returns 62.0 across the whole quarter. Now filter it to AOG work.

DAXAOG Hours, boolean shorthand
CALCULATE(
    [Labor Hours],
    DimWOType[WOType] = "AOG"
)

That is the shorthand, and it reads like a condition: keep the rows where WOType is AOG. With nothing selected on the page it returns 14.0, which is WO-1002 at 9.0 plus WO-1005 at 0 plus WO-1007 at 5.0. Here is the same measure written out in full, and the full form is closer to what the engine actually runs.

DAXAOG Hours, table form
CALCULATE(
    [Labor Hours],
    FILTER(
        ALL( DimWOType[WOType] ),
        DimWOType[WOType] = "AOG"
    )
)
Line 4
