ALL on the column produces every distinct WOType in the model, ignoring whatever the report has selected. Three values: Scheduled, AOG, Mod.
Line 5
The condition keeps the one row where WOType is AOG, so the FILTER opened on line 3 returns a one row table.
Lines 3 to 6
That one row table becomes the filter on DimWOType[WOType]. It is the whole filter, not an addition to the existing one, because the existing one was discarded by the ALL on line 4.

The two are the same expression. The shorthand is compiled into the table form with ALL on the referenced column. That expansion is the entire explanation for the behaviour people find surprising. The shorthand reads like a condition and behaves like a replacement, and the hidden ALL is why.

You will also meet a variant written as FILTER(ALL(DimWOType), DimWOType[WOType] = "AOG"), with ALL on the whole table instead of on the column. It returns the same 14.0 here, and on a two column dimension you will never see a difference. The expansion underneath differs, though. A table level ALL clears the filters on every column of DimWOType. The moment that dimension gains a description or a priority column that someone slices on, the table form quietly drops that slicer. The shorthand keeps it.

This is the production controller's screen, exactly. Put a slicer on the report page for DimWOType[WOType] and set it to Scheduled. A card showing [Labor Hours] reads 38.0, which is WO-1001 at 13.5 plus WO-1003 at 12.5 plus WO-1006 at 12.0 plus WO-1008 at 0. Put the AOG measure above it on the same page and it reads 14.0. The measure removed the slicer's Scheduled filter from the WOType column and put AOG there instead. He is looking at a card that answers a question he did not ask.

Both rows are correct answers to different questions. The first answers "how many AOG hours are there". The second answers "how many of the hours the user is currently looking at are AOG". The production controller was asking the second question and the report was answering the first. Decide which question your page is asking before you write the measure, because both compile and only one of them is right.

Why this and not that

Use the boolean shorthand for any comparison on a single column against constants. Reach for the explicit FILTER form only when you need it: a condition across two columns, a column compared against a measure, or a filter that has to be evaluated row by row over a fact table. FILTER over a large table forces the engine to materialise and iterate it, while the shorthand compiles to a filter the storage engine can push down. At Meridian's eight work orders that difference is unmeasurable, which is why habits formed on toy models get expensive later.

ALL, the blunt instrument

The finance manager wants a share column. Labor hours by aircraft type, and next to each type the percentage of the quarter it represents. She expects the percentages to add to 100. You put [Labor Hours] in the numerator, and then you need a denominator that holds still at 62.0 while the rows of the visual change underneath it. Holding a denominator still is what ALL is for.

ALL removes filters. What it removes depends on what you hand it. With no arguments at all it clears the entire filter context of the model. That is almost never what a report measure wants, and it is mostly useful inside a scoped calculation. Hand it a table and it clears every filter on that table. Hand it one or more columns and it clears the filters on those columns only, leaving the rest of the table alone.

DAXPct of Total Hours
DIVIDE(
    [Labor Hours],
    CALCULATE( [Labor Hours], ALL( DimAircraft ) )
)
Line 2
The numerator is evaluated in the visual's own filter context. On the E175 row it is 17.5, which is WO-1003 at 12.5 plus WO-1007 at 5.0.
Line 3
ALL(DimAircraft) drops every filter the aircraft dimension is contributing, including AircraftType, ACREG and Operator. The denominator becomes 62.0 on every row of the visual.
Line 1
DIVIDE rather than the slash operator, because DIVIDE returns blank on a zero denominator instead of raising an error, and a divide by zero error kills the whole visual rather than one cell.

The finance manager gets her share column and it adds to 100.0 percent. E175 is 17.5 divided by 62.0, which is 0.28226, shown as 28.2 percent. The fourth row exists only because the aircraft dimension was built by appending the tails found in the work orders. Point this measure at the raw registry instead and the 12.0 hours land in a blank row, while the three real types add to 80.6 percent with nothing on screen saying so.

Why this and not that

ALL(DimAircraft) rather than ALL(DimAircraft[AircraftType]). The visual might later gain a second field from the same dimension, Operator for instance. A column level ALL would leave that new filter in place. The denominator would quietly become the operator total instead of the grand total, and the percentages would still look plausible. Table level ALL is the safer default for a true grand total. Column level ALL is right when you deliberately want to hold some of the dimension's filters and release others.

REMOVEFILTERS, which is ALL with a clearer name

REMOVEFILTERS accepts the same arguments as ALL. In the modifier position inside CALCULATE it does exactly the same thing. Microsoft added the name, and the name is the whole contribution, and it is still worth adopting.

DAXPct of Total Hours, preferred spelling
DIVIDE(
    [Labor Hours],
    CALCULATE(
        [Labor Hours],
        REMOVEFILTERS( DimAircraft )
    )
)

Naming preferences are cheap, so here is REMOVEFILTERS carrying a calculation of its own. Put DimStation[StationCode] on the rows of a matrix and ask what share of the quarter each station worked.

DAXPct of Quarter Hours
Pct of Quarter Hours =
DIVIDE(
    [Labor Hours],
    CALCULATE(
        [Labor Hours],
        REMOVEFILTERS( DimStation )
    )
)
Line 3
The numerator keeps the row's own station filter. On the MSP row it is 34.5, being WO-1001 at 13.5 plus WO-1002 at 9.0 plus WO-1006 at 12.0, with WO-1008 contributing nothing.
Line 6
REMOVEFILTERS( DimStation ) drops the station filter and nothing else, so the denominator is 62.0 on every row of the visual. A month slicer, a WOType slicer or a technician slicer would still apply inside that denominator, because none of them sit on DimStation.

34.5 divided by 62.0 is 0.55645, shown as 55.6 percent. 22.5 divided by 62.0 is 0.36290, shown as 36.3 percent. 5.0 divided by 62.0 is 0.08065, shown as 8.1 percent, and those three add to 100.0. The last two rows are the ones worth pausing on. UNASSIGNED holds WO-1005, which has no labor rows. PHX exists only in the planning workbook and has no work orders at all. Both return a blank, so Power BI hides them from the visual by default. Turn on "Show items with no data" and they reappear with an empty share, which is the honest reading: neither station worked a share of anything.

The reason to prefer it is that ALL is overloaded. In the modifier position it removes filters. In an expression position it is a table function that returns rows. That is the job it is doing on line 4 of the table form earlier in this chapter, inside FILTER(ALL(DimWOType[WOType]), ...). Same identifier, two different jobs, and the reader has to work out which one from the surrounding syntax. REMOVEFILTERS only ever means "clear the filters here", so when a colleague reads your measure six months from now there is nothing to work out.

Why this and not that

Use REMOVEFILTERS in every filter argument position. Keep ALL for the places where you actually need a table of rows returned, typically as the source of a FILTER or SUMMARIZE. They are functionally identical as modifiers, so this costs nothing and buys readability. The one caveat is version support: REMOVEFILTERS arrived later than ALL, so very old Analysis Services models may not accept it. Current Power BI Desktop and current Fabric semantic models do.

The working rule is positional. If the name appears directly as an argument of CALCULATE or CALCULATETABLE, spell it REMOVEFILTERS. If it appears inside another table expression, spell it ALL.

ALLEXCEPT, and the trap it sets

The production controller wants a different share. For each work order, what proportion of its own station's hours did it take? WO-1001 measured against MSP, WO-1003 measured against TUS, one line at a time down the list. The denominator has to change from row to row, following whichever station that row belongs to, and you cannot hardcode a station into a measure that has to serve all of them.

ALLEXCEPT removes filters from a table and everything related to it, except the columns you list. That is the natural way to express "share of the parent group" while leaving the parent to be decided at query time.

DAXPct of Station Hours
DIVIDE(
    [Labor Hours],
    CALCULATE(
        [Labor Hours],
        ALLEXCEPT( FactWorkOrder, DimStation[StationCode] )
    )
)
Line 5
The first argument is the table whose filters are cleared. DimStation, DimAircraft, DimWOType and DimDate all sit on the one side of a relationship from FactWorkOrder. That makes them part of the expanded FactWorkOrder table, so their filters are cleared too.
Line 5
StationCode is named as the exception, so a filter already sitting on that column survives. Note the word already. ALLEXCEPT preserves a filter and it never creates one. The station has to be present in the visual for this measure to mean anything. Table 11.4 puts the work order and the station side by side on the rows, and the denominator becomes that station's total. Drop the station column from the visual and every denominator silently becomes 62.0, because there was no StationCode filter left to keep.

That is the controller's answer. WO-1001 is 13.5 divided by 34.5, which is 0.39130, shown as 39.1 percent. The three MSP work orders with hours come to 39.1 plus 26.1 plus 34.8, which is 100.0 percent. The fourth contributes nothing, because WO-1008 has no labor rows. WO-1005 returns a blank because DIVIDE was used, and that blank is honest: the UNASSIGNED station has no hours to take a share of.

There is a version of this that some architects prefer, which clears the fact table and then puts the visible station back as an explicit filter.

DAXThe explicit equivalent
CALCULATE(
    [Labor Hours],
    REMOVEFILTERS( FactWorkOrder ),
    VALUES( DimStation[StationCode] )
)

This reads better: clear the fact table, then put back the one thing you want to keep. On the visual behind Table 11.4 it produces the same numbers. File the two as different measures, though, because the scope they clear is different. REMOVEFILTERS(FactWorkOrder) clears the filters on the columns of FactWorkOrder itself and stops there. A slicer on DimDate or DimWOType still applies inside that denominator. ALLEXCEPT works on the expanded table and takes those slicers out as well.

Add a month slicer to the page and the two versions stop agreeing. The explicit form gives each work order its share of its station within the selected month. The ALLEXCEPT form gives its share of the station across the whole quarter. The March rows then add to something under 100 percent, and a reader who does not know the measure will report that as a bug. Both forms are correct. Decide which of the two questions the page is asking before you pick one.

Set that slicer to February and the divergence is easy to check by hand. The active date relationship runs to OpenedDate. The visual now shows the three work orders opened in February: WO-1004 at TUS, WO-1005 at UNASSIGNED and WO-1006 at MSP. February labor is L-506 at 10.0 hours on WO-1004 and L-507 at 12.0 hours on WO-1006. The numerators are 10.0, blank and 12.0 in both versions. Only the denominators move.

The explicit form gives 10.0 divided by 10.0 and 12.0 divided by 12.0, because WO-1004 is the whole of TUS in February and WO-1006 is the whole of MSP in February. Both rows with hours on them read 100.0 percent, which is correct and which tells the reader nothing they did not already know. The ALLEXCEPT form gives 10.0 divided by 22.5, which is 0.44444 and shows as 44.4 percent, and 12.0 divided by 34.5, which is 0.34783 and shows as 34.8 percent, both against the quarter totals from Table 11.4. February is the month that shows this cleanly. Try it in March instead and the only station with hours is LAS. The LAS March total and the LAS quarter total are both 5.0, so that row reads 100.0 percent under either form and the difference hides.

Common mistake

ALLEXCEPT(FactWorkOrder, DimStation[StationCode]) clears more than the filters you were thinking about. It clears DimDate, DimAircraft and DimWOType too, because those tables expand into FactWorkOrder. A user who slices to March and to AOG gets a denominator that ignores both selections. It also breaks in the future: add a dimension on the one side of FactWorkOrder next quarter and every ALLEXCEPT in the model starts clearing that one as well, with no error. Now the surprise in the other direction. DimTechnician relates to FactLabor, so it never expands into FactWorkOrder, and a technician slicer survives this ALLEXCEPT untouched.

KEEPFILTERS, the one everybody gets wrong

Here is where the production controller gets his answer. KEEPFILTERS is an instruction that changes how a filter argument is applied. It tells CALCULATE to intersect the argument with the existing filter on the column instead of replacing it. That is the whole function. It takes the default behaviour of CALCULATE and inverts it for one argument.

DAXTwo AOG measures that behave differently
// replaces the WOType filter, ignores the slicer
CALCULATE(
    [Labor Hours],
    DimWOType[WOType] = "AOG"
)

// intersects with the WOType filter, respects the slicer
CALCULATE(
    [Labor Hours],
    KEEPFILTERS( DimWOType[WOType] = "AOG" )
)
Lines 2 to 5
The shorthand expands to ALL on WOType then a filter for AOG. Whatever the slicer had chosen on that column is discarded. With the slicer on Scheduled this returns 14.0, being WO-1002 at 9.0 plus WO-1005 at 0 plus WO-1007 at 5.0.
Lines 8 to 11
KEEPFILTERS suppresses the implicit ALL. The AOG table is intersected with the slicer's table. Scheduled intersect AOG is the empty set, so the measure returns blank.
Trace this by hand, row by row

Slicer set to Scheduled. Outer filter context on DimWOType[WOType] is the one row table { Scheduled }.

Without KEEPFILTERS. The filter argument expands to FILTER(ALL(DimWOType[WOType]), WOType = "AOG"). ALL discards { Scheduled } and returns { Scheduled, AOG, Mod }. FILTER reduces that to { AOG }, and CALCULATE applies it in place of { Scheduled }. Three work orders now pass: WO-1002 with L-503 at 9.0 hours, WO-1005 with no labor rows at all, WO-1007 with L-508 at 5.0 hours. Sum is 14.0.

With KEEPFILTERS. The same { AOG } table is produced, and CALCULATE intersects instead of replacing. { Scheduled } intersect { AOG } is empty, so no work orders pass and no labor rows pass. SUM over zero rows returns a blank. The card shows nothing at all, and a conditional format keyed on "less than 1" will not fire, because a blank never reaches the comparison.

Now select both Scheduled and AOG in the slicer. Outer context is { Scheduled, AOG }. Without KEEPFILTERS you still get 14.0, because the replacement does not care what the slicer said. With KEEPFILTERS the intersection is { AOG }, so you also get 14.0. The two measures agree here, which is why this bug survives testing: it only diverges when the selection and the hardcoded value do not overlap.

KEEPFILTERS matters in a second place that has nothing to do with slicers. When a filter argument spans two columns of the same table, it replaces the filter on each column independently. That can resurrect column combinations the original context had excluded. KEEPFILTERS holds the original pairs intact. This is the difference between filtering on columns and filtering on rows, and it is why a filter argument that touches two columns almost always wants KEEPFILTERS around it.

Meridian has a two column case sitting in Built DimAircraft. Put AircraftType on the rows of a matrix and Operator on the columns and each populated cell is a filter on a pair of values, not two independent filters. There are seven such pairs in the dimension, one per tail, because no two tails share both a type and an operator. Now write a measure that asks for the Airbus fleet plus everything Northwind Regional operates.

DAXFleet Pair Hours, with and without KEEPFILTERS
// replaces the filter on BOTH columns
Fleet Pair Hours =
CALCULATE(
    [Labor Hours],
    FILTER(
        ALL( DimAircraft[AircraftType], DimAircraft[Operator] ),
        DimAircraft[AircraftType] = "A320-200"
            || DimAircraft[Operator] = "Northwind Regional"
    )
)

// intersects with the pair the cell already carries
Fleet Pair Hours Kept =
CALCULATE(
    [Labor Hours],
    KEEPFILTERS(
        FILTER(
            ALL( DimAircraft[AircraftType], DimAircraft[Operator] ),
            DimAircraft[AircraftType] = "A320-200"
                || DimAircraft[Operator] = "Northwind Regional"
        )
    )
)
Line 6
ALL over two columns returns the pairs that exist in the table, not the cross join of the two columns. Seven pairs go in, and the OR condition keeps three of them: A320-200 with Cascade Air, A320-200 with Northwind Regional, and E175 with Northwind Regional. Those three pairs reach N771QR, N615RB and N902TT.
Result of the first
That three row table is applied in place of whatever pair the cell was carrying, on both columns at once. N771QR contributes 23.5 from WO-1001 and WO-1004, N615RB contributes nothing because WO-1005 has no labor rows, and N902TT contributes 17.5 from WO-1003 and WO-1007. Every cell in the matrix returns 23.5 plus 0 plus 17.5, which is 41.0.
Result of the second
KEEPFILTERS intersects the three pairs with the cell's own pair, so only cells whose pair is in the list survive. The Cascade Air A320-200 cell keeps 23.5 and the Northwind Regional E175 cell keeps 17.5. Everything else is an empty intersection and returns blank.

The four shaded rows are the damage. The B737-800 row for Cascade Air reads 41.0, and not one of those 41.0 hours was worked on a B737-800. The pair filter replaced the cell's type and the cell's operator, then went and found aircraft the cell had excluded. The kept version puts blanks there instead. Its two surviving cells, 23.5 plus 17.5, add to exactly the 41.0 that the replace version was printing everywhere. That is the tell. When a measure repeats one number across every cell of a matrix, a filter argument has replaced the axis it was supposed to respect.

Performance note

KEEPFILTERS is cheap but not free. It adds no iterator and forces no materialisation. What it can do is reshape the query plan enough that a filter which used to be pushed to the storage engine now resolves in the formula engine. On Meridian's 8 fact rows this is undetectable. Take a high cardinality column on a fact table with 200 million rows. Measure that before you ship. The plan change is real even though the function is light.

ALLSELECTED, the one to verify before you trust it

The shift supervisor selects MSP and TUS in the station slicer, because those are the two stations he covers. The share column beside the hours now adds to 91.9 percent. He asks where the missing 8.1 percent went. He will not accept "it is at LAS, which you filtered out" as an answer on a page that shows him two stations and one total.

ALLSELECTED is built for exactly this. It restores the filter context that existed outside the current visual. Slicers, page filters and report filters survive. The filters the visual itself is applying, its rows, columns and legend, are removed. The denominator then equals what the user can currently see, and the model total stops leaking into it.

DAXPct of Visible Hours
DIVIDE(
    [Labor Hours],
    CALCULATE(
        [Labor Hours],
        ALLSELECTED( DimStation )
    )
)

Put stations on the rows of a matrix and set a station slicer to MSP and TUS only. The visible hours are 34.5 plus 22.5, which is 57.0. Compare the two denominators.

The REMOVEFILTERS column divides by 62.0 and lands at 91.9 percent, which is correct and which most users read as a defect. That is the shift supervisor's missing 8.1 percent, and it is at LAS. The ALLSELECTED column divides by 57.0 and adds to 100 percent, which is what people expect from a share column sitting next to a slicer. 34.5 divided by 57.0 is 0.60526, shown as 60.5 percent. 22.5 divided by 57.0 is 0.39474, shown as 39.5 percent. Give the supervisor the second column and tell him it is a share of what he selected.

Why this and not that

Use ALLSELECTED when the reader will compare the percentages to each other and expect them to total 100 within what they selected. Use REMOVEFILTERS when the reader will compare the percentage to an absolute baseline, such as share of the whole quarter. Do not use ALLSELECTED as a general purpose "remove filters but nicer". Its result depends on where it is called from, and the concept of "outside the visual" is defined by shadow filter contexts that the report author never sees.

Common mistake

Nest ALLSELECTED inside an iterator, inside another CALCULATE, or inside a calculated table, and it stops meaning what the same expression means in a measure a visual evaluates directly. Its formal semantics involve shadow filter contexts, and it has genuine edge cases. What is certain is the simple case shown above. Anything more nested should be checked in your own report against numbers you worked out by hand. This is the one function in this chapter where I would not defend a claim in a design review without a screenshot of the actual result.

VALUES and DISTINCT

Both return a one column table of the values visible in the current filter context. The difference is the blank row.

When a fact table contains a key that does not exist in the dimension, Power BI adds an invisible blank row to the dimension so those fact rows have somewhere to go. In the finished Meridian model that never happens for aircraft, because Built DimAircraft was created by appending the tails found in the work orders, which recovered N338WA. Point the relationship at the raw AircraftRegistry instead, with its 6 rows, and WO-1006 becomes an orphan and the blank row appears.

DAXTwo ways to count tails
Tails with VALUES =
    COUNTROWS( VALUES( AircraftRegistry[ACREG] ) )

Tails with DISTINCT =
    COUNTROWS( DISTINCT( AircraftRegistry[ACREG] ) )
Why this and not that

COUNTROWS wrapped around the table function, and not DISTINCTCOUNT, because the point of this pair is to make the blank member visible and DISTINCTCOUNT buries the choice of table function inside a single name. Its own treatment of blanks is then a separate question you have to go and look up, which is one lookup more than this comparison needs. Use VALUES when you are reapplying a filter, as in the ALLEXCEPT rewrite earlier. Dropping the blank member there would exclude the orphaned facts from your denominator, and the percentages would stop adding up. Use DISTINCT when you are counting real dimension members for a human to read, because "7 aircraft" against a fleet list of 6 is a number you will have to explain in a meeting. The right answer at Meridian is neither: fix the dimension so the blank row cannot occur, and the choice stops mattering.

SELECTEDVALUE, HASONEVALUE, ISFILTERED and ISCROSSFILTERED

SELECTEDVALUE is a wrapper. SELECTEDVALUE(DimWOType[WOType], "all types") is shorthand for "if exactly one value is visible in that column return it, otherwise return the alternate result". It is the safe way to read what a slicer is set to.

DAXDynamic title driven by a slicer
WO Type Header =
    "Labor hours, " &
    SELECTEDVALUE( DimWOType[WOType], "all types" )
Line 3
Slicer on AOG alone returns "Labor hours, AOG" and the card beneath it shows 14.0. Slicer on Scheduled and AOG together returns "Labor hours, all types" because two values are visible, which is honest: the header no longer claims a single type.
Why this and not that

SELECTEDVALUE rather than IF(HASONEVALUE(col), VALUES(col), "all types"). The long form is three functions where one will do, and a bare VALUES used as a scalar throws a runtime error the moment two values are visible. Keep the long form only when you need different branches for the zero value case and the many value case, since SELECTEDVALUE collapses both into one alternate result. Do not reach for FIRSTNONBLANK, which older blog posts suggest. It returns a value even when several are selected, so it will label your card AOG while the numbers behind it include Mod.

The last three are inspection functions, and the distinction between the first two is a standard interview question because it is a clean test of whether you understand propagation.

Say it precisely. ISFILTERED asks whether a filter was placed on that column. ISCROSSFILTERED asks whether the column ends up restricted for any reason, including a filter placed elsewhere that reached it. A direct filter restricts the column too, so ISFILTERED being TRUE always implies ISCROSSFILTERED is TRUE. The reverse holds only sometimes. Cross filtering also follows relationship direction. Meridian's relationships are single direction, so a filter on FactWorkOrder leaves DimAircraft uncrossfiltered: filters travel from the one side to the many side, and back the other way only when the relationship is bidirectional.

Composing filter arguments

Multiple filter arguments in a single CALCULATE are combined with AND. Each is applied independently to its own columns.

DAXThree ways to compose
// AND across two arguments: AOG work at MSP
CALCULATE(
    [Labor Hours],
    DimWOType[WOType] = "AOG",
    DimStation[StationCode] = "MSP"
)

// OR inside one argument: unplanned plus modification work
CALCULATE(
    [Labor Hours],
    DimWOType[WOType] = "AOG"
        || DimWOType[WOType] = "Mod"
)

// same thing with IN, which is easier to extend
CALCULATE(
    [Labor Hours],
    DimWOType[WOType] IN { "AOG", "Mod" }
)

AOG and MSP intersects to WO-1002 alone, since WO-1005 has a blank station that was mapped to UNASSIGNED and WO-1007 is at LAS. AOG or Mod is the 14.0 AOG hours plus WO-1004's 10.0 Mod hours, which is 24.0. The IN form and the || form compile to the same thing, so choose IN. Adding a third work order type later costs you one token inside the braces, where the || form costs you a whole new clause.

Here is the limitation that trips people. The boolean shorthand can reference only one column. Write DimWOType[WOType] = "AOG" || DimStation[StationCode] = "MSP" and it will not compile, because there is no single column for CALCULATE to place the resulting table on. OR across two columns needs a real table expression, typically FILTER over a summarised table or a TREATAS of value pairs. Treat that as information about cost. The language is telling you that OR across dimensions costs more than AND across dimensions, and it will be slower on a large model.

CALCULATE and variables

The planner opens the work order type breakdown you sent her and every row of the share column reads 100.0 percent. Scheduled, AOG, Mod, and the total underneath them. She asks whether the report is finished. The measure behind that column looks correct, and one variable in it was declared one line too early.

A variable declared with VAR is evaluated once, at the point of declaration, in the filter context that exists there. It holds a value from then on, and using it somewhere else re evaluates nothing. Move a VAR inside a CALCULATE and its value changes. Reference a VAR inside a CALCULATE and its value stays exactly what it was.

The wrong way
DAXPct of All Types, broken
VAR Hours = [Labor Hours]
RETURN
DIVIDE(
    Hours,
    CALCULATE(
        Hours,
        REMOVEFILTERS( DimWOType )
    )
)

The author expected CALCULATE to recompute Hours without the WOType filter. It cannot. Hours was already resolved to a number on line 1, in the row's own context. CALCULATE is handed a constant and returns that constant.

The fix
DAXPct of All Types
VAR Hours = [Labor Hours]
VAR AllTypes =
    CALCULATE(
        [Labor Hours],
        REMOVEFILTERS( DimWOType )
    )
RETURN
    DIVIDE( Hours, AllTypes )

The measure reference sits inside CALCULATE, so it is evaluated in the modified context. Each VAR now holds the number it was supposed to hold.

What you see in the report

The broken version shows 100.0 percent on the AOG row, 100.0 percent on the Scheduled row, 100.0 percent on the Mod row and 100.0 percent on the total. That is the planner's screen. Every cell divides 14.0 by 14.0, or 38.0 by 38.0, or 10.0 by 10.0. A column of identical values is the signature of a variable captured too early. Learn to recognise it on sight, because the formula bar gives you no hint at all. Move the measure reference inside the CALCULATE, as the fix on the right does, and the planner gets a column she can read: 14.0 over 62.0 for AOG, 38.0 over 62.0 for Scheduled, 10.0 over 62.0 for Mod.

The same behaviour is a tool. Because a variable freezes the current context, it is the cleanest way to hold onto "what this row is" before you go and change the context to get a comparison base.

DAXPct of Station Hours, variable form
VAR ThisWO = [Labor Hours]
VAR StationTotal =
    CALCULATE(
        [Labor Hours],
        ALLEXCEPT( FactWorkOrder, DimStation[StationCode] )
    )
RETURN
    DIVIDE( ThisWO, StationTotal )
Line 1
Captured in the work order's own context. On the WO-1001 row this is 13.5 and it stays 13.5 for the rest of the expression, no matter what happens below.
Lines 2 to 6
Evaluated in a context where everything except the station has been cleared. On the WO-1001 row this is the MSP total, 34.5.
Line 8
13.5 divided by 34.5, which is 39.1 percent, matching Table 11.4.
Rule of thumb

Name variables for the context they were captured in, not for the value they hold. ThisWO and StationTotal tell the next reader that one was taken before the context change and one after. Hours1 and Hours2 tell them nothing, and this class of bug is invisible unless the names carry the information.

The order of evaluation, restated

Every question about CALCULATE resolves against this list. When a measure returns something you did not expect, walk it.

  1. Copy the current filter context.
  2. Evaluate every filter argument in the outer filter context and any outer row context, independently of each other.
  3. Perform context transition if a row context is open, turning the iterated row's column values into filters.
  4. Apply the modifiers. REMOVEFILTERS, ALL, ALLEXCEPT and ALLSELECTED run here, after context transition. That ordering is why CALCULATE([Labor Hours], REMOVEFILTERS(FactWorkOrder)) inside an iterator over work orders returns the grand total. The transition put the row filter in, and the modifier took it straight back out.
  5. Apply the filter arguments, replacing existing filters on the same columns unless KEEPFILTERS asked for intersection.
  6. Evaluate the expression in the resulting context.

The last two rows of that table are the only entries that change the wiring of the model instead of the filters running through it, and they get a chapter to themselves. Chapter 12 works both through on Meridian: USERELATIONSHIP counting the same eight work orders as 8 opened, 6 closed and 8 promised through three relationships into one date table, and CROSSFILTER opening the certification bridge to produce 39.0, 10.5, 12.0 and 23.5 hours, which add to 85.0 against a true total of 62.0.

What to remember
  • Filter arguments replace the existing filter on the columns they touch. They do not add to it. That one rule accounts for most CALCULATE results that look wrong.
  • The boolean shorthand compiles into FILTER(ALL(column), condition). The hidden ALL is why replacement happens, so you never have to memorise the behaviour separately.
  • With a slicer on Scheduled, CALCULATE([Labor Hours], DimWOType[WOType]="AOG") returns 14.0 and the same expression wrapped in KEEPFILTERS returns blank. Both are correct answers to different questions.
  • A filter argument that spans two columns replaces the filter on both of them at once. Fleet Pair Hours prints 41.0 into every cell of an aircraft type by operator matrix, including the B737-800 cells that contributed none of those hours. Wrapped in KEEPFILTERS the same argument leaves 23.5 on A320-200 with Cascade Air, 17.5 on E175 with Northwind Regional and blank everywhere else, and those two add back to 41.0.
  • One number repeated across every cell of a matrix is the signature of a filter argument that replaced the axis it was meant to respect. Wrap it in KEEPFILTERS and check the cells again before you look anywhere else.
  • REMOVEFILTERS(DimStation) holds the denominator at 62.0, so MSP is 55.6 percent of the quarter, TUS 36.3 and LAS 8.1. ALLEXCEPT(FactWorkOrder, DimStation[StationCode]) looks like the same instrument and behaves differently. With a February slicer the TUS and MSP work orders read 44.4 and 34.8 percent under it, against 100.0 percent each under REMOVEFILTERS(FactWorkOrder) plus VALUES, because ALLEXCEPT removed the month as well.
  • Prefer REMOVEFILTERS over ALL as a modifier. They behave identically and only one of them says what it means.
  • ALLEXCEPT clears the expanded table, including dimensions you did not list and dimensions that do not exist yet. Audit every use whenever you add a relationship.
  • Modifiers apply after context transition, which is what lets REMOVEFILTERS undo a transition that has already happened inside an iterator.
  • Variables are evaluated where they are declared. A column of identical percentages is the symptom of one captured too early.
  • ALLSELECTED is the one function here whose nested behaviour you should verify against hand calculated numbers before you rely on it.
Part 4 . Evaluation context and DAX

12USERELATIONSHIP and CROSSFILTER

After this chapter you can activate an inactive relationship inside a single measure, change or cut the filter direction of one relationship for one calculation, and defend which of those two, or a model change, is the right instrument for the problem in front of you.

The production controller stops at your desk with one question. How many work orders closed in January? Your page has a month axis and a work order count, and the January cell reads 3. His board says two aircraft went out the door in January. You are both looking at the same eight work orders.

The report is counting the wrong date. It counts by opened date, because that is the relationship the model has switched on, and nothing in the visual says so. By the end of the first section that January cell reads 2 and you can say exactly why.

Every modifier you have used so far changes the filter. These two change the wiring the filter travels along. They hold for the length of one CALCULATE, and then the model snaps back to exactly what the relationship diagram says it is. USERELATIONSHIP swaps which relationship on a path is the active one. CROSSFILTER sets the direction a named relationship propagates in, or switches it off entirely.

That difference is worth holding onto, because it changes how you reason about a measure. When a modifier changes the filter, you ask what rows survive. When a modifier changes the model, you ask which way the filter went and where it arrived. Both modifiers are arguments to CALCULATE. Both are temporary. A report author looking at a field list sees no sign of either one.

USERELATIONSHIP: borrow a relationship for one calculation

Meridian has the standard role playing problem, and it sits underneath the controller's question. Fact FactWorkOrder carries three dates on every row: OpenedDate, PromisedDate and ClosedDate. There is one Dimension DimDate, marked as the date table, and it has three relationships into the fact. Only the one on OpenedDate is active. An active relationship is the one the engine uses when nothing in the query says otherwise, and a path between two tables can carry only one of them. The other two relationships are inactive. They are stored, they are fully defined, and they carry no filters until a measure asks for one by name. The shape is the one from Chapter 6, drawn here again. Chapter 6 covered the relationship settings. This chapter covers the measure that puts them to work.

Look at the three lines running from DimDate into FactWorkOrder. The top one is solid and labelled active. The two beneath it are dashed and labelled inactive. The three columns they land on are named beside the fact box: OpenedDate, PromisedDate, ClosedDate. Each dashed line is a working relationship waiting for a measure to name it. The figure can label which line is live, because the figure is drawing the model. A report field list cannot. That is the whole reason the measure has to say out loud which date it means. The first card underneath gives the two measures in their shortest form. The second gives the number this section is heading for: January counts 3 work orders by opened date and 2 by closed date.

USERELATIONSHIP names a relationship by its two columns. It tells the engine to treat that relationship as active while the surrounding CALCULATE evaluates. It does a second thing that people forget: it deactivates whatever relationship was previously active along the same path. There can only ever be one active relationship between two tables on a given path. Switching on DimDate[Date] to FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] therefore switches off DimDate[Date] to FactWorkOrder[OpenedDate] for that evaluation. You are not adding a second path. You are substituting one for another.

DAXWork Orders Opened
Work Orders Opened =
COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder )
Why this and not that

COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ) and not COUNT ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] ). COUNT ignores blanks. Two Meridian work orders, WO-1004 and WO-1008, have no closed date. Under the closed relationship the two expressions happen to agree. A blank date joins to no row in DimDate, so those rows fall out anyway. They stop agreeing the moment somebody reuses the measure without the modifier. Then COUNT quietly reports 6 and COUNTROWS reports 8. DISTINCTCOUNT ( FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID] ) is also correct today and costs more. It builds a distinct value list over a table whose grain is already one row per work order. Grain is what one row of a table stands for, and one row of FactWorkOrder stands for one work order. Count rows when the grain is the thing you are counting.

The other two measures are the same count with a relationship modifier added, and one of them needs a second argument as well. No table is duplicated and nothing is materialised.

DAXWork Orders Closed and Work Orders Promised
Work Orders Closed =
CALCULATE (
    COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ),
    USERELATIONSHIP (
        DimDate[Date],
        FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate]
    ),
    NOT ISBLANK ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
)

Work Orders Promised =
CALCULATE (
    COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ),
    USERELATIONSHIP (
        DimDate[Date],
        FactWorkOrder[PromisedDate]
    )
)
Line 2
CALCULATE, and not a bare COUNTROWS, because USERELATIONSHIP returns nothing and cannot stand on its own. It only has meaning as an argument to CALCULATE or to CALCULATETABLE. Reach for CALCULATETABLE when the surrounding expression needs a table. A visual cell needs a single value, so CALCULATE is the one here.
Line 3
The expression being modified. It is the identical count in all three measures. Nothing about the counting changes, only the route the date filter takes to reach the fact.
Lines 4 to 7
The modifier. The two columns identify an existing relationship. Order does not matter to the engine, and this book writes the date column first everywhere so the three role measures read the same way. If no relationship exists between those two columns, this is an error, not a silent virtual join.
Line 8
Excludes WO-1004 and WO-1008, which have no closed date. Inside a month it changes nothing. A blank date joins to no row in DimDate, so those two rows fall out anyway. It is there for the total row. Nothing filters DimDate on the total, the two unmatched rows come back, and the measure would otherwise read 8 instead of 6. Work Orders Promised needs no equivalent, because every work order carries a promised date.
Scope
The substitution holds for everything inside this CALCULATE, including any measure it calls. It ends when the CALCULATE ends. Nothing in the model file changes, and a second report page evaluating at the same moment is unaffected.

Put the three measures on one matrix with DimDate[MonthName] on rows and you get the table that makes the whole idea concrete. One axis, one date table, three different questions.

January is the row that pays for the chapter, and it is the row the production controller was arguing about. Three work orders opened: WO-1001, WO-1002 and WO-1003. Two closed. His board said two aircraft out in January, and the closed column agrees with his board. WO-1003 opened on 14 January and closed on 5 February, so it counts in the opened column against January and in the closed column against February. That single work order sitting in two different months is the thing a second date table would have made ambiguous and a shared date column would have made impossible.

Read the totals as a check on your own work. Opened sums to 3 plus 3 plus 2, which is 8, the full work order count. Promised sums to 2 plus 3 plus 3, also 8, because every work order carries a promised date. Closed sums to 2 plus 2 plus 2, which is 6. Six is right. WO-1004 and WO-1008 have a blank ClosedDate, a blank joins to nothing in DimDate, and those two work orders are correctly absent from every month of that column. Six is the closed work order count. Now subtract closed from opened, month by month, and you get 1, 1 and 0. That is a backlog. It grows by one in January, by one more in February, and holds in March. It ends at the two open work orders you already know about.

What USERELATIONSHIP will not do

Four things are certain, and I would defend all four in a design review. First, the modifier has to be inside CALCULATE or CALCULATETABLE. Second, both columns must already form a relationship in the model. The modifier activates a relationship; it never creates one. Third, activating a relationship on a path deactivates the one that was active on that path. Pass two USERELATIONSHIP arguments for the same path inside one CALCULATE and the engine raises an error. Fourth, several USERELATIONSHIP arguments in the same CALCULATE are fine when they address different paths.

Nesting is where careful people still get caught. If your CALCULATE calls a measure that sets its own USERELATIONSHIP on the same path, the inner one governs inside its own evaluation. That is scoping working as designed. It produces a classic symptom: a measure that is right on its own and wrong the moment somebody wraps it. If you build a base measure that already pins a relationship, treat it as pinned and stop reusing it as a generic building block.

Three more limitations, and I will mark which parts are certain. First, row level security, usually written RLS. RLS is a rule that restricts which rows a given user is allowed to see. The documentation states that USERELATIONSHIP cannot be used when RLS is defined on the table involved. If your tenant applies RLS to FactWorkOrder, test these three measures under a security role before you ship them. Second, weak relationships. A weak relationship is one with many-to-many cardinality, or one that crosses source groups in a composite model. The modifier is designed around regular strong relationships, and I will not claim every weak relationship case behaves the way the strong case does. Third, calculated columns. A calculated column has no filter context of its own and is evaluated at refresh. So a CALCULATE inside one behaves differently from the same expression in a measure. Whether a specific calculated column pattern with USERELATIONSHIP resolves the way you expect during refresh is something to prove in your own model, on your own version of Power BI, with a value you can check by hand. Meridian is small enough that checking by hand takes four minutes.

Rule of thumb

One date table, one active relationship, and a measure that names the date column it means. If a report needs to count by promised date, that requirement belongs in the measure, not in a second copy of the calendar.

The cost, which is close to nothing

There is no data movement here. The relationship already exists in the model. Its join structures were built at refresh time along with every other relationship. USERELATIONSHIP chooses which of them the engine uses while one CALCULATE runs. The engine copies no table and builds no filter list. Refresh costs exactly what it cost before.

Performance note

USERELATIONSHIP is a routing decision, not a data operation. It does not make a slow join fast, though. If ClosedDate is high cardinality against a large fact, the scan costs what that join costs, exactly as it would if you had made that relationship active in the model. Measure the join, not the modifier.

The argument that actually decides it

Eight months from now the planner asks for promised date counts on a second page. You open the file and find a measure called Work Order Count. Nothing in the name tells you which of the three dates it counts, so you have to open the definition and read it. Multiply that by every measure on every page.

Readability is why you choose this pattern. A measure called Work Orders Closed whose definition contains USERELATIONSHIP ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate], DimDate[Date] ) tells every future reader what it means, including you in eight months. The meaning lives in the measure and travels with it. Performance barely enters the argument.

Now consider the alternative that gets built instead, usually in a hurry. Somebody imports a second date table called DateClosed and relates it to FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] with a normal active relationship. It works. It also moves the meaning out of the measure and onto the report canvas. That single measure called Work Order Count now returns opened counts when somebody drags month from DimDate, and closed counts when somebody drags month from DateClosed. Nothing in the visual or the tooltip says which happened. You get two fields called MonthName in the same field list, and two slicers that look identical and do not filter each other. Time intelligence needs both tables marked as date tables. On Meridian the storage cost is trivial, since DimDate is 90 rows. Storage is the smaller of the two bills. The expensive one is correctness: the report is now right or wrong depending on which of two identical looking fields somebody happened to pick.

Here is the inconvenient part, and it is a real one. Measures can only fix measures. Suppose the planner asks for a cohort matrix with opened month down the rows and closed month across the columns. USERELATIONSHIP cannot deliver it. Both axes are columns supplying filters through relationships, and only one relationship on that path can be active during the query. A cross-tab of two different dates genuinely requires a second date table, deliberately named something like DateClosed, with the axis role written into the field names. That is the case where the second table is the right answer, and it is narrower than the number of models you will find it in.

CROSSFILTER: change the direction of one relationship for one calculation

The shift supervisor wants to know how many hours his A&P certified technicians booked this quarter. You put a certification slicer on the page next to total labor hours. Every certification returns 62.0, which is every hour in the quarter. The filter leaves the slicer and never arrives.

That is a direction problem, and CROSSFILTER is the instrument for it. CROSSFILTER names a relationship the way USERELATIONSHIP does, by its two columns, and sets that relationship's cross filter direction for the duration of the CALCULATE. Cross filter direction means which way a filter is allowed to travel along a relationship. Three settings exist. OneWay filters from the one side to the many side only. Both lets the filter travel in either direction. None stops the relationship propagating anything at all.

What is certain is that CROSSFILTER sets direction on a relationship that already exists. Whether setting a direction on an inactive relationship also activates it is behaviour I would test in your own build before relying on it. In a measure you hand to somebody else, USERELATIONSHIP states that intent far more plainly anyway.

Both panels draw the same pair of tables: DimTechnician above FactLabor, the pair Chapter 8 took apart. They differ in one property. On the left, under Single, the default, one arrow points down from the one side to the many side. The note beside it says what that costs. A selection on DimTechnician reaches FactLabor, and a selection on FactLabor stops where it started. On the right, under Both, bidirectional, the same line carries an arrow head at each end. The note beside it describes what people actually want from that: a slicer that hides technicians with no hours. The green card and the red card underneath are the trade itself. One path and one answer on the left. Convenience and the usual source of ambiguity on the right. That return path on the right is the edge CROSSFILTER opens for the length of one calculation instead of for the whole file.

Both, without committing the whole model

Meridian's certification structure is a classic bridge. A bridge table holds the pairs that link two other tables when neither side is unique. Dimension DimTechnician has one row per technician. Dimension DimCertification has four rows. Bridge BridgeTechCert has ten rows, one per technician per certification, produced by splitting the delimited Certifications column. Both relationships into the bridge point from the one side to the many side and both are single direction.

So the supervisor's certification slicer filters the bridge and stops there. The filter reaches BridgeTechCert. From there it needs to travel from the many side back up to DimTechnician before it can flow down into FactLabor, and a single direction relationship carries filters one way only. That is why hours by certification came back as the same 62.0 in every row. The fix for one measure is one argument.

DAXHours by Certification
Hours by Certification =
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ),
    CROSSFILTER (
        BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID],
        DimTechnician[TechnicianID],
        BOTH
    )
)
Line 3
SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ) and not SUMX ( FactLabor, FactLabor[Hours] ). Hours is a stored column, so SUM resolves to one storage engine scan with no row context involved. SUMX earns its place when the per-row expression is not a plain column, for example hours times hourly rate.
Lines 4 to 8
The relationship between the bridge and the technician dimension, set to filter in both directions for this evaluation only. The relationship in the model file stays single direction. Every other measure on the page keeps the model it was written against.
Path
With that edge opened, a certification selection travels DimCertification to BridgeTechCert, up to DimTechnician, then down to FactLabor. Four tables, three hops, one modifier.

Every one of those four rows is right. TECH-04 really did work 10.5 hours and really does hold three certifications, so those hours belong in three rows. The rows add to 85.0 against a true total of 62.0, a gap of 23.0 hours, and no report consumer will thank you for explaining that after they have quoted the wrong number to a customer.

Trace the 23 hour gap by hand

Take the certified technicians only. TECH-01 12.0, TECH-02 16.5, TECH-04 10.5 and TECH-05 13.0 add to 52.0. TECH-03 and TECH-06 hold certifications and logged no hours, so they add nothing.

Now count the repeats. TECH-01 appears in two certification rows, A&P and NDT, so their 12.0 hours are counted twice and 12.0 hours of excess are created. TECH-04 appears in three rows, A&P, Avionics and Engine Run, so 10.5 counted three times creates 21.0 of excess. TECH-02 and TECH-05 hold one certification each and create none. Excess is 12.0 plus 21.0, which is 33.0, and 52.0 plus 33.0 is 85.0.

Then the other direction. TECH-07 logged 10.0 hours on WO-1004 and is not in the source technician list at all, so that technician has no bridge rows and appears in no certification row. 52.0 plus those 10.0 hours is the true 62.0. The visible gap of 23.0 is 33.0 hours of double counting minus 10.0 hours that are missing entirely, which is why the total looks less wrong than it is.

CROSSFILTER and a permanently bidirectional relationship both do one job: they get the filter to travel. The arithmetic of a many-to-many is a separate decision. Somebody has to choose whether hours get allocated across certifications, deduplicated, or reported per certification with an explicit warning on the total. That decision is Chapter 14.

Common mistake

Setting the bridge relationship to Both in the model itself, watching the certification rows finally populate, and shipping it that afternoon. The four rows were always going to be right once the filter could travel. What changed is that every other measure in the file now answers a certification slicer, and this visual now shows a total of 85.0 next to a report header that still says 62.0 hours worked in Q1. Getting the filter to arrive is the easy half of the problem.

None, when a measure should ignore a relationship

The finance manager wants one number per technician: what share of Q1 labor hours did each of them book? You put hours on a bar chart with a technician slicer beside it. Pick TECH-02 and the numerator and the denominator both drop to 16.5, so every technician shows 100 percent. The denominator has to stop listening to that slicer.

Meridian's technician slicer is useful and occasionally in the way. Any share calculation needs a denominator that holds still when the slicer moves.

DAXLabor Hours Ignoring Technician
Labor Hours Ignoring Technician =
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ),
    CROSSFILTER (
        FactLabor[TechnicianID],
        DimTechnician[TechnicianID],
        NONE
    )
)
Why this and not that

REMOVEFILTERS ( DimTechnician ) returns the same 62.0 here and is the more common idiom, so use it when all you need is the total. The two do different jobs. REMOVEFILTERS clears the filter from the dimension itself. Anything else inside that same CALCULATE which reads DimTechnician, such as a row count or a home station test, also stops seeing the selection. CROSSFILTER with None leaves DimTechnician filtered to the selected technician and cuts one edge, the one into FactLabor. Reach for None when the selection still has work to do elsewhere in the expression, and for REMOVEFILTERS when you want the selection gone.

Select TECH-02 and the plain hours measure returns 16.5 while this one returns 62.0. 16.5 divided by 62.0 is 0.2661, so TECH-02 accounts for 26.6 percent of Q1 labor hours. That is the number the finance manager asked for, and the denominator holds whichever technician the user picks.

OneWay, the setting everyone forgets exists

Suppose somebody has already made the bridge relationship permanently bidirectional, either because they were asked for hours by certification or because a tutorial told them to. Now every measure in the file responds to a certification slicer, including the ones that should not. A denominator, a total hours reference line: both start moving.

DAXLabor Hours All Certifications
// use when the bridge relationship is bidirectional in the model
Labor Hours All Certifications =
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ),
    CROSSFILTER (
        BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID],
        DimTechnician[TechnicianID],
        ONEWAY
    )
)
Line 1
A comment that names the precondition. Without it the next reader deletes the modifier, because against a single direction model this measure looks like a no-op.
Lines 5 to 9
The same relationship as the Both example, pushed the other way. Filtering from DimTechnician to the bridge still works. A certification selection can no longer climb back up to the technicians, so it never reaches FactLabor and the measure returns 62.0 under any certification selection.
Use
Put it beside Hours by Certification and the double count becomes visible in the report rather than in a support ticket: 85.0 divided by 62.0 is 1.371, so the four shares add to 137.1 percent.

Four ways to change how a filter travels

Two of those requests landed in the same week, one from the production controller and one from the shift supervisor. You have four instruments to answer them with. They differ in what they touch and in how far the change spreads, and that spread is what decides it when you are choosing under time pressure.

TREATAS earns a row of its own next to CROSSFILTER because of one specific case: CROSSFILTER can only redirect a relationship that already exists in the model, and TREATAS needs no relationship at all. In Meridian that matters at the capacity join, where FactCapacity sits at station and month grain while FactLabor sits at day grain, and where the relationship you would want may not be one you are willing to create.

Interview-level insight

Asked to separate USERELATIONSHIP from CROSSFILTER, the short answer is that one changes which relationship is used and the other changes how an already chosen relationship propagates. The longer answer is the one worth giving. Both are arguments to CALCULATE, so both last exactly one evaluation, which means neither can repair a model whose grain is wrong. They redirect filters. They do not change what a row means, and 85.0 against 62.0 is a grain problem wearing a direction problem's clothes.

Which leaves the decision rule, and it is short enough to keep. Change the model when every measure needs it. Change the measure when one measure needs it. A bidirectional relationship you set once and never revisit is a promise you have made to every report author who will ever open the file, and a CROSSFILTER or USERELATIONSHIP argument is a note in the margin of one calculation. Most of the time the note is enough.

What to remember
  • USERELATIONSHIP activates an inactive relationship for one CALCULATE and deactivates whatever was active on that same path. It never creates a relationship and it never stands alone.
  • Meridian by month: opened 3, 3, 2 for a total of 8, closed 2, 2, 2 for a total of 6, promised 2, 3, 3 for a total of 8. January opens three and closes two, and WO-1003 sits in January opened and February closed.
  • Two work orders never appear in the closed column at all, because a blank ClosedDate joins to no date and 6 is the correct closed count.
  • The modifier is cheap because it copies nothing. Choose it for readability: the measure states which date it means, whereas a second date table lets the report author decide by accident.
  • A cross-tab of opened month against closed month is the case USERELATIONSHIP cannot serve. That is when a second, explicitly named date table is right.
  • CROSSFILTER sets one relationship to OneWay, Both or None for one CALCULATE. Both gives hours by certification of 39.0, 10.5, 12.0 and 23.5, which add to 85.0 against a true 62.0. Getting the filter to travel is not the same as getting the arithmetic right, and that is Chapter 14.
  • Verify in your own environment: behaviour under row level security, over weak or many-to-many relationships, and inside calculated columns evaluated at refresh.
  • Change the model when every measure needs it. Change the measure when one measure needs it.
Part 5 . Hard modelling cases

13Role-playing dimensions: one date table, many dates

After this chapter you can put opened, promised and closed counts side by side on a single month axis driven by one slicer, and you can argue which of the three role-playing strategies belongs in a given model instead of picking one by habit.

The production controller asks for one page. One month slicer, three numbers: work orders opened in the month, work orders promised in the month, work orders closed in the month. You build it in ten minutes and all three columns come back identical. He tells you the report is broken. The model is doing exactly what it was built to do, and by the end of the first section you will have the three columns he wanted.

Start with the raw material. Meridian has five date columns spread across three fact tables. Fact FactWorkOrder carries OpenedDate, PromisedDate and ClosedDate. FactLabor and FactParts carry one each, WorkDate and IssueDate. Only one of those columns can be the one a date slicer drives by default, and the controller wants three of them on the same page.

Those three numbers are not three views of one set of rows. They are three different sets. In January the opened set is WO-1001, WO-1002 and WO-1003, while the closed set is WO-1001 and WO-1002. February makes the point harder to miss. Opened is WO-1004, WO-1005 and WO-1006. Closed is WO-1003 and WO-1005. The only work order in both sets is WO-1005.

So the same eight rows have to be selected three different ways by the same slicer. A relationship in a tabular model joins exactly one column to one column. Between DimDate[Date] and FactWorkOrder you need three joins. The engine will happily store all three. It will only let one of them carry filters at a time. That is why the controller's three columns came back identical.

Role-playing dimension
One physical dimension table that answers several different questions about the same fact table, depending on which foreign key it is joined through. A date table joined to OpenedDate plays the role of intake date. Joined to ClosedDate it plays the role of completion date.
Active relationship
The relationship the engine uses when nothing in the query says otherwise. Solid line in the model view. At most one active relationship can exist on any given filter path between two tables.
Inactive relationship
A stored, validated relationship that propagates no filters until a measure asks for it by name. Dashed line in the model view. It costs storage and a small amount of processing time, and it changes nothing until it is invoked.

You have met this diagram before, in Chapter 6 where active and inactive were defined, and again in Chapter 12 beside USERELATIONSHIP. Read it once more for the line style. Three lines run from DimDate into FactWorkOrder. The three target column names are printed beside the fact box in the same order: OpenedDate, PromisedDate, ClosedDate. The top line is solid and carries the label active. The two beneath it are dashed and each carries the label inactive. The figure prints no cardinality on those lines, so take it from here. All three are one to many, from one date on DimDate[Date] to the many fact rows that share it, and all three run in that one direction. The only thing that separates them is which one is switched on.

The two cards underneath the boxes run ahead of the argument, and both are worth a look now. The first is headed One date table, three roles, and it is strategy 1 in miniature. Work Orders Opened is a bare COUNTROWS riding the solid line. Work Orders Closed is the same count wrapped in CALCULATE with USERELATIONSHIP pointed at ClosedDate. That card shows the wrapper in its shortest form. The version built later in this chapter adds one more filter argument, which changes the total row and leaves the month rows alone. The second card, titled Why it matters, counts a single January twice: 3 work orders by opened date against 2 by closed date. Same slicer, same eight rows, different question.

The reason the engine allows one at a time explains the whole chapter. If two of those relationships were active, a filter on DimDate[Date] equal to January would have two routes into FactWorkOrder, and the engine would have to decide on its own whether January meant opened or closed. It refuses to guess. That is the ambiguity rule from Chapter 8, applied to the simplest case there is: two roads between the same pair of tables.

Strategy 1: one date table, inactive relationships, USERELATIONSHIP

Build one Dimension DimDate covering 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31, mark it as a date table, and create all three relationships from DimDate[Date] to the three date columns on FactWorkOrder. Make OpenedDate active. Leave PromisedDate and ClosedDate inactive. Then write one measure per role.

DAXThree date roles from one date table
// Opened rides the active relationship, so no wrapper is needed
Work Orders Opened =
    COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder )

Work Orders Promised =
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ),
        USERELATIONSHIP ( DimDate[Date], FactWorkOrder[PromisedDate] )
    )

Work Orders Closed =
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ),
        USERELATIONSHIP ( DimDate[Date], FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] ),
        NOT ISBLANK ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
    )
Line 3
COUNTROWS and not COUNT ( FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID] ), because COUNT ignores blanks. Point COUNT at a date column and the two open work orders disappear without a warning. Not DISTINCTCOUNT either: WorkOrderID is already unique at this grain, so a distinct count buys nothing and pays for a hash pass over the column.
Lines 6 and 12
CALCULATE and not CALCULATETABLE, because a visual needs a scalar here. Both accept relationship modifiers, but CALCULATETABLE returns a table, which is what you want when you are feeding another iterator, not when you are filling a cell.
Lines 8 and 14
USERELATIONSHIP names the two endpoints of a relationship that already exists in the model. It does not create anything. For the duration of that CALCULATE it switches the named relationship on and switches the active one between the same two tables off.
Line 15
ISBLANK and not FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] = BLANK ( ). In DAX a blank coerces to zero in a comparison. A date is stored as a number, so the equality test also matches the date that sits at zero. ISBLANK tests for the absence of a value and nothing else. The predicate references a single column, so CALCULATE accepts it as a filter argument and expands it internally to a filter over all values of that column.

Two of Meridian's eight work orders, WO-1004 and WO-1008, have no ClosedDate. That is why line 15 is there, and the callout below explains what happens when you leave it out. Put the three measures in place, DimDate[MonthName] on the rows and one date slicer set to the quarter. The page the production controller asked for looks like this.

Read the January row against the March row. Three work orders opened in January and only two were promised in it. By March the shape has inverted: two opened, three promised, two closed. The closed column totals 6 because two work orders are still open. The controller has his three columns, and each one answers a different question off the same slicer.

Common mistake

Write Work Orders Closed without the ISBLANK guard and the month rows still read 2, 2 and 2, so the measure looks right. The total reads 8. The two work orders with no close date land in the blank member, which is the row the engine adds to DimDate to hold fact rows whose key matches nothing. Leave the visual unfiltered by a date slicer and that blank member shows up as an unlabelled row worth 2. A reviewer who checks only the month rows signs off on a total that says six closed work orders are eight.

The verdict on strategy 1: it is the default choice, and for most models it is the last word. One date table means one slicer, one set of time intelligence, one place to fix a fiscal calendar. You pay for it twice. Every measure on a non-default role has to be written with CALCULATE, so the measure list grows by one entry per role per question. And a report author who drags a bare column into a visual gets the active relationship with no warning. Put DimDate[MonthName] next to an implicit sum of FactWorkOrder[QuotedAmount] and you are reading quoted amount by opened month, whether or not you meant to.

Why this and not that

USERELATIONSHIP and not a virtual relationship built with TREATAS. They look like swap-for-swap alternatives and they divide the work differently. USERELATIONSHIP switches the active relationship off at the same moment it switches the named one on, so the January selection lands on ClosedDate and on nothing else. A TREATAS version has to do that second half itself: CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ), TREATAS ( VALUES ( DimDate[Date] ), FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] ), REMOVEFILTERS ( DimDate ) ). Leave the REMOVEFILTERS out and the month is still filtering OpenedDate down the active relationship. The two conditions intersect, and February returns 1 instead of 2. That 1 is the single work order that both opened and closed in February. USERELATIONSHIP also flips a join the engine has already built and indexed, where TREATAS materialises the selected dates and applies them as a filter on the target column at query time. Reach for TREATAS when the physical relationship cannot exist, for example when the target sits in a table produced by a DAX expression, or when you need two roles filtered at once. Otherwise use USERELATIONSHIP.

Strategy 2: one date table per role

Now the planner comes with a different question. Which work orders opened in February were still open at the end of February? You reach for the three measures you just built and find they cannot answer it. One month slicer produces one selection of dates, and this question needs two.

Strategy 2 answers it by duplicating the date table. Build DateOpened, DatePromised and DateClosed as three Built tables generated from the same Power Query function, and give each one an active relationship to its own column on FactWorkOrder. No inactive relationships, no CALCULATE wrappers, no measure per role. A report author drags DateClosed[MonthName] onto a visual and gets closed months, because the field name says what it does.

That convenience is the honest appeal of strategy 2, and it is real. The reason to reach for strategy 2 is narrower than the convenience. It is the only one of the three that lets a user filter two roles at the same time. Strategy 1 cannot do that, and no amount of USERELATIONSHIP will make it. One date table produces one selection of dates, and that selection has to mean one thing.

The planner's question sounds ordinary. Which work orders were opened in a given month and were still open at the end of a later month? Take Meridian work orders opened in February and still open on 2025-02-28. The answer is 2: WO-1004, which has never closed, and WO-1006, which opened 2025-02-17 and closed 2025-03-19. Now try opened in January and still open on 2025-02-28. The answer is 0, because WO-1001 closed 2025-01-16, WO-1002 closed 2025-01-13 and WO-1003 closed 2025-02-05. That takes two independent date inputs, one for the opened window and one for the as-of point, and one date table cannot supply both.

Trace this by hand, row by row

Opened in February: WO-1004 on 2025-02-03, WO-1005 on 2025-02-10, WO-1006 on 2025-02-17. That is the 3 in the February opened column of Table 13.1.

Now test each against the as-of date 2025-02-28. WO-1004 has a blank ClosedDate, so it was open. WO-1005 closed on 2025-02-12, before the as-of date, so it was not. WO-1006 closed on 2025-03-19, after the as-of date, so it was open. Count 2.

Now do it with two slicers instead of a measure: DateOpened on February, DateClosed on March or later. That returns 1, not 2. WO-1004 is missing, because a blank foreign key joins to nothing and no selection on DateClosed can include it. To make the slicer version correct you have to stamp open work orders with a sentinel close date in Power Query, something like 9999-12-31, and extend the date table to hold it. That fixes the count and makes every raw ClosedDate in the model a value that every downstream consumer has to know is fictional.

The narrower version of the question does work with one date table, as long as the as-of point is the end of the opened window. Opened in January and still open on 2025-01-31 returns 1: WO-1003, opened 2025-01-14 and closed 2025-02-05. That is the shape most backlog reports actually need, which is why many models never hit the wall at all.

If you only need the as-of point to float free of the opened window, one extra disconnected table is enough. A disconnected table has no relationship to anything, so it filters nothing by itself and a measure reads the user's selection out of it by hand. It is a cheaper version of the same idea, and it gives the planner her answer.

DAXStill Open As Of
// AsOfDate has NO relationship to anything. It is a picker.
Still Open As Of =
VAR AsOf =
    MAX ( AsOfDate[Date] )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ),
        FILTER (
            ALL ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] ),
            ISBLANK ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
                || FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] > AsOf
        )
    )
Line 4
MAX and not SELECTEDVALUE ( AsOfDate[Date] ). A user who drags a range across the as-of slicer selects many dates, and SELECTEDVALUE returns blank the moment there is more than one. MAX takes the last date in the selection, which is what "as of" means. Not LASTDATE either: LASTDATE returns a one row table meant to be used as a filter, and line 11 needs a scalar to compare against.
Lines 8 to 9
FILTER over ALL of the one column, not over ALL ( FactWorkOrder ). Filtering a single column keeps the filter narrow and leaves every other filter on the table in place, including the opened month coming down the active relationship. ALL removes any existing filter on ClosedDate so the as-of test is the only condition applied to it. If you wanted to intersect with an existing close date filter instead of replacing it, you would wrap the whole FILTER in KEEPFILTERS.
Lines 10 to 11
Two conditions joined by ||: never closed, or closed after the as-of point. The blank test has to be first and explicit, because a blank date compared to any real date with > behaves as zero and would quietly answer false.
The wrong way

Add a second slicer on the same DimDate and hope the two selections mean different things. They cannot. Both slicers write into the same filter on DimDate[Date], so the second one narrows the first. Set one to February and the other to March and you get an empty selection and a blank page, and the author usually concludes the model is broken.

The fix

Give the second question its own table. Either a full role table with its own relationship, or a disconnected picker read with MAX. Two independent tables produce two independent selections, and the measure decides how they combine. The cost is that a disconnected table filters nothing on its own, so anything it should affect has to be written into a measure by hand.

The verdict on strategy 2: correct when a user must filter two roles at the same time, and heavy everywhere else. Three date slicers on one page confuse people, because nobody can tell which one drives which visual. Three tables means three fiscal calendars to keep in step. It also means every time intelligence measure repeated once per table, since DATESYTD ( DateOpened[Date] ) and DATESYTD ( DateClosed[Date] ) are unrelated expressions. There is a subtler cost. Table 13.1 cannot be built this way at all. The month axis has to come from one of the three date tables, only that table filters the fact, and all three columns would return the same number.

Rule of thumb

Count the slicers a user would have to set before you count the measures you would have to write. A model with three date tables asks the user to understand your model. A model with one date table and three measures asks you to understand your model. Push the difficulty onto yourself.

Strategy 3: a calculation group with a date role item

Six weeks later the finance manager asks for quoted amount and actual cost by closed month. The next day the production controller asks for the same two by promised month. Each new measure needs its own wrapper for each role, and you are now writing the same USERELATIONSHIP line for the fifth time. That repetition is the signal for strategy 3.

A calculation group is a table in the model that holds no data. It has one visible column, and the values in that column are called calculation items. Each item is a name and a DAX expression. Inside that expression sits a placeholder, SELECTEDMEASURE ( ), standing in for whichever measure the visual happens to be evaluating. Put the calculation group's column on an axis and the engine evaluates every measure in the visual once per item, substituting the measure into the item's expression each time.

So a calculation item is a rewrite rule, and it applies to measures you have not written yet. In the model view a Meridian calculation group would appear as a small table with a column named Date Role and three rows: Opened, Promised, Closed. Drag Date Role onto the columns of a matrix, drop any work order measure into values, and you get one column per role. Add a fourth measure next month and it inherits all three roles the moment it is created, with no new DAX.

DAXCalculation group: Date Role
// Three items on the column DateRole[Date Role]

// Item 1: Opened
SELECTEDMEASURE ( )

// Item 2: Promised
CALCULATE (
    SELECTEDMEASURE ( ),
    USERELATIONSHIP ( DimDate[Date], FactWorkOrder[PromisedDate] )
)

// Item 3: Closed
CALCULATE (
    SELECTEDMEASURE ( ),
    USERELATIONSHIP ( DimDate[Date], FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
)
Item 1
The default role returns the measure untouched, riding the active relationship. Write it out. Leave it absent and the axis carries one blank-looking item the user has to guess at, where a labelled column for opened would have said what it was.
Items 2 and 3
Identical to the wrappers in strategy 1, with one difference that carries the whole idea: the thing being wrapped is a placeholder. SELECTEDMEASURE and not a specific measure reference, because the item has to work for every measure the report puts in scope. Naming a measure here would turn the calculation group back into an ordinary measure with extra steps.
Ordering
Give the items an explicit ordinal in the editor. Without one they sort alphabetically, and Closed, Opened, Promised is a reading order nobody wants for a work order lifecycle.

Now the arithmetic that decides it, and it settles the finance manager's request too. Suppose the work order page carries five measures: work order count 8, quoted amount 38,100, actual cost 29,671.50, average turn time 12.0 days and on time percentage 50.0%. One measure per role is 5 times 3, or 15 measures. Each of the 10 non-default ones is a hand-written CALCULATE that can be got wrong on its own. With a calculation group it is 5 measures plus 3 items, or 8 objects, and the 3 items are the only place the role logic lives. Strategy 1 multiplies. Strategy 3 adds.

Interview-level insight

A calculation group applies to every measure in scope, including the ones you had forgotten were on the page. On the Meridian model, DimDate reaches FactLabor by two routes: directly through WorkDate, and indirectly through the work order header. A date role item changes only the second route, so a measure such as labor hours can shift under the Closed item even though nothing in it mentions FactWorkOrder.
