The item rewrites the measure; that much is certain. Check the resulting number in your own model before you trust it. If both routes apply, January labor hours under the Closed item reads 7.5 plus 6.0 plus 9.0, which is 22.5, instead of the 35.0 that WorkDate alone gives. Test every measure under every item before you publish.

The verdict on strategy 3: the best answer when the model has many measures times many roles, and overkill when it does not. The costs are real. You need Tabular Editor or the calculation group editor built into recent Power BI Desktop releases. That is a tool your colleague may not have and a skill they may not want. Format strings need attention too. A calculation group can override the format of the measure flowing through it, so a currency measure can end up rendering as a plain number under one item and not another. Discovery is the third cost. A calculation group has no relationships, so no line in the model view connects it to anything. A colleague opening your file six months from now sees a table holding three text values and no obvious reason for the numbers to change when they click one.

One more thing catches people out: adding any calculation group to a model turns off implicit measures. Dragging FactWorkOrder[QuotedAmount] into a visual to get an automatic sum stops working, and every aggregation has to be an explicit measure from then on. That is good discipline, and it is a change of habit imposed on every report author in the workspace, usually without warning.

The choosing rule

One or two measures need the extra roles
Strategy 1: inactive relationships
Users must filter two roles at once
Strategy 2: one table per role
Many measures times many roles
Strategy 3: calculation group

The three combine. A common shape is strategy 1 as the base, plus one small disconnected as-of table for the backlog question, and no calculation group until the measure count justifies one. Meridian sits there today.

Role playing reaches past dates: the station case

The shift supervisor at Las Vegas says the report is wrong. It shows 5.0 hours at his station for the quarter and his whiteboard says 13.0. Both counts are right. The report and the whiteboard are answering two different questions about the same word, station.

Every dimension can play more than one role, and stations are the case that turns up in a maintenance, repair and overhaul shop, an MRO. DimStation could describe the station where the work was done, which reaches the facts through FactWorkOrder[StationCode]. It could equally describe a technician's home station, which lives as DimTechnician[HomeStation]. Same five members, two roles, and two very different numbers.

The home station column is the sum of each technician's hours grouped by the station on their personnel record. MSP is TECH-01 at 12.0 plus TECH-02 at 16.5 plus TECH-06 at 0, which is 28.5. TUS is TECH-03 at 0 plus TECH-04 at 10.5, so 10.5. LAS is TECH-05 alone at 13.0. The 10.0 against UNASSIGNED is TECH-07, the technician who exists in the timesheet and not in the personnel extract. Now look at the LAS row. The station absorbed 5.0 hours of work, and the technician based there logged 13.0, because K. Ibrahim spent 8.0 hours on WO-1003 at Tucson. That is the supervisor's whiteboard. He is counting his people. The report was counting his hangar.

All three strategies apply here mechanically. You could add a relationship from DimStation[StationCode] to DimTechnician[HomeStation] and leave it inactive. You could build a separate DimHomeStation. You could add a station role item to a calculation group. The inconvenient answer is to do none of them by default. In Meridian that second relationship is deliberately absent, because DimStation would then reach FactLabor by two paths, one through the work order and one through the technician. That is the ambiguity case from Chapter 8. The deeper reason is about the questions. Opened and closed are two readings of one question: when did this work order move? Where work happened and where a technician is based are two separate questions. Where work happened is a capacity question. Where a technician is based is a staffing and travel question. Put them on one axis and a reader will subtract one column from the other, which means nothing. Leave HomeStation as a descriptive attribute on DimTechnician, and if the staffing question earns its own page, build DimHomeStation for that page.

The other two date columns, and one slicer over three facts

The finance manager sets the date slicer to a single day, 9 January, and calls you. The page says zero work orders opened, zero promised and zero closed, and underneath that it says 15.0 labor hours and 2,450 of parts. He wants to know which half of the page is broken. Every number on it is right, and this section says why.

Start by closing the ledger this chapter opened with. Five date columns, three of them worked. FactLabor[WorkDate] and FactParts[IssueDate] each stand alone. Each is the only date its fact table carries, so each gets one plain active relationship from DimDate[Date] and nothing more: no inactive twin and no calculation item. Having just met role playing, you will be tempted to assume every date column in the model now needs the machinery. Two of the five stay plain, and adding inactive relationships to them would create objects nothing will ever invoke.

What all five share is the date table, and that is the part worth ten minutes. One DimDate means one slicer. One slicer means a single selection arrives at three fact tables, through three different columns, in the same instant. The three answers it produces have no obligation to agree with each other. Set the slicer to a single day and the point stops being theoretical. That is the day the finance manager picked.

Six measures, one date, and a page that reads as impossible: no work orders opened, none promised, none closed, fifteen hours booked and 2,450 of parts issued. Every cell is correct, and that is the answer the finance manager needed. Be precise about the first three. COUNTROWS over an empty set returns blank and not zero, so on the report those cells render empty. They are written as 0 in the table above only so the column reads as a column. If a card has to show a real zero, add + 0 to the measure. Accept that the measure is then never blank and will hold open every row on any axis you put it against. The ninth of January is a Thursday in the middle of two jobs that opened on the Monday and the Wednesday. Work happens on days when nothing in the work order lifecycle does. This is what a shared date table buys you and what it costs. One slicer governs everything, and the word "January" means intake on one visual, timesheets on the next and stores issues on the third.

Interview-level insight

Ask which measures on the page are anchored to which date column before you accept any date filtered number. Three fact tables against one calendar give you three separate answers to one date. On the Meridian quarter the month level answers happen to line up, because every labor row, and every parts row whose work order exists, falls in the same calendar month as that work order opened, so opened month and work month agree across the seven orders that carry any activity at all. WO-1008 has neither a labor row nor a parts line, and the orphan parts line P-9007 points at WO-1009, which is not in the header table and so has no opened month to agree with. That agreement is a property of this quarter's data, not of the model. One job that opens on the twenty eighth and gets worked on the second would break it, and every month level reconciliation built on the coincidence would break with it.

The second consequence is sharper, and it catches people who have just got strategy 1 working. A USERELATIONSHIP wrapper changes which column of FactWorkOrder the date filter lands on. It does nothing at all to FactLabor, which is filtered by its own active relationship on WorkDate. Put [Work Orders Closed] and [Labor Hours] side by side on a month axis and February reads 2 and 22.0. The two work orders closed in February are WO-1003 and WO-1005. The 22.0 hours are L-506 on WO-1004 and L-507 on WO-1006. The two sets do not share a single work order, and the row invites the reader to divide one by the other.

If the question really is hours booked against work that completed in the period, the filter has to travel through the work order header. The labor date is the wrong road for that question, and the next measure takes the right one.

DAXLabor Hours on Closed WOs
// The VAR is evaluated in the visual's own filter context,
// so it resolves the month before anything is cleared.
Labor Hours on Closed WOs =
VAR ClosedInPeriod =
    CALCULATETABLE (
        VALUES ( FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID] ),
        USERELATIONSHIP ( DimDate[Date], FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
    )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        [Labor Hours],
        REMOVEFILTERS ( DimDate ),
        ClosedInPeriod
    )
Lines 5 to 8
CALCULATETABLE and not CALCULATE, because what is wanted here is the list of work orders and not a number. This is the one place in the chapter where the table returning twin earns its keep. USERELATIONSHIP switches the close date relationship on for the duration of that table expression only. Under a February filter it returns WO-1003 and WO-1005. WO-1004 and WO-1008 have a blank ClosedDate, so they attach to the blank member of DimDate and never appear under any month.
Line 6
VALUES of one column and not CALCULATETABLE ( FactWorkOrder, ... ). Filtering a single column leaves every other filter on the header table in place, so a station or work order type slicer on the same page still applies. Handing back the whole table as a filter argument would replace those filters instead of intersecting with them, and the measure would quietly ignore the station the user selected.
Line 12
The line that makes the measure work, and the line people leave out. Without it the February filter still reaches FactLabor along the WorkDate relationship. The two conditions then intersect: labor dated February, on work orders closed in February. That intersection is empty, because the February labor rows sit on WO-1004 and WO-1006. The measure returns blank, so it looks broken rather than wrong. That is the better of the two failures and it is still a failure.
Line 13
A variable holding a table can be handed straight to CALCULATE as a filter argument. ClosedInPeriod still carries the lineage of FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID], so it filters the header, and the filter travels down the existing header to line relationship into FactLabor with no further help.

February now returns 12.5. That is L-504 at 8.0 hours plus L-505 at 4.5 hours, both booked in January against WO-1003, which closed on 2025-02-05. WO-1005 closed in February too and contributes nothing, because it has no labor rows at all. Read the pair honestly. 22.0 is hours worked in February. 12.5 is hours belonging to work that finished in February. The production controller wants one of them and not the other, so ask him which. The same shape gives you parts on closed work orders by swapping [Labor Hours] for [Parts Cost], and the same REMOVEFILTERS line is needed for the same reason.

Recount the roles when the heavy maintenance tables arrive

The planner sends you three more files from the heavy side of the shop and asks for the same page again, this time for the hangar checks. You open them and find two more date columns sitting on work orders you have already modelled three ways. That ledger was drawn against six source tables. Meridian has nine. Three of them come from the heavy side, two of those three carry dates, and the count you just closed does not survive them.

Start with where the new dates come from, because the reason they exist is the reason one pair of them will hurt. Heavy maintenance is base maintenance. An aircraft goes out of service into a hangar bay for days or weeks, jacked and opened up, worked to a package a planner built before it arrived. The function that owns the schedule for that work is commonly called the HMCC, the Heavy Maintenance Control Centre. Commonly, not universally. Plenty of shops call the identical function production control, or maintenance control, or the base maintenance control centre. The line maintenance equivalent is usually the MOC, the Maintenance Operations Control. The function is in every base shop. The acronym is not, so confirm the local one before you name a table after it.

The HMCC board owns the plan: which aircraft is in which bay, and the planned start and planned finish for every work order on it. It owns nothing that happened. Booked hours sit in the timesheet system, parts in stores, and the induction and release dates in the shop floor system. That split of ownership is how the industry is arranged, and Meridian's extracts reflect it. It is why HMCCSchedule turns up as its own file with its own dates.

HMCCSchedule holds one row per work order, which makes it one to one with WorkOrders. The recommended handling for one to one is a merge. Fold it into the header in Power Query and let its columns ride on Fact FactWorkOrder, with no relationship built at all. Once you do, PlannedStart and PlannedFinish become the fourth and fifth date column on the one fact you have spent this chapter joining three ways. ManhourForecast becomes Fact FactForecast and adds one more date on a table of its own, RevisionDate, the day production control reissued its estimate.

Eight is the count of columns joined to DimDate[Date]. FactCapacity[MonthStart] makes a ninth, and it joins to DimDate[MonthStart] at month grain. Grain is what one row of a table stands for, and one row of FactCapacity stands for one station in one month. That makes it a grain argument rather than a role argument, and grain belongs to Chapter 16.

RevisionDate needs one paragraph and can then be left alone. It is the only date on FactForecast, so it takes one plain active relationship, exactly like WorkDate and IssueDate. The awkward part is the measure sitting on it, not the relationship. Each revision replaces the one before it, so the answer for a period is the latest revision per work order and never a sum. Add the eight forecast rows together and you get 99.5, a figure that counts the same hours over and over as each revision lands. The correct total is 63.5. That is a semi-additive measure, and it is Chapter 16's problem.

Five date columns on one fact is where strategy 1 starts to cost more than it saves. The wrapper is per measure and per role, so the work grows as a product. Add one measure and you add one wrapper for every role. Count what a heavy maintenance page carries. The five measures from the strategy 3 arithmetic, plus the three numbers the shop actually argues about. Available is 57.0, the pre-input baseline the planner froze before the aircraft arrived. Pre-input is the planning and kitting work done on the package before the aircraft is in the bay. Projected is 63.5, production control's current estimate of the final total. Achieved is 62.0, the hours technicians really booked. Handle those three words carefully, because they do not travel. Available is planned in one shop, budgeted in the next and sold in the one after that, and the same word can mean the frozen baseline in one report and the live forecast in the next. Write the local definition down, get somebody in production control to agree it, and put it in the model description.

Eight measures, then. Eight times five is 40 measures. Take out the 8 that ride the active relationship and 32 hand-written CALCULATE wrappers are left, each able to be wrong on its own and each needing its own test. The calculation group version is 8 measures plus 5 items, which is 13 objects. Earlier in this chapter the same comparison came out at 15 objects against 8, close enough that either answer was reasonable. 40 against 13 is not.

Now take the five apart, because the honest count is lower and the reason matters more than the saving.

PlannedFinish is the easy one to dismiss and the easy one to get wrong. On all eight Meridian work orders it holds exactly the value in PromisedDate. Build it as a role today and you have paid for a relationship, an item and a test in order to reproduce a column you already have. The trap runs the other way. They hold equal values and they record different facts. One is the board's plan for when the bay frees up. The other is what the customer was told. The day the board slips a week and the customer date holds, the two diverge, and every report that treated them as interchangeable answers a different question without looking any different. Keep the column, give it no relationship, and compare the two on refresh.

PlannedStart is the one this section exists for. Seven of the eight rows agree with OpenedDate exactly. WO-1003 is the exception: the HMCC board says 2025-01-13 and the shop floor system says 2025-01-14, because the aircraft arrived a day late. Read what that actually is. Opened and closed are two different events in the life of a work order, which is what makes them roles. Planned start and opened date are one event, the aircraft arriving in the bay, recorded twice by two systems that disagree about it. Two events make a role. One event recorded twice makes a reconciliation, and a reconciliation takes a different kind of fix.

A second relationship is the wrong tool because of what a relationship is. It is a filter path, and a filter path answers exactly one shape of question: which rows belong in this period. Give PlannedStart an inactive relationship and a wrapper and you have built a second answer to a question that already has one. Nothing anywhere in the model would say which answer is the shop's. You would ship both. Turnaround on WO-1003 is 22 days from OpenedDate and 23 days from the planned start. So the average over the six closed work orders is 12.0 days one way, and 73 divided by 6, which is 12.17 days, the other. Two figures, both arithmetically correct, both labelled average turn time, differing because of one row out of eight. That is a meeting, not a report.

The disagreement is also invisible in the place most people look. Count work orders by planned start month and you get 3 in January, 3 in February and 2 in March, which is the opened column of Table 13.1 exactly, because WO-1003 moved from the thirteenth to the fourteenth and both dates sit in January. No month axis will ever show you this. It surfaces at day grain, and in anything that subtracts one date from another.

So measure turnaround from the induction date, write that down where the next section says to write it, and carry the disagreement itself as a number rather than as a second way to slice the same eight rows.

DAXTurn Days and Input Slip Days
// Turnaround from the shop floor date, and the name says which
Turn Days (actual input) =
    CALCULATE (
        AVERAGEX (
            FactWorkOrder,
            DATEDIFF ( FactWorkOrder[OpenedDate],
                FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate], DAY )
        ),
        NOT ISBLANK ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
    )

// The disagreement carried as a number, not as a second date role
Input Slip Days =
    SUMX (
        FactWorkOrder,
        DATEDIFF ( FactWorkOrder[PlannedStart],
            FactWorkOrder[OpenedDate], DAY )
    )
Lines 4 to 5
AVERAGEX and not AVERAGE. AVERAGE takes a column, and no column in this model holds turn days unless you add one. AVERAGEX iterates the header table, evaluates the difference once per row, and averages the values it gets back. That keeps the calculation in the measure where a reviewer can see it. A calculated column would hide it in a value computed at some refresh nobody remembers.
Lines 6 to 7
DATEDIFF and not FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] - FactWorkOrder[OpenedDate]. Both give a number of days when both columns are true dates. DATEDIFF names the unit inside the expression, so the next reader knows the result is days and not months, and the intent survives somebody changing a column type upstream.
Line 9
The same guard as Work Orders Closed, for the same reason. WO-1004 and WO-1008 have no ClosedDate. In arithmetic a blank behaves as the value at zero, so whatever difference it produces is not a turn time. Your build of DATEDIFF may return a large number or may raise an error on those rows, and the guard removes the question either way. With it in place the measure returns 12.0 days across the six closed work orders.
Lines 14 to 15
SUMX over FactWorkOrder and not a calculated column on the same table. Both return 1. The measure is the right form while you are still finding out whether anybody wants the number. If it survives to a second page, move it into Power Query as a column on the merged header, where it is computed once per refresh instead of once per query, and where the two source dates sit next to it for anyone auditing the row.
Why this and not that

SUMX and not AVERAGEX for the slip. An average across the eight work orders is 1 divided by 8, which is 0.125 days, and 0.125 rounds to nothing on a card and reads as two systems in agreement. The sum is 1, and one day is a fact somebody can act on, attached to an aircraft you can name. Averaging is the standard way to make a single bad row disappear, and a variance you are tracking precisely because it is rare is the last thing you should average. Put the count of disagreeing rows beside it, which here is also 1, and the pair tells the whole story without a paragraph of explanation underneath.

Turnaround time has a settled definition and it is worth holding to it. Input to output: from the moment the aircraft is inducted and towed to the bay, to the moment certifying staff release it. That makes OpenedDate the date turnaround is measured from, because nothing could be worked until the aircraft was there. The planned start answers a different question. Whether the check is where the board said it would be, day by day, is schedule adherence. Schedule adherence has its own audience and its own report. Keep the two apart. Name the measure so the name says which clock it ran on, as Turn Days (actual input) does above, and do not let the answer fall out of whichever relationship somebody happened to make active first.

What a date role does to a table that has no date of its own

Built FactPreInput is the planner's heavy pre-input work package, one row per work order per trade, and it carries no date column at all. A date filter can only reach it through FactWorkOrder. So a date role, whether it arrives as a USERELATIONSHIP wrapper or as a calculation item, changes the available hours number even though nothing in that measure mentions the header.

Available hours by work order are WO-1001 13.0, WO-1003 13.0, WO-1004 12.0, WO-1006 10.0 and WO-1008 9.0, which is 57.0 across the quarter. The other three work orders are light maintenance, have no pre-input pack, and contribute nothing.

Under the default opened role, February holds WO-1004, WO-1005 and WO-1006, so available reads 12.0 plus 0 plus 10.0, which is 22.0. Under a Closed item, February holds WO-1003 and WO-1005 instead, so it reads 13.0 plus 0, which is 13.0. January moves from 26.0 to 13.0, and March moves from 9.0 to 10.0.

Now the total, which is where it stops being interesting and starts being dangerous. Opened gives 26.0 plus 22.0 plus 9.0, which is 57.0 and ties to the figure above. Closed gives 13.0 plus 13.0 plus 10.0, which is 36.0, the available total for the three closed heavy checks WO-1001, WO-1003 and WO-1006. The missing 21.0 is WO-1004 at 12.0 and WO-1008 at 9.0, the two work orders that have never closed and therefore appear under no month at all. Both totals are arithmetically correct. Only one of them is the number somebody asked for, and nothing on the visual says which item is selected unless you put the item name on an axis.

So the real count on FactWorkOrder is three roles and not five, and the choosing rule earlier in this chapter has moved anyway. Eight measures times three roles is 24 measures, of which 16 are wrappers. A calculation group gives you 8 measures plus 3 items, which is 11 objects. Three roles against the five measures counted earlier was close enough to go either way. Three roles against eight measures is where a calculation group starts to earn its complexity. The heavy maintenance extension pushed it over the line from both directions at once. It put five date columns on the header, and it brought three more measures that all have to answer to them.

Which relationship should be active

The production controller builds his own page next week and drags DimDate[MonthName] next to a sum of FactWorkOrder[QuotedAmount]. Whatever number comes back, the active relationship picked the date for him, and nothing on screen said which one. Which relationship you make active is therefore a decision about everybody else's defaults, and it deserves five minutes of thought. Power BI creates one by default and it has no idea what your shop reports on.

The active relationship should be the role used by the majority of reports and by time intelligence, because those are the two places where the choice is invisible. For Meridian that is OpenedDate. Intake volume, current backlog, work in progress and quoted value by month are all opened-date questions, and they outnumber everything else on the shop floor pages.

The counter-case is real. If the main consumer of this model were finance, closing the month on work recognised at completion, ClosedDate would be the better default and every intake measure would carry the wrapper instead. Either choice is defensible. Leaving the choice implicit is not. Write it into the table description on FactWorkOrder in words: the active date role is OpenedDate, so any measure not wrapped in USERELATIONSHIP reports by opened date. That description surfaces as a tooltip in the field list, which is the one place a report author is already looking.

Performance note

Inactive relationships are close to free. They occupy storage for the join structures and add a little to refresh time, and they cost nothing at query time until a measure invokes one. USERELATIONSHIP materialises nothing. The storage engine runs against a different join. A TREATAS equivalent pushes a filter list in from the formula engine, which is why USERELATIONSHIP usually beats it on the same model. The cost shows up in a matrix with a calculation group on the columns, where each measure is evaluated once per item, so three roles means three storage engine queries where there was one.

Time intelligence has to be told too

The finance manager asks for closed work orders year to date. You already have Work Orders Closed, so you wrap it in a year to date function and ship it. At March it returns 8. Eight is the year to date count of work orders opened, and the report says closed.

Time intelligence functions read the date table and rewrite the filter on it. They know nothing about which relationship is active. So a year to date over a non-default role needs the role swap as well, and the swap has to sit inside the same CALCULATE that shifts the dates, or inside a measure that the shifting CALCULATE invokes.

DAXYear to date over the closed role
// Correct: the role swap lives inside the measure being shifted
Work Orders Closed YTD =
    CALCULATE (
        [Work Orders Closed],
        DATESYTD ( DimDate[Date] )
    )

// Broken: the VAR is resolved before the CALCULATE shifts anything
Work Orders Closed YTD (broken) =
VAR Closed =
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ),
        USERELATIONSHIP ( DimDate[Date], FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
    )
RETURN
    CALCULATE ( Closed, DATESYTD ( DimDate[Date] ) )
Lines 3 to 6
DATESYTD returns a table of dates from the first of the year to the last date in the current filter context, and it is applied as a filter argument to the outer CALCULATE. That filter lands on DimDate. The measure reference then runs its own CALCULATE, swaps in the close date relationship, and propagates the already shifted date filter through it. At March the result is 2 plus 2 plus 2, which is 6, and 6 is the number the finance manager wanted.
Lines 10 to 16
A variable is evaluated once, in the filter context where it is defined, and it is a constant everywhere after that. By the time line 16 applies DATESYTD, there is nothing left to filter. At March the broken measure returns 2, the March value, and it looks plausible enough to ship.
The silent version
Worse than either is TOTALYTD ( COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ), DimDate[Date] ) written for a closed report. It runs, it returns 3 plus 3 plus 2, which is 8 at March, and 8 is the year to date count of opened work orders. No error, no blank, no clue.
Why this and not that

DATESYTD and not TOTALYTD. TOTALYTD is a wrapper that performs the CALCULATE for you, and that is exactly the problem when a role swap is involved: the CALCULATE you would need to attach USERELATIONSHIP to is hidden inside the function. You can pass a measure that already carries its own wrapper, so TOTALYTD still gives you the right answer, and it puts the relationship decision one level out of sight. DATESYTD returns a table and forces you to write the CALCULATE yourself, which is where the role belongs and where the next reader will look for it.

The same reasoning covers SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, DATEADD and every other function in that family. They shift dates on the date table. Which column of the fact those shifted dates reach is a separate decision, and if you do not make it explicitly, the model makes it for you and reports opened.

What to remember
  • One date table, three relationships, one of them active. The engine allows a single active path between two tables because two would make January ambiguous, and inactive relationships cost almost nothing until a measure names one.
  • Strategy 1 is the default: CALCULATE plus USERELATIONSHIP per role. It produces Table 13.1 from one slicer, and it fails only when a user needs two roles filtered independently.
  • Strategy 2 exists for that one failure. Two independent date inputs, whether two role tables or one disconnected as-of picker, and remember that a blank close date joins to no date table at all.
  • Strategy 3 turns a multiplication into an addition: 5 measures times 3 roles is 15 measures, against 5 measures plus 3 calculation items. It needs a modelling tool, it disables implicit measures, and it is hard for a colleague to find.
  • Role playing on non-date dimensions is usually a signal that you have two different questions. Work station and technician home station total the same 62.0 hours and mean nothing when subtracted.
  • Only three of Meridian's five date columns are roles. WorkDate and IssueDate are the only date on their fact, so each takes one plain active relationship. They still share the calendar, so one slicer set to 2025-01-09 returns zero work orders beside 15.0 labor hours and 2,450 of parts, and all three numbers are right.
  • The heavy maintenance tables put five date columns on FactWorkOrder alone and eight in the model, and only three of those five header columns are roles. Count roles against measures before choosing: 8 measures times 3 roles is 24 measures with 16 wrappers, against 8 measures plus 3 calculation items, which is 11 objects. That is where strategy 3 stops being an indulgence.
  • PlannedStart and OpenedDate are one event recorded by two systems, one day apart on WO-1003. That is a reconciliation, not a role, and a second relationship ships both answers without choosing. Average turn days is 12.0 measured from OpenedDate and 12.17 measured from the HMCC planned start. Turnaround runs from induction, so 12.0 is the number, and the gap is carried as its own measure rather than as a second date role.
  • A USERELATIONSHIP wrapper redirects the date filter on FactWorkOrder and leaves FactLabor riding WorkDate. February shows 2 closed work orders next to 22.0 hours that belong to two different orders. Route the filter through the header and REMOVEFILTERS the calendar to get the 12.5 that answers the question asked.
  • Time intelligence does not inherit a role. Put USERELATIONSHIP inside the same CALCULATE that shifts the dates, or inside a measure that CALCULATE calls, and never inside a VAR that is resolved before the shift.
Part 5 . Hard modelling cases

14Many-to-many, and the total that does not add up

By the end of this chapter you will be able to trace a many to many result by hand, explain to a manager why the visible rows do not sum to the total shown underneath them, and pick deliberately between blanking the total, allocating the value, and changing the question.

The shop manager stops at your desk with one question. How many labor hours were booked by technicians holding each certification? She wants A&P, Avionics, NDT and Engine Run down the rows and hours across. You build the matrix in four minutes. The four rows add to 85.0 hours, and the total row printed underneath them says 62.0. Meridian booked 62.0 hours in Q1, so the total is right, and the rows are right too. By the end of this chapter you will be able to stand in front of her and say why both of those hold at the same time.

Why this question is genuinely many to many

Start with the term, because it is about to do a lot of work. A many to many relationship is one where a row on each side can match several rows on the other side. Look at the raw Technicians extract. TECH-04, D. Sandoval, has the value A&P; Avionics; Engine Run in the Certifications column. One technician, three certifications. Now read the same column down the other axis: A&P appears against TECH-01, TECH-02 and TECH-04. One certification, three technicians.

That is the definition, and it is why neither side is unique. Try to hold Sandoval's three certifications in one column on a technician table. You get the text A&P; Avionics; Engine Run, which nobody can filter on. Try to hold the three A&P holders in one column on a certification table and the same problem points the other way. The pairing itself has to become rows. One row per technician per certification, and that grain belongs to neither table. In the Meridian model those rows live in Bridge BridgeTechCert. That is a bridge table, meaning a table whose whole job is to hold one row per pair. Power Query built it by splitting the delimited column to rows.

Take the pause here. The model is right and the question is awkward, and both of those are true together. The awkwardness belongs to what the shop manager asked for. Ask the same question in SQL, in Excel or on paper and it follows you there.

Look at the two links that meet the bridge in the centre. Each is marked 1 at the dimension end and * at the bridge end, because the bridge sits on the many side of both. Study the link on the right, between BridgeTechCert and DimTechnician. It has an arrow head at each end and the label both, and it is the only relationship in the whole Meridian model you would ever set that way. The label records its cross filter direction, which is the setting that says which way a filter may travel along a relationship. Here is why it has to be both. A filter placed on DimCertification reaches the bridge easily. From the bridge it then has to climb into DimTechnician, against the one to many direction, before it can drop to Fact FactLabor underneath. Everything in this chapter follows from that one upstream hop.

The two notes beside the bridge state the same awkwardness from each side, TECH-04 holding three certifications and A&P being held by three technicians. The red card underneath gives away the ending before the chapter has argued for it: certification rows of 39.0, 10.5, 12.0 and 23.5, which add to 85.0, sitting under a grand total that prints 62.0. Every number in the rest of this chapter is an attempt to explain that card and then to decide what to do about it.

The three tables you need in front of you

Trace this by hand before you write any DAX. Ten bridge rows, four certifications, seven technicians. That is small enough to check with a pencil and large enough to reproduce every behaviour you will meet on a table with four million rows.

In the model the bridge carries two key columns and nothing else, TechnicianID and CertCode. It exists to be traversed. Keep it off report pages, and expect no measures and no dates on it.

The bridge row count reconciles to ten, which is the whole bridge. Good. If it did not, you would have lost a row in the split step and every number after this point would be quietly wrong.

TECH-07 is the orphan from L-506, an orphan being a fact row whose key matches nothing in the dimension. It sits in FactLabor and books ten hours against WO-1004. It appears in Built DimTechnician only because you appended an Unknown technician row for it. It holds no certifications, so it has no bridge rows at all. Keep that in view. It is going to explain a ten hour discrepancy later.

DAXLabor Hours
Labor Hours =
    SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )
Line 2
SUM and not SUMX. The value being aggregated is already a physical column on the fact table, so there is nothing to compute per row. SUMX ( FactLabor, FactLabor[Hours] ) returns the same number, and the engine usually reduces it to the same plan. The cost is in what an iterator tells the next reader: that a row by row calculation happens here, when none does.

The trace

Put DimCertification[CertCode] on the rows of a matrix and [Labor Hours] in the values. The relationship from DimTechnician to BridgeTechCert has its cross filter direction set to Both, which is what the double headed arrow in the figure earlier in this chapter records. Every other relationship in the documented Meridian model is single direction, so this one is a deliberate change. Here is what the engine does for each row. Beside it is the same arithmetic you would do by hand.

Rows add to
85.0
Total prints
62.0
Difference
23.0

Twenty three hours of daylight between the rows and the total. The shift supervisor will screenshot this and send it to you with a question mark on it.

Interview-level insight

The total row is not the sum of the rows above it. It never was, for any measure. Every cell in a matrix, including the total, is an independent evaluation of the measure in its own filter context. The row cells are evaluated with a certification filter on. The total cell is evaluated with that filter off. Power BI never adds the cells together to produce the total. For most measures over a star schema the two happen to agree, so people forget. A many to many is one of the cases where they part, and that is the moment the mechanism becomes visible.

Follow the individual hours. Sandoval's 10.5 hours appear in the A&P row, again in the Avionics row and again in the Engine Run row. Each of those three cells holds a correct answer. 10.5 hours really were booked by a technician holding A&P. The same 10.5 hours really were booked by a technician holding Avionics, and again by one holding Engine Run. All three statements describe the same timesheet lines, and all three are true. Okafor's 12.0 hours appear twice, under A&P and NDT.

In the grand total cell the filter on DimCertification is gone. Nothing propagates through the bridge, so FactLabor is unfiltered. Each of the eight labor rows is then counted exactly once, and the answer is 62.0. That 62.0 includes the ten hours from TECH-07. Those ten hours never appear in any row of the matrix, because that technician holds no certification.

Say this out loud once so it sticks: a measure evaluated over a many to many is non additive across that dimension. Non additive means the rows will never legitimately add up, in the same way a column of percentages never does. The question itself carries that property. Power BI is reporting it faithfully, and every relationship setting in the model leaves it exactly where it is.

Common mistake

Someone will ask you to "make the total match". The usual attempt is to redefine the total as the sum of the visible rows, which prints 85.0 and states that Meridian booked 85 hours in Q1 when the timesheets say 62. You have then replaced a total that is correct and confusing with a total that is wrong and comfortable. If you are ever tempted, remember that 85.0 changes the moment somebody adds a fifth certification to the reference data, without a single new hour being worked.

What to tell the business, with the numbers attached

The finance manager arrives at the desk next. He has seen the screenshot, he wants one number for the month, and he has no patience for a lecture about grain. You have three honest answers for him, and he is the one who picks between them. Each answer is a different agreement about what the report means, and the DAX follows from the agreement. Settle the agreement first.

Option A. Present it as coverage and refuse to print a total

The row values are correct as they stand. A&P covers 39.0 hours of work, Engine Run covers 23.5. The sum of those rows has no defined meaning, so do not print one. Relabel the column "Hours covered", and blank the total row.

DAXHours Covered
Hours Covered =
    IF (
        ISINSCOPE ( DimCertification[CertCode] ),
        [Labor Hours]
    )
Line 2
IF with no else branch returns blank when the condition is false. A blank measure result leaves the total row empty. A zero there would be read as "no hours", which is a different lie.
Line 3
ISINSCOPE asks whether DimCertification[CertCode] is one of the grouping columns of the cell being evaluated. In a row of the matrix it is, so the measure returns hours. In the total row it is not, so the measure returns blank.
Why this and not that

HASONEVALUE ( DimCertification[CertCode] ) is the function most people reach for, and it looks identical until a user drops a slicer on the page and selects A&P only. At that point the column has exactly one value in every cell of the visual, including the total. HASONEVALUE then returns true in the total row, and the total prints 39.0 as though it were a sum. ISINSCOPE asks a different question: is this column one of the columns grouping the visual? That is a fact about the layout of the matrix, so slicers cannot move it and the total stays blank. The cost is real and you should know it before you ship. ISINSCOPE returns true only when that specific column groups the visual, so the same measure on a card, or on a matrix grouped by station, returns blank. If the shop manager wants this number on a card as well, write a second measure for the card and leave this one alone.

Option B. Allocate the hours across certifications

If finance needs a set of numbers that reconcile, split each technician's hours evenly across the certifications they hold. Sandoval's 10.5 hours become 3.5 hours to each of A&P, Avionics and Engine Run. Okafor's 12.0 become 6.0 to each of A&P and NDT. Halvorsen holds one certification, so all 16.5 hours go to A&P unchanged.

Trace the allocation arithmetic by hand, row by row

One line per bridge row. The contribution is the technician's total hours divided by the number of certifications that technician holds.

Now roll the ten contributions up to the four certifications.

The allocated rows add to 52.0, which is exactly the hours booked by technicians who exist in the bridge. The remaining 10.0 hours belong to TECH-07, who holds no certification and so has nowhere to be allocated. The allocation therefore reconciles to 52.0, and the 10.0 hour gap is the orphan. To make it reconcile to 62.0 you have to add an Uncertified member to DimCertification and a bridge row pairing TECH-07 with it. That is a data decision. Somebody in HR owns it, and they have to agree to it before you build it.

DAXLabor Hours Allocated
Labor Hours Allocated =
    SUMX (
        BridgeTechCert,
        VAR TechHours = CALCULATE ( [Labor Hours] )
        VAR CertCount =
            CALCULATE (
                COUNTROWS ( BridgeTechCert ),
                REMOVEFILTERS ( DimCertification ),
                REMOVEFILTERS ( BridgeTechCert[CertCode] )
            )
        RETURN
            DIVIDE ( TechHours, CertCount )
    )
Line 2
SUMX and not SUM, and the table it iterates is the bridge itself. Iterating the bridge means the grand total sums ten technician to certification pairs and lands on 52.0. Iterate DISTINCT ( BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID] ) and each technician is visited once at the grand total, which gives 39.0. That number matches no row of the report and no timesheet.
Line 4
CALCULATE around the measure reference forces context transition. Context transition turns the current bridge row into a filter on BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID] and BridgeTechCert[CertCode]. That filter then travels up to DimTechnician and down to FactLabor. The engine already wraps a bare measure reference in an implicit CALCULATE, so the line behaves identically without it. Write it anyway. The transition is the entire mechanism of the measure, and hiding it costs the next reader ten minutes.
Lines 6 to 10
COUNTROWS and not COUNT, because you are counting bridge rows, not non blank values in a particular column, and COUNT would need a column argument that adds nothing. The two REMOVEFILTERS calls strip the certification restriction from both ends, the dimension and the bridge itself, leaving only the technician filter placed by the transition. For TECH-04 that returns 3.
Lines 6 to 10, function choice
REMOVEFILTERS and not ALL. They do the same job as CALCULATE modifiers. ALL is also a table function used to return rows, so a reader has to work out which of its two jobs is meant here. REMOVEFILTERS has only one job.
Line 12
DIVIDE and not the / operator, because DIVIDE returns blank on a zero denominator where / raises an error. Be honest about this one. CertCount cannot be zero here: the iterator walks rows that exist in the bridge, so every technician it visits holds at least one certification. DIVIDE is here to survive a future edit.
Performance note

This measure performs a context transition and a COUNTROWS per bridge row. Over ten rows that is free. Over a bridge with three hundred thousand customer to segment pairs it costs real time, and the query plan shows it as a large number of storage engine calls. The shipping version materialises the divisor once as a calculated column on DimTechnician, then the measure becomes SUMX ( BridgeTechCert, DIVIDE ( [Labor Hours], RELATED ( DimTechnician[CertCount] ) ) ). RELATED and not another CALCULATE. The bridge sits on the many side of a strong relationship to DimTechnician, which is the exact case RELATED exists for, and a lookup is cheaper than a filtered re-aggregation.

Option C. Change the question to one that behaves

The manager may not actually want hours. Ask her what decision the number feeds. If the answer is anything close to "do we have enough A&P cover on the floor", then the useful measure is a count of technicians, not a sum of hours: how many technicians holding this certification booked any time in the period.

DAXCertified Techs With Booked Time
Certified Techs With Booked Time =
    CALCULATE (
        DISTINCTCOUNT ( FactLabor[TechnicianID] ),
        TREATAS (
            DISTINCT ( BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID] ),
            FactLabor[TechnicianID]
        )
    )
Line 3
DISTINCTCOUNT and not COUNTROWS ( VALUES ( ... ) ). Be precise about where those two differ, because the usual shorthand gets it backwards. The blank member is added to the table on the one side of a relationship, so COUNTROWS ( VALUES ( DimTechnician[TechnicianID] ) ) can return one more than you expect when a fact row holds an unmatched key. The column being counted here is FactLabor[TechnicianID], which is the many side, so no blank member exists and the wrapped form would return the same number. Prefer DISTINCTCOUNT anyway: it states the intent in one function and resolves to a single storage engine operation instead of materialising a table and counting it.
Lines 4 to 7
TREATAS applies the list of technicians who hold the certification in scope as a filter on FactLabor[TechnicianID]. That filter lands in every cell of the visual, including the grand total, so the total counts only technicians who appear in the bridge. A relationship on its own leaves the total cell unfiltered, and the total then counts every technician in FactLabor.
Line 5
DISTINCT and not VALUES. BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID] sits on the many side of the relationship from DimTechnician, so the two return exactly the same rows today. The difference is what happens later. If somebody ever puts this column on the one side of a new relationship and a key fails to match, VALUES starts returning a blank member and DISTINCT does not. That list is being handed to TREATAS as a filter, and a blank that arrives inside a filter argument is a defect nobody spots for months.

The values are 3 for A&P, 1 for Avionics, 1 for NDT and 2 for Engine Run, and the grand total is 4. Work them through: A&P is held by TECH-01, TECH-02 and TECH-04, and all three booked time, so 3. Avionics is held by TECH-03, TECH-04 and TECH-06, and only TECH-04 booked time, so 1. NDT is held by TECH-01 and TECH-03, and only TECH-01 booked time, so 1. Engine Run is held by TECH-04 and TECH-05, both of whom booked time, so 2. The total is the four distinct technicians who both hold a certification and booked time: TECH-01, TECH-02, TECH-04 and TECH-05.

Here is the inconvenient part, and you should say it to the manager before she notices it herself. The rows add to 3 plus 1 plus 1 plus 2, which is 7, and the total is 4. A distinct count carries the same non additive property the hours did. The difference is expectation. Nobody expects a distinct count to add up, so the number stops generating support tickets. That is a smaller claim than "we fixed it", and it is the true one.

What I would ship

Option A, with Option C beside it on the same visual. Ship the coverage hours with a blanked total and a column header that says "Hours covered", and put the technician count next to it so the reader has an additive-looking number to anchor on. Two columns, one honest story: A&P touches 39.0 hours of work across 3 working technicians, Avionics touches 10.5 across 1.

I would not ship Option B by default, even though it is the one that reconciles. The allocation is a policy, and it was invented by whoever wrote the measure. D. Sandoval spent 10.5 hours on aircraft, and the even three way split of those hours is an arithmetic convenience. The moment the finance manager makes a staffing decision on 26.0 A&P hours, he is acting on a convention nobody at Meridian agreed to. Allocation belongs in the model when finance has a documented allocation rule that they own and can defend. In that case you also add the Uncertified member, so the number climbs from 52.0 and reconciles properly to 62.0.

Three ways to implement the same many to many

The agreement about meaning is settled, so now the model has to carry it. The planner who inherits this file will open it after you have moved on, see whatever you built, and work out what you meant from what is in front of her. That is the real difference between the three shapes below. All three produce the same four row values, 39.0, 10.5, 12.0 and 23.5. They differ in what they do to the model, in what the grand total prints, and in what a colleague can see without reading your DAX.

1. Bridge table with a bidirectional relationship

Two single direction relationships into the bridge, DimCertification[CertCode] to BridgeTechCert[CertCode] and DimTechnician[TechnicianID] to BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID], and then you set the cross filter direction on the second one to Both. Without that flag the certification filter reaches the bridge and stops there, and every row of the matrix prints 62.0 because FactLabor is never filtered. That symptom, every row identical to the total, is the fingerprint of a bridge with the flag not set.

This is the standard answer and the one to reach for first. The cost is that a bidirectional relationship is a permanent property of the model. It applies to every visual, every measure and every future table somebody adds. If a second bidirectional path from DimStation ever appears, the two paths from a dimension to FactLabor become ambiguous, and Power BI will refuse the relationship. If that worries you, leave the relationship single direction and switch the traversal on inside one measure with CROSSFILTER. CROSSFILTER gives you the same both directions behaviour, scoped to a single CALCULATE. USERELATIONSHIP is the wrong tool here: it activates an inactive relationship and leaves direction alone.

DAXBridge implementation
// With the bridge in place the measure needs no change.
Labor Hours =
    SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )

// Alternative, if you leave the relationship single
// direction and want both directions in one measure only:
Hours Covered Scoped =
    CALCULATE (
        [Labor Hours],
        CROSSFILTER (
            BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID],
            DimTechnician[TechnicianID],
            BOTH
        )
    )
Lines 2 to 3
That is the entire DAX cost of implementation 1. The base measure is untouched. All of the many to many behaviour lives in the model, in one checkbox on one relationship, which is why this is the default: a colleague can see what is happening by opening the model view, without reading a single measure.
Lines 8 to 15
CROSSFILTER and not USERELATIONSHIP. Both are CALCULATE modifiers that take a relationship, and people reach for the wrong one constantly. USERELATIONSHIP swaps which relationship is active, which is what you want for the role-playing date problem and useless here, because the technician to bridge relationship is already active. What is wrong with it is the direction, and direction is the only thing CROSSFILTER changes.
Lines 11 to 12
The many side column goes first and the one side column second. The engine matches the pair to a relationship either way round, but writing it many side first matches the argument order in the documentation and reads in the direction the filter is about to travel.
Line 13
BOTH, the third argument, is what makes the certification filter climb from the bridge into DimTechnician. The other accepted values are ONEWAY and NONE. NONE is the one worth remembering, because it lets you switch a relationship off for a single measure, which is occasionally the cleanest way out of an unwanted filter.
Whole block
Pay the honest cost here: the scoped version has to be repeated in every measure that needs the traversal. Two measures and it is fine. Fifteen measures and somebody will forget one, and that measure will quietly print 62.0 on every row. The model level flag cannot be forgotten.

2. Direct many to many cardinality on a shared column

Skip the separate bridge. Split Technicians[Certifications] to rows and leave the result on the technician table itself, so it now has ten rows and CertCode repeats down it. Relate DimCertification[CertCode] to DimTechnician[CertCode] and set the cardinality to Many to many.

Two things follow immediately. First, the technician table is no longer at one row per technician. TECH-04 now appears three times on what used to be the one side, so its relationship to FactLabor also has to become many to many. Second, every relationship you declare as many to many is a limited relationship, which the documentation also calls weak. A limited relationship behaves differently in three ways you will meet in production. No blank row is added on either side for unmatched keys. RELATED cannot be used across it. And the engine cannot apply the referential integrity optimisation it uses for strong relationships, so the join is resolved at query time.

The blank row point is the one that bites, and TECH-07 is the illustration. Across a strong relationship, Power BI keeps a FactLabor row whose TechnicianID matches nothing in the dimension. It adds a blank row to the dimension and parks those hours under it. So 10.0 hours show up under an empty label, and somebody eventually asks about it. Across a limited relationship there is no blank row, so those hours attach to no member at all. They vanish from every technician sliced visual while still sitting inside the unfiltered grand total. That is the worst combination: a number that is wrong on the rows and right at the bottom, with nothing on screen to signal it. Meridian escapes this only because you built DimTechnician with an explicit Unknown technician row for TECH-07. Had you skipped that step, the weak relationship would have hidden the loss.

DAXDirect many to many implementation
// The hours measure is unchanged. This shape is a model
// decision, not a DAX one.
Labor Hours =
    SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )

// This is what you give up. It is valid across the strong
// relationship the bridge model keeps, and it fails once
// that same hop is declared many to many:
Hours At Home Station MSP =
    SUMX (
        FactLabor,
        IF (
            RELATED ( DimTechnician[HomeStation] ) = "MSP",
            FactLabor[Hours]
        )
    )
Lines 3 to 4
Nothing new. Implementations 1 and 2 print the same four row values from the same measure text, which is precisely why the choice between them gets made carelessly. The difference shows up in what else the model can still do.
Lines 10 to 11
SUMX and not SUM this time, because the thing being summed is conditional and does not exist as a column. The first argument is FactLabor, a table, which is what gives the expression a row context for RELATED to work in. Written with the bridge model in place this returns 28.5, the hours booked by the three technicians whose home station is MSP: 12.0 from TECH-01 and 16.5 from TECH-02, with TECH-06 contributing nothing.
Line 13
RELATED and not RELATEDTABLE. You are standing on a FactLabor row, which is the many side, and reaching for one scalar attribute on the one side, which is what RELATED does. RELATEDTABLE goes the other way and would hand you every labor row for the technician, a table where the comparison needs a value. Under implementation 2 the relationship becomes limited and RELATED stops being available across it, so this measure has to be rewritten as a CALCULATE with an explicit filter. On its own that is a twenty minute job. It is one of a family of small taxes you keep paying for the life of the model.
Lines 12 to 15
IF with no else branch, and not IF ( ..., FactLabor[Hours], 0 ). Returning blank keeps the non matching rows out of the aggregation entirely. Adding zeros would change the answer as soon as the same pattern is used for an average.

I would not ship this shape for Meridian. It destroys the technician dimension as a dimension, and it trades a clean bridge for a limited relationship that gives you nothing in return.

3. TREATAS in the measure, no model change

Load BridgeTechCert and DimCertification with no relationships at all and do the propagation in DAX.

DAXHours Covered Virtual
Hours Covered Virtual =
    VAR CertsInScope =
        VALUES ( DimCertification[CertCode] )
    VAR TechsHolding =
        CALCULATETABLE (
            DISTINCT ( BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID] ),
            TREATAS ( CertsInScope, BridgeTechCert[CertCode] )
        )
    RETURN
        CALCULATE (
            [Labor Hours],
            TREATAS ( TechsHolding, FactLabor[TechnicianID] )
        )
Lines 2 to 3
VALUES here and not DISTINCT, deliberately reversing the earlier preference. DimCertification has no relationship in this design, so no blank member can exist, and VALUES reads as "whatever the visual selected", which is what you mean.
Lines 4 to 8
CALCULATETABLE and not FILTER. CALCULATETABLE applies the filter before the table is scanned. FILTER would run a row by row test over the whole bridge. The result is the set of technicians holding the certifications in scope.
Lines 7 and 12
TREATAS takes a table of values and stamps it with the data lineage of a target column, so the engine treats it as a filter on that column and can push it down to the storage engine. INTERSECT would produce the same set but leaves the lineage of its first argument, and a FILTER with a nested lookup forces a row context comparison per fact row. CROSSFILTER and USERELATIONSHIP are not options at all here, because both need a physical relationship to modify and there is none.
Line 12
The filter is applied to FactLabor[TechnicianID] and not to DimTechnician[TechnicianID] on purpose. Filtering the fact column leaves any technician slicer on the dimension in play, so the two intersect. Filtering the dimension column would override that slicer, which is almost never what the report author wanted.

Watch what this does to the grand total. Because the TREATAS filter is applied in every cell, the total cell is also restricted to the six technicians who appear in the bridge, so it prints 52.0, not 62.0. Whether that is an improvement depends on the agreement you made earlier. It is a cleaner total than 62.0 if the report is explicitly about certified staff, and it is a silent exclusion of ten hours if it is not.

The same shape, elsewhere in the shop

Once you have seen it you will find it everywhere at Meridian. A work order that touches several ATA chapters is the same structure: WO-1003 could easily carry both a hydraulics chapter and an engine chapter, and hours booked to it belong to both. A part that fits several aircraft types is already visible in the data you have: BRK-2210 was issued to WO-1001 on an A320-200 and to WO-1003 on an E175, and ENG-8802 went to both an E175 and the unregistered N338WA. An invoice line split across cost centres is the same shape again with a weight attached to each pair.

All three cases share one structure, and the structure is the part worth carrying to the next model you build. Two of those three columns are missing from the current extract, and I am leaving them missing. Inventing columns to fill the gap would teach you a pattern the data cannot back up. In each case the link between the two tables has its own grain, one row per pair, and the hours or the dollars you want to measure sit at neither table's grain. A measure that adds up cleanly along one table goes non additive along the other. You then face the same three choices this chapter has just worked through: present coverage, allocate with a documented rule, or count members instead of summing amounts. The weighted invoice case is the interesting one. The allocation rule already exists in the source system, so use theirs.

Telling a real many to many from a modelling mistake

The production controller wants labor cost and parts cost on one line per work order. You drag WorkOrderID from FactLabor onto WorkOrderID in FactParts, Power BI offers many to many cardinality, and the relationship is created. Both sides then fan out against each other and neither cost reconciles to anything. Power BI makes that offer whenever both join columns hold duplicates, and most of the time the offer is a warning. Read it as one.

Rule of thumb

Ask whether the many to many is a fact about the world or an artefact of a missing key. If a person at the business can name the pair as a noun and describe attributes of it, such as an issue date or an expiry, it is real and it deserves a bridge. If the only reason both sides have duplicates is that the table which would have been the one side is not in your model, it is an artefact and the fix is to find that table.

The real one in Meridian is technician to certification. "Sandoval's A&P" is a thing an HR manager would recognise on sight. It has a certificate number and a renewal date in the source system, even though this extract does not carry those columns. And there is no key you could add anywhere that would turn the pairing into one to many. Ten pairs, ten real facts about the world.

The artefact is the join the production controller asked for, FactLabor to FactParts. Both tables have WorkOrderID, and it repeats on both sides. WO-1001 appears on L-501 and L-502. WO-1003 appears on L-504 and L-505, and again on P-9003 and P-9004. The relationship even appears to work until labor cost and parts cost land in the same visual. Now apply the test. Ask what a single row of that join would describe. A labor line paired with a parts line describes nothing that happens on the floor, so the pair is meaningless. The table that is missing is the header, FactWorkOrder. It holds WorkOrderID exactly once per work order, and it gives both line tables a proper one side to hang from. Route the production controller's visual through it and the many to many disappears, because it was never there.

If you cannot describe the pair, do not model the pair.

What to remember
  • Every cell of a matrix, including the total, is an independent evaluation of the measure in its own filter context. The engine never sums the rows to make the total.
  • Hours by certification gives 39.0, 10.5, 12.0 and 23.5, which add to 85.0, against a printed total of 62.0. The 23.0 gap is correct. TECH-04 booked 10.5 hours while holding three certifications, so those hours belong under all three.
  • A measure over a many to many is non additive across that dimension. That property belongs to the question the shop manager asked, and the tool is reporting it faithfully.
  • Three honest answers: present coverage and blank the total with ISINSCOPE, allocate to 26.0, 3.5, 6.0 and 16.5 which reconcile to 52.0, or count certified technicians who booked time to get 3, 1, 1 and 2 with a total of 4.
  • Ship coverage with a blanked total plus the technician count beside it. Allocation only when someone owns the allocation rule, and then add an Uncertified member so it reconciles to 62.0 rather than 52.0.
  • A bridge with one bidirectional relationship is the default implementation. A direct many to many cardinality relationship is limited, adds no blank row for unmatched keys, and would have hidden TECH-07's ten hours entirely.
  • Before accepting a many to many, ask whether a business person can name the pair. Technician to certification passes. FactLabor to FactParts fails, and the answer there is the FactWorkOrder header.
Part 5 . Hard modelling cases

15Virtual relationships: TREATAS and friends

After this chapter you can push a filter from one table to another with no relationship between them, argue in a design review when that is the right call and when it is laziness, and recognise the two silent failures that make a TREATAS measure return blank with no error to explain it.

The production controller clicks 20 January on the date slicer, because that is the Monday he is asking about. Labor hours hold at 8.0, which is the time L-504 booked at TUS that day. Planned hours go blank. Utilisation divides one by the other, so it comes back empty too, and he wants to know which of the two numbers is broken. Both numbers are correct. The plan is stored by month, he asked for a day, and this chapter is about closing that gap without adding a relationship to the model.

A relationship is a standing instruction. Once it is in the model it applies to every query, every visual, every measure, and every user who opens the report at seven in the morning without asking you first. Most of the joins you need should work that way. A few should last for one calculation and then be gone, and the controller's question needs one of those. Some joins are true for exactly one measure. Some are true only for the question on one page. Some are true in a way the key columns cannot express. That is the gap TREATAS fills.

Meridian has three of these sitting in the model already. The certification bridge needs a filter to travel backwards up a many-to-many join. FactCapacity is keyed on station plus month, and no single column matches that pair. DimTechnician[HomeStation] holds station codes that would be useful as a filter, and the relationship list says in writing that it must never be related to DimStation. Three different problems, one function, no change to the model diagram.

That last part is the point people miss. TREATAS is not a shortcut for a relationship you were too busy to create. It is a way to keep a join out of the model on purpose.

Look at the gap between the two tables, and at the one thing that crosses it. Nothing joins FactCapacity to FactLabor in the model, so the only connection drawn is a dashed teal arrow. Its label reads "TREATAS, no relationship". Read the grain printed under each table as well. Grain means what one row of a table stands for: station and month on the left, day on the right. Those two labels are why no relationship can be drawn there at all. A relationship stored in the model would be a solid line, and a solid line carries a promise with it. The engine validated the keys at refresh, built structures to make the join fast, and will apply it to every query whether you want it or not. The dashed arrow is a virtual relationship, which is a join that lives inside the measure that writes it and nowhere else. It costs nothing at refresh, it stays out of the model view, and it lasts exactly as long as the one CALCULATE that creates it. For the rest of this book a dashed teal line drawn between two tables means that: a join written in DAX, alive for one evaluation, invisible to anyone reading the diagram.

The two cards underneath the tables run ahead of the argument on purpose. The first is headed Utilisation and sketches the shape of the measure that writes this join: a SUMMARIZE over FactLabor feeding a TREATAS inside CALCULATE. Situation 3 builds that skeleton out in full under the name Planned Hours Where Work Happened. Situation 4 turns it into the ratio the card is named for, which is the number the production controller was staring at. The green card beside it gives the two conditions that make the virtual version the better call here. The join needs two columns, and a Power BI relationship takes exactly one column on each side. The grain assumption also stays where a reader can see it, in the text of the measure. The card names the price too: the whole thing is evaluated per query, with no cached structure to help it.

What TREATAS actually does

Before the four situations, the mechanism. The signature is short, and the second half of it repeats.

DAXSignature
TREATAS ( <table expression>, <column> [, <column>] ... )
Argument 1
Any table expression. It can be a table in the model, a function that returns one, or a list of literal values you typed by hand. Its columns are what will be applied.
Arguments 2 onward
One model column per column of the table expression, in the same order. These are the columns that will be filtered.
Return
A table whose values are unchanged but whose lineage now points at the columns you named. Used as a filter argument to CALCULATE, it behaves exactly like a filter on those columns.

Lineage is the whole mechanism. Lineage is the tag every table expression in DAX carries, saying which model column each of its columns came from. VALUES ( DimStation[StationCode] ) returns a one column table, and that column is tagged DimStation[StationCode]. Hand it to CALCULATE as a filter and CALCULATE knows what to filter, because the tag says so. A list you type yourself, such as { "MSP", "TUS" }, arrives as two anonymous strings with the tag missing.

TREATAS rewrites the tag. It takes the values as they are, changes nothing about them, and declares that column one is now DimStation[StationCode]. From that moment they behave as if they had been read from that column, which means they filter it, and the filter propagates outward along the real relationships exactly like any other.

Argument type
Filter argument to CALCULATE
Match rule
Value equality, type sensitive
Column mapping
Positional, not by name
Lifetime
One evaluation of one CALCULATE

Here is the smallest honest example in the Meridian model. MSP and TUS are the two base stations. LAS is a line station and PHX exists only in the planning workbook. Suppose one measure, and only one, should count hours at the base stations regardless of what the station slicer says.

DAXHours at Base Stations
Hours at Base Stations =
    CALCULATE (
        [Labor Hours],
        TREATAS (
            { "MSP", "TUS" },
            DimStation[StationCode]
        )
    )
Line 2
CALCULATE and not CALCULATETABLE, because a visual needs one number in the cell. Both accept a TREATAS filter argument in the same way. The difference is what comes back: a table is what you want when the result feeds an iterator, and useless when it has to fill a cell.
Line 5
The table constructor braces build a two row, one column table with no lineage. Written on its own as a filter argument it is rejected, because CALCULATE has no idea which column those strings belong to.
Line 6
The target column. DimStation[StationCode] and not FactWorkOrder[StationCode]: filter the dimension and the filter reaches both FactWorkOrder and FactCapacity through the existing relationships. Filter the fact column directly and you have restricted one table and left the other wide open.

The result is 57.0 hours: 34.5 at MSP plus 22.5 at TUS. The UNASSIGNED member is excluded by the filter, which costs nothing here because WO-1005 has no labor rows at all, and LAS loses its 5.0 hours as intended.

Interview-level insight

Describe TREATAS as a lineage cast and the rest of its behaviour follows without being memorised. Column order matters, because the cast is positional. Data types matter, because the cast changes the tag and leaves the value alone. It costs what it costs, because nothing is stored. Calling it "a virtual relationship" repeats a phrase. Calling it "restamping the lineage of a table expression so CALCULATE filters the column you named" shows you understood it.

Situation 1: the join that must not become a relationship

The shop manager wants a slicer of target utilisation by station, so a report user can look at only the stations held to a target of fifty percent or better. The targets live in a small table with two columns and four rows. Build it as a calculated table so it stays in the model without a query refresh dependency.

DAXTargetUtil, a disconnected table
// Each target is that station's best Q1 month, from the
// utilisation figures: MSP 75%, TUS 50%, LAS 25%, PHX 0%.
TargetUtil =
    DATATABLE (
        "StationCode", STRING,
        "TargetPct", DOUBLE,
        {
            { "MSP", 0.75 },
            { "TUS", 0.50 },
            { "LAS", 0.25 },
            { "PHX", 0.00 }
        }
    )
Line 4
DATATABLE and not the table constructor { ... }. The constructor works and is shorter, but it names its columns Value1 and Value2 and infers their types from the first row. DATATABLE makes you declare both. Since TREATAS matches on value and is sensitive to type, a table whose types you declared yourself is worth the extra four lines.
Line 6
DOUBLE and not CURRENCY. Utilisation is a ratio, and the fixed four decimal places of the currency type would quietly round a target expressed to more precision later.

Now the measure. The slicer sits on TargetUtil[TargetPct], and whatever stations survive that selection have to filter the labor numbers.

DAXHours at Selected Targets
Hours at Selected Targets =
    CALCULATE (
        [Labor Hours],
        TREATAS (
            VALUES ( TargetUtil[StationCode] ),
            DimStation[StationCode]
        )
    )
Line 5
VALUES reads the station codes that survive whatever the user picked in the slicer. The slicer sits on TargetUtil[TargetPct], a different column of the same disconnected table, so the selection filters TargetUtil itself and VALUES then reads the codes on the rows that are left. No relationship is involved in that step at all.
Line 6
The one model column that receives the values. Note that TargetUtil stays disconnected: no relationship is created, and the only thing that ever crosses from it to the rest of the model is this one filter, inside this one measure.

Select the 0.75 and 0.50 targets in the slicer and VALUES returns MSP and TUS, so the measure reads 57.0 hours again. This time the report user drove it, and nothing is hard coded. Select nothing and all four stations pass through, which gives 62.0, because every hour Meridian booked in Q1 sits at MSP, TUS or LAS.

Why this and not that

VALUES and not DISTINCT. The two differ in one respect. When the column sits on the one side of a relationship, and the many side holds keys that match nothing, VALUES returns an extra blank row for those unmatched members. DISTINCT leaves that row out. TargetUtil is disconnected, so today both return the same four codes. I still write VALUES. If this table is ever related to something and an unmatched key appears, I want the blank member sitting visibly inside the filter where I can find it.

So why not relate TargetUtil[StationCode] to DimStation[StationCode] and stop writing DAX? Two reasons, both structural. Both columns are unique, so Power BI creates the relationship as one to one, and a one to one relationship always cross filters in both directions. The dialog gives you no option to make it single. The target table would then filter DimStation on every query in the report, which is the standing instruction this chapter exists to avoid. Try to route around that by relating TargetUtil straight to the facts and you hit the second reason. Relate it to both FactCapacity[StationCode] and FactWorkOrder[StationCode] and you have closed a loop, since DimStation already reaches both. Power BI accepts the first and refuses to activate the second.

Meridian has a second instance of this and it is written into the relationship list as a deliberate omission. DimStation[StationCode] is never related to DimTechnician[HomeStation], because that would give DimStation two roads to FactLabor, one through FactWorkOrder and one through DimTechnician, which is the ambiguity case from Chapter 8. The relationship stays out. The question it would answer does not have to.

DAXLabor Hours by Home Station
Labor Hours by Home Station =
VAR StationsInContext = VALUES ( DimStation[StationCode] )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        [Labor Hours],
        REMOVEFILTERS ( DimStation ),
        TREATAS (
            StationsInContext,
            DimTechnician[HomeStation]
        )
    )
Line 2
Capture the station codes visible right now, before anything is cleared. A VAR and not the expression written inline: a filter argument of CALCULATE is evaluated in the outer filter context anyway, so both forms return the same values, but the variable removes any need for the reader to know that rule to trust the measure.
Line 6
This line is the one people leave out, and leaving it out is why the measure looks broken. DimStation[StationCode] is on the matrix rows, so it is already filtering FactWorkOrder through the physical relationship. Without REMOVEFILTERS the measure returns hours that are both at that station and worked by a technician homed there, so TUS reads 4.5 rather than 10.5 and LAS reads 5.0 rather than 13.0. REMOVEFILTERS and not ALL. Used as a filter modifier inside CALCULATE the two behave identically, and only one of them is named after the job it is doing.
Lines 7 to 10
The captured codes are retagged onto DimTechnician[HomeStation], a plain descriptive text column with no relationship attached to it. That is the whole trick: a column does not need to be a key to be filtered.

Put DimStation[StationCode] on the rows of a matrix and you get a second answer to the question "hours by station". Both answers are right.
