Cardinality means which side of a relationship holds one row per key and which side holds many. The hop running many to one is your problem. Everything else in this chapter is a decision about getting past that hop, or living with it.

Read it top to bottom. Six numbered checks run down the left side. Each check carries a green card to its right with the fix for that check. A grey arrow drops to the next check when this one is not where your filter died. Check 3 asks whether every hop runs from the one side to the many side. That is the check this chapter is about, and its card sends you to chapters 7 and 8. Read check 4 before you touch the model at all, because Edit Interactions set to None leaves no trace anywhere in the relationship list. When all six pass, the grey card at the bottom tells you to open Performance Analyzer and read the filter arguments of the DAX the visual actually sends. One case needs no check at all. Two fields already sitting on one table cascade with nothing configured, and that is where this chapter starts. Everything else arrives at the three fixes below, and for any given pair of tables at most two of the three actually exist.

Case 1: operator and tail, same table

Start with the half that worked for the planner. Both DimAircraft[Operator] and DimAircraft[ACREG] sit on Dimension DimAircraft. ACREG is the aircraft registration, the tail number painted on the fin. Selecting Cascade Air filters that table to two of its seven rows. The tail slicer then runs its own query for distinct ACREG values, and that query inherits the two survivors. It shows N771QR and N448LM.

Notice the fourth row. N338WA is the tail recovered from WorkOrders, and its operator reads "Unknown operator". That wording earns its keep. A real value in a real column gets its own slicer entry, so whoever picks it lands on the one aircraft nobody can account for. A blank would have given them an unselectable row.

No relationship change, no bidirectional flag, no measure. If every cross-filtering question were shaped like this, the chapter would end here.

Case 2: station and technician, one on each side of the facts

Now the half that failed. Put a slicer on DimStation[StationCode] and another on DimTechnician[TechnicianName]. Select MSP, which is what the planner did. Nothing happens. All seven technicians stay, including J. Prieto and L. Petrov, who booked no hours all quarter.

Trace the route.

Source
DimStation
Target
DimTechnician
Hops
3
Blocking hop
FactLabor to DimTechnician
Slicer result
All 7 technicians stay

Hops 1 and 2 are fine. A station filter reaches FactWorkOrder and flows into FactLabor, which is why the card for MSP labor hours correctly reads 34.5. The measure works. The slicer needs one thing more. The filter has to keep going up the last relationship, from the many side of FactLabor into the one side of DimTechnician. A single direction relationship carries filters one way only, and that way is down.

Fix a: set the DimTechnician to FactLabor relationship to Both

You have met these two panels in Chapter 8. Look only at the arrowheads on the link between the dimension and the fact. The left panel is Single, the default. It has one arrowhead, pointing down into FactLabor. The note beside it says a selection on FactLabor does not reach DimTechnician, and that is your station filter arriving at FactLabor with nowhere further to go. The right panel is Both, also called bidirectional. It draws the same two boxes with a second arrowhead pointing back up. Its note states the effect plainly: a selection on FactLabor now narrows DimTechnician, which is what makes a slicer hide unused technicians. That second arrowhead is fix a in its entirety. Everything else in this section is about what else travels along it when you are not watching.

This works immediately and with no measure. Set the cross filter direction on DimTechnician[TechnicianID] to FactLabor[TechnicianID] to Both, select MSP, and the slicer drops to R. Okafor, M. Halvorsen and D. Sandoval: the three people with labor on an MSP work order.

Trace this by hand, row by row

MSP work orders are WO-1001, WO-1002, WO-1006 and WO-1008. The labor rows attached to them are L-501 and L-502 on WO-1001, L-503 on WO-1002, and L-507 on WO-1006. WO-1008 has no labor rows at all, so it contributes nothing.

That leaves TECH-02 with 7.5 plus 9.0 equals 16.5 hours, TECH-04 with 6.0 hours, and TECH-01 with 12.0 hours. The three add to 34.5, which is the MSP figure in the answer key, so the trace is consistent.

Note what TECH-04 does to the story. D. Sandoval's HomeStation is TUS, and he appears in an MSP-filtered slicer because he booked 6.0 hours there. Bidirectional propagation answers who worked here, not who is based here.

The cost is the one described in Chapter 8, plus one specific to this model. There is deliberately no relationship from DimStation[StationCode] to DimTechnician[HomeStation]. Such a relationship would hand a station filter two active routes into FactLabor, one through FactWorkOrder and one through DimTechnician. Faced with an ambiguous pair of active paths, the engine rejects the model instead of picking a route on your behalf. That refusal already stands today, with every relationship left single direction. Turning DimTechnician to FactLabor bidirectional makes the block permanent. A slicer somebody uses every day now depends on that edge, and nobody will trade it away later to get home station filtering back.

Both also lets everything through in that direction. Anything that filters FactLabor now filters the technician list, the date slicer included. Pick February and the list collapses to the two people with a February labor row: R. Okafor on 2025-02-19 and the Unknown technician on 2025-02-05. M. Halvorsen disappears from a list somebody was using to find a name.

Fix b: leave the model alone and filter the slicer with a measure

Select the technician slicer and add a visual level filter in the Filters pane on a measure, with the condition "is not blank". Leave Show items with no data off, so one mechanism decides membership. The measure is small.

DAXTechnician Has Labor
// Returns 1 when the current filter context leaves at
// least one row in FactLabor, and BLANK when it leaves none.
Technician Has Labor =
VAR LaborRows = COUNTROWS ( FactLabor )
RETURN
    IF ( LaborRows > 0, 1 )
Line 3
The measure declaration. Nothing is computed on this line, but it settles where the work happens. A measure placed in the Filters pane of a slicer is evaluated once per candidate member. That evaluation runs inside a filter context, which means the set of filters already in force from everything else on the page. With MSP selected, the filter context is station MSP plus one technician.
Line 4
COUNTROWS over FactLabor counts the rows surviving both filters. Station MSP arrives down hops 1 and 2, the technician arrives down the single relationship from DimTechnician, and the two intersect.
Line 6
IF written with two arguments returns BLANK when the test fails, and BLANK is exactly what the condition "is not blank" tests for. The member drops out of the list.
Why this and not that

COUNTROWS and not SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ). SUM returns 0 for a technician whose hours net to zero, and 0 passes an "is not blank" test. Meridian has no such row today. The first timesheet correction posting a plus and a minus creates one. Existence is the question here, so count rows. COUNTROWS and not DISTINCTCOUNT ( FactLabor[LaborID] ). Same answer in this model, but DISTINCTCOUNT hashes the column values while COUNTROWS reads a count the engine already keeps. And CROSSFILTER inside CALCULATE, the surgical version of fix a, does not help here. It changes propagation for one measure, and a member list is a column query, not a measure.

With MSP selected this returns the same three names as fix a. The difference is where the decision lives. Fix a lives in the model, and it applies to every report built on the dataset. Fix b lives on one visual, where a colleague can see it sitting in the Filters pane.

The catch is that "one visual" is literal. If the slicer appears on four pages, you set the filter four times. When someone copies a page and swaps the field, the filter travels with it in a state nobody checks.

Fix c: denormalise, which Meridian cannot do

The standard third answer is to flatten the problem. Put a Station column on DimTechnician so both slicers sit on one table, back in Case 1. Denormalise means exactly that: copy an attribute onto a table that did not carry it, so a lookup becomes a column. The data at Meridian blocks this one, and the tooling has nothing to do with it.

A denormalised Station column holds one value per technician. TECH-04 needs two. You could store HomeStation and call it Station. The MSP slicer would then return R. Okafor, M. Halvorsen and L. Petrov, at 12.0 plus 16.5 plus 0, which is 28.5. The card beside it reads 34.5. The 6.0 hour gap is TECH-04, who worked at MSP and is based at TUS.

Where two dimensions relate many to many through the facts, no flattening preserves the meaning. Either the fact table is the arbiter, or you accept a wrong answer that is easier to build.

What to do at Meridian

Use fix b. Keep DimTechnician to FactLabor single direction and put the measure filter on the technician slicer. That answers the planner. MSP now gives her R. Okafor, M. Halvorsen and D. Sandoval, and the setting she was hunting for turns out to be a measure.

The reason is about meaning, and performance has nothing to do with it. The correct technician list is ambiguous in the business as well as in the model. Planning wants technicians based at the station. Shop floor reporting wants technicians who booked hours there. The two lists differ by two names this quarter, L. Petrov in one and D. Sandoval in the other. A per visual filter lets you put both slicers on one page under different labels. Both hard-codes one answer where no reader can see it, and it forecloses the HomeStation relationship for good. Fix a is right when one answer is needed on many pages. Meridian needs two answers on one page.

Case 3: three things that look like the same setting

The shift supervisor asks for something that sounds simple. Hide the aircraft with no data. You do it, he opens the page, and N615RB has gone from the list. He knows that aircraft. It came in AOG, aircraft on ground, and went out two days later with 1,875 of parts on it. He did not mean that one.

People conflate three mechanisms, then argue about a slicer that is behaving correctly. Apply each to the aircraft registration slicer.

Show items with no data is a per field, per visual setting. It keeps members of that field even where the join produces nothing. On a slicer carrying one column and no measure it does nothing, because there is no join for rows to be dropped from. It earns its keep on a matrix crossing a dimension column with a measure.

A measure based visual level filter is the one that actually removes members. It evaluates a measure once per member and tests the result. It is a computation, and it costs what a computation costs.

A dimension member with no facts is a third thing entirely, and it is correct data. N120CE and N553KD are Sierra Charter aircraft in the fleet spreadsheet with no work orders at Meridian in Q1. Their absence from the report is a finding.

DAXTwo candidate filter measures
Work Order Count = COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder )

Labor Hours = SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )
Work Order Count
Tests whether the aircraft has any work order at all. Filtering the tail slicer on this keeps N615RB, which has WO-1005, and drops only N120CE and N553KD.
Labor Hours
Tests whether anyone booked time against the aircraft. This also drops N615RB, whose one work order was an AOG event closed in two days with 1,875 of parts and no timesheet rows.
SUM, not SUMX
SUM and not SUMX ( FactLabor, FactLabor[Hours] ), because there is no row by row expression to evaluate. SUMX would build an iterator to read one column that the engine can scan directly.

Read the N615RB row twice. Filtering on Labor Hours removes an aircraft with a genuine AOG event and 1,875 of parts issued, because no technician booked hours against it. That is the aircraft the shift supervisor came to ask about, and Work Order Count is the filter he actually wanted. The parts total reads 23,345 rather than 28,245 because the 4,900 on P-9007 belongs to WO-1009, which reaches no tail.

Common mistake

Building the technician slicer on FactLabor[TechnicianID] instead of on DimTechnician, because a fact column does narrow when you select a station. It looks solved. It is not. That slicer shows only the five technician codes present in labor rows, so J. Prieto and L. Petrov never appear even with nothing selected, and everyone else is listed as a raw code where a name was expected. A slicer belongs on a dimension unless the column is a degenerate key, which means a key that lives on the fact table and has no dimension of its own, like WorkOrderID.

Edit Interactions, per pair, every time

The shift supervisor is back. He clicks the station slicer at the top of the page, and the fleet table at the bottom sits there unchanged. He is right about what he is seeing. The relationship list will tell you nothing, because somebody set that pair of visuals to ignore each other.

Edit Interactions decides what one visual does to another when it acts as a filter source. Turn it on from the Format ribbon and every other visual gets a small control bar. Three states.

Filter
The target is filtered. Rows that do not match are gone, totals recalculate, and the target's own visual level filters apply on top.
Highlight
The target keeps its full data and shows the matching portion in solid colour against a dimmed remainder. It exists only on visuals that can draw a partial mark, so columns, bars, lines and maps offer it while cards and slicers do not.
None
The target ignores the source completely. The selection stays visible on the source, which is what confuses people: the slicer looks active and the visual does not move.

The default depends on the pair. A slicer defaults to Filter on everything on its page. A chart selection defaults to Highlight on another chart, because a chart can draw the matched portion against a dimmed remainder. On a card it falls back to Filter, because a card has one number and nothing to dim. Tables and matrices sit between the two cases and expose both buttons. Check the pair you care about.

None is right more often than people think. Put the station slicer and the capacity chart in the top half of a page. Put an operator slicer and a fleet table in the bottom half. The two halves have no reason to interfere. Setting each slicer to None against the other section is the honest build. Hoping users only click the slicer nearest what they meant is a wish, and a wish is not a design.

The trap is the word per. Interactions are stored per source visual per target visual. Three slicers and six visuals is eighteen pairs before chart to chart. Nothing shows you the grid at once, and a visual added later arrives with the defaults rather than your settings. That is how a page ends up with two slicers wired one way and the third not, and how the shift supervisor ends up with a table that ignores him.

Sync Slicers, and the two ways it goes wrong

The finance manager phones about page 3 of your report. Total labor hours reads 5.0, and he knows the quarter was 62.0. There is no slicer anywhere on that page for him to check. The explanation is two pages back, and this section is how it got there.

Sync Slicers makes one selection apply on more than one page. Open the Sync slicers pane and you get a row per page with two separate ticks: Sync and Visible. Sync means the selection applies there. Visible means the slicer is drawn there. They are independent, which is both the point of the feature and its second failure mode.

Membership is by group name. Slicers in one named group share a selection. Power BI derives the default group name from the field, so two slicers on DimStation[StationCode] land in one group when you tick Sync on both. Renaming the group links slicers Power BI would not have linked, deliberately or by accident.

Failure one: syncing slicers whose field is different on the two pages. Put DimStation[StationCode] on page 1 and DimTechnician[HomeStation] on page 2 under one group name. It appears to work: both columns hold the text MSP, TUS and LAS, and the selection passes across as a value. Page 2 then filters technicians whose home station is MSP: R. Okafor, M. Halvorsen and L. Petrov, at 12.0 plus 16.5 plus 0, or 28.5 hours. Page 1 reports 34.5. Select PHX and page 2 empties out entirely, because PHX has never been anybody's home station.

Failure two: forgetting that a hidden synced slicer still filters. Sync ticked and Visible unticked means the selection applies to a page showing no slicer. Leave LAS selected, walk to page 3, and total labor hours reads 5.0 instead of 62.0 with nothing on screen to explain it. That is the finance manager's page 3, and untick Sync for that page and his number comes back to 62.0. This is the usual cause of "the numbers are wrong on this page", and it survives export to PDF.

Performance note

Every slicer runs its own DAX query at page load, alongside the queries for your charts. Six slicers means six extra queries competing for the same capacity. A plain slicer scans distinct values on one column, cheap on a dimension of a few hundred members and expensive on a fact column of hundreds of thousands. A measure based visual filter changes the query shape: the engine groups by the column and evaluates the measure per group. At eight labor rows this is unmeasurable. On a real FactLabor of tens of millions it is one of the slowest things on the page, and it re-runs whenever another slicer changes.

Which slicer type, and what each one costs

The relative date row springs its trap only after handover, which is why it deserves a paragraph of its own. That slicer resolves against the system date, not the data. Point one at Meridian's Q1 2025 extract, open the report any month after June 2025, and every visual goes blank while the model and the measures are correct. Use relative date on data that keeps moving, an explicit range on a fixed extract.

The cascade you actually want: operator, then tail, then work order

Here is the pattern behind the original question, end to end. Three slicers, each narrowing the next, with the model exactly as the relationship list already has it.

Hop one is Case 1, two columns on one table. Hop two is the part people expect to be hard. DimAircraft[ACREG] to FactWorkOrder[ACREG] runs one to many, single direction, from the one side to the many side, which is the direction filters already flow. A slicer on FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID] is therefore narrowed by the tail slicer with nothing configured. Pick Cascade Air, then N771QR, and it holds WO-1001, WO-1004 and WO-1008. Pick N448LM and it holds WO-1002.

Make the work order slicer a dropdown, because in production it is the highest cardinality control on the page. Leave all three relationships single direction. To hide work orders with no labor, use the measure filter from fix b and leave the relationship alone.

The cost is that nothing forces the user down the cascade in order. Power BI has no required-selection state, so on page load the work order slicer sits at full cardinality and queries the whole column. Anyone clicking straight into it gets every work order in the model. That is the honest limit of the pattern, and why the dropdown is a correctness decision as much as a layout choice.

What to remember
  • Slicers cross-filter by the same propagation rules as every other visual. Trace the hops, find the one that runs many to one, and fix that.
  • Two fields on the same dimension always cascade for free. Operator to tail needs nothing.
  • Two dimensions either side of a fact need either a bidirectional relationship, which is global and permanent, or a measure based visual filter, which is local and repeated. At Meridian, choose the measure filter.
  • Denormalising is not always available. A technician works at more than one station, so no single Station column on DimTechnician can be correct.
  • Show items with no data, a measure filter, and a dimension member with no facts are three different things. Only the middle one removes members from a slicer.
  • Edit Interactions is stored per source visual per target visual, and a visual added later inherits defaults, not your settings.
  • Sync and Visible are separate. A synced hidden slicer still filters the page, and it is the usual explanation for numbers that look wrong with nothing on screen to blame.
Part 6 . Diagnosis and reference

18Diagnosis: my slicer is not filtering my visual

After this chapter you can pick up a report somebody else built, find the slicer that refuses to move a visual, and name the cause in under five minutes. Twelve checks in a fixed order get you there.

The shift supervisor at MSP walks over with his laptop open. He has clicked MSP on the station slicer, and the labor hours card still reads 62.0, the same number it read before he clicked. His whiteboard says 34.5. He wants to know why the report is lying to him, and he will decide it always was if you cannot tell him quickly.

Here is what actually happens when he clicks. A slicer contributes a filter to a query. The visual sends that query to the engine and prints whatever comes back. Between his click and the number there are four places that filter can be dropped: the report layer's interaction settings, the model's relationship paths, the measure's own code, and the three filter panes. Each layer is owned by a different part of the file. None of them announces itself when it swallows a filter.

Slicer
A visual whose only job is to send a filter. Click MSP on a station slicer and every other visual on the page is asked to answer for MSP.
Measure
A piece of DAX that produces one number for whatever filter arrives. Meridian's [Labor Hours] reads 62.0 with nothing selected and 34.5 with MSP selected.
Filter context
The set of filters in force when a measure is evaluated. The slicer, the row the visual is drawing, and every filter card in the panes all contribute to it.
Propagation
The way a filter travels along relationships from one table to another. A filter propagates from the one side of a relationship to the many side, and stops when the road runs the other way.

The ordering below runs cheapest and most likely first. Each check either eliminates a whole layer or points at one line of code. Do not start at check 5 because you enjoy reading DAX. You will read a perfectly correct measure for twenty minutes before discovering that someone set Edit interactions to None in 2023.

Checks in this chapter
12, in fixed order
First place to look
Model view, trace the route
Most common in inherited reports
Edit interactions set to None
Fastest shortcut
Performance Analyzer query

Read the numbered checks down the left, top to bottom. There are six of them in the figure, the short form of the twelve that follow. Each check has two exits. The yes arrow points right into the green card that names the fix, and the no arrow drops to the next check, so a yes ends the search and a no costs you one more question. The first three checks stay in the model, and one look at Model view answers all three: is there a relationship path at all, is every relationship on that path active, does every hop run from the one side to the many side. Check 4 leaves the model for the report layer. It asks whether Edit interactions has been set to None, which its card calls the most common cause in an inherited report and the one that leaves no trace in the model. Then come the two reading checks. Check 5 reads the measure for ALL, REMOVEFILTERS and ALLEXCEPT, and check 6 reads the key values for trailing spaces, case and data type. The grey card across the bottom is the escape hatch when all six pass: open Performance Analyzer, copy the DAX the visual actually sends, and read its filter arguments. The twelve checks below expand those six. They add the filter panes, the synced slicer and the case where nothing is broken at all.

The twelve checks, in order

1. Is there a route from the slicer's table to the visual's table?

Open Model view and trace from the table the slicer field lives on to the table the visual's measure sums. A slicer on Dimension DimTechnician against a parts cost visual is the case people hit first at Meridian. A route exists there: DimTechnician to FactLabor to FactWorkOrder to FactParts. The filter still dies on the middle hop, which runs from the many side to the one side. Total parts cost sits at 28,245 whichever technician you pick. There is a catch. In a finished star every table is reachable from every other by some route, so a genuine check 1 failure is nearly always a table someone loaded and never related, sitting as its own island on the canvas.

One line test

In Model view, click the slicer's table and see whether any unbroken chain of relationship lines reaches the visual's table.

2. Is every relationship on that route active?

An inactive relationship draws as a dashed line. It propagates nothing until a measure asks for it by name. Meridian has two by design: DimDate[Date] to FactWorkOrder[PromisedDate] and to FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate]. Only OpenedDate is active. So a date slicer set to January returns a work order count of 3, the ones opened in January. A reader expecting the 2 closed in January reports the slicer as broken. The slicer is answering a different question from the one in the reader's head. The fix is USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE in a second measure. A model holds only one active relationship per pair of tables, so activating the closed date one would deactivate the opened date one for every query in the file.

One line test

Look for a dashed line anywhere on the route. That hop is dead for every measure that does not name it.

3. Does every hop point the right way?

Walk the route hop by hop and confirm each one leaves the one side and arrives at the many side. The first hop pointing back at you is your answer, and you can stop walking. A slicer on DimPart against a labor hours visual shows it cleanly. DimPart to FactParts is one to many, fine. FactParts to FactWorkOrder is many to one, and single direction filtering does not travel that way, so labor hours sit at 62.0 for brakes, hydraulics, engine parts and avionics alike. A dimension filters its own fact. That is the one move single direction propagation makes. Asking a fact to filter a second fact through a shared header needs bidirectional filtering or a measure written for it, and check 9 covers both.

One line test

Put a finger on each arrowhead along the route and say "one to many" out loud at each hop. The first hop where you cannot is the cause.

4. Has Edit interactions been set to None between that slicer and that visual?

This is the most common cause in a report someone else built, which is why it comes before any DAX reading. Select the slicer and open the Format ribbon. Click Edit interactions, and every other visual on the page gains a small control showing filter, highlight or none. Someone turned it off years ago for a reason that has since expired. What makes it nasty is that it leaves no trace in the model. Relationships correct, measure correct, field on the right table, visual still showing the unfiltered grand total. No pane lists every interaction override in a report, so you check them one visual at a time or read the report definition as JSON.

One line test

Click the slicer, press Edit interactions on the Format ribbon, and read the icon that appears over the stubborn visual.

Interview-level insight

Interaction settings live in the report layer. The semantic model never sees them, which is why a model audit with Tabular Editor or VertiPaq Analyzer reports the file as clean. Two pages built on the identical model can behave differently with the identical slicer. When someone tells you the model is broken because a slicer does nothing, rebuild the pair on a fresh page. If it works there, the model was never involved.

5. Is the measure removing the filter itself?

Read the measure, then every measure it calls. You are hunting four shapes: ALL, REMOVEFILTERS, ALLEXCEPT, or a CALCULATE whose filter argument names the slicer's column. Any of them beats the slicer. A filter argument inside CALCULATE is applied after the external filter context and overwrites it on that column.

The wrong way
DAXLabor Hours All Stations
// Dropped straight into a card by mistake
[Labor Hours All Stations] =
CALCULATE(
    [Labor Hours],
    ALL( DimStation )
)
Line 3
CALCULATE, together with its table returning twin CALCULATETABLE, is how filter context gets changed at all. So this line is where the slicer gets overruled. Use CALCULATE here, because the result has to be a single value for a card, and CALCULATETABLE returns a table that a card cannot print.
Line 5
ALL(DimStation) clears every filter on the whole station dimension, so the card returns 62.0 for MSP, for TUS, for LAS and for a cleared slicer.
The fix
DAXLabor Hours Pct of All Stations
// The cleared context belongs in the denominator
[Labor Hours Pct of All Stations] =
DIVIDE(
    [Labor Hours],
    CALCULATE(
        [Labor Hours],
        REMOVEFILTERS( DimStation )
    )
)
Line 4
The numerator keeps the slicer, so MSP returns 34.5 and TUS returns 22.5.
Line 5 to 8
Only the denominator is cleared, giving 62.0, so MSP reads 55.6 percent from 34.5 divided by 62.0.
What you see in the report

The card reads 62.0 with MSP selected, 62.0 with TUS selected, and 62.0 with nothing selected, while every other visual on the page moves. That is the shift supervisor's card, and check 5 is where it gets its answer. One visual frozen at the grand total among neighbours that respond points straight at the measure, because a broken path would freeze every visual on that table. Point his card at the base measure [Labor Hours] and MSP reads 34.5, which is the number on his whiteboard.

Why this and not that

REMOVEFILTERS and ALL do the same job as a CALCULATE modifier. Use REMOVEFILTERS there, because its name states the intent, so the next reader does not have to work out whether you meant to clear filters or to return a table. ALL is still required where you need the table back, inside an iterator for example, because REMOVEFILTERS cannot be used as a table expression. ALLEXCEPT belongs only where you clear a table and keep named columns, and it is easy to misread at speed: it keeps what you list and clears everything else. Now DIVIDE, with a caveat about why. In this particular measure the denominator is a superset of the numerator, so it can only be blank when the numerator is blank too, and the slash operator would survive. The habit still earns its place. The moment someone narrows that denominator, by wrapping it in a work order filter for instance, a slash returns infinity and the visual prints an error, while DIVIDE returns blank and the row drops out quietly.

One line test

Read the measure and its dependencies, searching the text for ALL, REMOVEFILTERS, ALLEXCEPT and the slicer's column name.

6. Is the visual using a column from a different table than you think?

Two columns can carry the same name, the same values and different behaviour. Drag ACREG from Fact FactWorkOrder and the slicer offers 5 tails, because only 5 tails ever appear on a work order. Drag it from Built DimAircraft and it offers 7, because N120CE and N553KD never came in for work. The second case is worse. DimTechnician[HomeStation] reads like a station slicer on the chip and answers a technician question instead. Select MSP there and you filter to technicians 01, 02 and 06, giving 12.0 plus 16.5 plus 0, which is 28.5 hours. Select MSP on DimStation[StationCode] and you get 34.5, the hours worked at that station whoever performed them. Both numbers are correct answers to two different questions.

One line test

Hover each field in the visual's field well and read the table name in the tooltip. The column name printed on the chip is what fooled you in the first place.

7. Are the rows you expect sitting in the blank member?

When a fact holds a key the dimension does not, Power BI adds a blank row to the dimension and parks those fact rows against it. That added row is the blank member, and Chapter 19 is built around it. Meridian ships one deliberately. WO-1006 uses tail N338WA, missing from the stale AircraftRegistry spreadsheet. So before the aircraft dimension is built, the three real types total 50.0 hours and 12.0 hours live in a blank row nobody clicks. Select any aircraft type and WO-1006 never appears, which reads exactly like a broken slicer. What you are looking at is a referential integrity fault wearing a filtering fault's clothes.

One line test

Clear the slicer, group the visual by the dimension column, and look for a blank row at the bottom.

8. Do the key values actually match?

Trailing spaces, casing and data types break joins while looking perfect on screen. Meridian's L-505 carries the technician id "TECH-04 " with a trailing space. On screen it is indistinguishable from TECH-04. On the join it is a different value. TECH-04 shows 6.0 hours where it should show 10.5, and the missing 4.5 go to the blank row. The grand total stays 62.0, which is why this survives review. Nobody checks a total that ties.

MFactLabor key clean up
// Fix the key before the model loads
let
    Source = LaborEntries,
    Trimmed = Table.TransformColumns(
        Source,
        {{"TechnicianID", Text.Trim, type text}}
    )
in
    Trimmed
Line 4
Table.TransformColumns repairs the existing key in place, so every downstream relationship sees the fixed value. Add a second, cleaned column instead and the model holds two technician ids, and the relationship keeps using the broken one.
Line 6
Text.Trim removes leading and trailing whitespace only. DAX TRIM also collapses repeated spaces inside the text, which would quietly alter values like part descriptions. The narrower M function is the safer instrument for a key.
One line test

Add LEN of the key column to a table visual and look for the row one character longer than its neighbours. Use LEN here. An equality test tells you the two values differ without telling you why.

9. Is the relationship many to many, and are you expecting more than a weak relationship does?

Meridian's certification analysis runs DimCertification to Bridge BridgeTechCert to DimTechnician. A certification slicer filters the bridge and stops there, because the hop from bridge to technician dimension arrives at the one side. Nothing reaches FactLabor unless that bridge relationship filters both ways, or the measure uses CROSSFILTER. There is a second trap. A many to many cardinality relationship is a weak relationship. It gets no blank member, so unmatched values are simply dropped. That is the opposite of check 7: here the orphans go invisible, where check 7 left them merely awkward. When propagation does work, the certification rows total 85.0 hours against a true 62.0, because TECH-04 holds three certifications and his hours count under each.

One line test

Read the cardinality badge on the relationship. If it says many to many, expect no blank member and no propagation past the bridge without CROSSFILTER. Use CROSSFILTER rather than a permanent bidirectional setting, because it scopes the change to one measure instead of every future query in the file.

10. Is a visual, page or report level filter overriding the selection?

Filters combine with AND, so a page filter can make a slicer look inert by leaving it nothing to choose. Put a page filter of DimWOType[WOType] equals AOG on a Meridian page and labor hours drop to 14.0, which is WO-1002 at 9.0 plus WO-1005 at 0 plus WO-1007 at 5.0. Now the station slicer looks broken. MSP returns 9.0, LAS returns 5.0, and TUS returns blank, because both TUS work orders are Scheduled and Mod. The user reports that selecting TUS does nothing. Selecting TUS did everything it could. Check all three sections of the pane with the visual selected, because filter cards are often hidden from the consumer while remaining active.

One line test

Select the visual, expand the Filters pane fully, and read every card in all three sections including the hidden ones.

11. Is the slicer synced from another page?

Sync slicers separates two settings people assume are one: whether a slicer syncs its selection across pages, and whether it is visible on each of them. A slicer can be synced and invisible at once. A selection made three pages ago is then still applied here, with no control on screen to show it. The symptom is distinctive. The visible slicer reads All, the visual is plainly filtered, and clearing the visible slicer changes nothing.

One line test

Open View, then Sync slicers, and read the sync and visible checkboxes for the current page.

12. Is the measure a constant, or is the value legitimately identical?

Sometimes nothing is broken. Meridian plans MSP at 30 hours in January, 30 in February and 30 in March, totalling 90. A month slicer over a planned hours card for MSP looks dead, because the answer really is the same three times. The distinguishing move is to put the slicer's own field into the visual as a row. Three rows each showing 30 means the filter arrives and the data really is flat, so there is nothing to fix. Three rows each showing 176, the planned total for every station and every month, means the measure ignores context and you belong at check 5. One row where you expected three means something else has already narrowed the visual to a single month, which sends you back to check 10.

One line test

Drag the slicer's field into the visual as a category and see whether the rows split. A card using SELECTEDVALUE on that column does the same job in less space. Prefer it to HASONEVALUE paired with VALUES, because SELECTEDVALUE handles a multi selection with an explicit alternate result where the pair returns an error.

The shortcut: read the query the visual actually sent

The planner is standing behind you now. She set the January baseline three weeks ago, somebody has asked her why it moved, and she wants an answer before her one o'clock. You are at check 3 of twelve. Reading the tree is honest work and it is slow, so take the shortcut instead.

Two tools collapse most of the tree into a single fork. Performance Analyzer captures the DAX query each visual sends when it refreshes. Reading that query tells you whether the slicer's filter was ever put in the envelope. Working that out by inspection takes half an hour. Reading it off the query takes a minute.

  1. Open the View ribbon and turn on Performance Analyzer.
  2. Press Start recording, then Refresh visuals.
  3. Set the slicer to one value so a second set of rows is captured.
  4. Expand the row for the stubborn visual and choose Copy query.
  5. Paste it into DAX query view in Power BI Desktop, or into DAX Studio.
DAXQuery copied from Performance Analyzer
// Labor Hours by station, station slicer set to MSP
DEFINE
    VAR __DS0FilterTable =
        TREATAS(
            {"MSP"},
            'DimStation'[StationCode]
        )

    VAR __DS0Core =
        SUMMARIZECOLUMNS(
            'DimStation'[StationCode],
            __DS0FilterTable,
            "Labor_Hours", [Labor Hours]
        )

EVALUATE
    __DS0Core
The filter variables
Every applied slicer and filter card becomes one VAR named something like __DS0FilterTable. Count them and match them against what you think is applied. A missing one is your answer.
TREATAS
The generator uses TREATAS rather than a FILTER over the table, because it applies a list of literal values to one column without scanning anything. Slicer selections therefore appear as a readable list of the values you clicked.
SUMMARIZECOLUMNS
Group by columns first, filter tables next, then the measures as name and expression pairs. You did not choose this function, the engine did. It picks SUMMARIZECOLUMNS because that function accepts filter tables directly and drops empty combinations on its own, where SUMMARIZE needs a wrapper for both jobs.
What is absent
No KEEPFILTERS appears in this query, which is ordinary for one slicer feeding one group by column. Where you do meet it, wrapped around a filter argument, it means the filter intersects with what is already there. Leave it off and the filter replaces what is already there, and replacement is exactly how a measure overrules a slicer.

The fork is this. If the slicer's column appears in no filter variable, the visual never received the filter, and the cause is in the report layer: Edit interactions, a sync setting, or a bookmark that reset the selection. Checks 4 and 11 remain, plus the bookmark, and the other ten checks are eliminated in one read. A page or report level filter cannot be the culprit here, because a filter card that is applied always shows up as its own filter variable. If the column is present and the number still does not move, run the copied query again with that filter variable deleted. Identical numbers either way mean the measure ignores the column, and check 5 is where you are heading.

So the planner gets her answer. The recording takes one minute, the copied query carries __DS0FilterTable holding MSP, and the filter was sent. Ten checks fall away in one read. Check 5 then catches the ALL(DimStation) sitting in her card, and she walks into her one o'clock with a cause and a fix.

The honest limit of this tool: the query tells you a filter went missing and stops there. Interactions set to None, a slicer not synced to this page, and a bookmark that reset the selection all produce the same absence. You still check those three by hand. Three is a much better afternoon than twelve.

Trace the technician slicer against parts cost by hand

Select TECH-04 in a slicer on DimTechnician[TechnicianID]. The filter lands on the technician dimension and propagates to FactLabor, leaving L-502 and L-505 for 10.5 hours after the trim. That is where propagation stops.

To reach FactParts the filter would have to climb from FactLabor to FactWorkOrder, a many to one hop under a single direction relationship, so it does not travel. FactParts is never touched, and the parts card keeps showing 28,245, or 23,345 with the orphan WO-1009 excluded, for every selection.

Leave that relationship single direction. Two facts joined header to line with bidirectional filtering produce a second path from DimDate and an ambiguous model. If the business needs parts cost by technician, define it first. Parts issued to work orders a technician touched is defensible, and it belongs in a measure that applies the visible work order ids from FactLabor to FactParts.

The second tree: the filter arrives and the number is still wrong

The finance manager wants one number for January: what the shop spent on parts. He opens the summary page and the card says 28,245. He opens the page behind it and the matrix by station adds to 23,345. Both pages are yours, both slicers work perfectly, and one of those numbers is going into a board pack this afternoon.

A complaint like his needs a different tree. When the slicer clearly works and the value is still not the value, four causes cover most of it.

Double counting

Ask whether the parts sum to more than the whole. Meridian's certification rows are the clean case. A&P 39.0, Avionics 10.5, NDT 12.0 and Engine Run 23.5 sum to 85.0 against a real total of 62.0, because a technician with three certifications feeds three rows. That is what a bridge does, and the fix is a caption on the visual. The other case is a bug. If someone merged WorkOrders into LaborEntries in Power Query, summing QuotedAmount now runs at labor line grain. WO-1001 has 2 labor rows so its 3,000 counts twice, WO-1003 has 2 rows so its 12,500 counts twice, and the total becomes 6,000 plus 3,200 plus 25,000 plus 4,000 plus 7,500 plus 900, which is 46,600 against the true 38,100. WO-1005 and WO-1008 have no labor rows and vanish from that sum.

Blank rows and disappearing money

Ask whether the total drops when you slice. Meridian's parts cost is 28,245 in total and 23,345 once the orphan WO-1009 is excluded, a gap of 4,900. Group parts cost by aircraft type and the 4,900 vanishes without comment. The orphan sits against the blank work order, and the blank work order has no aircraft registration. The four visible type rows are 3,115 plus 2,450 plus 12,680 plus 5,100, which is 23,345. A total that shrinks the moment you add a grouping column is the signature. That is the finance manager's page exactly. His card counts every parts line and reads 28,245. His matrix counts every parts line that can be attributed to a station and reads 23,345. The 4,900 between them is one orphan work order, and Chapter 19 takes it apart line by line.

Wrong grain

Grain is what one row of a table means. Ask that question of both tables before you blame the measure. Fact FactCapacity sits at station and month grain and joins DimDate[MonthStart], so it answers at month level or coarser and returns blank for a day level filter on any date that is not the first of the month. Set a date slicer to 20 January and labor hours still read 8.0, the L-504 line on WO-1003, while planned hours go blank, which blanks utilisation too. Nothing is broken here. The two tables simply do not share a grain.

The totals row

Ask whether the total is the sum of the rows. It is always a separate evaluation. Meridian's utilisation reads 75.0 percent for MSP in January, 50.0 for TUS in January, 40.0 for MSP in February, 40.0 for TUS in February, 25.0 for LAS in March and 0 for the two remaining station months, which add to 230 percent. The total row shows 35.2 percent, because it computes 62.0 divided by 176 once at its own filter context. On time performance behaves the same way: 50.0 percent of closed work orders, with WO-1004 and WO-1008 excluded for having no closed date, so the denominator is 6 and not 8. When a total must behave differently from the rows, detect it with ISINSCOPE rather than ISFILTERED. ISINSCOPE tests whether a column is grouping in that cell, while ISFILTERED also returns true for a slicer selection and misfires on every row.

Rule of thumb

Prove where the filter died before you change anything. One test that separates the report layer from the model layer, either the Edit interactions check or the Performance Analyzer query, beats five speculative edits. Speculative edits are how a working model acquires a bidirectional relationship it never needed. If you are about to switch a relationship to filter both ways during a diagnosis, stop and finish the tree.

What to remember
  • Four places can eat a filter: interactions, relationships, the measure and the filter panes. Diagnose in that order, cheapest first.
  • Edit interactions set to None is the most common cause in an inherited report and leaves no trace in the model, so no model audit tool will find it.
  • Trace hop by hop and stop at the first hop that runs from the many side to the one side. That hop is the answer, and no measure rewrite will fix it.
  • The Performance Analyzer query answers one question fast: was the filter sent at all. If the slicer's column is absent from every filter variable, the model and the measure are innocent.
  • A slicer that appears dead is sometimes correct. MSP is planned at 30 hours in all three months, so the month slicer changes nothing and should not.
  • When the filter arrives and the number is still wrong, ask four questions. Do the parts exceed the whole, does the total shrink when you group, do the two tables share a grain, and is the total a separate evaluation.
Part 6 . Diagnosis and reference

19Data quality: orphans, blanks and unknown members

After this chapter you can look at a blank row in a visual and name which of nine defects produced it. You can prove which fact rows are responsible. Then you choose between three fixes: recover the key, map it to an explicit unknown member, or send it back to the source system.

The finance manager wants one number for the quarter: what the shop spent on parts. Your summary card says 28,245. The matrix by station on the page behind it adds to 23,345. He asks which one goes in the pack, and the uncomfortable answer is that both of them are right.

Every relationship you create in a Power BI model is an assertion about your data: that every value on the many side exists on the one side. Nothing verifies that assertion for you. The engine accepts the relationship, loads the data, and quietly invents a place to put whatever does not fit. The gap between his two numbers is one of those invented places.

Fact table
A table of events, one row per thing that happened. Meridian has four: Fact FactWorkOrder, FactLabor, FactParts and FactCapacity.
Dimension
A table of the things you group and filter by, one row per thing. Dimension DimAircraft holds one row per aircraft registration.
Foreign key
The column on the fact that names a row in the dimension. FactWorkOrder[ACREG] is the foreign key to DimAircraft[ACREG].
Orphan
A fact row whose foreign key has no matching row in the dimension. WO-1006 is an orphan of DimAircraft.
Blank member
The row Power BI adds to a dimension to hold the orphans. Its key is blank, it has no attributes, and it prints as an empty cell.

What the engine does when a key does not match

Build the relationship DimAircraft[ACREG] to FactWorkOrder[ACREG] and the engine scans the many side for values that have no partner on the one side. Meridian has one: N338WA on WO-1006, which the customer service desk never added to the fleet spreadsheet. The engine accepts all of it. It adds a single blank row to the one side of that relationship and attributes every unmatched fact row to that blank row. The refresh goes green. No warning appears anywhere a report author would see one.

That blank row is virtual. The engine keeps it outside the stored table, so COUNTROWS(DimAircraft) still returns 6. It carries no attribute values, so it renders as an empty cell wherever a visual groups by an aircraft attribute. And there is exactly one of it per relationship. That last part is the one that hurts. A hundred distinct broken aircraft registrations would collapse into the same single empty row, indistinguishable from each other and from a genuinely blank key.

Look at which side of the picture gains a row. On the left, DimAircraft holds the six aircraft registrations the stale registry actually delivered. The seventh box underneath them, drawn with a dashed red outline and labelled (blank), is annotated added by Power BI, not by you, because that is exactly what it is. Follow the dashed red curve back to its other end and it starts on N338WA, the single work order row tinted red on the right, whose 12.0 hours have nowhere else to land. The blank member appears on the one side, the dimension. The bad key itself lives on the fact, one hop away. That is why the defect surfaces as a category with no name instead of a fact row you can click into. Nothing is lost arithmetically. Across this one relationship the rows still sum to the grand total, blank member included, because the unmatched fact row is attributed to the blank member and kept. What the engine loses is the ability to describe it, which is the point the grey card at the foot of the figure makes when it calls the blank row a silent bucket.

Defect 1. The orphan foreign key

The planner wants labor hours by aircraft type for the quarter review. You build the matrix in about a minute. It comes back with four rows, and the fourth row has no name on it at all. That row holds 12.0 hours, and she wants to know whose airframe they went on.

WO-1006 is a scheduled visit on tail N338WA, 12.0 labor hours from TECH-01 and one ENG-8802 engine part at 5,100. The tail is real. The registry is stale. Put aircraft type on the rows of a matrix and the visit moves into a row with no label, and it stays inside the total.

Two defects, two relationships, and only one of them is given a row to sit in. The 12.0 hours and the 5,100 failed the DimAircraft join, so they land on the blank member, which is at least a row a reader can point at. The 4,900 failed a different join, header to line, and it is the next section. That parts line has no work order. With no work order it has no aircraft registration, so it has no aircraft type, and the matrix has nowhere to put it. It appears in the total and in none of the rows. When a visual's total is larger than the sum of the rows printed above it, this is the first thing to test. The difference, here 4,900, is usually the whole of your evidence.

Detection, method one: a left anti join in Power Query

MOrphan aircraft registrations
let
    Source = WorkOrders,
    Unmatched = Table.NestedJoin(
        Source, {"ACREG"},
        AircraftRegistry, {"ACREG"},
        "RegistryHit", JoinKind.LeftAnti
    ),
    Cleaned = Table.RemoveColumns(Unmatched, {"RegistryHit"})
in
    Cleaned
Line 3
Table.NestedJoin with JoinKind.LeftAnti rather than a normal left outer merge followed by a filter on nulls. The anti join returns only the left rows with no partner, so the answer is the row count, and it never materialises the matched side. The outer-merge-then-filter version builds the full joined table first and then throws most of it away.
Line 8
The anti join still adds the nested column, always empty, so drop it. Leaving it in the query costs nothing at refresh but confuses the next person who opens it.
Result
One row, WO-1006. Point a card at the row count of this query and you have a permanent check. Zero is healthy.

Detection, method two: a measure in the model

DAXOrphan Aircraft Rows
Orphan Aircraft Rows =
COUNTROWS (
    FILTER (
        FactWorkOrder,
        ISBLANK ( RELATED ( DimAircraft[ACREG] ) )
    )
)
COUNTROWS
COUNTROWS counts rows of a table, blank keys included. COUNT on a column skips blanks, and blank keys are precisely what you are trying to count, so it would report zero on the worst data you own.
FILTER
FILTER supplies a row context, and this test needs one, because RELATED only means something while the engine is standing on a specific fact row. A boolean predicate inside CALCULATE is evaluated with no row context, so it cannot do this job at all.
RELATED
RELATED walks the relationship that already exists, which is the cheapest route to the dimension. LOOKUPVALUE ignores relationships and performs its own match per row: the same answer at higher cost, and different behaviour if the key is ever duplicated.
ISBLANK
ISBLANK tests for blank and stops there. Write = BLANK() and DAX treats an empty string as equal to blank, so the test would also flag a key that exists but is empty. Those are two different defects with two different owners, and you want them counted separately.
Result
1 on the raw Meridian model. The fact row lands on the virtual blank member, RELATED finds no attribute to return, and the row is counted.

There is a shorter trick. Run it on the raw model, where the aircraft dimension is still the registry as it arrived, 6 rows. COUNTROWS(VALUES(DimAircraft[ACREG])) returns 7 while COUNTROWS(DISTINCT(DimAircraft[ACREG])) returns 6, because VALUES includes the virtual blank row of an invalid relationship and DISTINCT leaves it out. The difference is 1 whenever any orphan exists. The limitation is that it is always 1, however many orphans there are, so it tells you the model is broken without telling you how badly.

The fix

Build DimAircraft from the union of the registry and the distinct aircraft registrations actually used on work orders, exactly as in Chapter 3. That takes the dimension to 7 rows and gives N338WA a home. The 12.0 hours and the 5,100 move out of the blank row into a labelled row that says the type is unknown. The number keeps its value. What changes is its address.

So the planner gets her fourth row back with a name on it. It reads Unknown type, it still holds 12.0 hours, and she can walk to customer service and ask which airframe N338WA is. Somebody can answer that question in a minute. Nobody can answer a blank row.

Rule of thumb

A blank row in a visual is the model reporting a failed assertion in the only vocabulary it has. Read it the way you would read a null in a foreign key column in a database. It is an incident with an owner, and somebody has to go and chase it.

Defect 2. The orphan header key

P-9007 issues two HYD-4471 units at 2,450 each against WO-1009. There is no WO-1009 in WorkOrders. The stores clerk typed a work order number that the shop floor system never created, or created and voided. The parts left the store either way, and the cost is real.

This orphan behaves differently from the first one, because the broken relationship is fact to fact, header to line. Fact FactWorkOrder is the one side. It gains the blank row. So the 4,900 has no work order. With no work order it has no station, no aircraft, no work order type and no opened date. It falls out of every breakdown you can build.

MSP at 8,790 is arithmetic on the source lines: 1,240 plus 2,450 plus 5,100. The rest of the column comes straight from the answer key. Read this table for the shape of the failure. Which station carries which number matters far less than the two rows at the bottom.

What you see in the report

Two visuals on the same page, fed by the same measure, disagreeing by 4,900. The card says 28,245. The matrix by station adds to 23,345. Both are correct, and neither is a bug. The matrix shows every parts line that can be attributed to a station. The card shows every parts line. The gap between those two statements is a data quality defect that neither visual has any way to declare. A finance reviewer will assume the matrix is broken and stop trusting the page.

That answers the finance manager, and he will not enjoy it. Both of his numbers are correct, so neither one can be fixed. What he actually needs is the third number, 4,900, and the sentence that goes with it: two hydraulic units left the store against a work order that no system in the shop can find.

Trace the 4,900 gap by hand, line by line

Seven lines in FactParts. Six carry a WorkOrderID that exists in FactWorkOrder, so each inherits a station through its header.

  • P-9001, WO-1001, 4 times 310 equals 1,240, station MSP.
  • P-9002, WO-1002, 1 times 2,450 equals 2,450, station MSP.
  • P-9003, WO-1003, 2 times 5,100 equals 10,200, station TUS.
  • P-9004, WO-1003, 8 times 310 equals 2,480, station TUS.
  • P-9005, WO-1005, 1 times 1,875 equals 1,875, station blank, mapped to UNASSIGNED.
  • P-9006, WO-1006, 1 times 5,100 equals 5,100, station MSP.
  • P-9007, WO-1009, 2 times 2,450 equals 4,900, no header, so no station at all.

Six attributable lines sum to 23,345. Add P-9007 and you get 28,245. Both visuals compute the same measure over different row sets, and the only thing deciding which row set you get is whether the visual groups by an attribute on the far side of a broken join.

Detection is the same anti join as before, with PartsIssued on the left and WorkOrders on the right, keyed on WorkOrderID. The fix has three options. Two of them tell the reader the truth, and the middle one buys a tidy report by hiding the problem. You can chase WO-1009 in the shop floor system and find out whether it was voided, mistyped, or belongs to a different period. You can create an inferred header row for WO-1009 with a quoted amount of zero and an unknown station, which makes the matrix add up. Or you can leave it visible and labelled. Meridian ships with this one deliberately unfixed so the unknown member lesson has something to catch.

The inferred header carries a price. Total quoted amount is 38,100 and total actual cost is 29,671.50, which is 6,326.50 of labor plus the 23,345 of attributable parts. Add an inferred WO-1009 with quoted zero and total actual cost becomes 6,326.50 plus 28,245, which is 34,571.50, while quoted stays at 38,100. Your quote to actual variance moves by 4,900, because you invented a work order that was quoted at nothing. Fixing the join broke the margin report. That is the trade, and you should make it consciously.

Defect 3. The blank foreign key

WO-1005 has no StationCode. The field is empty. It is an AOG job that someone opened before deciding where the aircraft would be recovered to, and nobody went back to fill the field in.

A blank on the many side behaves exactly like an unmatched key. It is attributed to the blank member on the one side. In a labor hours by station visual the effect is invisible, because WO-1005 has no labor rows. In a parts cost by station visual its 1,875 sits in an empty row beside MSP and TUS, and readers take that row for a station whose name did not print.

Detection: count the blanks before you map them

MBlank station codes
let
    Source = WorkOrders,
    Blanks = Table.SelectRows(
        Source,
        each [StationCode] = null
             or Text.Trim([StationCode]) = ""
    ),
    Count = Table.RowCount(Blanks)
in
    Count
Line 3
Table.SelectRows counts the rows yourself, over the whole table, which is the answer. The Empty percentage on the column quality bar is the faster look, and it samples the first 1,000 rows unless you switch it to the whole data set, so a single bad row in a large table rounds to zero percent and the bar tells you the column is fine. Treat the bar as a prompt and this query as the answer.
Lines 5 and 6
Both tests, for the same reason the mapping step below uses both. A CSV export delivers null and an Excel export delivers an empty string, and a column that arrived from two sources over two quarters holds both. Text.Trim catches the third form, a cell holding nothing but spaces, which passes a null test and an empty string test and still joins to nothing.
Result
1 on the Meridian work orders, WO-1005. Point a card at it and zero is the healthy reading. The DAX equivalent is Blank Station Keys, later in this chapter, which reads 1 on the raw work orders and 0 once the mapping runs, because the key is then the string UNASSIGNED.
Scope
Run the same three lines over FactLabor[TechnicianID], FactParts[WorkOrderID] and every other relationship column before you build the model. Running them after a reader queries a number is running them late. Blank keys are the one defect class you can enumerate completely in advance, because the test does not depend on the other side of the join.

The fix

MMap blank station to an explicit member
let
    Source = WorkOrders,
    Mapped = Table.TransformColumns(
        Source,
        {{"StationCode", each
            if _ = null or Text.Trim(_) = ""
            then "UNASSIGNED"
            else Text.Upper(Text.Trim(_)), type text}}
    )
in
    Mapped
Line 3
Table.TransformColumns takes a function, so one step catches null, empty string and whitespace-only in a single pass. Replace Values from the ribbon generates a step that matches one literal, which means three steps and three chances to forget one.
Line 6
Both tests, because a blank cell in a CSV export arrives as null and a blank cell in an Excel export often arrives as an empty string. The two look the same in the preview pane and behave differently in a join.
Line 8
The normalisation is applied to the good values as well as the bad ones. Cleaning only the failures leaves you with a column that is half normalised, which is how you get a defect that appears one month and not the next.
Pairing
Add a matching UNASSIGNED | Unassigned | n/a row to Built DimStation, taking it to 5 rows. A mapped fact key with no dimension member is still an orphan.

An explicit UNASSIGNED member beats a blank for one reason. A blank is indistinguishable from a join failure, so as long as the row is blank you cannot tell whether the station is genuinely unknown or whether your model is broken.

Defect 4. Two keys that print the same and join differently

L-505 records 4.5 hours from "TECH-04 ". The trailing space is invisible in the query editor preview, in a table visual, in a tooltip and in the filter pane. Drop TechnicianID into a table visual and you get two rows that both read TECH-04. They are two different values. One joins to D. Sandoval, the other joins to nothing.

MMake the invisible visible
let
    Source = LaborEntries,
    Lengths = Table.AddColumn(Source, "KeyLength",
        each Text.Length([TechnicianID]), Int64.Type),
    Codes = Table.AddColumn(Lengths, "CharCodes",
        each Text.Combine(
            List.Transform(
                Text.ToList([TechnicianID]),
                each Text.From(Character.ToNumber(_))
            ), "."), type text)
in
    Codes
KeyLength
Use Text.Length for the test. A trim-and-compare test tells you the value changed, and it stays silent on any character that trim leaves in place, and those are the ones that cost you a week.
CharCodes
The definitive test. Character 32 is an ordinary space. Character 160 is a non breaking space, which is what you get when a key is copied out of a web page or lifted from a PDF, and Text.Trim will not always remove it, because its remit is the standard whitespace set. If you see 160 in this column, replace it explicitly.
In DAX
The same test is a calculated column, LEN(FactLabor[TechnicianID]). Use LEN for detection. DAX TRIM removes character 32 only, so a trim-based test would silently hide the case you most need to see. Delete the column once you have the answer.
MNormalise the key, both sides
let
    Source = LaborEntries,
    Normalised = Table.TransformColumns(
        Source,
        {{"TechnicianID", each
            Text.Upper(
                Text.Trim(
                    Text.Replace(_, Character.FromNumber(160), " ")
                )
            ), type text}}
    )
in
    Normalised
Order
Replace the non breaking space first, then trim, then case. Trimming first leaves a character 160 sitting at the end of the string where trim cannot see it.
Text.Upper
Applied on both the fact and the dimension, always as a pair. Normalising one side and leaving the other converts a matching key into a non matching one.
Effect
L-505 joins, TECH-04 goes from 6.0 hours to 10.5, and the 4.5 hours leave the blank row. Total labor hours stays at 62.0 throughout, which is why nobody noticed.

Defect 5. Case variation, which the two engines disagree about

No row in the Meridian extract carries a case problem today. This one arrives the afternoon somebody tidies a key by hand, or the day a second source starts feeding the same column, and the two tools you use to build the model take opposite views of what happened.

Power Query is case sensitive. TECH-04 and tech-04 are two values to a merge, to Remove Duplicates, and to Table.Group. The DAX engine, as it is used to resolve relationships and to group in a visual, is case insensitive under the default collation. It treats those two strings as one key.

The two behaviours point in opposite directions, and both directions bite.

  • A key that fails a Power Query merge can still match in the model. You spend an afternoon fixing a merge that produced nulls, load the result, and the relationship works fine, which makes you doubt your own diagnosis.
  • A dimension that Power Query considers clean can be rejected by the model. Run Remove Duplicates on a DimTechnician containing both TECH-04 and tech-04 and Power Query keeps both, because to it they are distinct. Then the model refuses to build the relationship, because to it they are one duplicated key.

The fix is to make the difference stop mattering. Normalise case explicitly in Power Query, on both the fact and the dimension, so that neither behaviour is load bearing.

Common mistake

Changing a text key to a numeric type because the profile pane says it is all digits. A technician id of 04 becomes 4, a part sequence of 0812 becomes 812, and the join to a dimension that kept the text form fails on every row with a leading zero. Meridian happens to escape this because every key carries a letter prefix, which forces text detection. That is luck. Nobody designed it. The moment someone strips the TECH- prefix to make a chart look tidier, the defect arrives, and Power Query's automatic Changed Type step will do it without asking.

Defect 6. Duplicate keys on the one side

The refresh failed overnight and the Monday manpower report is empty. The production controller has asked about it twice already. This is the friendliest defect in the chapter, because the refresh history hands you a table name, a column name and the offending value.

This one stops you dead before a blank row is ever drawn. Build DimAircraft by appending AircraftRegistry to the distinct aircraft registrations from WorkOrders, forget the deduplication step, and you have 11 rows for 7 aircraft, because the four tails present in both sources appear twice.

At design time, the relationship dialog refuses with a message along the lines of "You can't create a relationship between these two columns because one of the columns must have unique values". At refresh time, a relationship that was valid and has since gone bad fails the whole refresh with a message naming the offending value: "Column 'ACREG' in Table 'DimAircraft' contains a duplicate value 'N771QR' and this is not allowed for columns on the one side of a many-to-one relationship". The exact wording drifts between versions. The second form is more useful because it names the value, and it is the one you will meet in production at seven in the morning.

MFind the offending keys
let
    Source = DimAircraft,
    Counted = Table.Group(
        Source, {"ACREG"},
        {{"Rows", each Table.RowCount(_), Int64.Type}}
    ),
    Offenders = Table.SelectRows(Counted, each [Rows] > 1)
in
    Offenders
Table.Group
Rather than Remove Duplicates. Remove Duplicates makes the problem go away without telling you which key was duplicated or how many times, and on a real dimension the duplicate is usually the symptom of something upstream that you want to know about.
Line 7
An empty result is the healthy state. Keep this query in the file, disable its load, and check it whenever a refresh fails on a relationship.
Caution
Because this runs in Power Query it is case sensitive, so it will report a clean dimension that the model still rejects. Normalise case before you group, or you are testing a different question from the one the engine asks.

So the production controller gets a straight answer inside five minutes. Four aircraft registrations appear twice in the appended dimension, the deduplication step went missing when somebody reordered the query, and the refresh will run as soon as it goes back in. He can tell the shift that the manpower report will be there by eight.

Unknown members, done properly

Defects 1, 2 and 3 all end at the same fix, so this section builds that fix properly once and the numbered list picks up again afterwards.

An unknown member is a real row in the dimension, with a key you control and descriptive text that states what it means. It exists so that unmatched facts land somewhere labelled instead of nowhere. There are two ways to build one, and swapping one for the other changes what you can find out afterwards.

Mapped unknown
The dimension gets a hard coded row with a fixed key, UNASSIGNED or -1. Power Query rewrites the fact key to that value wherever it is blank or unmatched. The original value, if any, is discarded.
Recovered key, sometimes called an inferred member
The dimension gets one row per unmatched key, carrying the actual key value with unknown attributes filled in. The fact is untouched. Every distinct broken key stays distinguishable.

Variant one: the mapped unknown

Two halves, and both are compulsory. The dimension gets a row you wrote by hand, with a key you chose and text that states what the row means. The fact gets a step that redirects any key that is blank or absent from the dimension onto that chosen key. Ship only the first half and nothing lands on your new row. Ship only the second half and you have converted an orphan into a different orphan.

MUnknown member, dimension side and fact side
// Query 1. DimStation gains the row.
let
    Known = StationsAppended,
    Unknown = #table(
        type table [
            StationCode = text,
            StationName = text,
            StationRole = text
        ],
        {{"UNASSIGNED", "Unassigned",
          "No station recorded on the work order"}}
    ),
    Combined = Table.Combine({Known, Unknown})
in
    Combined

// Query 2. FactWorkOrder is redirected onto it.
let
    Source = WorkOrders,
    Valid = List.Buffer(StationsAppended[StationCode]),
    Mapped = Table.AddColumn(Source, "StationKey",
        each if [StationCode] = null
                or not List.Contains(Valid, [StationCode])
             then "UNASSIGNED"
             else [StationCode], type text),
    Dropped = Table.RemoveColumns(Mapped, {"StationCode"}),
    Renamed = Table.RenameColumns(Dropped,
        {{"StationKey", "StationCode"}})
in
    Renamed
#table
Rather than Enter Data from the ribbon. Enter Data writes the row into the query as a compressed base64 string, which nobody can read, review or diff, and which pins the column types at whatever they were the day you typed it. A #table literal is plain text in the query, so the next person can see the member exists and change its wording without re-entering the data.
The key you choose
A word for text keys, -1 for numeric surrogate keys, because real surrogates are positive. Avoid 0 and avoid an empty string. Both occur naturally in source systems, and the day one arrives for real you will have two meanings sharing one key with no way to separate them.
List.Buffer
Buffer the list of valid codes once, before the each starts running. Reference StationsAppended[StationCode] inside the each and the column is re-evaluated per fact row, so the cost becomes rows times members. On eight work orders that is invisible. On two million rows it is the difference between a refresh and a cancelled refresh.
Both tests
List.Contains catches the unmatched key and the null test catches the missing one, because they are different defects that happen to deserve the same destination here. If you want them separated later, send them to two members.
New column, then drop, then rename
The redirect writes StationKey, the next step removes the original StationCode, and the last step renames StationKey back to StationCode. While you are developing you can see both side by side. The rename matters because the relationship to DimStation and the Blank Station Keys measure later in this chapter both name that column, and a column rename inside Power Query breaks every one of them silently. For Meridian nothing is lost by dropping the original, because the value being replaced is blank.
Result
Built DimStation goes from 4 rows to 5. WO-1005 groups under Unassigned. Labor hours by station stays where it was, because WO-1005 has no labor rows, and parts cost by station moves 1,875 out of the blank row and into a labelled one.

Variant two: the recovered key

MDimAircraft with the recovered key
let
    Registry = AircraftRegistry,
    Tails = Table.Distinct(
        Table.SelectColumns(WorkOrders, {"ACREG"})),
    Missing = Table.NestedJoin(
        Tails, {"ACREG"}, Registry, {"ACREG"},
        "Hit", JoinKind.LeftAnti),
    Keys = Table.SelectColumns(Missing, {"ACREG"}),
    A = Table.AddColumn(Keys, "AircraftType",
        each "Unknown type", type text),
    B = Table.AddColumn(A, "Operator",
        each "Unknown operator", type text),
    C = Table.AddColumn(B, "EngineType",
        each "Unknown engine", type text),
    D = Table.AddColumn(C, "YearBuilt",
        each null, Int64.Type),
    Combined = Table.Combine({Registry, D})
in
    Combined
Lines 5 to 7
The anti join does all the work here. It produces exactly the keys the registry is missing, which for Meridian is N338WA and nothing else. Next quarter it might be three tails, and the query needs no change.
Lines 9 to 16
Literal text in the descriptive columns. A null here would put the row straight back into a blank cell in every visual and you would have gained nothing.
YearBuilt
Left null on purpose, because it is numeric and the text "Unknown" cannot go in a numeric column without changing the type and breaking any measure that averages it. Not every attribute can carry an unknown label, and pretending otherwise is how you get a fleet whose average age is wrong.
Result
7 rows. The relationship becomes valid, the virtual blank member disappears, and WO-1006 groups under "Unknown type" where a human can see it and act.

Which variant to use is decided by one question: is the key itself information? For Meridian's aircraft it is. N338WA is a real aircraft registration, it identifies a specific airframe, and someone in customer service can look it up and tell you who operates it. Recover it. Mapping it to a generic unknown would throw away the one piece of evidence that lets somebody resolve the defect.

For Meridian's station on WO-1005 the answer is the opposite. There is no value to recover. The field was never filled in, so there is nothing to look up, and every future blank belongs in the same bucket as this one. Map it to UNASSIGNED. The general rule: recover when a broken key is a real identifier you failed to resolve, map when the key is genuinely absent.

Defect 7. Type mismatches on the relationship columns

Two columns can hold what looks like the same value and still refuse to join, because the model compares stored values and not printed ones.

  • Text against number. A MonthKey of 202501 stored as whole number in DimDate and as text in FactCapacity. Power BI will refuse to create the relationship at all. This is the benign case, because it fails loudly at design time.
  • Date against date and time. This is the one that hurts. If the timesheet export delivers WorkDate with a time component and DimDate[Date] holds midnight values, the relationship is accepted, because both columns are date based. Then every labor row whose time is not exactly midnight matches nothing. Total labor hours still reads 62.0. Labor hours by month reads zero. Totals agreeing while breakdowns collapse is the signature of this defect.
  • Locale on the type conversion. Meridian's dates arrive ISO formatted, so 2025-01-06 is unambiguous. Change the export to 06/01/2025 and the Changed Type step will read it as 6 January or 1 June depending on the locale of the machine that authored the step, which is not necessarily the locale of the service that refreshes it. Set the locale explicitly in Table.TransformColumnTypes. The default is whatever the authoring machine happened to be set to.

The habit that prevents all three: set the type on every key column deliberately, in a named step near the end of the query, and never rely on the automatic Changed Type that Power Query adds when you first connect. That step is generated from a sample of the first rows and it will change its mind when the data changes.

Defect 8. Attributes that change under you

DimAircraft says N615RB is operated by Northwind Regional. Suppose it transfers to Cascade Air in April. The customer service desk updates the fleet spreadsheet, you refresh, and Q1 rewrites itself. Parts cost for Northwind Regional falls from 14,555, which is 12,680 on N902TT plus 1,875 on N615RB, to 12,680. Cascade Air rises from 3,690, which is 1,240 plus 2,450, to 5,565.
