Nobody touched a fact row. A number you reported in April is a different number in May.

That is a type 1 slowly changing dimension. The attribute is overwritten and history is restated. It is the default behaviour of every dimension you build by reloading the source, and it is sometimes correct, when you want current attributes applied to all history. A type 2 dimension adds a new row per version, with a surrogate key and validity dates, and the fact stores the surrogate that was current when the work order opened.

The cost is real. Type 2 means ACREG can no longer be the relationship key, because it is no longer unique. Every fact load has to resolve the correct version by date before it lands, which Power Query does badly and slowly. For a shop this size the honest answer is usually to stay on type 1 and document that operator describes the aircraft today, and that Q1 restates whenever an aircraft changes hands.

Defect 9. The key your own mapping table has not heard of

The production controller wants to know which crews delivered the quarter. You build him a bar chart of labor hours by service line, routed through the technician who booked each hour. Four bars carry a name. The fifth bar carries 10.0 hours and no name at all. He points at it and asks what that one is, and you do not have an answer for him yet.

Three terms before the mechanism, because this defect lives in the space between them. A service line is one of the four ways Meridian groups its work: Heavy, Light, Line, and Cabin and IFE. A crew code is the roster system's identifier for a crew, such as CRW-AF1 for Airframe Heavy. Built CrewCodeMap is the six row table that turns a crew code into a service line, and no system in the shop produces it. You typed it.

Labor hours reach a service line in three hops. FactLabor carries a technician id. CrewAssignment says which crew that technician belongs to. CrewCodeMap says which service line that crew works for. Two of those hops run on tables a real system maintains and refreshes. The third runs on yours.

TECH-07 booked 10.0 hours to WO-1004 in February. The roster system has TECH-07 on crew CRW-XX9, and the roster system is right. CRW-XX9 is a live crew code that the resource scheduler opened and never thought to mention to you. CrewCodeMap holds CRW-AF1, CRW-AV1, CRW-CAB, CRW-LN1, CRW-LT1 and CRW-LT2. The seventh code is missing from it, the lookup returns nothing, and 10.0 of the quarter's 62.0 hours land in a service line with no name.

Read the last two rows together, because they fail in opposite directions. Light shows 0.0 hours under a name, and that is a true statement about the shop. L. Petrov is on crew CRW-LT1, the crew is mapped, and he booked nothing in Q1. The blank row shows 10.0 hours under no name, and that is a statement about your model. Nothing on the chart separates the two, and the controller has no way to tell a quiet crew from a hole in your mapping.

Why this class is worse than an ordinary orphan

N338WA in defect 1 is somebody else's problem as well as yours. The customer service desk owns the fleet spreadsheet, the tail is missing from it, and an email can end with the registry gaining a row. CRW-XX9 has no route out like that. Four things make it a harder class to live with.

  • No upstream system will ever fix it. The roster system issued CRW-XX9 correctly and holds no opinion about service lines. It has never heard of CrewCodeMap and it never will. The crew code is valid in every system that stores it, and the only place it fails is a table that exists inside your report file.
  • Nothing raises an error. The refresh is green. No relationship is invalid, no key is duplicated, no type is wrong. A left outer merge that finds no match returns null, which in Power Query is an ordinary answer to an ordinary question, and null is what arrives on the report as a blank bar.
  • The total still reconciles. The crew route adds to 62.0 with the blank row included, and so does the work order route. Any reconciliation you built to catch this passes, because the defect moves hours between rows and never loses one.
  • You are the only person who can notice. Every other defect in this chapter has a second pair of eyes somewhere: a stores clerk, a planner, a refresh log, a failed relationship dialog. This one has you. And it grows, because every crew code the scheduler opens from now on lands in the same unnamed bar until somebody tells you it exists.

Detection: count the codes, then price them

Two numbers, and you need both. The count says whether the map is complete. The hours say whether the gap matters. One unmapped code covering a technician who books nothing is a note for the backlog. One covering 10.0 hours a quarter is a hole in the manpower report.

DAXUnmapped Crew Codes
Unmapped Crew Codes =
COALESCE (
    COUNTROWS (
        EXCEPT (
            DISTINCT ( CrewAssignment[CrewCode] ),
            DISTINCT ( CrewCodeMap[CrewCode] )
        )
    ),
    0
)
EXCEPT
The same choice, and the same reason, as Parts Rows With No Header later in this chapter. EXCEPT returns the rows of the first table that are absent from the second in one set operation, and it keeps the lineage of the first table. The alternative, FILTER over CrewAssignment with NOT CONTAINS, performs a lookup for every candidate row and gives you a table with no lineage to reuse.
DISTINCT
DISTINCT here, for the reason set out in the why box further down. If you ever relate CrewCodeMap to CrewAssignment, VALUES on the mapped side starts returning the virtual blank member, that blank joins the set of valid codes, and the check quietly certifies the defect as clean. A measure whose job is finding broken keys must never call the function that hides them.
COALESCE
COUNTROWS over an empty table returns blank, so a healthy model would show an empty card and look like a measure somebody broke. COALESCE states the fallback once. The IF ( ISBLANK ( ... ) , 0, ... ) form writes the whole expression twice to say the same thing.
Reading
1 on Meridian, and the code behind it is CRW-XX9. Swap COUNTROWS for CONCATENATEX over the same EXCEPT and the card prints the code itself, which is the difference between knowing something is wrong and knowing who to ask.
DAXHours On Unmapped Crews
Hours On Unmapped Crews =
VAR MissingCodes =
    EXCEPT (
        DISTINCT ( CrewAssignment[CrewCode] ),
        DISTINCT ( CrewCodeMap[CrewCode] )
    )
VAR MissingTechs =
    CALCULATETABLE (
        DISTINCT ( CrewAssignment[TechnicianID] ),
        MissingCodes
    )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] ),
        TREATAS ( MissingTechs, FactLabor[TechnicianID] )
    )
CALCULATETABLE
MissingCodes carries lineage on CrewAssignment[CrewCode], so handing it to CALCULATETABLE filters CrewAssignment directly, with no relationship involved, before DISTINCT is evaluated. FILTER would iterate the assignment table and test each row against the list.
TREATAS
There is no relationship from CrewAssignment to FactLabor, and you should not create one. TREATAS stamps the lineage of FactLabor[TechnicianID] onto the list of technicians for the life of this one calculation and leaves the model alone.
SUM
The measure adds one stored column with no per row expression to evaluate, so SUM is resolved entirely by the storage engine. SUMX would open a row context that nothing in this measure needs.
Reading
10.0 on Meridian, which is L-506 and nothing else.
Limitation
This counts hours booked by technicians on an unmapped crew. It matches the blank row on the report only while the technician key itself is clean. Leave the trailing space on "TECH-04 " from defect 4 in place and 4.5 more hours sit in the blank bar that this measure will never see, because that row fails one hop earlier.
Why this and not that

Use TREATAS here and leave the model alone. A new relationship from CrewAssignment to FactLabor looks tidier and would let the measure use a plain CALCULATE. It also creates a second filter path from the technician to the labor rows, one through DimTechnician and one through CrewAssignment, which is the ambiguity the model already avoids on DimStation to DimTechnician[HomeStation]. Adding a permanent relationship to serve one diagnostic measure is the wrong trade. TREATAS buys the same filter for the duration of one evaluation and disappears afterwards.

Run the same set difference with the two sides swapped and you get the opposite finding, crew codes you have mapped that nobody is rostered to, which today returns CRW-LT2. That one is tidiness and not correctness, so review it once a quarter instead of watching it daily.

The fix: an explicit Unmapped member

You cannot invent the service line for CRW-XX9, and guessing it would be worse than leaving it. What you can do is stop the gap being invisible. Give the missing case a name, write that name into the model at refresh, and the chart shows a bar labelled Unmapped where it used to show a bar labelled nothing.

MCrew to service line, with the gap given a name
let
    Source = CrewAssignment,
    Merged = Table.NestedJoin(
        Source, {"CrewCode"},
        CrewCodeMap, {"CrewCode"},
        "MapRows", JoinKind.LeftOuter
    ),
    Expanded = Table.ExpandTableColumn(
        Merged, "MapRows",
        {"ServiceLine"}, {"ServiceLine"}
    ),
    Named = Table.TransformColumns(
        Expanded,
        {{"ServiceLine", each
            if _ = null then "Unmapped"
            else _, type text}}
    )
in
    Named
JoinKind.LeftOuter
This step has to carry all seven technicians forward with a service line attached, so it keeps everything and labels the failure. JoinKind.LeftAnti, the kind used for detection higher up this chapter, answers "which codes are missing" and throws away the six that matched.
Table.ExpandTableColumn
Expand the nested column at refresh instead of leaving it and reaching into it from DAX. A plain text column is something a slicer, a legend, a matrix row header and a report level filter can all use. A nested table column is none of those things.
The literal Unmapped
A word a reader can see. A null and an empty string both render as the same blank cell you are trying to leave behind. Unmapped is a value a reader can see on an axis, click on, filter to, and complain about, and complaints are how this defect gets closed.
Both halves
The query runs over CrewAssignment, which holds one row per technician, so its output merges straight onto Dimension DimTechnician and the service line becomes a plain text attribute there. Nothing else is needed. If you instead relate that column to Built DimServiceLine, that dimension needs a matching Unmapped row of its own, exactly like the UNASSIGNED pairing in the unknown member section. A mapped fact key with no dimension member is still an orphan.
Result
The seventh technician carries the text Unmapped. The chart gains a labelled bar holding 10.0 hours, the crew route still totals 62.0, and the work order route is untouched. The number keeps its value. What changes is its address.

Now go back to the production controller. The fifth bar says Unmapped, it still holds 10.0 hours, and you can tell him what it means: those hours were booked by a technician on crew CRW-XX9, a crew the roster system opened and your service line map has never been told about. That is a sentence he can act on. He knows the resource scheduler, and one message closes it.

A bar labelled Unmapped on a page a customer sees is embarrassing, and the embarrassment is the point. A blank bar gets scrolled past. A bar with that word on it gets asked about, and the question travels to the one person who can answer it. Until somebody does, the report is at least telling the truth about how much it knows.

Common mistake

Reading a green refresh as evidence that the mappings are complete. A refresh succeeds when every query returns a table, and a left outer merge that matched nothing returns a table full of nulls. Delete all six rows from CrewCodeMap and Meridian still refreshes green, the crew route still totals 62.0, and every named service line reports zero while the blank reports the whole quarter. The only thing standing between you and that report is a check you wrote yourself.

Keep Unmapped Crew Codes and Hours On Unmapped Crews next to the measure set in the following section, on the same hidden diagnostics page, and leave them out of the Model Health Issues total. A count of codes and a count of orphan fact rows are different units, and adding them produces a number that rises for two unrelated reasons. Two cards side by side, reading 1 and 10.0 today, and 0 and 0.0 on a day when somebody has been paying attention.

A data quality measure set you can paste into any model

You have found five live defects by hand in this chapter: N338WA, WO-1009, the blank station on WO-1005, the trailing space on "TECH-04 " and CRW-XX9. Next quarter there will be a sixth, and the planner who spotted the last one will be looking at a different report when it lands. Hand checking runs out of road quickly. Six measures put the checks on a page and give you a number to watch.

You have already written the first of them, Orphan Aircraft Rows, earlier in this chapter. Three more follow, then the two that roll all four into a card. Rename the tables and columns and they work anywhere. Put them on a hidden diagnostics page. The page the customer sees has no use for them.

DAXBlank Key Rows
Blank Station Keys =
CALCULATE (
    COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ),
    ISBLANK ( FactWorkOrder[StationCode] )
)
CALCULATE
The predicate form, because the test touches one column and needs no row context. It is shorter and cheaper than a bare COUNTROWS wrapped in FILTER. CALCULATE is the only function that can evaluate an aggregate under an added filter.
Expansion
The predicate is expanded internally into a filter over ALL(FactWorkOrder[StationCode]), which means the measure ignores any station slicer on the page. That is what you want on a diagnostics page. Wrap the predicate in KEEPFILTERS if you want it to respect the slicer instead.
Limitation
ISBLANK is deliberately narrow and will not see an empty string, which is exactly what an Excel or CSV source often delivers. If your source can produce both, use the predicate FactWorkOrder[StationCode] = "", which is true for a blank and for an empty string, and accept that you have then lost the ability to tell the two apart in DAX. The clean separation only exists in Power Query, which is an argument for doing the test there.
Reading
1 on the raw Meridian work orders, WO-1005. 0 after the Power Query mapping, because the key is then the string UNASSIGNED and is no longer blank.
DAXDuplicate Key Count
Duplicate Aircraft Keys =
VAR KeyRows =
    ADDCOLUMNS (
        DISTINCT ( DimAircraft[ACREG] ),
        "@Rows", CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( DimAircraft ) )
    )
RETURN
    COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( KeyRows, [@Rows] > 1 ) )
ADDCOLUMNS
Over a key list rather than SUMMARIZE with an added column. SUMMARIZE applies a context transition to its extension columns in a way that is difficult to predict and that the published guidance advises against. ADDCOLUMNS with an explicit CALCULATE makes the transition visible in the code.
DISTINCT
DISTINCT and never VALUES, for the reason set out in the why box further down this section. Any key list inside a measure that hunts broken keys has to exclude the virtual blank member, or the measure starts reporting on the thing it was written to expose.
CALCULATE
Wrapping COUNTROWS is what performs the context transition. It turns the current key into a filter, so the count applies to that one key.
Alternative
COUNTROWS(DimAircraft) - DISTINCTCOUNT(DimAircraft[ACREG]) is faster and shorter, and it returns the number of excess rows where this measure returns the number of offending keys. On the un-deduplicated append that reads 4, and so does this measure, by coincidence. Do not rely on the coincidence.
DAXFact Rows Not Matching a Dimension
Parts Rows With No Header =
VAR PartKeys = DISTINCT ( FactParts[WorkOrderID] )
VAR HeaderKeys = DISTINCT ( FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID] )
VAR Missing = EXCEPT ( PartKeys, HeaderKeys )
RETURN
    CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( FactParts ), Missing )
EXCEPT
Rather than FILTER with NOT CONTAINS. EXCEPT is a set operation the engine resolves in one pass and it preserves the data lineage of its first argument, which is what lets the result be used directly as a CALCULATE filter on line 6. The CONTAINS version performs a lookup per candidate key and has no lineage to reuse.
Line 6
Because Missing carries lineage on FactParts[WorkOrderID], passing it as a filter needs no TREATAS. Adding one here would be harmless and redundant.
Independence
This measure works without the relationship, so it still returns a number when the relationship was never created or is inactive, which is exactly when you most need one.
Reading
1 on Meridian, P-9007. Change COUNTROWS to SUMX(FactParts, FactParts[Qty] * FactParts[UnitCost]) and it reads 4,900, which is the money at stake.
Why this and not that

Use DISTINCT in that measure, even though DISTINCT and VALUES are usually interchangeable. VALUES returns the virtual blank row that the engine adds to the one side of an invalid relationship, and DISTINCT leaves it out. FactWorkOrder is the one side of the header to line relationships, so it already carries a blank member because of P-9007. Use VALUES for HeaderKeys and the blank row joins the set of valid headers, which is the defect quietly certifying itself as clean. When you are writing a measure whose whole job is to find broken keys, never use the function that hides them.

DAXModel Health
Model Health Issues =
COALESCE (
    [Orphan Aircraft Rows]
        + [Blank Station Keys]
        + [Duplicate Aircraft Keys]
        + [Parts Rows With No Header],
    0
)

Model Health =
VAR Issues = [Model Health Issues]
RETURN
    SWITCH (
        TRUE (),
        Issues = 0, "Keys clean",
        Issues <= 5, Issues & " rows to review",
        Issues & " rows failing key checks"
    )
COALESCE
All four inputs are a COUNTROWS over a table that is empty on a healthy model, and COUNTROWS over an empty table returns blank. Blank plus blank stays blank in DAX, so the sum on a fully clean model would return blank and the card would print nothing at all on the one day you wanted to see a zero. COALESCE wraps the whole sum once and turns that case into 0. Wrapping each of the four separately would say the same thing four times.
Two measures
A numeric one and a text one. The numeric measure is what conditional formatting rules, alerts and any future aggregation can consume. The text measure is only for a card a human reads. Ship the text version alone and you cannot set a data alert on model health, which is usually the thing you actually wanted.
SWITCH
With TRUE() as the expression, rather than nested IF. The semantics are identical, conditions are tested in order until one holds, but the branches sit at one indent level instead of three, and adding a fifth check later does not require rebalancing brackets.
Reading
On the raw Meridian sources: 1 plus 1 plus 0 plus 1 equals 3. After building DimAircraft from the union and mapping the blank station: 0 plus 0 plus 0 plus 1 equals 1, the WO-1009 orphan that Meridian keeps on purpose.
Orphan aircraft rows
1 raw, 0 fixed
Blank station keys
1 raw, 0 fixed
Duplicate dimension keys
0 fixed, 4 if the append is not deduplicated
Parts rows with no header
1, worth 4,900
Performance note

Three of these measures scan a fact table with no filter applied, and one of them does it inside a FILTER that cannot be pushed into the storage engine cleanly. On Meridian's 8 and 7 row facts that is free. On a 40 million row parts table it is a query that runs every time someone opens the page. Either move the checks into Power Query so they are evaluated once at refresh and loaded as a small results table, or keep them on a page that is hidden and only opened deliberately. A diagnostics page that slows down the report is a diagnostics page that gets deleted.

Where each defect should be fixed

You now have a fix for all nine defects. The remaining question is where each fix lives, and it matters more than it sounds. The trim on TECH-04 can go in three different places, and only one of them stops the same trailing space arriving again next month.

Three layers are available: the source system, Power Query, and the model. The general rule is that you fix as far upstream as you can influence, because a defect fixed in a report is a defect that will reappear. The trailing space on TECH-04 came from a timesheet screen with no input validation. Trim it in Power Query and it is gone from your model, and still there next month, and still there in the payroll extract that a different team is about to build.

Two rows in that table are worth arguing about. Case normalisation belongs in Power Query and nowhere else, because the model treats case-different values as equal and therefore cannot report the discrepancy back to you. And the orphan header key belongs in the source alone, because there is no correct value for you to invent.

The bottom row breaks the rule this section opens with. You cannot push an unmapped crew code further upstream, because upstream of CrewCodeMap there is only you. Where the rule still bites is the input to your table. Ask the resource scheduler to tell you when a crew code is opened, and the defect moves one layer up to somebody who sees it before you do.

Interview-level insight

Hiding a data quality problem and resolving one look identical in the report and are opposites in the business. Mapping WO-1009's parts to an unknown work order makes the station matrix add to 28,245 and the page stops looking broken. The 4,900 of hydraulics that left the store against a work order nobody can find is still unaccounted for, and now it has a label that implies somebody accounted for it. Resolution means the defect count falls because the underlying record was corrected or written off. Concealment means the defect count falls because you changed where the number is displayed. The test is simple: after your change, can anyone still find out how many rows failed, and who owns them? If the answer is no, you removed the evidence and left the model exactly where it was.

What to remember
  • An unmatched key on the many side adds one virtual blank row to the one side and every unmatched fact row is attributed to it. Grand totals stay correct, breakdowns do not, and there is only ever one blank row no matter how many distinct keys are broken.
  • Two visuals disagreeing by a fixed amount, 23,345 against 28,245, is the standard signature of an orphan key. The visual that groups by an attribute behind the broken join loses those rows. The visual with no such grouping keeps them.
  • A blank member is indistinguishable from a join failure, so map genuine absences to an explicit member such as UNASSIGNED and recover real identifiers such as N338WA into the dimension with unknown attributes.
  • Keys that look identical are tested with Text.Length or LEN, never by eye. 7 and 8 on the same displayed TECH-04 is the whole diagnosis, and 4.5 hours is the whole cost.
  • Power Query is case sensitive, the model's relationships are not. Do not rely on either. Normalise case explicitly on both sides of every key.
  • Duplicate keys on the one side stop the relationship being created and fail the refresh once it exists. Find them with Group By and a count over 1, and normalise case before you group.
  • A foreign key can be valid in every system that holds it and still fail, when the table it has to join to is one you maintain by hand. CRW-XX9 is a real crew code that CrewCodeMap is missing, and the 10.0 hours behind it sit in an unnamed service line with no error raised anywhere. Nothing upstream will fix it, so write the unmapped check yourself and label the gap Unmapped so it shows on the page.
  • Fix as far upstream as your influence reaches. A defect fixed in a report reappears at the next refresh, in the next report, and in the next team's extract.
Part 6 . Diagnosis and reference

20Anti-patterns and how to recognise them

After this chapter you will be able to open a model you did not build, name what is wrong with it inside ten minutes, and say which of the fourteen failures you are looking at and what it will cost the report.

The finance manager forwards you a file at nine in the morning. Last month the quoted value of the quarter's work read 38,100. This morning the same page reads 53,600. Nobody has touched the source data, and he wants to know which of the two numbers goes in the board pack. You have never opened this file before.

You can answer him in about four minutes. Reviewing a model is pattern matching. You do not open every measure. You look for a small number of shapes that reliably mean trouble. Each shape leaves a signal you can see in model view or in the field list within a minute of opening the file.

What follows is fourteen of them, each with the same three parts: the signal you can see, the mechanism that makes it hurt, and the fix. Where Meridian shows the failure with real numbers, the numbers are here. Read it as reference material. You will come back to it when someone hands you a file and asks why the totals moved.

One caution before you start. Several of these are sometimes the right call. You may be working under a constraint you do not control, or at a scale where the cost stays theoretical, and the entries say so where that applies. Treat an anti-pattern as a default that is usually wrong. The reviewer who calls every snowflake a defect loses credibility with the person who snowflaked on purpose.

Anti-patterns 1 to 5: the shape of the model

1. The one big flat table

You open model view and there is one table. Sixty columns, a name like Master or Data, and QuotedAmount sitting three columns away from Hours and two away from UnitCost. Those come from three systems at three grains. There are no relationship lines because there is nothing to relate.

The mechanism is repetition. Joining the work order header to its labor lines repeats the header values once per line, so any additive measure over a header column counts that header more than once. Compression suffers separately. The wide table stores every column at the finest grain in the join. The high cardinality columns carried along for the ride, LaborID, IssueID and three separate dates, then dominate the dictionary.

The fix is to split the wide table by grain. Grain is what one row of a table means, said out loud in a sentence: one row per work order, or one row per technician per work order per day. Give each event its own Fact table at its own grain. Then share the descriptive tables between them. A Dimension is one of those descriptive tables, the list of things you group and slice by: stations, aircraft, technicians, dates.

You met this table in Chapter 2, where it was the argument. Here it is the signal. Read the columns downward and the repetition jumps out. Five labor lines, six columns, and the repeated cells in QuotedAmount, ACREG and AircraftType are tinted so you can watch the header value arrive once per labor line beneath it. 3,000 appears twice for a work order that was quoted once. 12,500 does the same. The tint belongs to the diagram. In the real table there is no tint, and nothing marks which of the two rows is the copy. The red card sums the drawn column to 34,200 and names the true total of 38,100. It also says plainly that these five rows are only an extract, which is why the full count below comes to a larger number. The grey card beside it is the second failure, AircraftType repeating on every row. The threshold is attached to it: nothing at eight rows, a dictionary entry per distinct value and the loss of run length encoding at eighty million.

Trace the quoted amount by hand, row by row

Join the eight work orders to their labor rows with a left join, so work orders with no labor survive. WO-1001 and WO-1003 have two labor rows each, WO-1005 and WO-1008 have none, the rest have one.

The true total quoted is 38,100. The flat table returns 53,600, an overstatement of 15,500, and every one of those dollars comes from two work orders that happened to have a second technician on them. Nobody looking at 53,600 has any way to know which two.

That is the finance manager's file, and that is his answer. The number for the board pack is 38,100. The page reads 53,600 because somebody joined the work order header onto the labor lines, and the shape that did it was visible in model view before you read a single measure.

2. Bidirectional everywhere

Every relationship line in model view has an arrowhead at both ends. Almost always this is residue. Someone wanted a slicer to filter something it would not filter, flipped the setting until the visual changed, and moved on.

Two things go wrong. The first is ambiguity. Once filters travel both ways, one dimension can reach a fact by more than one route, and the engine has to pick a route without telling anybody. Meridian sits one flip away from that. Filters already run from DimStation to FactLabor through FactWorkOrder. Relate DimStation[StationCode] to DimTechnician[HomeStation] as well and a second route opens, DimStation to DimTechnician to FactLabor. That is exactly why the relationship is deliberately absent from the model. Bidirectional filtering produces the same condition without anyone adding a relationship. Set DimTechnician to FactLabor to filter both ways, and a station selection now travels backwards into DimTechnician through FactWorkOrder and FactLabor. The technician list then changes for a reason nobody wrote down. Power BI refuses to activate some of these configurations and resolves others by an internal path preference you should not build a report on. The second problem is cost. The engine may have to propagate filters both ways on every query that touches the relationship. Where row level security is in place, bidirectional filtering needs an explicit opt in and changes what a restricted user is allowed to see.

These are the two panels from Chapter 8, and for a review you need only the arrowheads on them. The left panel, headed Single, the default, joins DimTechnician down to FactLabor with a single downward arrow, and the note beside it says a selection on FactLabor does not reach DimTechnician. The green card underneath calls that one path, one answer. The right panel, headed Both, bidirectional, draws the same two boxes with an arrowhead at each end. Its red card names both halves of the trade. Convenient, and the usual source of ambiguity, because the engine must now build a set on the one side where a lookup would have been enough. It pays that cost on every query. In an inherited file you are scanning model view for that second arrowhead line after line, and for any sign that somebody wrote down why it is there.

Default to single direction. Where one measure genuinely needs the reverse flow, use CROSSFILTER as a modifier inside a CALCULATE in that measure. Leave the model setting alone. CROSSFILTER is only legal inside CALCULATE, and that restriction is the point: the change is scoped to one calculation, and every other query in the file keeps a single filter path.

3. Dimensions built with DISTINCT from a single fact

The signal is arithmetic. The dimension row count is exactly equal to the distinct key count in one fact table. Look at DimStation. Three rows, and the non blank stations in FactWorkOrder are MSP, TUS and LAS. Somebody built the dimension out of the fact. A DimAircraft with five rows against five distinct tails in WorkOrders came from the same place.

The mechanism is coverage. A dimension built from one fact covers that fact completely and covers every other fact by luck, so it breaks the moment a second fact uses the same key. PHX is the Meridian case. It exists only in ShopCapacity, never on a work order. A station list derived from WorkOrders therefore has no PHX row, and the station slicer never offers PHX. The 16 planned hours for PHX in March no longer match a dimension row. They land in the blank member, the unlabelled line the engine adds for keys it cannot match, and authors routinely filter that line away. Select the three named stations and planned capacity drops from 176 to 160. Utilisation moves from 62.0 divided by 176, which is 35.2%, to 62.0 divided by 160, which is 38.75%. The model looks busier because a station disappeared.

Build the key list by appending every source that carries it, then deduplicate and add the UNASSIGNED member. Meridian's Built DimStation has five rows for that reason. Sometimes you are forced to derive the list in DAX, the formula language Power BI uses for measures and calculated columns. Use DISTINCT there. VALUES returns the blank member the engine adds for unmatched keys, so it would hand you a dimension with a phantom empty row sitting in it.

4. Date columns with no date table

Open the field list. Every date column has a small hierarchy under it offering Year, Quarter, Month, Day. That is the auto date/time feature, and it means there is no real date table.

Power BI creates one hidden date table per date column. Meridian has five date columns across the facts: OpenedDate, PromisedDate, ClosedDate, WorkDate and IssueDate. That is five hidden tables, each spanning the full calendar years covered by its own column, each with its own hierarchy, all stored and all refreshed. The bloat is annoying. The blocking problem is that each hidden table is attached to exactly one column. Nothing can put labor by WorkDate and work orders by ClosedDate on the same axis, and no time intelligence calculation can span them.

Turn it off explicitly. File, Options and settings, Options, Data Load, then clear Auto date/time under Time intelligence. Do it for the current file and for the global setting. Then build DimDate as 90 rows covering 2025-01-01 to 2025-03-31, and mark it as a date table. One active relationship on OpenedDate, two inactive ones for the other two roles.

5. Snowflaking everything because it looks normalised

Count the hops from a fact to a description. Does FactLabor reach a station name through DimTechnician to DimStation to DimRegion to DimCountry? Has DimAircraft been split so that operator and engine type each sit in a table of their own? Either one means the same thing. You are looking at a transactional schema copied into a reporting model without being reshaped.

Chapter 2 used this one to price the trade. Read it from the left again. Last time you chose this shape. This time you have found it in a file somebody handed you. DimOperator and DimEngineType both feed DimAircraft. Only DimAircraft touches FactWorkOrder. The three lines between the four boxes each carry a 1 at the outer end and a star at the inner end. An operator name is no longer an attribute of the aircraft. It sits out past DimAircraft, which holds only OperatorID to point at it, and the note underneath counts the extra hops that costs and says when they are worth paying.

Each hop is a relationship the engine resolves at query time, so cost grows with the chain. The larger cost is human. A model snowflaked throughout shows eight tables in the field list where three would do. No analyst can tell you whether Operator lives on the aircraft table or on the operator table without opening both. That is the confusion the two key columns in the figure create in miniature. Authors then drag the first field whose name matches, which is how two visuals end up grouping by different things.

Flatten to one dimension per business entity. DimAircraft holds AircraftType, Operator, EngineType and YearBuilt as plain attributes across seven rows. The honest exception: a sub dimension that is large and maintained separately upstream can justify its own table. Seven rows never does.

Anti-patterns 6 to 9: calculation in the wrong place

The production controller has a page filtered to Scheduled work. The labor cost card reads 1,295.00. He moves the slicer to AOG, which stands for aircraft on ground and means the aircraft cannot fly until the work is finished, and the card reads 1,295.00 again. He moves it back twice more to be sure, then calls you. Nothing on the page tells him that the slicer was never in charge of that number.

6. Calculated columns doing the work of measures

Two things in a model can hold a calculation. A calculated column is worked out once for every row when the model refreshes, and the answer is stored on the row. A measure is worked out when a visual asks for it, against whatever the user has filtered to. Now scan the fact tables for columns named TotalSales, Rank, PercentOfTotal or ShareOfHours. The name is the tell. A total, a rank and a share are all statements about a set of rows, and a column can only describe one row.

A calculated column is evaluated once at refresh, in row context. Row context means the engine can see the one row it is standing on and nothing else. No report filter is applied anywhere at that moment. By the time the slicer exists, the value is already stored. So a column holding a share of total hours keeps showing that share when the user filters to January. It adds to 100% while every visible number on the page contradicts it. It costs memory too, since a computed share has near unique values and compresses badly.

The nuance worth keeping: a row level product is a legitimate column. Hours times HourlyRate describes one timesheet line and nothing else. Even then, prefer the measure form, and see Chapter 10 for the full decision.

DAXLabor Cost without a stored column
Labor Cost :=
SUMX ( FactLabor, FactLabor[Hours] * FactLabor[HourlyRate] )
Line 2
SUMX here. SUM takes exactly one stored column, and the product of two columns is stored nowhere. Storing it as a calculated column just to let SUM work is the anti-pattern itself. SUMX iterates FactLabor in row context, multiplies, and adds, returning 6,326.50 across the eight rows.

7. Measures that hard code a filter a slicer should control

Search the measure list for a literal string, then check whether the same column appears on a slicer. CALCULATE with FactWorkOrder[WOType] = "AOG" on a page that also has a work order type slicer is the classic pairing. This is the production controller's page.

The mechanism is filter replacement. A predicate inside CALCULATE does not narrow the filter that is already on that column, it replaces it. So when the user moves the slicer to Scheduled, the measure overrides him and keeps returning the AOG figure. In Meridian the AOG work orders are WO-1002, WO-1005 and WO-1007. Their labor costs are 855.00, nothing at all, and 440.00. The measure therefore returns 855.00 plus 440.00, which is 1,295.00, wherever the slicer sits. That is the 1,295.00 the production controller could not shift, and it is why the same figure survived every move he made.

DAXAOG Labor Cost, fighting the slicer and not
// The measure wins and the user loses
AOG Labor Cost :=
CALCULATE ( [Labor Cost], FactWorkOrder[WOType] = "AOG" )

// The measure and the slicer agree
AOG Labor Cost :=
CALCULATE (
    [Labor Cost],
    KEEPFILTERS ( FactWorkOrder[WOType] = "AOG" )
)
Line 3
The predicate is expanded into a table of WOType values and applied as a replacement, so any slicer selection on that column is discarded.
Line 9
KEEPFILTERS here. A bare predicate overwrites the slicer. KEEPFILTERS intersects the new filter with whatever is already there, so the slicer on Scheduled now gives blank. That is the honest answer, and it is the one the production controller was owed.
Better
Delete the measure. If the page has a type slicer, [Labor Cost] alone answers the question and the user controls the filter.

8. ALL used where REMOVEFILTERS or ALLEXCEPT was meant

The symptom shows in the report before it shows in the code. A percent of total column whose values do not add to 100% inside a filtered page, or a total row that stays fixed while the page filter changes, points straight at a filter removal that was too broad.

Removing filters from an entire fact table removes the dimension filters with them. A table modifier acts on the expanded table, and the expanded table carries every column on the one side of its relationships. Put a page filter on January and ask for each station's share of labor hours. January hours are MSP 22.5 plus TUS 12.5, which is 35.0, so MSP should read 22.5 divided by 35.0, or 64.3%. Clearing the whole of FactLabor makes the denominator the full quarter, 62.0, and MSP reads 22.5 divided by 62.0, or 36.3%. Both numbers are plausible. Only one answers the question on the page.

DAXThree ways to build a denominator
// Too broad: the page filter on January is cleared too
Station Share Wrong :=
DIVIDE (
    [Labor Hours],
    CALCULATE ( [Labor Hours], ALL ( FactLabor ) )
)

// Clears the station only, keeps the date
Station Share :=
DIVIDE (
    [Labor Hours],
    CALCULATE ( [Labor Hours], REMOVEFILTERS ( DimStation ) )
)

// Keeps the station, clears trade and month
Station Planned Hours :=
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( FactCapacity[PlannedHours] ),
    ALLEXCEPT ( FactCapacity, DimStation[StationCode] )
)
Line 5
ALL over a table applies to that table expanded, meaning its own columns plus the columns of every table on the one side of its relationships. Clearing FactLabor therefore also clears DimDate and DimStation, so the denominator becomes the whole quarter, 62.0. This is the defect.
Line 12
Naming the dimension restricts the removal to station. The date filter still arrives through DimDate, so the denominator stays inside January at 35.0.
Line 18
SUM here. PlannedHours is a single stored column with no row level expression to evaluate, so SUMX would add a scan and return the same number.
Line 19
ALLEXCEPT states what survives, and everything it fails to name is cleared. Note the column it names. It is DimStation[StationCode]. The visual groups on the dimension, and that is where the filter actually sits. Name FactCapacity[StationCode] instead and you preserve a filter that was never there, handing every station the full 176. As written, every trade row for MSP shares one denominator, MSP's 90 planned hours, whatever the trade and month in the row.
Why this and not that

Reach for REMOVEFILTERS. As a CALCULATE modifier it behaves identically to ALL. The difference is what a reader can tell at a glance. ALL also works as a table function, so the line alone leaves your reader guessing whether you meant to return rows or to clear filters. REMOVEFILTERS carries one meaning. Reach for ALLEXCEPT in place of a list of REMOVEFILTERS calls. The exception list keeps working when someone adds a column to the table, while a removal list silently stops covering the new column. Use DIVIDE for the ratio itself. The denominator here can legitimately be zero or blank. A page filtered to a week with no timesheet lines gives no labor hours at all, and PHX and UNASSIGNED carry no labor rows in the whole quarter. DIVIDE returns blank in both cases. The slash operator returns Infinity when the numerator is not zero, and NaN when both sides are zero, and the visual prints those words where a percentage should be. There is a third option worth knowing. If you want the percentage to follow the slicer instead of the whole dimension, ALLSELECTED restores the filter context from outside the visual, which is what a share of the visible total actually means.

9. Using LOOKUPVALUE instead of a relationship

Find LOOKUPVALUE in a calculated column, then look at model view. If the table it points at has no line connecting it, you have found the pattern. They rarely appear alone: once one column has been fetched this way, the next request gets a second copy.

It works, which is why it survives. It is also slower. Every row runs a filtered match over the target column pair, and it has to handle the case where two rows match, while a relationship is resolved through an index the engine builds once. The worse problem is documentation. The model diagram shows two unconnected tables. The next analyst reads that as no path between parts and aircraft, and builds a second workaround of their own. The relationship still never gets created.

Meridian invites this. FactParts has no ACREG, so slicing parts cost by aircraft needs the work order in between. Create the header to line relationship instead, and in most cases you then need no column at all, because filters propagate from DimAircraft through FactWorkOrder into FactParts on their own.

DAXAircraft registration on FactParts, two ways
// The anti-pattern: a calculated column on FactParts
Aircraft Registration =
LOOKUPVALUE (
    FactWorkOrder[ACREG],
    FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID],
    FactParts[WorkOrderID]
)

// With the header to line relationship in place
Aircraft Registration = RELATED ( FactWorkOrder[ACREG] )
Lines 3 to 7
Three arguments, a scan per row, and nothing in the model diagram to show it happened. P-9007 points at WO-1009, which does not exist, so the result is blank and its 4,900 of hydraulic cost is untraceable to any aircraft.
Line 10
RELATED here. It will not compile unless the relationship exists, so the dependency becomes visible in the diagram to everyone who opens the file. LOOKUPVALUE leaves no such trace. The orphan still returns blank, but now it lands in the blank member and shows as a row in the visual, which is how 28,245 and 23,345 differ in the first place.
Caveat
LOOKUPVALUE earns its place when the match needs two or more columns and you are unwilling to build a concatenated key. That case is real. Keep the exception that narrow.

Anti-patterns 10 to 14: relationships, storage and intent

The shift supervisor at MSP keeps a whiteboard. It says his station did 34.5 hours of labour this quarter. The station report on the wall says 28.5. He has decided the report is broken, and he has said so to the production controller. Both numbers came out of the same model, from the same measure, and both of them are right.

10. Fact to fact relationships without a shared dimension

Look for a relationship line drawn directly between two tables that both hold events. A join from FactCapacity[StationCode] to FactWorkOrder[StationCode] qualifies, because station repeats in both. So does FactLabor to FactParts on WorkOrderID.

Since neither side is unique, the relationship has to be many to many, and Power BI marks it as a weak relationship. No blank member is created on either side. Keys present in one table and missing from the other therefore never show up as a blank row. They are dropped when the filter crosses. Totals taken through the relationship then disagree with totals taken straight from the same table, and no row anywhere in the report accounts for the difference.

Route through the shared dimension instead. Station belongs to DimStation, which filters both facts as a proper one to many on each side.

Interview-level insight

Two of Meridian's relationships connect two fact tables and both are correct: FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID] to FactLabor[WorkOrderID] and to FactParts[WorkOrderID]. What makes those two correct is uniqueness. WorkOrderID appears once and only once across the eight rows of FactWorkOrder, so the relationship is one to many and the header behaves as a dimension for its own lines. The word fact in a table name decides nothing. Header to line is a grain relationship. Fact to fact on a shared attribute is a missing dimension. Ask which side is unique and the answer falls out.

11. Hiding columns instead of removing them

The signal is size. A model whose sources amount to a few dozen rows takes 40 MB and two minutes to refresh. Open a metadata tool and you find columns with large dictionaries that no measure, relationship or sort property references.

Hidden means hidden from the field list and nothing else. The column is still pulled from the source, still stored in memory, still refreshed on every load. A free text remarks field or a system GUID is expensive precisely because its values are nearly unique, and hiding it saves not one byte.

Remove unneeded columns in Power Query, and prefer choosing the columns you want over removing the ones you do not, because a chosen list is a whitelist that ignores whatever new column the source adds next quarter. Meridian does this with Technicians[Certifications]: once the delimited string is split into BridgeTechCert, the original column is dropped rather than hidden. Hiding stays right for columns the model needs but the user should not see, such as keys and sort order columns, so do not read this as an instruction to delete everything hidden.

12. Storing the same attribute on both the fact and the dimension

Type a word into the field list search box. If "Station" returns FactWorkOrder[StationCode], DimStation[StationCode], FactCapacity[StationCode] and DimTechnician[HomeStation], the model offers four ways to group by station and no guidance about which one is meant.

Two of those give genuinely different answers. Group labor hours by the station on the work order and MSP is 34.5 hours. Group the same measure by the technician's home station and MSP is 12.0 for TECH-01 plus 16.5 for TECH-02, which is 28.5. Both totals reconcile to 62.0. Both are correct answers to different questions, and neither field name says which question it answers.

That is the shift supervisor's argument in one sentence. His whiteboard counts work done at MSP. The report counts hours booked by technicians whose home station is MSP. The 6.0 hour gap is made of hours worked at MSP by people posted somewhere else, or posted nowhere the data knows about. The UNASSIGNED row in the table below carries 10.0 hours of exactly that kind.

Keep the groupable attribute on exactly one table. Hide the key on the fact so nobody can drag it onto a chart. Rename anything that survives so the name carries the question: "Work station" on DimStation, "Technician home station" on DimTechnician. Do that and the shift supervisor and the report are arguing about two named things instead of one word. One duplicate stays safe, and that is the key itself. A key on the fact side exists to join, and joining is all it does.

13. Text keys where an integer key was available

Look at what each relationship is built on. Long text values, concatenated composites such as "WO-1001|BRK-2210", or a 36 character GUID stored as text, all mean the join carries more bytes than it needs to.

A relationship column gets a dictionary and a join structure. Text is held in a hash dictionary and compared by dictionary position, while integers in a bounded range can be value encoded and packed into fewer bits per row. The difference shows in storage engine time on scans and joins, and in dictionary memory, both scaling with row count.

The threshold matters more than the principle. Meridian's largest fact table is FactCapacity at 28 rows, and its largest table of any kind is DimDate at 90, and "BRK-2210" as a key costs nothing measurable there. Converting to surrogate integers would add a merge per fact in Power Query and buy an improvement nobody could detect. Change keys when a fact reaches several million rows, when the key text is long, or when profiling names the relationship as the cost.

Performance note

Do not reach for surrogate keys as a first response to a slow report. On models under a few million rows the usual causes are elsewhere: a measure iterating a large table row by row, a bidirectional relationship expanding a filter, a calculated column materialising millions of distinct values, or a visual asking for a matrix with tens of thousands of cells. Measure first with the performance analyser and a query trace, then change the key if the trace still points there. Rebuilding keys is the most disruptive change on this list and the one least likely to be the cause.

14. Modelling the report instead of the business

Read the table names. ExecSummaryData, StationTab and Page3 are the names of report pages. Confirm it by looking inside. The columns are already aggregated, and often generically named, because the table was shaped to fill one visual.

A table built to answer a page answers that page and stops. The aggregation destroys the grain the page did not need, so the next question cannot be answered by drilling. It needs another table, another refresh path, and another chance for two summaries of the same thing to disagree.

Meridian shows it cleanly. A table called UtilisationPage holding station, month, hours and planned hours reports 35.2% for the quarter and cannot be asked about trades at all, because Airframe, Avionics, Engine and NDT were summed away before the model saw them. The unpivoted FactCapacity, 28 rows at station, month and trade, answers the utilisation question and the trade question and the ones after that. Model the entities and the events, and let the pages ask.

The ten minute model review

Run these against any file you inherit. Every question is answerable from model view, the field list and a text search over the measures, and a yes is the healthy answer in each case. Thirteen of the fourteen anti-patterns have a question here. Text keys, number 13, do not, because whether they cost anything depends on row count and on what a trace says, so a yes or no question about them produces false alarms on every small model you will ever review.

The checklist has a real limitation, and you should say so when you hand the results to whoever owns the model. It tests structure. Meaning stays outside its reach. A model can pass all fifteen and still measure the wrong thing, because nothing here checks whether turn time was defined as closed minus opened or as closed minus promised, or whether hours by certification should have been 62.0 rather than the 85.0 a bridge produces. Structure is what you can audit in ten minutes. Definitions take a conversation with the person who runs the shop.

What to remember
  • Anti-patterns are recognised by signals you can see in a minute: a table named Master, arrowheads on both ends, a date hierarchy under every date column, a dimension whose row count exactly matches one fact.
  • Flattening repeats header values onto line rows. Meridian's quoted total goes from 38,100 to 53,600 the moment work orders are joined to labor.
  • A dimension built from one fact is complete for one fact. PHX drops into an unlabelled blank row, planned hours fall from 176 to 160 once anyone selects the named stations, and utilisation reads 38.75% instead of 35.2%.
  • Filter removal has to be narrow. Clearing a whole fact table takes the page filter with it, turning a 64.3% station share into 36.3%.
  • Header to line between two facts is correct when the header key is unique. Fact to fact on a shared attribute is a missing dimension.
  • A hidden column is still loaded, still stored and still refreshed. Text keys only matter at scale. Remove the column every time. Change the key only when a trace tells you to.
  • The fifteen question review audits structure. It cannot tell you whether the business definitions underneath are right.
Part 6 . Diagnosis and reference

21Cheat sheet, measure library and review checklist

Everything the previous twenty chapters proved, compressed into tables you can read at speed while a report is broken and someone is waiting. Symptom to cause to fix, the complete Meridian measure library, the filter modifiers, and a fifteen point review you run before you publish.

It is twenty past four. The finance manager needs the month's labour cost for a call at five. The production controller wants to know why the closed work order count moved since Friday. And the report you published on Monday has a blank row in it that nobody can explain. You have forty minutes and no time to reread three chapters.

That is what this chapter is for. It teaches nothing new. It exists so that you do not have to reread a chapter to remember which modifier keeps a filter and which one throws it away. Read the first table when something is wrong. Read the measure library when you are writing DAX, the formula language Power BI uses for measures, and you want a form already known to return the right number against the Meridian rows. Everything here matches the answer key exactly. If you build the model and a measure returns something different, look at the model first. These definitions are the tested ones.

The symptom table

Take the blank row first, because that is the one on your screen. Somebody in the meeting pointed at it, asked what it was, and you had nothing to say. Twelve hours of work on N338WA are sitting inside it. Here is how you find that out in under a minute.

Filter the visual down to the blank member and look at the raw keys behind it. Within seconds you will know which of four things you have: whitespace on one side of a key, a key with no dimension member, a date outside the calendar, or a source column that arrived genuinely empty.

Order matters in the third column. The first thing to check is the one that splits the possible causes roughly in half, chosen for how fast it rules things out. Work down the column in order.

Two words in the table are worth pinning down first. Grain is what one row of a table stands for, written as a sentence: one row of FactLabor is one technician on one work order on one day. Semi additive describes a number you may add across some things and never across others. A forecast revision adds across work orders. It must never be added across the revisions of one work order, because each revision replaces the one before it.

Common mistake

Reaching for the fix column before the check column. Half the entries in this table share a symptom with another entry, and the wrong fix applied confidently is worse than no fix, because it removes the evidence. If a blank row disappears after you switch a relationship to bidirectional, you have not solved anything. You have hidden 12.0 hours of work on N338WA behind a setting nobody will look at again.

The Meridian measure library

The finance manager wants one number for the month and does not care how you get it. He asks for the cost of the work. You open the file and find three measures with cost in the name, two of them written by somebody who has left, and the three disagree by thousands. He is waiting.

That is the situation this library removes. Every measure below is written against the finished model built in Chapter 3 and returns the figure stated underneath it. Names are stable across the whole document. Where a measure has a variant that is deliberately wrong, the wrong version stays in the chapter that discusses it. This library carries only the forms that return the right number. Store all of them in a dedicated measures table with no columns, so the field list groups them away from the data.

This is the model diagram from Chapter 3, repeated here so that you do not have to page back for it. Keep it next to you while you read the library. Every measure below assumes these twelve tables and these joins, with two exceptions. The six heavy maintenance measures reach into three extension tables the figure does not draw, and the eight manpower planning measures after them reach into four more. When a number fails to reproduce, the first question is whether your model has the same shape. Two details in the figure explain most of the awkward measures that follow. The first is the dashed curve running from DimDate across to FactCapacity, labelled month grain only, see chapter 16. The second is the pair of lines that meet at BridgeTechCert along the bottom. One drops into it from DimTechnician above, one arrives from DimCertification to its right, and that meeting point is where a technician's hours get counted once per certification held. The single straight line from DimDate down into FactWorkOrder is the OpenedDate role. The two inactive roles are not drawn at all, because an inactive relationship moves no filter until a measure asks for it.

Base measures

Seven measures cover the additive quantities in the model. Every other measure in this library is built from these or from the same pattern. If one of these returns the wrong number, stop and fix the model before writing anything else.

Total hours booked to labour lines.

DAXLabor Hours
Labor Hours =
    SUM ( FactLabor[Hours] )
Returns
62.0 with no filter. MSP 34.5, TUS 22.5, LAS 5.0. It is additive on every dimension in the model, which is what makes it safe as the base of everything else.

Count of timesheet lines, useful as a denominator and as a sanity check.

DAXLabor Entries
Labor Entries =
    COUNTROWS ( FactLabor )
Returns
8. Chosen over COUNT(FactLabor[LaborID]) because COUNTROWS counts rows including any with a blank in the column you happened to name, and it does not need a column at all.

Labour cost computed at line grain, then summed.

DAXLabor Cost
Labor Cost =
    SUMX (
        FactLabor,
        FactLabor[Hours] * FactLabor[HourlyRate]
    )
Returns
6,326.50. Line by line: 712.50, 660.00, 855.00, 704.00, 495.00, 1,020.00, 1,440.00, 440.00.
Choice
SUMX here. SUM([Hours]) * SUM([HourlyRate]) would give 62.0 times 808, which is meaningless. The multiplication has to happen inside the row.

Parts cost including the orphan issue line, which is the honest stores total.

DAXParts Cost
Parts Cost =
    SUMX (
        FactParts,
        FactParts[Qty] * FactParts[UnitCost]
    )
Returns
28,245 across seven issue lines. By category: Brakes 3,720, Hydraulics 7,350, Engine 15,300, Avionics 1,875.

Quoted value of the work, from the work order header.

DAXQuoted Amount
Quoted Amount =
    SUM ( FactWorkOrder[QuotedAmount] )
Returns
38,100 across eight work orders. Header grain, and as a measure it stays correct in any visual, including one that lists labour lines underneath. What it will not do there is look correct. WO-1001 shows 3,000 against both of its labour rows, so a reader who adds the visible column by hand reaches 46,600 while the total row still reads 38,100.

Work order count at header grain.

DAXWork Order Count
Work Order Count =
    COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder )
Returns
8. By opened month: Jan 3, Feb 3, Mar 2. This counts headers, so it never fans out even when the visual also carries a technician.

Planned capacity, summed from the unpivoted capacity fact.

DAXPlanned Hours
Planned Hours =
    SUM ( FactCapacity[PlannedHours] )
Returns
176 over 28 rows. By station: MSP 90, TUS 50, LAS 20, PHX 16. By trade: Airframe 80, Avionics 44, Engine 39, NDT 13.

Cost measures

Cost is where the finance manager's three disagreeing numbers come from, and where the orphan in PartsIssued starts to matter. P-9007 charges 4,900 against WO-1009, and WO-1009 does not exist. Two different totals are both defensible. Carry both in the model, under names that say which is which, so that nobody has to guess what a visual is showing. What he gets is Total Cost Attributable at 29,671.50, with Orphan Parts Cost at 4,900 on the page beside it.

Parts cost restricted to lines that resolve to a real work order.

DAXParts Cost Attributable
Parts Cost Attributable =
    SUMX (
        FILTER (
            FactParts,
            NOT ISBLANK (
                RELATED ( FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID] )
            )
        ),
        FactParts[Qty] * FactParts[UnitCost]
    )
Returns
23,345, which is 28,245 less the 4,900 charged to WO-1009.
Choice
RELATED here. A relationship already exists from FactWorkOrder to FactParts, and RELATED follows it directly. LOOKUPVALUE would rescan the header table for every one of the seven lines and would still be wrong the day a work order number repeats.

The cost that fell out of the report, published as a number of its own.

DAXOrphan Parts Cost
Orphan Parts Cost =
    [Parts Cost] - [Parts Cost Attributable]
Returns
4,900. Put this on the data quality page. A number that is visible gets fixed at source. A number hidden inside a difference does not.

Total cost that can be charged against work actually on the books.

DAXActual Cost
Actual Cost =
    [Labor Cost] + [Parts Cost Attributable]
Returns
29,671.50, which is 6,326.50 plus 23,345. WO-1003 alone accounts for 13,879.00 of it.
Earlier form
Chapter 10 and Chapter 16 wrote this as [Labor Cost] + [Parts Cost], because neither chapter had built Parts Cost Attributable yet. The two agree on every work order row, since the orphan line belongs to no work order. They differ by 4,900 on the grand total, where the earlier form reads 34,571.50 and this one reads 29,671.50. The library keeps the attributable version so that the total reconciles against the rows above it, and keeps Orphan Parts Cost beside it so that the 4,900 is still reported somewhere.

Quote against actual, positive when the shop kept money.

DAXQuote Variance
Quote Variance =
    [Quoted Amount] - [Actual Cost]
Returns
38,100 less 29,671.50 gives 8,428.50 across the quarter. Two work orders are negative: WO-1002 by 105.00 and WO-1003 by 1,379.00.
Caution
WO-1004 and WO-1008 are still open, so their variance of 2,980.00 and 5,000.00 is not profit. Filter to closed work orders before anyone reads this as margin.

The same variance as a proportion of what was quoted.

DAXQuote Variance Pct
Quote Variance Pct =
    DIVIDE ( [Quote Variance], [Quoted Amount] )
Returns
8,428.50 divided by 38,100 is 0.2212, so 22.1 percent at the all up level.
Choice
DIVIDE here. A work order with a zero quote makes the slash operator raise an error, and that error propagates through every subtotal above it. DIVIDE returns blank and the visual keeps working.

Work order measures with role playing dates

The production controller has two pages open, built by two different people. One says February had 3 work orders. The other says February had 2. He wants to know which of his colleagues got it wrong. The answer is neither of them.

DimDate joins FactWorkOrder three times. That arrangement is called a role playing date: one calendar table, serving more than one date column on the same fact. OpenedDate is the active role. PromisedDate and ClosedDate are inactive, meaning they carry no filter until a measure asks for them by name. Each of the three measures below is the same count with a different relationship switched on, which is why they must never be given generic names. February has 3 opened, 2 closed and 3 promised, and the only work order that appears in all three sets is WO-1005. Both of the controller's pages are right. Both are missing one word in the title.

Work orders opened in the period, using the active relationship.

DAXWork Orders Opened
// The active DimDate[Date] to OpenedDate relationship applies
Work Orders Opened =
    COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder )
Returns
Jan 3, Feb 3, Mar 2, total 8. No modifier needed, which is exactly why the default role has to be the one the business asks about most often.

Work orders closed in the period, switching to the inactive ClosedDate join.

DAXWork Orders Closed
Work Orders Closed =
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ),
        USERELATIONSHIP (
            DimDate[Date],
            FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate]
        ),
        NOT ISBLANK ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
    )
Returns
Jan 2, Feb 2, Mar 2, total 6.
Why the predicate
Drop the NOT ISBLANK line and the monthly figures stay right while the total becomes 8. USERELATIONSHIP only changes which relationship a date filter travels down. On a grand total row there is no date filter to travel, so nothing excludes WO-1004 and WO-1008, and the measure quietly counts two work orders that have never closed.
Choice
USERELATIONSHIP here. A second copy of DimDate would also work. Every date slicer, every time intelligence measure and every drill path would then have to be built twice, and users would face two fields called Month.

Work orders promised in the period, which is the commitment view of the same eight work orders.

DAXWork Orders Promised
Work Orders Promised =
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ),
        USERELATIONSHIP (
            DimDate[Date],
            FactWorkOrder[PromisedDate]
        )
    )
Returns
Jan 2, Feb 3, Mar 3, total 8. Every work order has a promise, including the two that are still open, so this total matches the opened total while the monthly split does not.

Work orders with no close date, at whatever date the report is filtered to.

DAXOpen Work Orders
Open Work Orders =
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ),
        ISBLANK ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
    )
Returns
2, being WO-1004 and WO-1008.
Choice
A boolean predicate inside CALCULATE here. The predicate names one column, so the engine can turn it into a column filter and never materialise the table. FILTER over the whole fact would work on eight rows and would not work on eight million.

The complement, kept as its own measure so that ratios have a stable denominator.

DAXClosed Work Orders
Closed Work Orders =
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ),
        NOT ISBLANK ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
    )
Returns
6. Every on time and turn time measure below divides by this, never by Work Order Count, because an open work order has no turn time to average.
Not the same as
Work Orders Closed, above. That one counts work orders whose close date falls inside the selected period. This one counts work orders that have a close date at all, inside whatever the active OpenedDate relationship has already selected. Both read 6 on an unfiltered page. Slice to January and Work Orders Closed returns 2, being WO-1001 and WO-1002, while Closed Work Orders returns 3, being the three January openings that have since closed.

Average days from open to close, closed work orders only.

DAXAvg Turn Time Days
Avg Turn Time Days =
    AVERAGEX (
        FILTER (
            FactWorkOrder,
            NOT ISBLANK ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
        ),
        DATEDIFF (
            FactWorkOrder[OpenedDate],
            FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate],
            DAY
        )
    )
Returns
12.0 days. The six values are 10, 5, 22, 2, 30 and 3, summing to 72 over six work orders.
Choice
DATEDIFF here. Subtracting one date from the other returns a decimal number that carries any time component along with it, and it gives you no place to state the unit. DATEDIFF forces you to write DAY, which is the thing a reviewer needs to see.
Choice
AVERAGEX here. AVERAGE over a stored turn days column gives the same 12.0. The iterator version keeps the open work orders out of the denominator without needing a second column to hold the exclusion.

Work orders closed on or before the promised date.

DAXOn Time Work Orders
On Time Work Orders =
    COUNTROWS (
        FILTER (
            FactWorkOrder,
            NOT ISBLANK ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
                && FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate]
                    <= FactWorkOrder[PromisedDate]
        )
    )
Returns
3, being WO-1001, WO-1003 and WO-1005.
Choice
FILTER here. The condition compares two columns of the same table, and a boolean predicate inside CALCULATE may reference only one column. This is one of the few places where the iterator is not optional.

On time delivery as a share of work actually completed.

DAXOn Time Pct
On Time Pct =
    DIVIDE ( [On Time Work Orders], [Closed Work Orders] )
Returns
3 divided by 6, so 50.0 percent. Against all eight work orders it would read 37.5 percent, which would be a different and less useful claim.

Total days late across the quarter, counting only overruns.

DAXDays Late
Days Late =
    SUMX (
        FILTER (
            FactWorkOrder,
            NOT ISBLANK ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] )
        ),
        MAX (
            DATEDIFF (
                FactWorkOrder[PromisedDate],
                FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate],
                DAY
            ),
            0
        )
    )
Returns
9 days: WO-1002 by 3, WO-1006 by 5, WO-1007 by 1, and zero for the three that were on time.
Choice
The two argument form of MAX here. It compares two scalars and reads as a floor, so early deliveries contribute nothing instead of subtracting from the lateness of others. An IF says the same thing in more words.

Closures accumulated from the start of the year, or year to date, which is the one time intelligence measure this model needs. The name carries the abbreviation because that is what a reader scanning a field list expects to see.

DAXWork Orders Closed YTD
Work Orders Closed YTD =
    CALCULATE (
        [Work Orders Closed],
        DATESYTD ( DimDate[Date] )
    )
Returns
Jan 2, Feb 4, Mar 6. The quarter is the whole year in this dataset, so March and the grand total agree at 6.
Choice
DATESYTD rather than TOTALYTD. Both give the same six numbers. DATESYTD returns a table of dates that you hand to CALCULATE yourself. The role swap then sits where you can see it, inside the measure being shifted. TOTALYTD buries it in a wrapper function's second argument.
Order
Call the measure, do not inline its definition into a variable here. A variable holding the closed count is resolved before CALCULATE shifts the dates, so the shift would apply to a number that has already been computed and every month would read 2, 2, 2 again.
Cost
This returns blank on every row if DimDate is not marked as a date table, or if the calendar has a gap. It gives no error and no warning, which is why the marked date table check sits in the review list below.
Performance note

Three of the measures above wrap FILTER(FactWorkOrder, ...). On eight rows that is free. On a fact with tens of millions of rows, FILTER over the table forces a row by row scan with the full row context available. A single column predicate inside CALCULATE can often be pushed down into the storage engine instead. When you migrate these patterns to a real shop floor extract, rewrite anything that filters on one column, and leave the two column comparisons alone because they have no alternative.

Utilisation

The planner clicks 15 January on the date slicer and the utilisation card goes blank. She clicks 1 January and it comes back. She has decided the report only works on the first of the month, and that is closer to the truth than she realises.

Utilisation is the hardest thing in this model, and the DAX is the easy part of it. Labour is recorded per technician per day. Capacity is planned per trade per station per month. The relationship on MonthStart works when the report is filtered to a whole month or coarser. On any single day that is not the first of a month, it returns blank. The measure below papers over that, and you need to know exactly what it is doing before you put it in front of that planner.

Capacity for whatever months the current date filter touches.

DAXPlanned Hours Month Safe
Planned Hours Month Safe =
    CALCULATE (
        SUM ( FactCapacity[PlannedHours] ),
        REMOVEFILTERS ( DimDate ),
        TREATAS (
            VALUES ( DimDate[MonthStart] ),
            FactCapacity[MonthStart]
        )
    )
Line 4
REMOVEFILTERS(DimDate) drops the day level filter that the physical relationship cannot use.
Line 5
TREATAS puts the filter back at month grain. Filter arguments are evaluated in the context outside CALCULATE, so VALUES(DimDate[MonthStart]) still sees the original selection and returns 2025-01-01 for any day in January.
Returns
176 unfiltered. MSP January 30, TUS January 25, LAS March 20, PHX March 16.
Choice
TREATAS here. It applies an existing single column table as a filter without scanning the fact, and it does not require the relationship to be usable at day grain. FILTER(ALL(FactCapacity), ...) scans the whole fact to do the same job.
Cost
Filter to 2025-01-15 alone and this returns a full month of capacity against one day of labour. There is no honest daily number, because the source has none. Put "capacity is monthly" in the visual title and mean it. The planner's 15 January click now returns a figure, and the title tells her it is a month of capacity standing behind one day of work.

Hours booked against hours planned.

DAXUtilisation Pct
Utilisation Pct =
    DIVIDE ( [Labor Hours], [Planned Hours Month Safe] )
Returns
62.0 over 176, so 35.2 percent overall. MSP January 22.5 over 30 is 75.0 percent, TUS January 50.0 percent, MSP February 40.0 percent, TUS February 40.0 percent, LAS March 25.0 percent, MSP March and PHX March both zero.
Earlier name
Chapter 2 and Chapter 7 call this Utilisation and divide by the plain Planned Hours. Every figure above is identical under either denominator, because both read the same 176 planned hours at month grain or coarser. They part company only below month grain, where the plain Planned Hours returns blank for any day that is not the first of a month and Planned Hours Month Safe returns the whole month. Chapter 16 sets out four ways to handle that, and this measure is the second of them. That chapter folds the same TREATAS step into Planned Hours itself, keyed on MonthKey instead of MonthStart, and then keeps a guarded Utilisation that refuses to answer below month grain.

Planned hours at station and month combinations where nobody booked any time.

DAXIdle Planned Hours
Idle Planned Hours =
    SUMX (
        SUMMARIZE (
            FactCapacity,
            DimStation[StationCode],
            DimDate[MonthStart]
        ),
        VAR Planned = [Planned Hours]
        VAR Booked = [Labor Hours]
        RETURN
            IF ( Booked = 0, Planned, 0 )
    )
Returns
46 hours: MSP March 30 plus PHX March 16. Both are planned capacity that produced no recorded work.
Choice
SUMMARIZE over columns of DimStation and DimDate here. Grouping on the fact's own columns would give the right list of pairs. The engine then turns the row the iterator is standing on into a filter, a move called context transition, and that filter would reach FactCapacity only. FactLabor would stay unfiltered, because filters do not travel from the many side to the one side.

Heavy maintenance planning

The planner froze a baseline for WO-1003 weeks before the aircraft arrived: 13.0 hours of work. The check was released on 2025-02-05 having taken 12.5. Somewhere in between, production control revised the forecast to 16.5. Three numbers, one work order, and a meeting in which all three people believe theirs is the manhour figure.

Six measures settle that meeting. Nothing else in the library depends on them, and they depend on three tables the diagram above does not draw, because Meridian sends nine extracts and the diagram covers six. HMCCSchedule is the control board kept by the Heavy Maintenance Control Centre, one row per work order, and it is the only place ServiceLine and CheckType exist at all. Its four service lines are Heavy, Light, Line, and Cabin and IFE, where IFE stands for in-flight entertainment. It is merged into FactWorkOrder in Power Query. One row on each side makes it a one to one, and a one to one is a merge waiting to happen. HeavyPreInput is the pre-input pack, the tab a planner fills in weeks before the aircraft arrives, at one row per work order per trade, loaded as FactPreInput with 8 rows. ManhourForecast is production control's re-forecast, one row per work order per revision, loaded as FactForecast with 8 rows. Chapter B builds all six of these from the source rows and argues for each choice. What follows is the reference copy.

The three numbers underneath them are available, projected and achieved. Learn those three words, because this section uses them and nothing else. Available is what the pre-input pack said the work should take, frozen at induction so that performance has something stable to be measured against. That is the planner's 13.0.
