Projected is the current estimate of the final total, revised as findings land. A technician opens a panel, finds corrosion that no routine task card covers, raises a non-routine card, and the number moves. That is production control's 16.5. Each revision supersedes the one before it, so revisions are never added together. Achieved is booked time from the timesheet system, and of the three it is the one that records something that actually happened. That is the shop floor's 12.5. The function that owns the second number is that control centre, HMCC for short. Treat those four letters with more suspicion than you treat AOG, which means the same thing in every shop. Other shops call the identical function production control or the base maintenance control centre, and the line maintenance equivalent is usually MOC, Maintenance Operations Control.

The planner's frozen baseline, summed from the pre-input pack.

DAXAvailable Hours
Available Hours =
    SUM ( FactPreInput[PlannedHours] )
Returns
57.0 over eight rows. By work order, WO-1001 13.0, WO-1003 13.0, WO-1004 12.0, WO-1006 10.0 and WO-1008 9.0. By trade, Airframe 34.0, Avionics 4.0, Engine 5.0, Cabin 12.0 and NDT 2.0.
Choice
SUM here, for the same reason Planned Hours uses it. Each row is one trade on one work order, so no row overlaps another and available is fully additive across every dimension in the model. SUMX would add a scan and change nothing.
Watch the name
FactPreInput[PlannedHours] and FactCapacity[PlannedHours] are two different columns with one name. The first is demand, what the work needs. The second is supply, what the shop can staff. Utilisation compares them, so rename one of the two in Power Query before somebody drags the wrong field onto a chart and gets a number that looks reasonable.

Booked time, under the name production control reads it in.

DAXAchieved Hours
Achieved Hours =
    [Labor Hours]
Returns
62.0 unfiltered. By service line, Heavy 38.0, Cabin and IFE 10.0, Light 9.0 plus Line 5.0. Restricted to the five work orders that have a pre-input pack it is 48.0, and 48.0 plus 14.0 ties back to the 62.0 that every other measure in this library reports.
Same measure
Chapter B writes this out as SUM(FactLabor[Hours]), which is the definition of Labor Hours at the top of this library. Two definitions of one expression is a defect. One definition carrying a second name is fine, and the second name earns its place here. Put Labor Hours in a matrix beside Available Hours and Projected Hours, and the reader takes it for a different kind of number.

The current estimate of the final total, taking the newest revision of each work order and discarding the rest.

DAXProjected Hours
Projected Hours =
    SUMX (
        VALUES ( FactForecast[WorkOrderID] ),
        VAR LatestRevision =
            CALCULATE ( MAX ( FactForecast[RevisionDate] ) )
        RETURN
            CALCULATE (
                SUM ( FactForecast[ProjectedHours] ),
                FactForecast[RevisionDate] = LatestRevision
            )
    )
Line 3
VALUES returns the work orders visible in the current filter context. Five of them here, because only five work orders were ever forecast.
Lines 4 and 5
The bare CALCULATE performs a context transition. It turns the work order the iterator is standing on into a filter, so MAX returns the latest revision date for that one work order. An unfiltered MAX would return the latest date in the whole table.
Lines 7 to 10
The inner CALCULATE keeps the work order and replaces the date filter with the single date found above. One row survives per work order, and SUMX adds the five.
Returns
63.5, being WO-1001 14.0, WO-1003 16.5, WO-1004 12.0, WO-1006 13.5 and WO-1008 7.5. A plain SUM of the same table returns 99.5, which adds superseded revisions to live ones and describes nothing that ever happened.
Choice
MAX of the revision date here. MAX of the projected hours also returns 63.5, because every Meridian revision happens to move upwards, and it fails the first day a controller cuts a forecast after a finding turns out to be cosmetic. A measure that is right for the wrong reason cannot be tested, because the test passes. Filtering on the text Rev 1 is worse again: it loses the three work orders that were never revised, and it sorts Rev 10 ahead of Rev 2 the moment a check runs long.
Cost
This is semi additive, so the date selection decides which revision is the latest one, assuming you joined RevisionDate to the calendar. Slice to March and only the two work orders revised in March survive, 13.5 plus 7.5, so the card reads 21.0 and looks like the workload collapsed. That is arguably right, in that it answers what production control thought during March, and arguably wrong on a card labelled Projected Hours. Decide which, then say so on the visual. Chapter 16 covers the family.

The planner graded against the shop floor: what the plan said, over what the work took.

DAXPerformance Factor
// above 100 percent means the work came in under the
// frozen plan. Confirm the direction locally.
Performance Factor =
    DIVIDE ( [Available Hours], [Achieved Hours] )
Returns
94.7 percent across the three closed heavy checks, being 36.0 available over 38.0 achieved. WO-1001 reads 96.3 percent, WO-1003 104.0 percent and WO-1006 83.3 percent.
Direction
Plenty of shops invert this and divide achieved by available, so that a figure above 100 percent is bad news rather than good. Neither convention is more correct and both are in use. Ask production control which way they read it, write the answer into the measure description, and never assume the report you inherited used your convention.
Scope
Filter to closed heavy checks before anyone sees it. On an unfiltered page it divides 57.0 by 62.0 and reads 91.9 percent, which sets a plan that excludes light maintenance against hours that include it. The number is arithmetically fine and answers no question.
Choice
DIVIDE with no third argument, so a work order with no pre-input pack comes back blank instead of zero. Supply a zero and the three light work orders report a performance factor of zero percent, which reads as a team that achieved nothing against its plan. They had no plan. Those are different statements and only one of them starts an argument you cannot win.

Production control graded instead: what the work took, over what the last forecast said it would take.

DAXForecast Accuracy
// measured at close. Below 100 percent means the last
// forecast was too high.
Forecast Accuracy =
    DIVIDE ( [Achieved Hours], [Projected Hours] )
Returns
86.4 percent across the same three closed checks, being 38.0 achieved over 44.0 projected. WO-1001 reads 96.4 percent, WO-1003 75.8 percent and WO-1006 88.9 percent.
Read it with the one above
WO-1003 scores 104.0 percent on performance and 75.8 percent on forecast accuracy. The plan was sound, the check beat it, and the forecast written in between said 16.5 against an eventual 12.5, so it was 4.0 hours too high. That is a forecasting problem, and the pair of measures is what separates it from an execution problem. Either one on its own would have blamed the wrong department. That is the WO-1003 argument settled. The planner's 13.0 was sound, the shop beat it at 12.5, and the 16.5 written in between is the number that needs explaining.
Scope
Closed work only. On an open check the numerator is still growing, so the ratio starts near zero and climbs all week, and anybody reading it before the aircraft leaves is reading progress as accuracy.

What the current forecast still expects to be booked on work that has not finished.

DAXRemaining To Go
Remaining To Go =
    VAR Forecast = [Projected Hours]
    VAR Booked = [Achieved Hours]
    VAR IsOpen =
        ISBLANK (
            CALCULATE ( MAX ( FactWorkOrder[ClosedDate] ) )
        )
    RETURN
        IF (
            IsOpen && NOT ISBLANK ( Forecast ),
            Forecast - Booked
        )
Lines 2 and 3
Evaluate each measure once and hold it. Both are referenced below, and the forecast selection is the expensive one to repeat.
Lines 4 to 7
A work order with no close date is still in the hangar. ISBLANK of the maximum close date in the current context is true for WO-1004 and WO-1008 and false for the other six.
Lines 9 to 12
Two guards, and only one of them earns its keep against these eight rows. Drop the open test and closed checks report work still to come: WO-1003 would show 16.5 less 12.5, which is 4.0 hours outstanding on an aircraft released on 2025-02-05. The blank test changes nothing here, because every light work order is already closed and the open test catches it first. Keep it anyway. It is there for the first quarter in which a light job is still in the hangar at the cutoff. A blank forecast less 9.0 booked hours evaluates to minus 9.0, and the card then reports negative work outstanding.
Returns
9.5 hours, being 2.0 on WO-1004 (12.0 less 10.0) and 7.5 on WO-1008 (7.5 less 0.0). Without the guards the same subtraction totals 15.5 across the five forecast work orders, and 6.0 of that belongs to checks that were released weeks ago.
Choice
An IF with the else branch left out, so the result comes back blank. Zero would put a closed check on the same footing as an open check that is running exactly to forecast, and a production controller reads those two cells very differently at eight in the morning.
Rule of thumb

None of these words is standardised. Available is planned in one shop, budgeted in the next and sold in a third, and sold is the figure the customer was quoted, which is allowed to differ from the internal estimate on purpose. Projected is also called forecast, or estimate at completion. Achieved is actual, booked, expended or clocked. The same word can mean the frozen baseline in one report and the live forecast in the next, inside the same building. Before you write any of these six measures against a real extract, write down the local definition of each term. Get somebody in production control to agree it in writing. Paste it into the measure description, so that the definition travels with the model instead of living in your head.

Manpower planning

The cabin line missed February by one hour. The production controller wants to know why. The shift supervisor says his crew worked every hour it was given, and the planner who set the roster back in January has already moved on to March. All three of them are right, and the eight measures below are how you show that in a meeting instead of arguing about it.

These measures come from the resource planning side of the shop, which sends its own set of extracts again. The heavy maintenance section above took Meridian from six extracts to nine. Manpower planning sends six more, and five of them stay as tables of their own. RPODemand is what the central resource planning function asked the shop to deliver, at one row per service line per month, six rows and 75.0 hours. CrewRoster is attended hours, meaning hours people are rostered to be present and paid. It sits at the same service line and month grain, six rows and 109.0 hours. ProductivityFactor holds one row per service line, carrying the fraction of attended time that reaches a job card. DeptSubmission is the official month end figure each department reports upward, six rows and 63.0 hours. CrewCodeMap is the crew code to service line mapping you maintain by hand. The sixth file, CrewAssignment, says which crew each technician belongs to, and it merges onto DimTechnician because one row per technician is a one to one. Chapter C builds the planning chain from these rows and Chapter D builds the crew route. What follows is the reference copy.

The factor is the one number in this chain that people argue about, so read it slowly. Meridian books 0.88 for heavy and 0.68 for line, for light, and for cabin and IFE. Those two values are illustrative and they belong to Meridian. Every shop sets its own and reviews them, and heavy normally runs higher because a hangar crew works a continuous shift on one aircraft while a line crew waits for arrivals. The factor absorbs briefings, tool collection, travel to stand, waiting for access and paperwork. All of that is paid time. None of it lands on a job card.

What the resource planning function asked the shop to deliver.

DAXDemand Hours
// what the business asked for, before any roster exists
Demand Hours =
    SUM ( RPODemand[DemandHours] )
Returns
75.0 over six rows. Heavy 48.0, being 30.0 in January, 14.0 in February and 4.0 in March. Light 10.0, cabin and IFE 11.0, line 6.0.
Why SUM
One row per service line per month, and nothing on the row needs multiplying before it is added. SUMX would add a scan and return the same 75.0.
Cost
Demand is published for six service line and month combinations only. Filter to light in February and the measure comes back blank, because the planning function asked for no light work that month. Blank there means not asked for. A visual that prints zero instead is making a claim the source never made.

Hours the roster says people will be present and paid for.

DAXAttended Hours
// hours people are rostered to be present and paid
Attended Hours =
    SUM ( CrewRoster[AttendedHours] )
Returns
109.0 over six rows. Heavy 68.0, being 40.0, 20.0 and 8.0 across the three months. Light 16.0, cabin and IFE 15.0, line 10.0.
Why SUM
The roster already holds hours. Counting technicians and multiplying by a shift length would have to model part shifts, overtime and absence before it agreed with 109.0, and every one of those assumptions would be yours to defend.
Watch the word
Attended hours are paid presence. All 109.0 of them are on the payroll and only some of them reach a job card. The distance between those two statements is the next measure.

The ceiling: attended hours multiplied by the productivity factor for that service line.

DAXAchievable Hours
// attended times factor, the real ceiling.  87.72
Achievable Hours =
    SUMX (
        CrewRoster,
        CrewRoster[AttendedHours]
            * RELATED ( ProductivityFactor[Factor] )
    )
Lines 3 to 7
SUMX walks CrewRoster one row at a time. RELATED reads that row's factor from ProductivityFactor, which sits on the one side of a many to one relationship on the service line.
Returns
87.72. Row by row, heavy January is 40.0 times 0.88, which is 35.20. Light January is 16.0 times 0.68, which is 10.88. Heavy February is 20.0 times 0.88, which is 17.60. Cabin February is 15.0 times 0.68, which is 10.20. Line March is 10.0 times 0.68, which is 6.80. Heavy March is 8.0 times 0.88, which is 7.04.
Why SUMX
The factor changes with the service line, so the multiplication belongs inside the row. Summing attended hours first and multiplying once picks a single factor for all 109.0 hours, and no such factor exists in this shop.
Why RELATED
A relationship already runs from ProductivityFactor down to CrewRoster, and RELATED follows it from the many side. LOOKUPVALUE would rescan the factor table once per roster row to read the same four values.

The weighted ratio of those two, which is the number a planning pack gets wrong most often.

DAXOverall Productivity Factor
// weighted.  87.72 over 109.0 is 80.5 percent
Overall Productivity Factor =
    DIVIDE ( [Achievable Hours], [Attended Hours] )
Returns
87.72 divided by 109.0 is 0.80477, so 80.5 percent. The same two measures give the ratio for any service line, any month, or the whole quarter, because both halves are recomputed at whatever level the visual asks for.
The trap
Put the factor on the roster as a calculated column and average it and you get 4.68 divided by 6, which is 0.78, so 78.0 percent. Every row gets one vote. Heavy carries 68.0 of the 109.0 attended hours and the cabin row carries 15.0, so one vote each is the wrong arithmetic. This is the average of averages error and it is the most common wrong number in a planning pack.
Why DIVIDE
The slash operator would error on any service line with no roster hours at all, and that error travels up into every subtotal above it. DIVIDE returns blank and the visual keeps working.
Earlier name
Chapter C calls this Productivity Factor and writes both halves out as SUMX expressions. It is the same 80.5 percent. The library puts Overall in the name so that nobody reads it as Performance Factor above, which divides available hours by achieved hours and answers a question about a check rather than about a roster.

Achieved hours are booked time from the timesheet, and that measure is already in this library under heavy maintenance planning, where Achieved Hours reads [Labor Hours] and returns 62.0. The planning chain uses it unchanged. Across the six planning rows it reads heavy January 26.0, light January 9.0, heavy February 12.0, cabin February 10.0, line March 5.0 and heavy March 0.0. Those six add to 62.0, which ties back to every other total in this chapter.

The other achieved number, and the one the business actually reports.

DAXSubmitted Hours
// the official month end figure the department reported
Submitted Hours =
    SUM ( DeptSubmission[SubmittedHours] )
Returns
63.0 over six rows. Heavy 39.0, being 27.0, 12.0 and 0.0. Light 9.0, cabin and IFE 10.0, line 5.0.
Why a second measure
DeptSubmission and FactLabor measure the same hours on different days. The department submits at the month end cutoff and the timesheet keeps moving afterwards. Both get quoted in the same meeting, so both get a measure and a name that says which one it is.

The gap between the two achieved numbers, published as a number of its own.

DAXSubmission Variance
Submission Variance =
    VAR Submitted = [Submitted Hours]
    VAR Booked = [Achieved Hours]
    RETURN
        IF (
            NOT ISBLANK ( Submitted )
                || NOT ISBLANK ( Booked ),
            Submitted - Booked
        )
Returns
1.0 hour across the quarter, all of it on heavy January, where the department submitted 27.0 against 26.0 in the timesheet. One late booking was corrected after the submission cutoff.
Lines 5 to 9
The guard. On a service line and month where neither figure exists, a bare subtraction returns zero, and a zero variance reads as two systems agreeing. Blank reads as nothing to compare, which is the truth.
Earlier name
Chapter D writes the two inputs as Achieved Hours (Submitted) and Achieved Hours (Timesheet). That is the same pair of sums, under names built to sit next to each other in a field list. Same 1.0 hour.
Scope
This belongs on the data quality page beside Orphan Parts Cost. One hour is small, and it is the entire distance between two numbers that both get quoted as the achieved figure for January.

The last pair splits a missed target into the two things that cause it.

DAXStructural Shortfall, Execution Shortfall
// the roster was too small for the demand
Structural Shortfall =
    [Demand Hours] - [Achievable Hours]

// the crew did not convert the ceiling it was given
Execution Shortfall =
    [Achievable Hours] - [Achieved Hours]
Returns, cabin February
Demand 11.0, achievable 10.20, achieved 10.00. Structural shortfall is 11.0 less 10.20, which is 0.80. Execution shortfall is 10.20 less 10.00, which is 0.20. The two add to the 1.00 hour the line missed against demand, and four fifths of that miss was a rostering decision taken in January.
Returns, quarter
Structural shortfall reads 75.0 less 87.72, which is minus 12.72. Execution shortfall reads 87.72 less 62.0, which is 25.72. A negative structural shortfall means the roster gave more ceiling than the demand needed, which it did on five of the six rows.
Cost
A grand total nets the rows against each other, so the 0.80 that matters disappears into the minus 12.72. Put this pair on a matrix by service line and month. On a card it says nothing useful.
Why two measures
A single variance cannot say which of the two happened, and the two owners are different people. Resource scheduling owns the roster size. The shift supervisor owns the conversion. Give a meeting one number and it will pick an owner by seniority.
Cost again
Both measures stand on the factor, so both are worth exactly what the factor is worth. If 0.68 was set three years ago and nobody has looked at it since, structural shortfall is measuring an assumption and calling it a shortfall.
Common mistake

Averaging the productivity factor. It is the shortest route to a wrong number in this whole chapter, and it survives review because 78.0 percent and 80.5 percent both look like reasonable answers. Weight it by attended hours every time: divide 87.72 by 109.0, once, at whatever level the visual asks for. That rule already governs cost per hour and utilisation earlier in this library, and it will govern the next ratio anybody asks you for.

The planning chain traced by hand, all six rows

Six rows carry every number in this section. Read each one across: demand is what was asked for, attended is what was rostered, achievable is attended times the factor, achieved is what the timesheet recorded, and submitted is what the department reported at the month end.

  • Heavy, January. Demand 30.0, attended 40.0, factor 0.88, achievable 35.20, achieved 26.0, submitted 27.0. The one row in the quarter where the two achieved numbers disagree.
  • Light, January. Demand 10.0, attended 16.0, factor 0.68, achievable 10.88, achieved 9.0, submitted 9.0.
  • Heavy, February. Demand 14.0, attended 20.0, factor 0.88, achievable 17.60, achieved 12.0, submitted 12.0.
  • Cabin and IFE, February. Demand 11.0, attended 15.0, factor 0.68, achievable 10.20, achieved 10.0, submitted 10.0. The only row where demand sits above achievable.
  • Line, March. Demand 6.0, attended 10.0, factor 0.68, achievable 6.80, achieved 5.0, submitted 5.0.
  • Heavy, March. Demand 4.0, attended 8.0, factor 0.88, achievable 7.04, achieved 0.0, submitted 0.0.

Add the columns and you have the five totals the measures return: demand 75.0, attended 109.0, achievable 87.72, achieved 62.0, submitted 63.0. Three headline ratios fall straight out of them. Demand over achievable is 75.0 divided by 87.72, which is 85.5 percent, and it answers whether there was enough capacity for the ask. Achieved over achievable is 62.0 divided by 87.72, which is 70.7 percent, and it answers whether the capacity was used. Achieved over demand is 62.0 divided by 75.0, which is 82.7 percent, and it answers whether the shop delivered what was asked.

Run the cabin row backwards and the rostering decision turns into a number a planner can act on. Cabin and IFE was asked for 11.0 hours at a factor of 0.68, so the roster had to supply 11.0 divided by 0.68, which is 16.18 attended hours. It supplied 15.0. The line was 1.18 attended hours short before anybody picked up a tool, and 1.18 multiplied by 0.68 brings you back to the 0.80 of structural shortfall the measure reported. Same fact, stated in attended hours instead of achievable hours. Every other row in the quarter was covered: heavy January needed 34.09 against 40.0 rostered, light January 14.71 against 16.0, heavy February 15.91 against 20.0, line March 8.82 against 10.0, and heavy March 4.55 against 8.0.

Many to many and the bridge

The resourcing manager wants to know how much A&P work the shop did this quarter. You put certification down the rows and labour hours in the values. The four certification rows add to 85.0. The total row underneath them reads 62.0. He asks which figure he should quote, and both of them are correct.

Certifications are held by technicians, and technicians book hours. A bridge table is what sits between the two: one row per technician per certification held, which is BridgeTechCert in this model. Nothing in the data says which certification was actually used on which job, so any attribution of hours to a certification is an assumption. The first measure below makes that assumption visible. The second counts people instead of hours, which is usually the honest answer. The third allocates, which makes totals reconcile at the cost of inventing a fraction that no timesheet supports.

Hours belonging to technicians who hold the selected certification.

DAXHours With Certification
Hours With Certification =
    CALCULATE (
        [Labor Hours],
        CROSSFILTER (
            DimTechnician[TechnicianID],
            BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID],
            BOTH
        )
    )
Returns
A&P 39.0, Avionics 10.5, NDT 12.0, Engine Run 23.5. Those four add to 85.0 against a true total of 62.0.
Earlier name
Chapter 8 and Chapter 12 call this measure Hours by Certification and define it identically. Chapter 14 calls the same expression Hours Covered Scoped, to sit beside the two other implementations it compares there. The library renames it once more only so that it pairs with Technicians With Certification below. All three are one measure: A&P 39.0, Avionics 10.5, NDT 12.0, Engine Run 23.5, and 62.0 on a total row. Chapter 14 and Chapter 15 also give TREATAS forms that need no bidirectional hop at all and return the same four row values. Their totals are the thing to watch. Hours Covered Virtual in Chapter 14 restricts the total to certified staff and prints 52.0. The Chapter 15 version wraps the traversal in ISFILTERED, so its total comes back to 62.0. Both chapters say which they are doing and why.
Choice
CROSSFILTER inside the measure here. Set the relationship to both directions in the model and the double counting spreads across the whole file. Written into the measure, it exists only where a certification is on the axis, and every other measure keeps a single unambiguous filter path.

Technicians holding the selected certification, which is additive in a way hours are not.

DAXTechnicians With Certification
Technicians With Certification =
    DISTINCTCOUNT ( BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID] )
Returns
A&P 3, Avionics 3, NDT 2, Engine Run 2, and 6 with no certification selected. The row values still add to more than 6, because the same people are counted under several certifications, but nobody reads a headcount as a sum without checking.

The overlap, stated as a number so the reader knows how much of the difference is real.

DAXCertification Overlap Hours
Certification Overlap Hours =
    VAR AcrossCerts =
        SUMX (
            VALUES ( DimCertification[CertCode] ),
            [Hours With Certification]
        )
    VAR Covered = [Hours With Certification]
    RETURN
        AcrossCerts - Covered
Returns
85.0 less 62.0, so 23.0 hours of overlap. That figure is the entire distance between a bridge table and a lie, and it is the number to hand the resourcing manager alongside the 85.0.
Choice
VALUES inside the iterator here, so that the overlap responds to a certification slicer. ALL would ignore the slicer entirely. Pick two certifications and the measure reports the overlap between those two, which is the question a resourcing manager actually asks.
Choice
The subtrahend is [Hours With Certification]. Using [Labor Hours] there looks identical at first, because both read 62.0 on an unfiltered page, and the difference stays invisible until somebody uses the slicer the line above promises. Select A&P and NDT: the iterator adds 39.0 and 12.0 to reach 51.0, and the honest comparison is the 39.0 hours belonging to the four technicians who hold either certification, which leaves 12.0 of overlap. Subtracting a flat 62.0 there would return minus 11.0, and a negative overlap is not a number anyone can act on.
The allocation variant, and the arithmetic that makes it reconcile

Allocation divides each technician's hours by the number of certifications they hold, then gives each certification its share. Totals reconcile. The individual numbers describe nothing that happened.

DAXAllocated Hours
Allocated Hours =
    SUMX (
        CALCULATETABLE (
            VALUES ( DimTechnician[TechnicianID] ),
            CROSSFILTER (
                DimTechnician[TechnicianID],
                BridgeTechCert[TechnicianID],
                BOTH
            )
        ),
        VAR CertsHeld =
            CALCULATE (
                COUNTROWS ( BridgeTechCert ),
                REMOVEFILTERS ( DimCertification )
            )
        VAR CertsInScope =
            CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( BridgeTechCert ) )
        VAR HoursForTech = [Labor Hours]
        RETURN
            DIVIDE ( HoursForTech * CertsInScope, CertsHeld )
    )
Mechanism
The iterator moves one technician at a time, so [Labor Hours] is that technician's hours through context transition. CertsHeld ignores the certification filter and counts everything the person holds. CertsInScope counts only the certifications on the axis, which is 1 in a normal matrix row.
Returns
A&P 26.0, Avionics 3.5, NDT 6.0, Engine Run 16.5. Those add to 52.0, which is the total for known technicians.
Earlier form
Chapter 14 calls this Labor Hours Allocated and iterates BridgeTechCert instead of the technician list, with DIVIDE ( TechHours, CertCount ) and no CertsInScope factor. It returns the same four figures and the same 52.0. Chapter 14 also warns that swapping its bridge iterator for a technician iterator drops the total to 39.0, and that warning applies to the expression written there. This one behaves differently, because CertsInScope puts the multiplier back, so a technician holding three certifications contributes all three thirds on a total row instead of one.

Read the last row carefully before you ship this. The allocated total is 52.0 and the real total is 62.0, because the ten hours booked by the unknown technician TECH-07 have no certifications to be divided between. Allocation always leaks somewhere. Here it leaks exactly where the data quality problem is, which is the one place a leak is tolerable.

Percent of total variants

The finance manager asks for MSP's share of labour hours. Three percent of total measures are already on the page. One reads 55.6%, one reads 60.5%, and the third moves the moment he touches the station slicer. He wants to know which one is right. All three are.

Four measures, four different denominators, all built on Labor Hours. Choosing the wrong one is the most common way a correct model produces a wrong report, because every version returns a plausible percentage. Name the denominator in the measure name, and put that name on the visual. Then the answer to his question is whichever measure divides by the thing he meant.

Share of everything in the model, regardless of any filter on the page.

DAXPct of All Hours
Pct of All Hours =
    DIVIDE (
        [Labor Hours],
        CALCULATE ( [Labor Hours], REMOVEFILTERS () )
    )
Returns
MSP is 34.5 divided by 62.0, which is 0.5565, so 55.6 percent. It stays 55.6 percent even if the page is filtered to January, which is either exactly what you want or a serious bug.

Share within the station column only, leaving every other filter intact.

DAXPct of Station
Pct of Station =
    DIVIDE (
        [Labor Hours],
        CALCULATE (
            [Labor Hours],
            REMOVEFILTERS ( DimStation )
        )
    )
Returns
Station shares that respond to a date slicer. In January the denominator is 35.0, where the measure above would use 62.0. MSP January therefore reads 22.5 over 35.0.
Choice
REMOVEFILTERS here. It behaves identically to ALL as a CALCULATE modifier. REMOVEFILTERS cannot be misread as returning a table, which matters when someone else edits your measure at speed.

Share of what the user can currently see, which follows the station slicer but not the row axis.

DAXPct of Visible Hours
Pct of Visible Hours =
    DIVIDE (
        [Labor Hours],
        CALCULATE (
            [Labor Hours],
            ALLSELECTED ( DimStation )
        )
    )
Returns
Station percentages that always add to 100 within the visual. A column of shares that adds to 100 is taken to be this measure, whichever of the four actually produced it.
Against Pct of Station
The two agree until somebody selects a subset of stations. Slice to MSP and TUS and this measure divides MSP by 57.0, the total of what is on screen, so MSP reads 60.5 percent. Pct of Station divides the same 34.5 by 62.0 and reads 55.6 percent, because REMOVEFILTERS throws the selection away instead of restoring it.
Choice
ALLSELECTED(DimStation) here, with the table named. Put months down the rows and stations across the columns. The scoped form releases only the station grouping, so each month row adds to 100 percent. A bare ALLSELECTED() releases the month grouping too, so every cell becomes a share of the whole matrix and only the grand total reaches 100.

Share of the level above, for a matrix with more than one field on the rows.

DAXPct of Parent
Pct of Parent =
    VAR Numerator = [Labor Hours]
    VAR Denominator =
        SWITCH (
            TRUE (),
            ISINSCOPE ( DimTechnician[TechnicianName] ),
                CALCULATE (
                    [Labor Hours],
                    REMOVEFILTERS ( DimTechnician )
                ),
            ISINSCOPE ( DimStation[StationCode] ),
                CALCULATE (
                    [Labor Hours],
                    REMOVEFILTERS ( DimStation )
                ),
            [Labor Hours]
        )
    RETURN
        DIVIDE ( Numerator, Denominator )
Returns
On a station then technician matrix, TECH-02 inside MSP reads 16.5 over 34.5. MSP itself reads 34.5 over 62.0. The grand total reads 100 percent.
Choice
ISINSCOPE rather than HASONEVALUE. HASONEVALUE is true whenever a column happens to be filtered to one member, including by a slicer, so a single station selection would make the measure think it is on the technician level. ISINSCOPE tests grouping, which is the actual question.
Order
The SWITCH conditions run deepest level first. Reverse them and every technician row is divided by the station total's parent instead of by the station.

Data quality measures

These belong on a page that only you and the data owner look at. They exist so that a broken source shows up as a number on a screen, weeks before somebody discovers it in a board meeting. Three of them count keys that failed to match, and in a model whose sources agree all three read zero: hours booked to an unknown technician, work orders with no station, and orphan parts lines. None of the three reads zero here. The other two count dimension members that have no facts. That is a legitimate state, and it earns a place on this page anyway, because a figure that has read 2 all quarter and suddenly reads 4 is telling you something changed upstream.

Hours booked by a technician who is not in the HR extract.

DAXHours On Unknown Technician
Hours On Unknown Technician =
    CALCULATE (
        [Labor Hours],
        DimTechnician[TechnicianName] = "Unknown technician"
    )
Returns
10.0 hours, all of them L-506 booked by TECH-07. Known technicians account for 52.0 of the 62.0 total.

Work orders that arrived with no station on them.

DAXWork Orders Without Station
Work Orders Without Station =
    CALCULATE (
        COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ),
        DimStation[StationCode] = "UNASSIGNED"
    )
Returns
1, being WO-1005. It carries 1,875 of parts cost and no labour at all, so it disappears from any station report that filters the blank away instead of mapping it.

Dimension members that have never appeared on a work order.

DAXAircraft With No Work Orders
Aircraft With No Work Orders =
    COUNTROWS (
        FILTER (
            VALUES ( DimAircraft[ACREG] ),
            ISBLANK (
                CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( FactWorkOrder ) )
            )
        )
    )
Returns
2, being N120CE and N553KD. Both are legitimate. The registry lists aircraft the shop has not touched this quarter, and a dimension is allowed to be ahead of its facts.
Choice
The bare CALCULATE(COUNTROWS(...)) is there for context transition. Without it the inner count would ignore the row of the iterator entirely and return 8 every time.

The same test, run against people.

DAXTechnicians With No Hours
Technicians With No Hours =
    COUNTROWS (
        FILTER (
            VALUES ( DimTechnician[TechnicianID] ),
            ISBLANK ( [Labor Hours] )
        )
    )
Returns
2, being TECH-03 and TECH-06. Both are real staff with no timesheet lines in the quarter, which makes it a question for the roster. The model is behaving correctly.

Parts issue lines that point at a work order number nobody has ever seen.

DAXOrphan Parts Lines
Orphan Parts Lines =
    COUNTROWS (
        FILTER (
            FactParts,
            ISBLANK (
                RELATED ( FactWorkOrder[WorkOrderID] )
            )
        )
    )
Returns
1, being P-9007 against WO-1009 for 4,900. One row out of seven, and 4,900 of 28,245 by value, which is 17.3 percent of parts spend.
Why this and not that

Almost every measure above uses CALCULATE rather than a plain aggregation with a visual level filter. The reason is portability. A visual level filter lives in one visual on one page, cannot be tested or reused, and disappears the moment somebody copies the chart onto a new page. The filter written inside the measure travels with the measure, appears in the definition when a reviewer reads it, and behaves identically in a card, a matrix and an export. The cost is that the filter no longer shows up in the filter pane. A reader who wonders why Closed Work Orders shows 6 while Work Order Count shows 8 has to open the measure to find out. Name measures so that the question does not arise.

Filter modifier quick reference

Most of these are arguments you pass to CALCULATE to change the filter context instead of adding to it. The last three are table functions and a level test that turn up in the same measures, and the table says where each one belongs. The trap column is the failure each one causes most often in a real report.

Interview-level insight

Asked to explain the difference between ALL and ALLSELECTED, the stock answer is that one ignores filters and the other respects them. That is close enough to be wrong. Both remove filters. The difference is where they get the replacement from: ALL replaces the filter with nothing, and ALLSELECTED replaces it with the filter state that existed before the visual added its own row and column grouping. That is why ALLSELECTED gives 62.0 as a denominator with no slicers applied and 35.0 when January is selected, while ALL gives 62.0 in both cases.

Cardinality and direction quick reference

Six settings, and the whole model is built from them. Every one of the sixteen Meridian relationships is many to one and single direction. Two of them, the PromisedDate and ClosedDate date roles, are switched off, and no relationship anywhere in the model filters in both directions.

Function choice at a glance

No function goes into a measure without a reason it beat the obvious alternative, and a reviewer is entitled to ask for that reason on any line. Here are the answers for the functions this library uses to aggregate, iterate and test. The filter modifiers have their own table above and are argued for there.

Where does this work belong

The compact version of the layer table from Chapter 4. If you can only remember one rule, remember this one. Anything that has to appear on an axis, in a slicer or in a sort order must be a column. Anything whose value depends on what the user selected must be a measure.

Fifteen point measure review

The model level review is in Chapter 20. This one is for the DAX. Run it on every measure before it goes into a report that someone else will read. Run it again on any measure that produced a number a stakeholder questioned. A measure that has been questioned once will be questioned again.

  1. Does the name say which date role and which denominator it uses? Work Orders Closed and Work Orders Opened are two measures, never one measure and a bookmark.
  2. Does it return the answer key figure with no filters at all? If Labor Hours is not 62.0 on an empty page, nothing downstream is worth checking.
  3. Does the total equal the sum of the rows, and if not, do you know precisely why? Certification rows adding to 85.0 against a total of 62.0 is acceptable only when it is labelled.
  4. Does every division use DIVIDE? Search the definition for a slash character.
  5. Does every ratio divide a sum by a sum, rather than averaging a per row ratio?
  6. Is every filter modifier scoped to a named table or column? A bare REMOVEFILTERS() should appear only in a measure whose name contains the words all or model wide.
  7. Does the measure survive a date slicer? Set the page to February and check that the number moves in the direction you expect, and by how much.
  8. Does it survive a station slicer, a technician slicer, and both at once?
  9. Does it behave in a card as well as in a table? A card evaluates once, at the top, with no grouping to lean on.
  10. Does it behave at a matrix subtotal? Add the children by hand for one group and compare.
  11. Are there any hidden iterators over a whole fact table that could be a single column predicate instead?
  12. Does it reference a calculated column that could have been made in Power Query? If so, note the refresh cost and decide deliberately.
  13. Does it handle blank inputs the way the audience needs? Blank and zero mean different things, and WO-1008 with no activity is not the same as a work order with zero cost.
  14. Is the format string set on the measure itself, so that every visual inherits it? A percentage that only looks like a percentage in one chart will be exported as a raw decimal.
  15. Can you explain the measure out loud, in one sentence, without reading the code? If not, split it into two measures and let one call the other.
Rule of thumb

Point two of that list catches more defects than the other fourteen combined. Before you write a single measure against a new model, build a table with the four base aggregates and no slicers, and compare it against figures you calculated by hand from the source. It takes ten minutes. Skipping it means every later number you check has two possible explanations, and you will spend a day telling them apart.

What to do next

Rebuild the Meridian model from the six raw tables without looking at the answers. Compare every figure against the key in one table. Pay attention to which ones you got wrong, and let the count of them go, because the pattern is what teaches you something. Write the grain of each table into its description field in model view, in the form one row per technician per work order per day. Grain is the one fact about a table that everybody forgets and nobody can reconstruct from a screenshot. Then do the same on a model of your own, with your own data, where you cannot check the answer at the back of the book, and where the missing station code belongs to a person you can go and talk to. This document has covered the modelling core: grain, keys, relationships, filter context, role playing dimensions, many to many, and the diagnosis of each of those when it goes wrong. It has not covered composite models and the mixed storage modes that come with them, user defined aggregations over a large fact, incremental refresh policies and partitioning, row level security beyond the shape of the problem, or calculation groups past the brief treatment in Chapter 13. Those five sit on top of what you have just learned, and each one is a poor idea in a model whose grain and keys are not already correct. When you meet them, you will meet them because a model that works has become too slow or too large, which is a better problem than the one you started with.

What to remember
  • Diagnose in the order symptom, cause, check, fix. The check column exists to rule causes out, and applying a fix first destroys the evidence you would need if it was the wrong fix.
  • Every measure in the library is a base aggregate plus a filter change. If you know what Labor Hours returns and what the modifier does, you can predict the result before you run it.
  • Name measures after their denominator and their date role. Pct of All Hours and Pct of Visible Hours differ by one modifier, agree on an unfiltered page, and disagree the moment anybody touches a slicer.
  • Many to one, single direction is the default. Bidirectional filtering belongs in one measure, through CROSSFILTER. Set it in the model and it reaches visuals you have not built yet.
  • 62.0 hours, 6,326.50 labour cost, 28,245 parts, 176 planned hours, 8 work orders. Check these four aggregates and the count against a new build before you write anything else.
  • Utilisation at day grain is not available in this data, and no DAX will create it. Say so in the visual title. A measure that stays silent is making a promise the data cannot keep.
  • Demand 75.0, attended 109.0, achievable 87.72, achieved 62.0, submitted 63.0. Five words, five numbers, and the productivity factor is the only bridge between attended and achievable. Weight that factor by attended hours or it reads 78.0 percent instead of 80.5.
Appendix

EYour shop, mapped onto this document

After this appendix you will be able to translate every Meridian term into the word your own shop uses, and model a service line that carries two reporting groupings. You will also keep a report working when somebody edits its source workbook under you, and walk into a maintenance system migration with your headline numbers already written down.

The shift supervisor stops at your desk holding a printout of your report. One column is headed Available hours and it reads 57.0. His whiteboard uses the word Estimate, and it reads 57.0 too. He wants to know why you renamed his number, and whether this report is even about his hangar. Two words, one number, half an hour gone. This appendix is the translation layer that stops that conversation happening a second time.

Start with the shop those numbers come from. Meridian Aero Services is invented, and it was invented on purpose. Every table in this document belongs to a fictional shop with eight work orders, six technicians and three months of history. None of it came from a real operator or a real customer contract. You can copy a Meridian table into an email or argue about it in a meeting, and there is nobody whose commercial data you have just moved.

That freedom is also why the sample data is deliberately broken in places. A blank station code. An aircraft registration that matches nothing. A technician key with a trailing space. In a real extract those faults are somebody's problem. In Meridian they are teaching material, and you can break them open in public.

The cost of an invented shop is that its vocabulary was chosen for it. Your shop will call some of these things by other names. It will also use one or two of these names for something else entirely. This appendix maps the Meridian words onto the words you will hear on the hangar floor. Then it works through the four places where that mapping gets hard. A service line that carries two reporting groupings. A service line that nobody stores at all. A planning workbook that its owner edits while your report reads it. And the quarter the maintenance system gets replaced.

1. The vocabulary map

The finance manager calls on the last working day of the month. He wants one number from you: how many hours did the shop do this quarter. You have three defensible answers sitting in front of you and he wants a single figure for a slide. Hold that request for a moment. You cannot answer him until you can name all three, and the table below is where the names live.

Aviation regulation is standardised. Aviation vocabulary is not. Two shops twenty miles apart will use different words for the same number, and the same word for two different numbers, and both will be certain that theirs is the industry standard. Read the middle column below as likely. Your own shop gets the final say on every row of it. The right column says where the concept lives in the Meridian model, and says so plainly when Meridian holds nothing for it at all.

Three of those rows will get you into an argument if you use them loosely. Available, projected and achieved are the three manhour numbers, and they are the words people use most carelessly. In Meridian they are 57.0, 63.5 and 62.0 hours. Three numbers, one quarter of work, all three correct.

So the finance manager gets a question back before he gets a figure. Which of the three does he mean? If he wants what the shop actually did, that is achieved, 62.0 hours, and the word achieved goes on the slide next to it. If he wants what the shop said it would do, that is available, 57.0, and it covers only the five work orders that had a pre-input pack. Ask before you build anything. The build is the cheap part and the retraction is not.

The shift supervisor from the top of this appendix gets his answer from one row of the same table. Estimate is his word for what this document calls available hours. Both read 57.0 because both come off the same pre-input pack, and nobody renamed his number. Whether the report is about his hangar is the harder half of his question, and section 3 answers it.

Productivity factor is the next word worth pinning down. It measures the fraction of attended time that reaches a job card, and it absorbs briefings, tool collection, walking to the stand and paperwork. Meridian uses 0.88 for heavy work and 0.68 for line, light and cabin work. Those two values are illustrative, chosen for this document. Every shop sets its own and reviews them periodically. People hear the name as a verdict on how hard the crew works, so say what the factor actually measures out loud every time you put it on a page.

Turnaround time has a start and a stop that people quietly disagree about. Meridian measures ClosedDate minus OpenedDate. Over the six closed work orders that averages 12.0 days. Now move one date. Measure WO-1003 from the HMCC planned start of 2025-01-13 instead of the actual induction on 2025-01-14, and its turn time becomes 23 days. The total moves from 72 days to 73. The average becomes 73 divided by 6, which is 12.17 days. One row, one day, and a headline average that two people now quote differently.

Rule of thumb

Before you publish a number, write its definition in one sentence, name the table it comes from, and get the person who owns that table to agree the sentence in writing. An email is enough. Do it once per term and you spend the next two years pointing at the email instead of re-arguing the definition from memory.

2. The four service lines, and the clubbing problem

The production controller stops you after a review. Your chart says base maintenance did 48.0 hours in the quarter. The pack he circulates every Monday says heavy did 38.0. He wants to know which one is wrong. Both are right, and by the end of this section you will be able to say why in one sentence.

A shop of any size runs several service lines, and four is the common set. Take them one at a time, because the first two get conflated constantly by people who work in neither.

Line maintenance happens on the ramp, at the gate or on a stand, driven by arrivals. Transit checks, defect rectification, a tyre, an AOG recovery. AOG means aircraft on ground: the aircraft cannot fly, and it costs its operator money every hour that stays true. Line work runs from minutes to a shift, and the work is only known when the defect is reported.

Light maintenance is a short planned input, usually in a hangar, often overnight. Scheduled service checks and defect clearance, with its own crew and its own bay. Outsiders hear both of these as the quick stuff and club them together. They are two service lines with different crews, different bays and different planning behaviour, and a shop that runs both reports them separately.

Heavy maintenance is base maintenance. The aircraft is out of service in a bay for days to weeks, jacked and opened up. Its economics are dominated by findings that nobody could estimate in advance.

Cabin and IFE covers seats, monuments, panels, carpets and in-flight entertainment. IFE means In-Flight Entertainment: the head-end servers, the seat-back units and the wiring between them. Most of this work is a modification embodied under an STC or a service bulletin. STC means Supplemental Type Certificate, an approval for a design change to an aircraft that is already certified. So cabin work sits in a hangar and looks like heavy maintenance from the outside, while being a different job with a different trade mix.

Heavy
38.0 hours
Light
9.0 hours
Line
5.0 hours
Cabin and IFE
10.0 hours

Meridian's quarter splits across those four lines as shown above, and they add to 62.0 hours, which ties to the grand total of achieved hours. Now the grouping. Heavy and Cabin and IFE are both hangar work with the aircraft out of service, so most shops club them together and call the pair base maintenance. Line and Light are the non-base pair. That gives a second, coarser view of exactly the same 62.0 hours.

Do the arithmetic in your head once. Base is 38.0 plus 10.0, which is 48.0. Non-base is 9.0 plus 5.0, which is 14.0. Base plus non-base is 48.0 plus 14.0, which is 62.0. The two views agree at the top and differ only in how many rows they show. That equality is the diagnostic. When two breakdowns of a number agree at the grand total and disagree only in their row labels, you are looking at two groupings of one dimension.

Which gives the production controller his sentence. Both figures are achieved hours: his 38.0 is the Heavy service line on its own, and your 48.0 is Heavy plus the 10.0 hours of Cabin and IFE, grouped together as base maintenance. Say that, show him the four rows, and the argument is over in a minute.

Here is where it gets awkward in practice. Cabin and IFE moves. Some months the pack reports it inside base maintenance, because the aircraft was in a bay and the finance manager wants base against non-base. Other months it is broken out on its own, because a retrofit programme is running and the customer wants to see it separately. Both are legitimate, and both will be asked for by the same person in the same week.

The modelling answer is short. Two groupings over one dimension means two columns on one dimension table. Build a second table instead and you buy yourself the failure described at the end of this section.

Dimension DimServiceLine has one row per service line. Apply the grain test from Chapter 1. Grain means the one thing that a single row of a table stands for. Here the grain is one row per service line. ReportingGroup is completely determined by ServiceLine, so it is an attribute at that grain and it belongs on that row. SortOrder is there because alphabetical ordering puts Cabin and IFE first, which nobody in a hangar reads as sensible.

Two report-side mechanisms let the reader switch views. A hierarchy with ReportingGroup above ServiceLine gives drill down: the visual opens on two rows, Base 48.0 and Non-base 14.0, and the user drills into four. A field parameter is the other option. A field parameter is a small table you create that holds a list of fields. Put it on a slicer and the user chooses which column the visual groups by, so the same chart shows two rows or four depending on what they picked. Both mechanisms read from the one dimension table, so both stay consistent with each other.

Now the failure mode, because it is common and it is expensive. Somebody decides that base and non-base deserve their own table. They build DimReportingGroup with two rows, push a ReportingGroup column onto the fact so it can be joined, and relate it. Two objects in the model now claim to define what base maintenance means. In March a decision is taken that cabin retrofits should be reported outside base while the programme runs. Somebody edits DimServiceLine. Nobody edits DimReportingGroup. From that day the service line report says base is 38.0 and the group report says base is 48.0. Both refresh cleanly. The difference is exactly the 10.0 hours of cabin work, and nothing in either report shows a defect. You will spend a morning finding it, and you will find it again next year.

Interview-level insight

"How do you model two different hierarchies over the same set of members?" is a standard modelling question, and the answer is one dimension table with one row per member and one column per grouping, surfaced with a hierarchy or a field parameter. The follow up separates people: what happens when the two groupings disagree. With one table they cannot disagree, because there is one row per member and one place to edit it.

3. Deriving the service line when nobody stores it

The shift supervisor wants his own crew's hours for the quarter. You hand him the Line figure, 5.0. He puts his pen on it and says that cannot be right, because TECH-05 works for him and TECH-05 booked more than that on his own. He is right. So are you. Table E.4 is the reason, and the fix turns out to be a naming decision.

Meridian is generous about service line, so start with what it gives you. Its HMCCSchedule extract carries a ServiceLine column, and every work order arrives already labelled. Plenty of shops carry nothing of the kind. The work order has no service line, the check type is free text, and what you actually hold is a crew code against each technician. You ask the resource manager and he tells you from memory that CRW-AF1 is the airframe heavy crew and CRW-LN1 is the line team. It has been in his head for years, and no system holds it.

Meridian models that situation too. CrewAssignment has seven rows, one crew code per technician. CrewCodeMap has six rows and turns a crew code into a service line, and the dataset records its source as built by the analyst, held by no system. That is you. You own it.

Before the mechanics, one warning that will save you a bad meeting. Deriving the service line from the crew gives a different answer from taking it off the work order, and both answers are right.

Take one row and the disagreement stops being mysterious. TECH-05 belongs to CRW-LN1, the line crew, and booked 13.0 hours in the quarter. Of those, 8.0 hours went on WO-1003, which is a heavy C-check, and 5.0 hours went on WO-1007, which is line work. Route A splits those 13.0 hours across two service lines because it follows the work order. Route B puts all 13.0 on Line because it follows the person.

That is the shift supervisor's answer, and it is the Route B column. His crew booked 13.0 hours, and 8.0 of them went on somebody else's C-check. Both routes are correct. They answer two different questions, and they must be two differently named measures, because the moment they share a name somebody will drop them into the same visual.

Now the mechanics, in short form. The full treatment of hand-maintained mapping tables is Chapter D. What matters here is the shape of the thing you build.

The wrong way

Merge the crew code onto DimTechnician, then write the mapping into a DAX calculated column as a chain of nested IF calls.

DAXCrew Service Line, the version nobody can review
-- calculated column on DimTechnician
Crew Service Line =
    IF ( DimTechnician[CrewCode] = "CRW-AF1",
        "Heavy",
    IF ( DimTechnician[CrewCode] = "CRW-AV1",
        "Heavy",
    IF ( DimTechnician[CrewCode] = "CRW-CAB",
        "Cabin and IFE",
    IF ( DimTechnician[CrewCode] = "CRW-LN1",
        "Line",
    IF ( DimTechnician[CrewCode] = "CRW-LT1",
        "Light",
        "Other" ) ) ) ) )
The five branches
One per crew code. Adding CRW-LT2 means editing DAX and republishing the model.
The last line
Every unknown code falls into "Other". CRW-XX9 lands there quietly, and the label tells nobody that a code was missed.
The real defect
The resource manager is the only person who knows these codes, and he cannot read this. So it never gets reviewed, and it drifts out of date without anybody noticing.
The fix

Keep the mapping as a two column table and merge it in Power Query, with the unmatched case labelled out loud.

MDimTechnician, with crew and service line merged in
let
    Source = Technicians,
    WithCrew = Table.NestedJoin(Source, {"TechnicianID"},
        CrewAssignment, {"TechnicianID"},
        "crew", JoinKind.LeftOuter),
    CrewCol = Table.ExpandTableColumn(WithCrew, "crew",
        {"CrewCode"}),
    WithLine = Table.NestedJoin(CrewCol, {"CrewCode"},
        CrewCodeMap, {"CrewCode"},
        "map", JoinKind.LeftOuter),
    LineCol = Table.ExpandTableColumn(WithLine, "map",
        {"ServiceLine"}, {"CrewServiceLine"}),
    Labelled = Table.ReplaceValue(LineCol, null,
        "Unmapped crew code",
        Replacer.ReplaceValue, {"CrewServiceLine"})
in
    Labelled
WithCrew
A left outer join keeps every technician even when the roster system has no crew for them. An inner join drops those people and your hours stop reconciling to 62.0.
WithLine
The second join reads CrewCodeMap, the table you maintain. It is data, so anybody can open it, and it can live in a shared workbook the resource manager edits himself.
Labelled
Unmatched crew codes come back as null. Replacing null with the text "Unmapped crew code" puts a visible label on the axis, so the 10.0 hours on CRW-XX9 appear as a named row somebody will ask about.
Why this and not that

Two DAX alternatives look tidier than the nested IF chain and both keep the defect. SWITCH ( TRUE(), ... ) flattens the nesting and reads better, and the mapping is still written in a formula that only a report developer can open. LOOKUPVALUE is the honest DAX way to read a mapping table, and it earns its place when the mapping has to be evaluated at query time, for example when the user picks the mapping with a slicer. Here it does not: the crew a technician belongs to does not change when somebody clicks something. So the join belongs at refresh time in Power Query, where it is computed once, stored as a plain text column, and compressed like any other low cardinality column. The deciding argument is reviewability. A two column table can be read and corrected by the one person who knows the codes, and a formula cannot.

Rule of thumb

Any mapping table you own gets three things: a row for every code you have ever seen including the ones you cannot explain, an explicit label for the unmatched case, and a named human who reviews it. Meridian shows what happens without them. CRW-XX9 sits in CrewAssignment and is missing from CrewCodeMap, so 10.0 of the 62.0 achieved hours have no service line, and because you own the map, nobody else is going to fix it.

4. Reading a workbook while its owner is still editing it

The capacity workbook belongs to the resource manager. It lives in a shared document library, he edits it most days, and your report reads it live so the numbers are never stale. At 06:10 on a Monday the refresh fails. By the time you look, the file opens cleanly and nothing seems wrong. On Friday afternoon he renamed the Airframe column to Airframe Hrs, because that reads better in his own sheet, and it did not occur to him that anything downstream cared.

That is the trade, stated honestly. Reading a live workbook gives you numbers that are always current, and it hands you a schema you have no control over. Nobody is doing anything wrong here. The workbook is his working document and he is entitled to work in it. Your model is a consumer he never agreed to have.

The breakages are predictable, so name them before they happen. A renamed column. A row inserted above the header, which pushes the real header down a line. A renamed or duplicated sheet. A column inserted in the middle, harmless when you select columns by name and fatal when any step depends on position. A file renamed or dragged into a subfolder, which breaks a path-based reference. A number typed as text, so 14 arrives as "14 hrs" and your sum drops it. A total row added at the bottom out of politeness, which then behaves like a station called Total.

Six defences, in the order I would add them. First, reference the file by a stable identifier where your connector allows it. Some connectors address a file in a document library by an identifier that survives a rename or a move. Others take a path and break the moment somebody reorganises a folder. Find out which one you have before you promise anybody that a rename is safe.

Second, select the columns you want by name, and let the query tolerate a missing one long enough to say which one it was. The habit worth breaking is removing the columns you do not want, because every new column the owner adds then flows straight into your model. Third and fourth, count the rows and count the nulls, and fail loudly when either looks wrong. All of that fits in one query.

MShopCapacity, loaded from the library with its own checks
let
    // LibraryFile is the binary your connector returns
    Book = Excel.Workbook(LibraryFile, null, true),
    Sheet = Book{[Item = "Capacity", Kind = "Sheet"]}[Data],
    Headers = Table.PromoteHeaders(Sheet,
        [PromoteAllScalars = true]),
    Wanted = {"StationCode", "Month", "Airframe",
        "Avionics", "Engine", "NDT"},
    Missing = List.Difference(Wanted,
        Table.ColumnNames(Headers)),
    Kept = Table.SelectColumns(Headers, Wanted,
        MissingField.UseNull),
    Rows = Table.RowCount(Kept),
    Blanks = List.Count(List.Select(Kept[StationCode],
        each _ = null)),
    Checked =
        if List.Count(Missing) > 0 then
            error "ShopCapacity is missing: "
                & Text.Combine(Missing, ", ")
        else if Rows < 4 then
            error "ShopCapacity is below the row floor of 4"
        else if Blanks > 0 then
            error "ShopCapacity has a blank StationCode"
        else Kept
in
    Checked
Sheet
The tab is addressed by name, so a renamed or duplicated sheet fails right here, before any check of yours gets to speak. That one break carries the connector's message and not your sentence, and there is no tidy way around it.
Wanted
The six column names are the contract, written down in one place. Anything the owner adds beyond these six is ignored, so a new working column on the right of his sheet cannot reach your model.
Missing
List.Difference gives you the names you asked for that are absent. That turns "the refresh failed" into "the Airframe column is gone", which is the difference between a morning of guessing and a two minute conversation.
Kept
Table.SelectColumns with MissingField.UseNull keeps the query alive when a column is absent, so the checks below get their chance to run and report. The default behaviour errors immediately with a much less useful message.
Rows
A floor, not an exact count. Meridian's capacity workbook holds seven rows today and gains one every time a station opens a month, so a floor of 4 catches a truncated load without fighting legitimate growth.
Blanks
A null station code is how a total row or a stray note at the bottom of the sheet announces itself.
Checked
Each branch raises an error with a message that names the problem. A refresh that fails with a sentence you wrote yourself is worth far more than one that fails with a generic connector message.

Go back to that Monday. With this query in place the refresh still fails at 06:10, and it fails with the words "ShopCapacity is missing: Airframe". You read that at 08:00, you walk over, and the resource manager puts the header back in ten seconds. The break itself was never preventable. The morning of guessing was.

This is the query that produces ShopCapacity. What Chapter 5 does next, unpivoting those four trade columns into FactCapacity, assumes it was handed clean input. Checks belong here, at the door, before any reshaping has hidden the problem. One cost is worth knowing while you are standing at that door. A workbook in a document library does not fold. Folding is when Power Query hands your filters back to the source and lets the source do the work. A file cannot do that, so every refresh pulls the whole workbook across and Power Query filters afterwards. Seven rows costs nothing. A forty tab planning workbook that somebody combined at folder level is why a dataset starts timing out with nobody having changed a line of code.

Fifth, keep a dated snapshot. After the checks pass, write the result somewhere you control, stamped with the date it was read.

Why the snapshot earns its keep, and what it costs you

In June the finance manager asks why the March capacity number in his own deck differs from your report. Your report reads the workbook live, so it shows what the workbook says today. The resource manager has since corrected March, which he was right to do. Without a snapshot you cannot show what the number was on the day you published it, and the conversation becomes a question of who remembers better. With a dated snapshot you open the March file and it closes in a minute.

The costs are real. You accumulate a file per refresh unless you keep only month end copies, and somebody will eventually ask why there are ninety versions of a capacity workbook in a folder. Snapshots also drift out of agreement with the live source by design, so anybody who finds one and reads it as current will be misled. Name them with the date they were taken, keep them in a folder that says archive on it, and tell one other person they exist.

Last, agree with the owner that the header row is a contract. One short email does it: the header row of the Capacity sheet is read by a report every morning, so tell me before you change it, and add columns on the right whenever you like. Most owners are glad to be told. Nobody enjoys finding out that a change of theirs broke something two floors away.

One more mechanical fact about live workbooks. A file that several people edit at once will sometimes be locked or mid-save when your refresh runs, and that failure is genuinely transient. A retry a few minutes later will succeed.

Common mistake

Treating a scheduled retry as the fix for every refresh failure. A retry clears the lock failures, which is why it feels like it works. It does nothing for a structural break, because the renamed column will be exactly as renamed on the second attempt. What the retry actually buys you is silence: the alert stops arriving, the dataset keeps serving whatever it last loaded successfully, and the report goes quietly stale until somebody notices a number that has not moved for nine days.

5. When the source system changes

You hear it in a corridor. The maintenance and engineering system is being replaced in the spring, the project has been running for eight months, and nobody told the reporting team because nobody thinks of reporting as a consumer of the system. This section stays vendor neutral on purpose. Every migration moves the same five things, whatever the products involved.

Identifier formats and lengths
WO-1001 becomes a longer key, or gains a prefix, or picks up leading zeros, or keeps its old identifier in a legacy field that only some extracts carry. Every join you own is keyed on one of these.
Code lists
Station codes, trade codes, check types, crew codes. The new system arrives with its own lists, somebody maps old to new by hand once during the migration, and that mapping is then never looked at again.
The grain at which labour is booked
One row per technician per work order per day can become one row per clock-in against a task card. The row count multiplies, the total hours do not, and every measure that counts rows instead of summing hours changes meaning overnight.
Status value names
Closed becomes Complete. A new intermediate status appears that nobody mentions, because it was obvious to the people who chose it. Any measure filtering on a status string now filters on a value that no longer exists, and it returns zero without complaining.
The meaning of date fields
This is the one that ruins a week. If the new system stamps a created date on every record as it loads, every migrated work order gets the cutover date, the day the new system took over, and your work orders by month chart shows the entire history landing in a single month.

You cannot stop any of that. You can arrive already holding the evidence, which moves you from complaining to reconciling. Work through this list before the cutover date.

  1. Inventory every hand maintained mapping table you own. List its name, its keys, its row count and who reviews it. Meridian has exactly one: CrewCodeMap, six rows, keyed on CrewCode, reviewed by nobody. Yours will have more than you expect.
  2. Snapshot your headline numbers for a closed period and store them outside the model, in a file the migration cannot touch. For Meridian's quarter that is achieved 62.0, available 57.0, projected 63.5, submitted 63.0, capacity 176 and a work order count of 8. They are worthless if you take them the week after go-live.
  3. Write the orphan check and the unmapped check now, and run them against the old system so you know today's baseline. An orphan is a key on a fact row that matches no row in its dimension, for example a labour row pointing at a work order that the header table has never heard of. Meridian's baseline is four known breaks: WO-1009 on parts, TECH-07 on labour, N338WA on work orders and CRW-XX9 on crew. A break you already knew about is not a migration problem, and you can only say that if you wrote it down first.
  4. Ask whether history is migrated or only open work. If only open work moves, your year on year comparison needs the old extract preserved somewhere readable, and somebody has to agree to keep it available.
  5. Ask which system is the source of truth during the parallel run, and until what date. Get the answer in writing, because during a parallel run both systems produce a defensible number for the same month and you will be asked to publish one of them.
  6. Ask for the new code lists in advance and compare them against the ones you hold. Every code in the old list and missing from the new one is a row your mapping table will fail to match on day one.
  7. Confirm the labour booking grain in writing, with one example row. One sentence: one row per what, per what, per what. If nobody can produce that sentence, the project has not decided yet, and you have found that out early.
  8. Confirm what every date column means in the new system, field by field. Take your own list of date columns to the meeting as the agenda, because a general question gets a general answer and a column by column question gets facts.
  9. Get a test extract at real volumes and point a copy of your model at it. A hundred row sample tells you nothing about whether a key format change breaks a join at scale.
  10. Agree who tells you when a code list changes, and get a person's name for it. A team has no memory. A person does.
  11. Freeze your own report changes across the cutover window. When a number moves you want exactly one candidate explanation.

Then in the first week after go-live, in this order.

  1. Re-run the snapshot for the same closed period and reconcile it against the numbers you stored. Grand totals first, then by month, then by service line.
  2. Look at every blank member in every dimension. A new blank is almost always a new key format arriving somewhere you did not expect.
  3. Compare row counts by month against the old system. A row count that doubles while the hours stay put is the labour grain change, and it will otherwise be reported to you as the report counting things twice.
  4. Check your mapping tables before anything else when a number looks wrong. New codes land there first and they land silently.
  5. Keep the old model, with its scheduled refresh switched off, until the reconciliation is signed off by somebody other than you. Deleting it early is a decision you cannot reverse.

Back to the corridor. You cannot stop the replacement, and nobody was ever going to consult you about it. What you can do that same afternoon is step 2: write achieved 62.0, available 57.0, projected 63.5, submitted 63.0, capacity 176 and eight work orders into a file the project cannot reach. Six months later, when somebody says the numbers have moved, that file is the difference between an investigation and an argument.

6. A short checklist for taking over a reporting workload

Three weeks in, the planner asks what your report means by attended hours. You do not know. The person who built the measure has left, nothing was written down, and the number goes to the customer on Friday. Four habits stop that happening. They carry more weight than any technique in this document, and all four are cheap to start now.

  1. Name the grain of every table in one sentence and put that sentence in the table description inside the model. One row per technician per work order per day. One row per work order per trade. One row per work order per revision. When you cannot write the sentence, you do not yet understand the table, and every measure you build on it is a guess that happens to be right.
  2. Write down the definition of every ambiguous word and get it agreed in writing. Available, projected, achieved, attended, achievable, demand, submitted, capacity. In Meridian's quarter those eight words carry 57.0, 63.5, 62.0, 109.0, 87.72, 75.0, 63.0 and 176. Eight words, eight different numbers, every one correct in its own frame. Put each definition in the measure description so it travels with the model.
  3. Build the data quality checks before you build the dashboards. An orphan count per fact table, a null key count, a row count by month, and a coverage count for every mapping table you own. They take an afternoon, nobody will ask you for them, and they are how you hear about a break before the production controller hears about it from a wrong number in a meeting.
  4. Find the one person per source system who will tell you when something changes, and write their name next to that source in your documentation. One human being, with a name you could ring. Check every six months whether they still do that job, because the day they move on is the day your model starts ageing without you knowing.

Habit 2 is the planner's answer, written down before he asks. Attended hours are the 109.0 hours in CrewRoster: rostered and paid, before any productivity factor is applied. That sentence lives in the measure description, so next time he can read it himself and the two of you never have that conversation again.

Meridian's eight work orders were built so that every one of those habits has something to catch. A blank station code, an orphaned registration, a trailing space in a key, a forecast table that must never be summed, a crew code with no mapping row, and two achieved numbers for heavy work in January that differ by one hour and are both official. Your shop has all of these. It has more rows, better systems and worse documentation, and the same faults are sitting in there waiting for somebody to name them. Name them first, in writing, and the rest of the job is modelling.

What to remember
  • Meridian is fictional so its data is unambiguously invented and safe to share. Table E.1 is the bridge from its vocabulary to your own, and the middle column lists what you are likely to hear. Your own shop's word wins every time.
  • Four service lines: Heavy 38.0, Cabin and IFE 10.0, Light 9.0 and Line 5.0 achieved hours, totalling 62.0. Base is 38.0 plus 10.0, which is 48.0. Non-base is 9.0 plus 5.0, which is 14.0.
  • Base and non-base is a second grouping over one dimension, so it is a second column on DimServiceLine, surfaced with a hierarchy or a field parameter. A second table gives you two definitions of base maintenance and two reports that will one day disagree by exactly the cabin hours.
